findings.situation: A filer who filed jointly for 2024 and not jointly with that spouse for 2025 (for example, after a divorce) has no 2024 capital loss carryover because the 2024 Schedule D line 21 was not a loss, yet must answer YES and is refused.
findings.irs_text: Question: "the 2024 return these figures come from was a joint return, and for 2025 you are not filing a joint return with the same spouse". i1040sd p. 10: "if your 2024 Schedule D, line 21, is a loss and... Otherwise, you don't have any carryovers."
findings.why: The first limb has no loss or carryover condition, unlike the second limb, so it catches filers with nothing to allocate. The tool correctly computes a zero carryover for them, and the spouse-allocation rule has no effect.

findings.situation: A filer who filed jointly for 2024 and not jointly with that spouse for 2025 actually had the entire loss behind the joint carryover, yet must answer YES and is refused.
findings.irs_text: Question: "the 2024 return these figures come from was a joint return, and for 2025 you are not filing a joint return with the same spouse". i1040sd p. 10: "any capital loss carryover from the joint return can be deducted only on the return of the spouse who actually had the loss."
findings.why: When all of the loss belongs to the filer, the whole carryover figured from the joint return's amounts is deductible on the filer's return, so no allocation is needed. The worksheet computation is therefore correct, but the question's wording still forces a refusal.

findings.situation: A parent with a post-2008 divorce decree that gives the noncustodial parent the claim, but no signed Form 8332 or similar statement, answers YES even though the special rule does not apply and the tool's ordinary computation would be correct.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "If the divorce decree or separation agreement went into effect after 2008, the noncustodial parent can't include pages from the decree or agreement instead of Form 8332. The custodial parent must sign either Form 8332 or a substantially similar statement"
findings.why: The question says to answer yes when "a decree lets the noncustodial parent claim the child" and when "your decree or agreement lets the other parent claim the child." It never says that a post-2008 decree alone does not trigger the rule, and the same is true of a release that depends on support payments.

findings.situation: A Form 8332 release or a decree exists, but the other conditions fail (the child got half or less of their support from the parents, a multiple support agreement applies, or neither parent had custody for more than half of 2025), so the rule does not apply, yet the filer answers YES.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "A child will be treated as the qualifying child or qualifying relative of the child's noncustodial parent ... if all of the following conditions apply ... 2. The child received over half of the child's support for 2025 from the parents ... 3. The child is in custody of one or both of the parents for more than half of 2025."
findings.why: The question offers the existence of a release or decree as the example that makes the rule apply. It omits the support and custody conditions, so a filer who fails them still answers yes and is refused for a case the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A noncustodial parent under a pre-1985 decree that allows the claim, but who provided less than $600 of support in 2025 (or whose decree was changed after 1984 to deny the claim), answers YES.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 22: "A pre-1985 decree ... states that the noncustodial parent can claim the child as a dependent, the decree or agreement wasn't changed after 1984 to say the noncustodial parent can't claim the child as a dependent, and the noncustodial parent provides at least $600 for the child's support during the year."
findings.why: The wording "a decree lets the noncustodial parent claim the child" leads to a yes without the $600 condition or the no-later-change condition, both of which must be met for the rule to apply.

findings.situation: A divorced or never-married custodial parent with no release, decree provision, or agreement shifting the claim may read "Does the special rule for children of divorced or separated parents ... apply to this person" as asking simply whether the child's parents are apart.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "Children of divorced or separated parents. A child will be treated as the qualifying child or qualifying relative of the child's noncustodial parent (defined later) if all of the following conditions apply."
findings.why: The question's title names the parents' status rather than the transfer of the claim, so some filers will answer yes simply because the parents live apart. The tool would compute that case correctly as an ordinary custodial-parent claim.

findings.situation: The question says "parents who lived apart" without the time requirement, so parents who lived apart for only part of the last 6 months of 2025 may answer either way.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "or lived apart at all times during the last 6 months of 2025 (whether or not they are or were married)."
findings.why: The rule requires living apart at all times during the last 6 months of the year, and the question's wording does not say so.

question: Does the special rule for children of divorced or separated parents, or parents who lived apart (including parents who never married), apply to this person, for example because a Form 8332 release or a decree lets the noncustodial parent claim the child? Answer yes whether you are the custodial parent who signed the release (or whose decree or agreement lets the other parent claim the child) or the noncustodial parent using it. A release the custodial parent has revoked still applies for 2025 unless written notice of the revocation was given (or reasonable efforts were made to give it) to the noncustodial parent in 2024 or earlier.

locators: p. 19, Step 4, "But see Children of divorced or separated parents"; p. 20, Children of divorced or separated parents, "If conditions (1) through (4) apply, only the noncustodial parent can claim the child for purposes of the child tax credit and credit for other dependents"; , Revocation of release of claim to an exemption, "For the revocation to be effective for 2025, the custodial parent must have given (or made reasonable efforts to give) written notice of the revocation to the noncustodial parent in 2024 or earlier."

findings.situation: A child disappeared in mid-2025, but law enforcement did not presume a non-family kidnapping until early 2026, before the return was filed, so the months-lived count could fall to 6 or fewer.
findings.irs_text: "The child is presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped by someone who isn't a member of your family or the child's family." (p501, 2025, p. 13); "In the year the kidnapping occurred, the child lived with you for more than half of the part of the year before the date of the kidnapping." (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The IRS text ties the year to when the kidnapping occurred and sets no deadline for the presumption, but the question asks whether the child was presumed kidnapped "at any time during 2025." This filer could truthfully answer NO, and the tool would then compute the residency lines as false even though the kidnapped-child treatment may apply.

findings.situation: A child was presumed kidnapped for a few days in 2025, was returned, and lived with the filer for well over six months anyway.
findings.irs_text: Question: "at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped ... (even if the child has since been returned)"; IRS: "To meet this test, your child must have lived with you for more than half the year." (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The filer must answer YES, but the child meets the residency test on actual time lived, so the months count gives the correct result. The tool refuses a case it computes correctly.

findings.situation: A child was presumed kidnapped during 2025 but did not live with the filer for more than half of the part of the year before the kidnapping, or for more than half of the part of the year after the child's return.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Is this person a child who, at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped"; IRS: "You can treat your child as meeting the residency test even if the child has been kidnapped, but the following statements must be true." followed by statements 2 and 3 on time lived before the kidnapping and after the return (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The question tests only statement 1, so the filer answers YES even though the special treatment is unavailable. The ordinary months count, which the tool computes, would correctly apply if the child also fell short of more than half the year.

findings.situation: A child still presumed kidnapped during 2025 is past the end of the special treatment because the child would have reached age 18, or there was a determination of death, in an earlier year.
findings.irs_text: Question: "at any time during 2025, was presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped"; IRS: "This treatment applies for all years until the earlier of: 1. The year there is a determination that the child is dead, or 2. The year the child would have reached age 18." (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: The question has no age or death cutoff, so a filer with a continuing presumption answers YES after the treatment has ended. The ordinary months count would correctly decide these lines, so the refusal is unnecessary.

findings.situation: The person presumed kidnapped was 18 or older, or was a relative such as a sibling, niece, or nephew rather than the filer's own child.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Is this person a child"; IRS: "You can treat your child as meeting the residency test even if the child has been kidnapped" (p501, 2025, p. 13); "To meet this test, a child must be: Your son, daughter, stepchild, or foster child, or a descendant ... Your brother, sister, half brother, half sister, stepbrother, or stepsister, or a descendant" (p501, 2025, p. 13)
findings.why: "A child" could mean a minor, the filer's own offspring, or anyone who fits the qualifying-child relationship test. Filers in the same situation could therefore answer differently, and the question does not say which meaning applies.

findings.situation: The filer is one of several contributors in a multiple support situation, but another contributor claims the person (or the filer gave 10% or less), so the filer cannot treat themselves as providing over half the support. The tool's support test correctly finds the person is not the filer's qualifying relative.
findings.irs_text: Question: "...with no one person providing over half (a multiple support situation), whether you or another contributor claims the person?" IRS: "For whom you provided over half of the person's support in 2025. But see ... Multiple support agreements" (i1040gi p. 19); "special rules may apply that would treat you as having provided over half of the support" (i1040gi p. 21).
findings.why: The special rule only changes the result for the contributor who is treated as providing over half. The clause "whether you or another contributor claims the person" forces a YES from filers whose correct result, not a dependent, the tool already computes.

findings.situation: The filer provided part of the support and the rest came from the person themselves or from public or other sources that could not claim the person. The filer may count these as "others" and answer YES, although no multiple support agreement is possible and the tool's no-dependent result is correct.
findings.irs_text: "If no one person contributed over half of the support of your relative ... but you and another person(s) provided more than half of your relative's support, special rules may apply" (i1040gi p. 21).
findings.why: The question does not say whether "others" means only people who could claim the person apart from the support test, or also the person themselves, government assistance, or similar sources. Filers could reasonably read it either way.

findings.situation: A custodial parent has released the claim to the child on Form 8332, and the noncustodial parent, with whom the child did not live for more than half of 2025, claims the child.
findings.irs_text: "A child will be treated as the qualifying child or qualifying relative of the child's noncustodial parent... only the noncustodial parent can claim the child for purposes of the child tax credit and credit for other dependents" (i1040gi 2025, p. 20); see also "unless the special rule for Children of divorced or separated parents... applies" (p. 21).
findings.why: The noncustodial parent fails the lived-with test and is only treated as having a qualifying child, so the custodial filer can truthfully answer NO to "meet the conditions." The tool then computes dependent.qualifying_child as true for a filer who has released the claim, and the question also does not catch a noncustodial filer whose line computes false on the lived-with helper.

findings.situation: A child who was married at the end of 2025 and is not filing a joint return lives with the filer, but the filer cannot claim the child as a dependent and the divorced-or-separated-parents exception does not apply.
findings.irs_text: "If the child was married, see Married child, later" (i1040gi 2025, p. 41); "A child who was married at the end of 2025 is a qualifying child only if (a) you can claim the child as your dependent, or (b) you could have claimed the child as your dependent except for the special rule for Children of divorced or separated parents" (p. 44).
findings.why: The question asks only about other people's claims, so a filer can truthfully answer NO when no one else qualifies. The computed dependent.eic_child has no married-child condition and returns true for a child the text excludes.

findings.situation: The child lives with the filer and another person and provided over half of their own support, so the child fails the support test for dependent.qualifying_child but meets the EIC conditions for the other person.
findings.irs_text: Question: "under the dependent rules or under the EIC rules (which have no support test)"; IRS: "Who didn't provide over half of their own support for 2025" (i1040gi 2025, p. 17).
findings.why: The EIC branch forces YES, which also refuses dependent.qualifying_child. That line would correctly compute false from the support helper without any tie-breaker, because the child is not a dependent-rule qualifying child of anyone.

findings.situation: The filer is the child's only parent among the eligible claimants, such as a parent living with the child and the filer's own parent, so the tie-breaker necessarily resolves in the filer's favor.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Does this person meet the conditions to be the qualifying child of any other person for 2025"; IRS: "If only one of the persons is the child's parent, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the parent" and "you can claim Lee as a qualifying child" (i1040gi 2025, pp. 21, 44).
findings.why: The filer must truthfully answer YES and is refused, although the tool's computed true result is the correct outcome. This over-refusal is conservative, but it does block a case the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: Another person meets the qualifying-child tests on paper but will not or need not claim the child, for example because that person is not filing or is filing only for a refund.
findings.irs_text: "Even if a child meets the conditions to be the qualifying child of more than one person" and "If you and any other person can claim the child as a qualifying child" (i1040gi 2025, p. 21); compare "Check 'No' if the other person isn't required to file, and isn't filing" (p. 41, Step 3, question 6).
findings.why: A filer could read "meet the conditions" as covering only the listed relationship, age, joint-return, residency and support tests, and answer YES. A filer could also read it as requiring someone who can actually claim the child, by analogy to the non-filer carve-out on p. 41, and answer NO.

findings.situation: A filer has foreign-source qualified dividends but no foreign-source capital gain, loss, or capital gain distribution, and those dividends must be adjusted (or included only under the adjustment-exception election) before going on line 1a.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 9: "If you have foreign source qualified dividends or foreign source capital gains (including any foreign source capital gain distributions) or losses, you may be required to make certain adjustments to those amounts before taking them into account on line 1a"; "multiply your foreign source qualified dividends or capital gain distributions in each separate category by 0.4054 ... by 0.5405 ..."
findings.why: The question asks only about capital gains or losses and capital gain distributions, so a filer whose only foreign rate-preferred income is qualified dividends truthfully answers NO. Yet the cited adjustment rule applies to those dividends, and its result flows through line 19 to line 35.

findings.situation: A filer has only U.S.-source qualified dividends or capital gains, and Qualified Dividends and Capital Gain Tax Worksheet line 5 exceeds $197,300 with line 23 less than line 24, so line 18 must come from the Worksheet for Line 18.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 23: "you must use the Worksheet for Line 18 to figure the amount to enter on line 18 if: 1. Line 5 of your Qualified Dividends and Capital Gain Tax Worksheet is greater than zero, and 2. Line 23 ... is less than line 24"; the exception requires that "Line 5 ... doesn't exceed ... $197,300 if single".
findings.why: The line 18 adjustment uses worldwide gains and dividends and is not limited to foreign-source amounts. This filer has nothing foreign-source in the capital category and answers NO, but the tool then uses unadjusted taxable income on line 18, which misstates lines 19 through 35.

findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 20, Line 16: "1. Adjustment for disallowed business loss under section 461(l). Increase the amount on line 15 by the amount of any business loss that is disallowed under section 461(l) to the extent it is attributable to the separate category of income"

findings.situation: In the current year the filer has a loss on line 15 of one Form 1116 and income on line 15 of another, and has no earlier loss account, so they answer NO.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 21: "2. Allocation of foreign losses. If you have a loss on line 15 of one Form 1116 and you have income on line 15 of one or more other Forms 1116, you must reduce the foreign income by a pro rata share of the loss"

findings.situation: The filer has a net loss from U.S. sources this year, such as a U.S. rental loss, and has no earlier loss account, so they answer NO.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 21: "3. Allocation of U.S. losses. If you have a net loss from U.S. sources, proportionately allocate that loss among the separate categories of your foreign income. Reduce the income on line 15 ... by including (in parentheses) on line 16 the allocable portion of any U.S. loss."
findings.why: This is a required reduction on line 16 for the current year, not the recapture of an earlier account. The question's wording excludes it, and the tool skips it.

findings.situation: The filer had an overall foreign loss in a prior year that offset U.S. source income, but did not file Form 1116 that year (for example, they had no creditable taxes, used the no-Form-1116 election, or deducted foreign taxes), so no earlier Form 1116 shows the account.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 21: "4. Recapture of prior-year overall foreign loss accounts. If you had an overall foreign loss in a prior year that offset U.S. source income, a part of your foreign income (in the same category as the loss) is recharacterized as U.S. source income in each following tax year."
findings.why: The IRS trigger is a prior-year loss, whether or not a Form 1116 was filed that year. The question and its help text tie the answer to what 'an earlier Form 1116 shows,' so this filer can truthfully answer NO.

findings.situation: The filer had a prior-year foreign loss in one category that reduced income in another category, or a U.S. loss that reduced foreign income, but no earlier Form 1116 labels a balance as an 'account.'
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 21: "If the loss reduces foreign source income, you must create, or increase the balance in, a separate limitation loss account"; "In later years, you will be allowed to treat part of your U.S. source income as foreign source income."
findings.why: Form 1116 has no line for account balances; they appear only on attached statements, if at all. The help text says an earlier Form 1116 'shows such a loss as' an account, so a filer who never kept a statement could read the question as not applying to them.

findings.situation: A partner or S corporation shareholder receives a Schedule K-3 that reports a foreign tax redetermination made at the entity level, but no foreign tax was refunded to the filer personally and nothing on the filer's own foreign tax bill changed.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 9: "Form 1120-S, Schedule K-3, Part III, Section 3, line 3—Foreign tax redeterminations. The partnership or S corporation has already apportioned the change in foreign income tax liability and has reported it to you ... Include these amounts on each of the applicable Schedules C (Form 1116)"
findings.why: The question asks about foreign tax "refunded to you, or changed", so a filer whose own taxes were never refunded or changed can truthfully answer NO. Schedule C is still required, and line 35 is computed without it.

findings.situation: A filer who claimed an earlier year's credit on an accrual basis paid that accrued tax in 2025 in a different amount, or paid it at a different exchange rate than the one used to accrue it.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 2: "Use Schedule C (Form 1116) to report foreign tax redeterminations that occurred in the current tax year and that relate to prior tax years."
findings.why: Nothing was refunded, and the filer may not see paying a previously accrued liability as foreign tax being "changed". The question gives no hint that a payment differing from the accrued amount counts as a redetermination.

findings.situation: A foreign authority decides in 2025 to refund or assess tax for an earlier year, but the money moves in 2026; or the refund is credited against later foreign tax instead of being paid out.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 2: "foreign tax redeterminations that occurred in the current tax year and that relate to prior tax years"
findings.why: "Refunded to you ... in 2025" could mean the year the decision was made or the year the cash arrived. A refund applied as a credit may not read as "refunded to you", so filers could answer either way.

findings.situation: A filer receives a 2025 refund of a non-income foreign tax from an earlier year, such as VAT or foreign property tax. That tax was never part of the foreign tax credit, so Form 1116 is unaffected.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Was foreign tax of an earlier year refunded to you, or changed, in 2025?"; i1116 p. 2: "You can take a credit for income, war profits, and excess profits taxes paid or accrued"
findings.why: "Foreign tax" is not limited to creditable foreign income taxes, so this filer answers YES and is refused. The tool would have computed line 35 correctly because no creditable tax was redetermined.

findings.situation: A partner or S corporation shareholder receives a Schedule K-3 reporting a reduction of taxes available for credit and must enter it on line 12, but that instruction appears outside the Line 12 heading.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 9: "Forms 1065 and 8865, Schedule K-3, Part III, Section 4, line 2; and Form 1120-S, Schedule K-3, Part III, Section 3, line 2—Reduction of taxes. ... Include these amounts on line 12 of each of the applicable Forms 1116"
findings.why: The question asks only about items 'listed under Line 12 of the Form 1116 instructions,' and the help text does not mention K-3 amounts. This filer can truthfully answer NO, and the tool then treats a required line 12 reduction as zero.

findings.situation: A filer who participated in an international boycott and cannot figure the taxes attributable to it must reduce the credit by the boycott factor on line 34, not reduce the foreign taxes.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 20: "you must reduce either the total taxes available for credit or the credit otherwise allowable ... If you can't figure the amount of taxes specifically attributable to boycott operations, multiply the credit otherwise allowable by the international boycott factor ... and enter the result on Form 1116, line 34."
findings.why: The question asks whether 'the foreign taxes' must be reduced. Here the credit is reduced, not the taxes, so the filer can truthfully answer NO, and line 35 is computed without the line 34 reduction. The help text does not mention boycotts.

findings.situation: A filer had a foreign tax credit splitting event in a prior year and takes the related income into account in 2025, so the previously suspended taxes are now allowed and need no line 12 reduction.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 18: "Enter in Part II the foreign taxes that were previously suspended under section 909 and that are allowed in 2025 because the related income is taken into account in 2025."; question help: "a splitting event"
findings.why: The help text names 'a splitting event' without limiting it to taxes still suspended in the current year. A filer whose splitting-event taxes are released this year could read it as requiring YES, although line 12 calls for no reduction.

findings.situation: The amount carried out of the 2024 Schedule B (line 8) was wrong when filed, for example a miscomputed excess limitation or a carryforward column that was dropped. The filer adjusts it on the 2025 Schedule B, but nothing has happened since filing that the filer would call a change.
findings.irs_text: i1116sb p. 2, Lines 2c, 2d, 2e: "Any other adjustments needed to properly reflect the total carryover amount from the prior tax year that is available for credit in the current tax year."
findings.why: The question asks only whether something changed the carryover since the 2024 return was filed. A filer correcting an error in the original line 8 can truthfully answer No, and the tool then uses an uncorrected line 1 amount.

findings.situation: The filer entered no estimate on line 7 of the 2024 Schedule B but later carried 2024 excess tax back to 2023, for example on an amended 2023 return.
findings.irs_text: i1116sb p. 2, Line 2a: "Enter on line 2a, column (xii), the difference between any estimated carryback amount you may have used on your prior year carryover schedule ... and the actual carryback amount."
findings.why: "A carryback to 2023 that differs from the estimate on line 7" assumes an estimate was made. A filer who left line 7 blank may read the example as not applying and answer No, even though an actual carryback against a zero estimate needs a line 2a adjustment.

findings.situation: An event since the 2024 filing changes only the carryover from an older year, such as 2019 or 2022, that passed through the 2024 Schedule B, not the unused tax generated in 2024.
findings.irs_text: i1116sb p. 1, Line 1: "Enter on line 1 the amounts from the appropriate columns of line 8 of the prior year Schedule B"; Line 2: "any adjustments resulting from events that occurred between the filing of your prior year tax return and the filing of your current year tax return."
findings.why: "The foreign tax carried from it" could be read as only the tax left unused in 2024 itself, rather than every column carried forward through the 2024 Schedule B. A filer whose change affects an older column could reasonably answer No.

You and your spouse file separate returns for the current tax year, to which you carry an unused foreign tax from a tax year for which you and your spouse filed separate returns, but through a tax year for which you and your spouse filed joint return." findings.situation: A filer covered in 2025 by two employers' dependent care plans that each cap exclusions at the same amount below $5,000 (for example, $3,000 each) truthfully answers NO, and the tool enters $3,000 on line 21.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 5, Line 21: "Enter on line 21 the maximum amount that you may exclude for the year under your dependent care plan... Don't enter more than the maximum amount allowed under your dependent care plan."
findings.why: The IRS text speaks of a single plan, so with two plans the line 21 amount is just as unsettled when the maximums are equal (it could be $3,000 or up to $5,000 combined). The question asks only about plans with 'different maximum amounts,' so these filers get a computed result instead of the refusal.

findings.situation: A filer who was eligible for two plans in 2025 but received benefits under only one, or who changed employers mid-year and had two plans one after the other, may not know whether that counts as being 'covered by two or more dependent care plans.'
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 5, Line 21: "the maximum amount that you may exclude for the year under your dependent care plan"
findings.why: 'Covered' could mean enrolled or eligible, or it could mean actually receiving benefits. Filers could reasonably answer either way, and the line 21 maximum is ambiguous in each of these cases.

findings.situation: A filer whose plans have different annual election or contribution limits, but who does not know each plan's exclusion maximum, may not know whether the plans 'allow different maximum amounts to be excluded.'
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 5, Line 21: "if your dependent care plan only allows a maximum of $4,000 to be excluded, substitute $4,000 for the $5,000 amount"
findings.why: Filers usually see an election or contribution limit, not an exclusion maximum. Some will equate the two and others will not, so answers will vary.

findings.situation: A filer paid 2024 care expenses in 2025, but their 2024 credit was already figured on the maximum qualified expenses ($3,000 or $6,000). Worksheet A then gives no additional credit, so the tool's zero on line 9b is correct, yet the question makes them answer YES and be refused.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'Did you ... pay in 2025 any qualified expenses for care provided in 2024?' vs. i2441 (2025) p. 4, Line 9b: 'If you had qualified expenses for 2024 that you didn't pay until 2025 and you didn't claim a credit on the maximum amount of qualified expenses for 2024, you may be able to increase the amount of the credit'
findings.why: The IRS text allows an increase only when the 2024 credit was not taken on the maximum expenses. The question asks only whether the payment happened, so it also catches filers whose correct line 9b is zero, which the tool already computes.

findings.situation: An unmarried filer (single or head of household) who was a full-time student or unable to care for themselves must answer YES and is refused, even though deemed income appears to be available only on a joint return, so the tool's actual earned income would be correct.
findings.irs_text: p503 (2025) p. 11: 'These rules also apply if you are a student or not able to care for yourself and are filing a joint return.' Compare i2441 (2025) p. 4: 'These rules for a spouse who was a student or disabled also apply to you if you were a student or disabled.'
findings.why: The question asks 'were you ... a full-time student ... or physically or mentally not able to care for yourself' without regard to filing status. Pub. 503 limits the filer's own deemed income to joint returns, although i2441 p. 4 states no such limit, so this finding depends on following Pub. 503.

findings.situation: A filer who was a student or unable to care for themselves, and whose actual earned income met or exceeded the $250 or $500 floor in every such month, must answer YES although deemed income would not change lines 4 or 18.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 4: 'If you also worked during that month, enter the higher of $250 (or $500) or your actual earned income for that month.'
findings.why: The question asks only about status ('were you ... a full-time student ... or ... not able to care for yourself'), not whether the floor raises income in any month. Where actual earnings are the higher figure every month, the tool's sum of actual earned income is the correct result.

findings.situation: A filer enrolled full-time for 5 or more months only in a correspondence school, an internet-only school, or an on-the-job training course can truthfully answer YES and is refused, although that enrollment does not qualify for deemed income.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 4: 'A school doesn't include an on-the-job training course, a correspondence school, or a school offering courses only through the Internet.'
findings.why: The question says 'a full-time student at a school' and does not give this exclusion, so an ordinary reading of 'school' includes these programs. Without deemed income, the tool's actual earned income is correct for this filer.

findings.situation: A filer with a temporary illness or injury, or a disability that did not prevent self-care, could reasonably answer either way to 'physically or mentally not able to care for yourself at any time'.
findings.irs_text: i2441 (2025) p. 1: 'Persons who can't dress, clean, or feed themselves because of physical or mental disabilities are considered not able to care for themselves. Also, persons who must have constant attention to prevent them from injuring themselves or others are considered not able to care for themselves.'
findings.why: The question omits the IRS test, and 'not able to care for yourself at any time' could be read to include short periods of needing help. A filer who reads it loosely may be refused unnecessarily, while one who reads it strictly may answer NO despite meeting the IRS test.

findings.situation: A filer with allowed investment expenses other than interest, such as depreciation or depletion on assets that produce investment income or investment expenses passed through on a Schedule K-1, would answer NO, and the tool would then enter zero on line 5.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 4, Line 5: "Investment expenses are your allowed deductions, other than interest expense, directly connected with the production of investment income. For example, depreciation or depletion allowed on assets that produce investment income is an investment expense. Include investment expenses incurred directly by you or reported to you on Schedule K-1..."
findings.why: The question asks only about the line 4e/4b allocation election, so nothing in it leads a filer with nonzero line 5 expenses to answer YES. Line 5 is hard-coded to zero, which overstates net investment income on line 6 and the deduction on line 8.

findings.situation: A filer with qualified dividends and no net capital gain on line 4e who simply elects to include qualified dividends in investment income on line 4g could read the question as asking about that election and answer YES, although the tool computes the ordinary line 4g election.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Elect an alternative allocation of Form 4952 line 4g to qualified dividends instead of capital gains first?"; f4952 p. 3, Line 4g: "But you can elect to include part or all of these amounts in investment income."; f4952 p. 4: "you can treat less of the amount on line 4e as attributable to line 4g and more to line 4b ... enter on the dotted line next to line 4e 'Elec.'"
findings.why: The question never mentions the line 4e 'Elec.' entry or Form 1116. A filer who includes qualified dividends on line 4g, especially when line 4e is zero so all of line 4g is necessarily dividends, could think that counts as allocating line 4g to qualified dividends and be refused unnecessarily.

findings.situation: A filer has no carryover but does have other deductible investment expenses, such as depreciation or depletion on investment assets or K-1 investment expenses, so they answer NO and line 5 is computed as zero.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 4, Line 5: "Investment expenses are your allowed deductions, other than interest expense, directly connected with the production of investment income. For example, depreciation or depletion allowed on assets that produce investment income is an investment expense. Include investment expenses incurred directly by you or reported to you on Schedule K-1..."
findings.why: Line 5 and the filing-exception test in the `required` helper depend on these expenses, but the question asks only about a prior-year carryover. A filer with investment expenses and no carryover truthfully answers NO, and the tool treats line 5 as zero, which overstates net investment income and can wrongly apply the filing exception (p. 3: "You don't have any other deductible investment expenses").

findings.situation: A filer had disallowed investment interest in an earlier year that was fully used by 2024, so their 2024 Form 4952 line 7 is zero, but they may still answer YES because they once had a carryover.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 1, line 2: "Disallowed investment interest expense from 2024 Form 4952, line 7"; p. 3: "You don't have any carryover of disallowed investment interest expense from 2024."
findings.why: "Any prior-year disallowed investment interest carryover" does not tie the answer to the amount on 2024 Form 4952 line 7. A filer could read it as any past carryover, even one already used up, and the tool would refuse a case it computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer with a line 4g election who also files Form 1116 may want to treat less of line 4e as attributable to line 4g and more to line 4b, but none of the question's clauses asks about this, so the filer truthfully answers NO.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 4, Note: "However, you can treat less of the amount on line 4e as attributable to line 4g and more to line 4b. You may want to do this if you are filing Form 1116 ... To do so, enter on the dotted line next to line 4e 'Elec.' and the part of line 4e that you elect to treat as being attributable to line 4g"
findings.why: The tool's election line is a 'default-allocation' election, so it only supports the default ordering (line 4e first, then line 4b). The 'Elec.' alternative allocation is not computed, and the screening question never mentions it.

findings.situation: A filer whose Schedule K-1 reports investment expenses that are miscellaneous itemized deductions (not allowed for 2025) answers YES, although line 5 is correctly zero.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 4, Line 5: "Include investment expenses ... reported to you on Schedule K-1 ... but only if you are allowed a deduction on your return for the expense ... Don't include any miscellaneous itemized deductions, which aren't allowed deductions in tax years beginning after December 31, 2017, and before January 1, 2026."
findings.why: The question offers "investment expenses on a Schedule K-1" as an example of a deductible investment expense. A filer will likely answer YES for nondeductible K-1 investment expenses, even though line 5 correctly stays zero.

findings.situation: A filer with annuity income, royalty income, or a gain on investment property other than securities (for example, land), but no other investment expenses, answers YES, although line 2, the election, line 5 and the filing test are all computed correctly.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 3, Line 4a: "Gross income from property held for investment includes income ... from interest, ordinary dividends ..., annuities, and royalties"; Who Must File exception: "Your investment income from interest and ordinary dividends minus any qualified dividends is more than your investment interest expense. • You don't have any other deductible investment expenses. • You don't have any carryover"
findings.why: The clause "any other investment income or expense beyond interest, dividends and securities sales" covers types of income that do not affect any of the refused lines. Only deductible expenses (line 5) and the carryforward (line 2) feed these lines.

findings.situation: A filer whose interest relates to tax-exempt income, or is disallowed under section 264 or capitalized, may not know whether that interest is 'interest you count as investment interest'.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 3, Line 1: "Investment interest expense doesn't include ... Interest expense related to tax-exempt interest income under section 265" and "Any interest expense that is capitalized" and "Interest expense, disallowed under section 264"
findings.why: Under the IRS text, interest related to tax-exempt income is never investment interest. Yet the question asks whether investment interest is 'attributable to ... tax-exempt income', so a filer could answer YES or NO. The question also says nothing about capitalized or section 264 interest.

findings.why: The question asks about 'a home whose original use by you did not begin in 2025', and the help says costs count 'in the year you first live in it'. Under the IRS rule these costs are paid in 2025, so the tool computes them correctly, but the question refuses the filer.

findings.situation: A filer who adds solar or battery storage during a major remodel of an existing home they live in cannot tell whether the work counts as 'reconstruction'. If it does, the costs are deferred until use of the reconstructed home begins; if it does not, they are paid when installation is complete.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 1, Costs: "costs are treated as being paid when the original installation of the item is completed, or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins"
findings.why: Neither the question nor its help explains what makes work 'reconstruction' rather than an ordinary installation or renovation. A filer could reasonably answer either way, and the two answers can put the costs in different tax years.

If the aggregate credit that would be allowed to all occupants for any item of property exceeds the credit limit below, then you must figure your allocable share"; question: "Did you occupy any home for which you enter Part II costs jointly with someone other than your spouse ... answer Yes if you shared any one of them."
findings.why: Allocation and the line 32a statement are required only when the occupants' combined credit exceeds a limit. Below the limits, each occupant simply enters what they paid, which the tool computes. The question asks Yes for every case of joint occupancy, so it refuses cases the tool would get right.

findings.situation: A filer shares a home with a roommate or relative who paid for some Part II items, but the filer does not think of themselves as having entered costs 'jointly' with that person.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 3: "If you occupied your home jointly with someone, each occupant must complete their own Form 5695."
findings.why: In "occupy any home for which you enter Part II costs jointly with someone," the word "jointly" can attach either to occupying the home or to entering the costs. If a filer reads it as shared payment of the same costs, a filer whose co-occupant paid for separate items could answer No. The parenthetical points the other way, but the main clause stays ambiguous.

findings.situation: A filer whose Section A insulation, doors or windows are improvements to an existing main home, but whose Section B property (for example a heat pump, furnace, central air conditioner, panelboard or audit) was installed while a new home was being built, truthfully answers NO because the question asks only about the Section A improvements.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 5, Line 17e: "You cannot claim the credit for expenses related to the construction of a new home." i5695 (2025) p. 1: "The energy efficient home improvement credit (Part II) is only available for existing homes."
findings.why: Line 30 adds line 28 (which includes lines 22d–26c) and line 29h, so it includes Section B costs, and the bar on new-home construction expenses applies to all of Part II. The question asks only whether 'these qualified energy efficiency improvements' were related to construction, so the tool computes new-construction Section B costs that the IRS text excludes.

findings.situation: A filer whose Section A improvements are on the existing main home, but who installed Section B qualified energy property in a different, newly constructed home they use as a residence, answers NO because the question asks only about 'this main home'.
findings.irs_text: f5695 (2025) p. 3, line 21a: "installed on or in connection with a home located in the United States that you use as a residence"; i5695 (2025) p. 5, Line 17e: "You cannot claim the credit for expenses related to the construction of a new home."
findings.why: Section B property does not have to be in the main home. The question's wording limits the construction test to 'this main home', so construction-related expenses for another new home reach line 30 without being screened.

findings.why: "Have you elected" is true for a filer whose election was revoked, so that filer answers Yes and is refused. The ordinary ordering the tool computes is actually correct once the revocation applies.

findings.situation: The filer made the election on an amended return, or on a return for this tax year that was already filed, and must decide whether that counts as 'an earlier return'.

findings.situation: A shareholder who guaranteed or co-signed a corporate loan has made payments on that guarantee, so they now hold debt basis, but the help text tells them guaranteed loans are 'not meant', so they answer NO.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 2: "Shareholders only obtain basis from acting as a guarantor or in a similar capacity to the extent the shareholder makes a payment pursuant to the guarantee"; i7203 p. 3: "aren't part of a shareholder's loan basis except to the extent the shareholder makes a payment on the loan guaranteed or co-signed."
findings.why: The help excludes guaranteed loans without saying that payments made under a guarantee create debt basis that Part II must track, so this filer is steered to NO and the tool ignores that debt basis.

findings.situation: A shareholder advanced money informally, for example by paying corporate expenses personally on an open account, and does not think of this as 'lending money'; Item I may also be blank or misreported, and the question tells them to look there.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 3: "Loans made to the S corporation that aren't evidenced by a written instrument are referred to as an open account debt ... Enter any net advances on line 17"; "You must complete this section if you have personally loaned money to the corporation."
findings.why: The wording 'lent money' and the pointer to K-1 Item I let a filer with open-account advances answer NO, even though those advances are shareholder debt that Part II must track.

findings.situation: For a fiscal-year S corporation, a shareholder lends money in early 2026 during the corporation's tax year that began in 2025, and had no loan outstanding at the start of 2025.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 3, Line 17: "Enter any new loans made during the tax year"; Line 16: "balance of each loan to the S corporation at the beginning of the corporation's tax year."
findings.why: The question uses calendar 2025 rather than the corporation's tax year, so a loan made in 2026 inside that tax year falls outside both clauses and the filer truthfully answers NO.

findings.situation: A shareholder holds corporate debt they acquired by purchase or assignment rather than by lending the money themselves.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 2: "The basis of your loans to the corporation is generally the balance the corporation owes you".
findings.why: The IRS text turns on debt the corporation owes the shareholder, but the question asks whether 'you lent money', so a holder of acquired debt could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: The filer's reimbursements came under a pre-August 1, 1996 contract that was exchanged or modified after July 31, 1996 to increase per diem payments or reimbursements. Those reimbursements belong on line 24 like any other, and the tool computes line 25 correctly, but the wording makes the filer answer YES.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Was any of those reimbursements received under a long-term care contract issued before August 1, 1996?" i8853 (2025) p. 9, Line 24: "However, you must include reimbursements if the contract was exchanged or modified after July 31, 1996, to increase per diem payments or reimbursements."
findings.why: The question asks only about the issue date and ignores the exchange/modification exception. A filer whose reimbursements are properly on line 24 and handled by the plain line 23 minus line 24 subtraction is refused anyway.

findings.situation: The filer received some reimbursements under a pre-August 1, 1996 contract and left them off line 24 as instructed. Line 24 still holds reimbursements from other contracts. The filer cannot tell whether "those reimbursements" means only the amount entered on line 24 or every reimbursement received.
findings.irs_text: i8853 (2025) p. 9, Line 24: "Generally, don't include on line 24 reimbursements for qualified LTC services you received under a contract issued before August 1, 1996." f8853 (2025) p. 2, line 24 caution: "If you received any reimbursements from LTC contracts issued before August 1, 1996, see instructions."
findings.why: If "those" means every reimbursement received, the filer answers YES and is refused even though line 24 was entered correctly and line 25 computes correctly. If it means the amount on line 24, the filer answers NO. The question and its help do not say which.

findings.situation: A filer's 1099-LTC box 4 does not match the contract's actual status, for example a grandfathered pre-1997 contract that is qualified but has box 4 unchecked, or the reverse.
findings.irs_text: i8853 (2025) p.8: "A qualified LTC insurance contract is a contract issued: • After December 31, 1996, that meets the requirements of section 7702B ... or • Before January 1, 1997, that met state law requirements for LTC insurance contracts ... and hasn't been changed materially."
findings.why: The question equates "not a qualified long-term care insurance contract" with the box 4 "Qualified contract" box being unchecked, but the IRS text defines qualified status by the contract itself. findings.situation: Someone else received a lump-sum (not periodic) accelerated death benefit under a policy on the same insured, for example because the insured was terminally ill, so nothing reduces the filer's $420-a-day limit and the tool's single-payee line 26 is correct.
findings.irs_text: i8853 p. 8, Line 15: "Special rules apply in determining the taxable payments if other individuals received per diem payments under a qualified LTC insurance contract or as accelerated death benefits with respect to the insured"; p. 8, Accelerated Death Benefits: amounts paid when the insured is terminally ill "are fully excludable"
findings.why: The question asks about 'accelerated death benefits under a life insurance policy covering this person' with no per-diem or periodic limit, so this filer must answer YES and is refused. Per the Line 15 instruction, sharing the limit only matters when the other person's payments were per diem or periodic. The form's own line 15 is equally broad, and the Multiple Payees instruction asks for a statement 'in all other cases', so this widening comes straight from the form.

findings.situation: The filer's own LTC per diem payments are assigned to and paid directly to a nursing home or other third party, so a filer could think 'someone other than you' received payments under the contract covering this person.
findings.irs_text: i8853 p. 8, Policyholder: "The policyholder is required to report the income, even if payment is assigned to a third party or parties."
findings.why: 'Did anyone other than you ... receive payments' could be read to include a third party who physically received the filer's own assigned payments, which the tool computes correctly. The help example (a sibling who owns another policy) suggests a separate policyholder but does not rule out the assignee reading.

findings.situation: A single contract pays $175 a day from March through May, stops while the insured is out of care, and resumes at the same $175 a day from September through December, with no second contract.
findings.irs_text: i8853 p. 9, Method 2: "your LTC period is the period during which the insurance company uses the same payment rate to compute your benefits"; i8853 p. 8, Line 18: "If you have more than one LTC period, you must separately calculate the taxable amount of the payments received during each LTC period."
findings.why: The rate never changed and only the same contract stopped and restarted, so the filer truthfully answers NO. The two separated stretches can be separate LTC periods, and the per-period comparison of $420 × days against costs on lines 21–23 can then give a different line 26 than one combined calculation.

findings.situation: Two contracts both begin paying on March 1, 2025 at fixed rates ($100/day and $1,500/month) and both pay through December 31, which the IRS treats as a single LTC period.
findings.irs_text: i8853 p. 9, Method 2: "You have one LTC period because each payment rate doesn't vary during the LTC period of March 1 through December 31."
findings.why: The question asks whether "another contract for this person start[ed] or stop[ped] paying". A filer whose second contract started paying in 2025 may answer YES even though it started together with the first, and the tool computes that case correctly. A filer may also be unsure whether two different rates running together count as payments "not at one rate".

findings.situation: A contract pays a fixed $1,500 per month, so the amount per day differs between 30- and 31-day months.
findings.irs_text: i8853 p. 9, Method 2: "a second contract that pays $1,500 per month ... You have one LTC period because each payment rate doesn't vary"
findings.why: The question names a "daily, weekly or monthly rate". A filer could compute a daily rate that varies from month to month and answer YES, even though the IRS treats a constant monthly rate as one LTC period and the tool computes it correctly.

findings.situation: A filer whose final determination of reckless or intentional disregard came, say, in mid-2024 cannot tell whether they are 'within 2 years' of it when claiming the credit for 2025 on a return filed in 2026.
findings.irs_text: i8863 (2025) p. 3: "Don't claim the American opportunity credit for 2 years after there was a final determination that your claim was due to reckless or intentional disregard of the rules or 10 years after there was a final determination that your claim was due to fraud."
findings.why: The question asks whether the filer is 'within 2 years' (or 10 years) of the determination but does not say what date to measure to. A filer could measure to the filing date and answer No, or to the tax year being claimed and answer Yes, so the same facts can produce either answer.

findings.situation: A filer whose credit was denied or reduced on a tax year that began in 2015 and ended in 2016, or who isn't sure whether the reduction was a math or clerical error, has to judge from the wording alone whether Form 8862 is 'required'.
findings.irs_text: i8863 (2025) p. 1: "If your American opportunity credit was denied or reduced for any reason other than a math or clerical error for any tax year beginning after 2015, you must attach a completed Form 8862"
findings.why: The question says 'a tax year after 2015' where the IRS says 'beginning after 2015'. It also ends with 'so that Form 8862 is required', which leaves the filer to decide whether the form is needed. Both points can be read either way.

question: Was your American opportunity credit denied or reduced, for a reason other than a math or clerical error, for a tax year after 2015, so that Form 8862 is required (it is not, if since then you filed Form 8862 with the return for a later year and the credit was allowed), or are you within 2 years of a final determination that a claim was due to reckless or intentional disregard of the rules, or within 10 years of one that it was due to fraud?

findings.situation: A filer with no Archer MSA contributions for 2025 who received a 2025 Archer MSA distribution, including one rolled over into an HSA, must answer YES, yet line 13 does not depend on Archer MSA distributions, so the tool would compute it correctly with line 4 as zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'did you receive a distribution from an Archer MSA in 2025 (including one rolled over into an HSA)'. f8889 p.1 line 4: 'Enter the amount you and your employer contributed to your Archer MSAs for 2025 from Form 8853, lines 1 and 2'; i8889 p.4 Line 2: 'Do not include ... amounts rolled over from another HSA or Archer MSA.'
findings.why: Only Archer MSA contributions for 2025 reach line 13, through line 4. Distributions, including rollovers into an HSA, are kept out of lines 2 through 13, so refusing line 13 for them is broader than the line needs.

findings.situation: A filer who only acquired an interest in an Archer MSA in 2025 because the account holder died, with no contributions for 2025, must answer YES, although nothing from that event enters lines 2 through 13.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'did you acquire an interest in an Archer MSA in 2025 because its account holder died?' i8853 p.1 Who Must File: 'You ... acquired an interest in an Archer MSA ... because of the death of the account holder.' f8889 p.1 line 4 counts only amounts 'contributed to your Archer MSAs for 2025'.
findings.why: This event triggers the Form 8853 filing requirement, but it does not change line 4 or the HSA deduction. Line 13 would therefore be computed correctly at the tool's zero for line 4.

findings.situation: The filer engaged in a prohibited transaction with an HSA in 2025, but no Form 1099-SA shows code 5 (the trustee did not know, issued no form, or coded the year's ordinary payments as 1).
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 3, Deemed Distributions From HSAs: "You engaged in any transaction prohibited by section 4975 with respect to any of your HSAs, at any time in 2025. Your account ceases to be an HSA as of January 1, 2025, and you must include the fair market value of all assets in the account as of January 1, 2025, on line 14a." and "Any deemed distribution will not be treated as used to pay qualified medical expenses."
findings.why: The question asks only what box 3 shows, not whether a prohibited transaction happened, so this filer truthfully answers NO. Line 16 is then computed from actual distributions only, leaving out the deemed distribution of the whole account.

findings.situation: The filer inherited an HSA in 2025 from someone who was not their spouse but received no payment from it in 2025 (or no Form 1099-SA for it), while having distributions from their own HSA so the gate holds.
findings.irs_text: f1099sa (Rev. April 2025) p. 3, Nonspouse beneficiary: "Report the FMV on your tax return for the year the account owner died even if you received the distribution from the account in a later year."; i8889 (2025) p. 3, Death of Account Beneficiary: "On Part II, line 14a, enter the fair market value of the HSA as of the date of death."
findings.why: With no 2025 Form 1099-SA showing code 4 or 6, the filer truthfully answers NO. The date-of-death value that belongs on line 14a and flows to line 16 is omitted, as is the separate "Death of HSA account beneficiary" Form 8889.

findings.situation: The return is the final return of an HSA owner who died in 2025 with the estate as beneficiary; the code 4 Form 1099-SA, if any, is issued to the estate, while the decedent's own forms show code 1.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 3: "If the account beneficiary's estate is the beneficiary, the value of the HSA as of the date of death is included on the account beneficiary's final income tax return."; f1099sa p. 3, Estate beneficiary: "the fair market value (FMV) of the account on the date of death is includible in the account holder's gross income. Report the amount on the account holder's final income tax return."
findings.why: "Your 2025 Forms 1099-SA" read as the decedent's own forms show only code 1, so the answer is NO. Line 16 then leaves out the date-of-death value.

findings.situation: The filer pledged part of an HSA as security for a loan in 2025 and also had ordinary code 1 distributions.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 3, Deemed Distributions From HSAs: "You used any portion of any of your HSAs as security for a loan at any time in 2025. You must include the fair market value of the assets used as security for the loan as income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8f."
findings.why: No distribution code flags a pledge, so the filer answers NO. The deemed distribution, which goes into the same Schedule 1 line 8f total that line 16 feeds and is generally subject to the 20% tax, is not captured by this screen.

findings.situation: A surviving spouse who is the designated beneficiary receives a 2025 Form 1099-SA with code 4 for a payment from the deceased spouse's HSA and files as a single-type filer.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 3, Death of Account Beneficiary: "If the account beneficiary's surviving spouse is the designated beneficiary, the HSA is treated as if the surviving spouse were the account beneficiary. The surviving spouse completes Form 8889 as though the HSA belonged to the surviving spouse."
findings.why: The question says "4 (death distribution other than code 6)", so this filer must answer YES and is refused. Yet for a spouse beneficiary line 16 is the ordinary line 14c minus line 15, which the tool computes.

findings.situation: A filer who received an HSA distribution but no Form 1099-SA, or a form with box 3 blank or wrong, cannot tell whether the question is about the printed code or the nature of the distribution.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 8, Line 14a: "Enter the total distributions your HSAs made in 2025. These amounts should be shown on Form 1099-SA, box 1."
findings.why: The question is framed entirely on what box 3 "shows", while the Form 8889 treatment depends on what the distribution actually was (excess withdrawal, death, prohibited transaction). A filer with a missing or miscoded form could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: A filer files the 2025 return on time without requesting an extension, then withdraws the 2025 excess contributions and their earnings between April 15 and October 15, 2026, and prepares an amended return.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8, Note: 'If you timely filed your return without withdrawing the excess contributions, you can still make the withdrawal no later than 6 months after the due date of your tax return, excluding extensions. If you do, file an amended return...' and Line 14b: 'Also include any excess contributions (and the earnings on those excess contributions) included on line 14a that were withdrawn by the due date, including extensions, of your return.'
findings.why: A filer who never requested an extension can read 'by the due date of your 2025 return including extensions' as April 15, 2026, and answer NO. The tool then sets line 14b to zero and taxes the withdrawal on line 16, even though the IRS text treats it as a timely withdrawal of excess contributions.

findings.situation: In 2025 the filer withdrew excess contributions from an earlier year after that year's return due date had passed, so the withdrawal is an ordinary distribution.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8, Line 15: 'Do not include the distribution of an excess contribution taken out after the due date, including extensions, of your return even if used for qualified medical expenses.'
findings.why: The question asks 'Did you withdraw from your HSA any excess contributions ... in 2025', and the 2025 branch has no due-date limit. This filer therefore answers YES, but the withdrawal is an ordinary taxable distribution that the tool computes through lines 14a–16 without a line 14b entry.

findings.situation: In early 2026, before the 2025 return due date, the filer withdrew excess contributions made for tax year 2026, not 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8, Excess Contributions You Make: 'you can withdraw some or all of your excess contributions for 2025 and they will be treated as if they had not been contributed if: • You make the withdrawal by the due date, including extensions, of your 2025 tax return'
findings.why: The question says 'any excess contributions' and does not limit them to contributions for 2025 or earlier years. A 2026-year excess withdrawn in 2026 therefore triggers YES, although it does not touch lines 13, 14b or 16 of the 2025 form.

findings.why: The question asks only whether "you" acquired an interest because of another person's death, so the decedent's own final return answers NO and line 16 is computed from actual distributions (or zero) without the date-of-death value on line 14a. findings.situation: An unmarried filer who became the owner of a late spouse's HSA as designated beneficiary in an earlier year, and now uses it as their own, must answer YES although their Form 8889 is an ordinary one.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 3: "If the account beneficiary's surviving spouse is the designated beneficiary, the HSA is treated as if the surviving spouse were the account beneficiary. The surviving spouse completes Form 8889 as though the HSA belonged to the surviving spouse."
findings.why: The question says "as the surviving spouse or as any other beneficiary" and "in 2025 or in an earlier year", so this filer is refused. The IRS text has lines 13 and 16 figured exactly as for the filer's own HSA, which the tool computes.

findings.situation: A non-spouse beneficiary whose HSA owner died in an earlier year, who reported the date-of-death value that year and received nothing from the inherited account in 2025, must answer YES although nothing from it belongs on the 2025 Form 8889.
findings.irs_text: f1099sa (Rev. April 2025) p. 3: "Report the FMV on your tax return for the year the account owner died even if you received the distribution from the account in a later year." i8889 (2025) p. 3: "the account ceases to be an HSA as of the date of death."
findings.why: The question says "in 2025 or in an earlier year" and the help says "Answer Yes whatever year the owner died in", so this filer is refused. The inherited account adds nothing to 2025 lines 13 or 16, and the tool would compute the filer's own HSA correctly.

findings.situation: An heir who received the HSA money through the decedent's estate (the estate was the beneficiary, or there was no designated beneficiary) may not know whether they "acquired an interest in an HSA".
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 3: "If the designated beneficiary is not the account beneficiary's surviving spouse, or there is no designated beneficiary, the account ceases to be an HSA as of the date of death." and "If the account beneficiary's estate is the beneficiary, the value of the HSA as of the date of death is included on the account beneficiary's final income tax return."
findings.why: The words "as any other beneficiary" and "only received a distribution after the death" could lead such an heir to answer YES, although the value belongs on the decedent's final return. The help text mentions only being named as beneficiary, so the heir could equally answer NO.

findings.situation: A filer whose 2025 HSA funding distribution came by direct trustee-to-trustee transfer from a SEP IRA or SIMPLE IRA that is not ongoing could answer NO, because the question names only a 'traditional IRA or Roth IRA'.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 7, Line 10: 'This distribution cannot be made from an ongoing SEP IRA or SIMPLE IRA. For this purpose, a SEP IRA or SIMPLE IRA is ongoing if an employer contribution is made for the plan year ending with or within your tax year'
findings.why: The IRS text implies that a transfer from a SEP or SIMPLE IRA that is not ongoing can be a qualified HSA funding distribution. Such a transfer reduces the line 12 limit, but a filer who reads 'traditional IRA or Roth IRA' literally would answer NO, and the tool would then figure line 13 against an unreduced limit.

findings.situation: A filer who made a direct IRA-to-HSA transfer but believes it was not 'qualified' could answer NO. Reasons might be that it exceeded the age- and coverage-based maximum or was a second lifetime transfer.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 7, Line 10: 'A distribution from your traditional IRA or Roth IRA to your HSA in a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer is called an HSA funding distribution ... Enter this amount on line 10 ... The maximum amount that can be excluded from income is based on your age ... You can make only one qualified HSA funding distribution during your lifetime.'
findings.why: The question asks whether the distribution was 'qualified', which makes the filer judge the limits that the IRS text applies after line 10 is entered. A filer who decides the transfer failed those limits answers NO, and the tool then ignores a transfer that line 10 and the excess-contribution rules still need.

findings.situation: A filer with a 2025 IRA-to-HSA transfer and no other HSA contributions answers YES, and line13_none is refused even though the HSA deduction is zero either way.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'Was a qualified HSA funding distribution made to your HSA in 2025'; i8889 p. 7, Line 10: 'The qualified HSA funding distribution is not included in your income, is not deductible'; i8889 p. 8, Line 13: 'enter the smaller of line 2 or line 12'
findings.why: A qualified HSA funding distribution is excluded from line 2 and is not deductible. With no other contributions, line 13 is zero whatever the distribution's amount, so the zero line13_none computes is correct, but the screen still refuses it.

findings.situation: A filer personally used, or took a transfer of, an asset held by the HSA (or dealt with it indirectly, for example through a family member or an entity they own) without any sale, lease, loan or furnishing of goods or services.
findings.irs_text: p969 (2025) p. 9: "Examples of prohibited transactions include the direct or indirect: ... Transfer to or use by you or for your benefit of any assets of the HSA."
findings.why: The question defines prohibited transactions only by citing section 4975 and listing three of the four Pub. 969 examples, leaving out transfer or use for your benefit and the words "direct or indirect". findings.situation: A filer who was already 65 or disabled when they pledged the HSA as security for a loan or engaged in a prohibited transaction must answer YES, although line 17b itself is not increased by that deemed distribution.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 9: "The additional 20% tax does not apply to distributions made after the account beneficiary: • Dies, • Becomes disabled or • Turns age 65." and i8889 p. 3: "Generally, these distributions are subject to the additional 20% tax."

findings.situation: A mistaken distribution was taken in 2024 (or earlier) and repaid during 2025, and the filer has only ordinary 2025 distributions, or none.
findings.irs_text: f8889 (2025) p. 1, line 14a: 'Total distributions you received in 2025 from all HSAs'; line 17b: 'Enter 20% (0.20) of the distributions included on line 16 that are subject to the additional 20% tax'; i1099sa p. 1: 'Do not treat the repayment as a contribution on Form 5498-SA'.
findings.why: The question's clause 'or one made earlier and repaid in 2025' forces YES, but an earlier-year distribution is never in 2025 line 14a or line 16 and the repayment is not a contribution. The 2025 line 17b the tool computes is already correct, so the refusal is unnecessary.

findings.situation: A 2025 mistaken distribution was repaid and the trustee left it off (or corrected) Form 1099-SA, so the amounts the filer enters for 2025 distributions already exclude it.
findings.irs_text: i1099sa p. 1, HSA Mistaken Distributions: 'Do not report the mistaken distribution on Form 1099-SA. Correct any filed Form 1099-SA with the IRS and the account beneficiary as soon as you become aware of the error.'
findings.why: The filer must truthfully answer YES to 'Was a distribution from your HSA made by mistake and repaid to the HSA', yet the repaid amount is in neither box 1 nor line 14a. The ordinary computation of 20% of line 16 is already right.

findings.situation: The filer was 65 or older or disabled before the mistaken distribution was made and repaid it, so line 17b is zero with or without the special rule.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 9, Lines 17a and 17b: 'The additional 20% tax does not apply to distributions made after the account beneficiary: Dies, Becomes disabled or Turns age 65.'
findings.why: The question forces YES and refuses line 17b even though the exception already removes the distribution from the 20% tax. For this line the mistaken-distribution rule changes nothing (its effect is only on line 16 income).

findings.situation: The filer withdrew HSA money in the reasonable but wrong belief that an expense was qualified and then repaid it; the trustee made no error.
findings.irs_text: i1099sa p. 1: 'the account beneficiary reasonably, but mistakenly, believed that an expense was a qualified medical expense and was reimbursed for that expense from the HSA. The account beneficiary then repays the mistaken distribution to the HSA.'
findings.why: 'Made by mistake' with the help example 'the HSA paid a bill that turned out not to be a medical cost' can be read as an error by the HSA or trustee. A filer whose own mistaken belief caused the withdrawal might answer NO, and the tool would then charge the 20% tax on an amount the IRS text excludes.

findings.situation: The filer took a mistaken distribution in 2025 and intends to return it, but the trustee may not accept repayments or the repayment may not happen by the deadline.
findings.irs_text: f1099sa p. 3: 'You may repay a mistaken distribution from an HSA no later than the due date of the tax return (not including extensions) following the first year you knew or should have known the distribution was a mistake, providing the trustee allows the repayment.'
findings.why: The help says 'Answer Yes also if you plan to return it' and the question says 'to be repaid by the date allowed', without naming the date or the trustee-consent condition. A filer cannot tell whether an intended repayment that may not be permitted calls for YES (refusal) or NO (ordinary 20% tax, which would be correct if the repayment cannot be made).

findings.situation: A filer who is not the surviving spouse inherited an HSA from someone who died in 2025 and must file their own Form 8889 reporting the account's date-of-death value, but answers NO because the form is for the filer, who is alive, and it is not the dead person's final return.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 3, Death of Account Beneficiary: "If the designated beneficiary is not the account beneficiary's surviving spouse, or there is no designated beneficiary, the account ceases to be an HSA as of the date of death. The beneficiary completes Form 8889 as follows... skip Part I. On Part II, line 14a, enter the fair market value of the HSA as of the date of death. On Part II, line 15, for a beneficiary other than the estate, enter qualified medical expenses incurred by the account beneficiary before the date of death that the beneficiary paid within 1 year after the date of death."
findings.why: The question and its help tie YES to "the person this Form 8889 is for" and to the dead person's final or joint return, so an inheritor truthfully answers NO. The tool then computes line 16 by the ordinary rule (line 14c less line 15) and line 13 as an ordinary deduction, without the date-of-death value on line 14a, the special line 15 rule, the skipped Part I, or the separate statement forms needed when the filer also has their own HSA.

findings.situation: A non-spouse beneficiary receives a 2025 distribution (Form 1099-SA code 6) from an HSA whose owner died before 2025, and answers NO because the death was not in 2025.
findings.irs_text: f1099sa (Rev. April 2025) p. 3, Nonspouse beneficiary: "Report the FMV on your tax return for the year the account owner died even if you received the distribution from the account in a later year... Any earnings on the account after the date of death (box 1 minus box 4 of Form 1099-SA) are taxable. Include the earnings on the 'Other income' line of your tax return." Box 3: "6—Death distribution after year of death to a nonspouse beneficiary."
findings.why: The question is limited to deaths "in 2025", so this filer answers NO and the tool treats the box 1 amount as an ordinary distribution on line 14a, taxing on line 16 value that belonged in the year of death. Only the earnings after death are taxable, and they belong on the other income line, not line 16.

findings.situation: For an inherited HSA, the question's two descriptions of the same person point to different people: the account beneficiary is the person who died, while the person the Form 8889 is for is the living inheritor.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 2, Account Beneficiary: "The account beneficiary is the individual on whose behalf the HSA was established." p. 3: "Enter the name(s) shown on the beneficiary's tax return and the beneficiary's SSN in the spaces provided at the top of the form."
findings.why: The question says "the account beneficiary of this HSA (the person this Form 8889 is for)", which an inheritor can read as YES (the account's owner died in 2025) or NO (I am the person the form is for and I am alive). The help's "on that person's final return" pushes toward NO, but the sentence "It includes an HSA whose beneficiary is the estate" adds to the confusion over which return is meant.
