findings.situation: In a post-2012 year the filer's MAGI was below the threshold, so no Form 8960 was filed, but that year produced an NOL with a section 1411 portion. In 2025 the filer recovers a state income tax refund for that year.
findings.irs_text: i8960 p. 15, Deduction Recoveries Worksheet line 1: 'Don't include recoveries of items if ... you weren't subject to the NIIT solely because your MAGI was below the applicable threshold. This rule doesn't apply if you incurred an NOL in such year, and a portion of such NOL constitutes a section 1411 NOL'; lines 14–16 'Calculation of recoveries when the deduction is taken into account in computing your section 1411 NOL ... include on Form 8960, line 7'
findings.why: The question asks only about amounts 'deducted on an earlier Form 8960'. This filer filed no Form 8960 that year, so they can truthfully answer NO, yet the instructions require a line 7 recovery that the tool sets to zero.

findings.situation: The filer recovers an amount deducted on an earlier Form 8960 that does not belong on line 7. Either the deduction did not reduce that year's NIIT (for example, MAGI was below the threshold and there was no section 1411 NOL), or the recovery is already in NII on lines 1–6 (for example, a recovered rental expense reported on Schedule E and flowing to line 4a).
findings.irs_text: Question: 'Any recovery or refund in 2025 of an amount deducted on an earlier Form 8960'. IRS text, i8960 p. 15: 'properly allocable deductions aren't reduced in the year of the recovery if the amount deducted in the prior year didn't reduce the amount of section 1411 liability'; worksheet line 1: 'Don't include recoveries of items that are included in NII in the year of recovery (included on lines 1–6)'
findings.why: The wording forces a YES for any such recovery. In these cases nothing goes on line 7 and the computed lines are already correct, so the tool refuses returns it handles properly.

findings.situation: The filer got a state or foreign income tax refund in 2025 and does not know whether the tax refunded was part of the prior year's Form 8960 line 9b deduction. Line 9b may have used only an allocated portion, or the prior Form 8960 may have been prepared by someone else.

findings.situation: A filer received a 2025 state income tax refund that is taxable on Schedule 1 line 1, and deducted that tax on a prior-year Form 8960 line 9b, so the recovery must be added on line 7; the tool sets line 7 to zero.
findings.irs_text: i8960 p. 14, Deduction recoveries: "A recovery or refund of a previously deducted item increases NII in the year of the recovery... if a taxpayer receives a refund of state income taxes from a prior year, such a refund would be included"; p. 15 worksheet line 13: "include on Form 8960, line 7"
findings.why: The question names no refund or recovery of a prior-year deduction. A filer would not recognize an ordinary state tax refund as "another net investment income adjustment" and would truthfully answer NO.

findings.situation: A parent includes a child's interest and dividends by filing Form 8814, or receives substitute dividend or interest payments (Form 1099-MISC) or notional principal contract payments reported on Schedule 1 line 8z, and these must go on line 7, which the tool sets to zero.
findings.irs_text: i8960 p. 13, Line 7: "Other items of NII ... not otherwise included on Form 8960 reported on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8z ... 1. Amounts reported on Form 8814 ... line 12. 2. Substitute interest and dividend payments"
findings.why: None of these items is listed. The catch-all "another net investment income adjustment" requires the filer to already know that these items are Form 8960 modifications, so they would answer NO.

findings.situation: A filer has a casualty or theft loss on Schedule A line 15 from investment property, which must be entered as a negative amount on line 7; the tool ignores it.
findings.irs_text: i8960 p. 13, Line 7: "Gains and losses from the disposition of property not included on line 5a ... 2. Casualty and theft losses reported on Schedule A (Form 1040), Itemized Deductions, line 15 (enter as a negative amount)"
findings.why: The question lists only life insurance contract dispositions and line 5b/5c items. A casualty loss does not fit "a disposition adjustment (Form 8960 line 5b or 5c)", so the filer could answer NO.

findings.situation: A filer with only Schedule E Part I rental income is a real estate professional, or has a self-rental or a rental grouped with a trade or business, so line 4b needs an adjustment for nonpassive rental income; the tool sets line 4b to zero.
findings.irs_text: i8960 p. 8, Line 4b: "Nonpassive net rental income or loss of a real estate professional where the rental activity rises to a section 162 trade or business. • Net rental income or loss that's a nonpassive activity because it was grouped with a trade or business"
findings.why: Whether directly held rental real estate counts as "business ... income" is ambiguous. A landlord could read the question as asking only about Schedule C income or K-1s and answer NO.

findings.situation: A filer whose only annuity income is a pension or IRA annuity from a section 401, 403, 408 or 457(b) plan must answer YES, although line 3 is correctly zero for that income.
findings.irs_text: Question: "annuity, business or pass-through income"; i8960 p. 7, Line 3: "Enter the gross income from all annuities, except annuities paid from ... Section 401 ... Section 408—individual retirement accounts (IRAs) or annuities"
findings.why: Qualified-plan annuities are excluded from NII, so the tool's zero on line 3 is correct for them. The question's unqualified "annuity" still forces a refusal.

findings.situation: A filer who excludes savings bond interest on Form 8815 must answer YES, although that exclusion is already reflected in Form 1040 line 2b and in AGI, which the tool uses for lines 1 and 13.
findings.irs_text: Question: "excluded savings bond interest (Form 8815)"; i8960 p. 7, Line 1: "Include the following amount from your return. • Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 2b"; p. 22, Line 13: "If you didn't exclude any amounts from your gross income under section 911 and you don't own an interest in a CFC or PFIC, your MAGI is your AGI"
findings.why: Form 8815 interest is already removed before line 2b and AGI. Form 8960 needs no further adjustment for it, so the tool computes this case correctly.

findings.situation: A filer whose only pass-through income is passive partnership or S corporation income reported on Schedule 1 line 5 must answer YES, although line 4a takes that amount and no line 4b adjustment applies.
findings.irs_text: Question: "annuity, business or pass-through income"; i8960 p. 8, Line 4a: "Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 5"; Line 4b covers only items "that aren't included in determining NII" such as nonpassive section 162 income
findings.why: Passive pass-through income is fully NII and is already captured on line 4a. Refusal is needed only for nonpassive or otherwise excepted pass-through items, but the question refuses all pass-through income.

findings.situation: An employer offer was in fact affordable under 9.02% of actual household income, but the filer gave the Marketplace accurate information and the Marketplace found the filer eligible for APTC.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 5: "employer-sponsored coverage is not considered affordable if, when you or a family member enrolled in a qualified health plan, you gave accurate information about the availability of employer coverage to the Marketplace, and the Marketplace determined that you were eligible for APTC"
findings.why: The question's affordability test only looks at the 9.02% threshold, so the filer answers YES. Under the IRS text the person is not eligible for that coverage, so the tool computes the lines correctly.

findings.situation: Actual 2025 income made a family member income-eligible for Medicaid or CHIP, but the Marketplace, given accurate information, had determined the person ineligible for Medicaid or CHIP and eligible for APTC.

findings.why: The bullet 'eligible for ... Medicaid' leads this filer to answer YES. The person is treated as not eligible, so the tool's computation is correct. The question's separate bullet only covers determinations based on intentionally or recklessly incorrect information.

findings.situation: After leaving a job, a former employee was offered affordable, minimum-value COBRA or retiree coverage but did not enroll in it.

findings.situation: A family member was eligible for other MEC for only part of a month, for example Medicaid or employer coverage that began mid-month.

findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 17, Column (f): "Enter on lines 12 through 23, column (f), the amount of the monthly APTC reported on Form 1095-A, lines 21 through 32, column C"; i8962 p. 18, Line 25: "Enter the amount from line 11(f) or add lines 12(f) through 23(f)"
findings.why: Both adjustments in the question act only on the monthly credit amount, through enrollment premiums and first-of-month enrollment. They feed column (e) and line 24, not column (f) and line 25. The tool computes line 25 correctly in every YES situation.

findings.situation: A filer whose 2025 premium refund the Marketplace has already netted out of Form 1095-A column A must answer YES to "any premiums for a 2025 month of that Marketplace coverage were refunded in 2025", even though the tool's use of column A as reported is already correct.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 4: "The enrollment premiums are the total amount of the premiums for the month, reduced by any premium amounts for that month that were refunded in 2025 ... Form 1095-A, Part III, column A, reports the enrollment premiums."
findings.why: The IRS text says column A reports enrollment premiums, which are defined net of 2025 refunds. A refund already reflected there needs no adjustment by the filer. The question asks only whether a refund happened, not whether column A omits it.

findings.situation: A filer whose coverage began mid-month cannot tell whether to answer YES when Form 1095-A column A already shows no premium for that partial month, a case the tool already treats correctly.

findings.why: The question asks only about the start date. It does not ask whether the 1095-A reports a premium or APTC for that month. A filer could reasonably answer either way when the 1095-A already shows nothing for the partial month.

findings.situation: A filer claims the 60% allowance in 2025 for used long-production-period property or certain aircraft acquired before January 20, 2025, and placed in service in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 6: "Property with a long production period and certain aircraft acquired after September 27, 2017, and before January 20, 2025, is eligible for a special depreciation allowance of 60% ... and can be either new property or certain used property." The 40% election for post-January 19 property also allows "60% for property with a long production period and certain aircraft."
findings.why: The computed helper reads "the full allowance or the 40% allowance." A filer claiming the 60% allowance could truthfully answer no, so the used-property line is never asked even though the allowance applies to used property.

findings.situation: A filer elects the qualified production property allowance in 2025 for used nonresidential real property placed in service after July 4, 2025.
findings.irs_text: i4562 pp. 7-8: "You can elect to take a special depreciation allowance for qualified production property (QPP) by designating up to 100% of the depreciable basis... Eligible property can be either new property or certain used property."
findings.why: The QPP allowance is a designation of basis, not a class-wide allowance. It is also not "the full allowance or the 40% allowance" named in the helper, so a filer could answer no. Used QPP would then be treated as not used.

findings.situation: A filer who elected the special allowance for a specified fruit or nut plant grafted in 2025 but not yet placed in service.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 6: "the special depreciation allowance only applies for the first tax year in which the plant is planted or grafted. The plant will not be treated as qualified property ... in the subsequent tax year in which it is placed in service."
findings.why: The gate requires the property to be placed in service in 2025, but this allowance is claimed in the planting or grafting year, before the plant is placed in service. Grafting onto existing stock could raise an original-use question that the gate never reaches.

findings.situation: Property placed in service in 2025 with the 50% allowance for qualified reuse and recycling property.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 7: "The original use of the property must begin with you after August 31, 2008."
findings.why: Used property cannot qualify for this allowance, so asking whether it was used before adds questions without affecting any amount.

findings.situation: A business that is not an energy producer, such as a retailer, farm, or office, installs solar, wind, or geothermal equipment on its own premises and truthfully answers no to the gate.
findings.irs_text: 5-year property includes the following. ... • Certain energy property specified in section 168(e)(3)(B)(vi). (i4562 2025 p. 10)
findings.why: Energy property under 168(e)(3)(B)(vi) is classified by what the asset is, not by the owner's industry. Any business that puts in qualifying solar or wind equipment owns it, so the gate drops the 5-year classification for owners who are not energy producers.

findings.situation: A manufacturer, retailer, or waste hauler that does not see itself as a recycler buys machinery used exclusively to collect or distribute reuse and recyclable materials, such as a baler or sorting equipment, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: Qualified reuse and recycling property includes any machinery and equipment ... that is used exclusively to collect, distribute, or recycle qualified reuse and recyclable materials. (i4562 2025 p. 6)
findings.why: The definition depends on how the equipment is used, including collection and distribution, not on whether the business is a recycler. A business with in-house or collection-only equipment could truthfully answer no.

findings.situation: A midstream or pipeline gathering company, or a stand-alone electric transmission company, decides whether it is a 'utility or energy producer'.
findings.irs_text: Any natural gas gathering line (as defined in section 168(i)(17)) placed in service after April 11, 2005 ... (i4562 2025 p. 10); electric transmission property ... used in the transmission at 69 or more kilovolts of electricity (p946 2025 p. 31)
findings.why: Gathering lines and transmission assets are often owned by companies that neither produce energy nor see themselves as utilities. A filer could read 'utility or energy producer' either way.

findings.situation: A business that leases vehicles, boats, or trailers, rather than selling them, used floor plan financing, and decides whether it is 'a dealer that finances its stock'.
findings.irs_text: Property described in section 168(k)(9)(A) or 168(k)(9)(B) (i4562 2025 p. 7); the gated question restates 168(k)(9)(B) as covering motor vehicles, boats, farm machinery or equipment, or trailers or campers 'held for sale or lease'
findings.why: Floor plan financing under 168(k)(9)(B) covers inventory held for lease as well as for sale. The word 'dealer' in the gate could lead a lessor to answer no.

findings.situation: A filer has a passenger automobile, pickup truck, SUV, motorcycle or aircraft whose qualified business use is 50% or less, and truthfully answers no because the gate asks only about entertainment or recreation equipment and computers.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 3, Listed Property: "Passenger automobiles weighing 6,000 pounds or less" ... "Any other property used for transportation if the nature of the property lends itself to personal use, such as motorcycles, pickup trucks, SUVs, aircraft, etc."; p. 14: "Use line 27 to figure the depreciation for property used 50% or less in a qualified business use."
findings.why: Transportation property is listed property, and a low qualified-business-use vehicle or aircraft goes on line 27. The gate never asks about it, so asset.qbu_low_if_listed is forced to false.

findings.situation: A filer has computer peripheral equipment (for example a printer) placed in service before 2018 that is not used only at a regular business establishment, and answers no because the question mentions only 'a computer'.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 3, Exceptions: "Any computer or peripheral equipment used exclusively at a regular business establishment and owned or leased by the person operating the establishment"; p. 14: "computers and peripheral equipment placed in service before 2018"
findings.why: Pre-2018 peripheral equipment is listed property under the same rule as computers, but the question names only computers.

findings.situation: A pre-2018 computer is used only at a regular business establishment, but the filer (for example an employee using it at the employer's office) does not own or lease the establishment, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 3: "used exclusively at a regular business establishment and owned or leased by the person operating the establishment"
findings.why: The exception requires that the person operating the establishment own or lease the computer. The question drops that requirement, so a truthful no excludes a computer that is still listed property.

findings.situation: An employee uses a camera or video equipment only in a home office that meets the home-office requirements, then reads the help text and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 3: "However, for any property listed in (1) above, the regular business establishment of an employee is their employer's regular business establishment."
findings.why: The help says a qualifying part of the home is a regular business establishment. It omits the rule that an employee's regular establishment is the employer's, so an employee could reasonably treat the home as the regular place of business and answer no.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the property is used in the spouse's business or at the spouse's regular place of business.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 3: "used exclusively in a taxpayer's trade or business or at the taxpayer's regular business establishment"
findings.why: The question says 'your business' and 'your regular place of business' and does not mention the spouse. A filer could read it as covering only their own business.

findings.situation: A filer has communication equipment that is not used only in the business and is unsure whether it is 'equipment of a kind used for entertainment or recreation'.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 3: "Any property used for entertainment or recreational purposes (such as photographic, phonographic, communication, and video recording equipment)."
findings.why: The question's examples leave out communication equipment, which the IRS text names. A filer could read the question as excluding it.

findings.situation: A filer bought a computer for personal use before 2018 and converted it to business use after 2017, and answers yes because they 'began using' it before 2018.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 14, Column (b): "If property held for personal use is converted to business/investment use, treat the property as placed in service on the date of conversion."
findings.why: The computer's placed-in-service date is after 2017, so it is not listed property, yet the question's 'began using' wording leads the filer to answer yes.

findings.situation: An asset placed in service before 2025 whose business-use share has since changed (for example, listed property that dropped to 50% or less) needs this line, but the computed gate 'Placed in service in 2025' is false for that asset, so the question is never asked.

findings.why: The gated line covers only pre-2025 property. The gate passes only for 2025 property, so the two never overlap and the line is always zero. The gate is the inverse of the condition the line needs.

findings.situation: A joint return filed for 2025 where one spouse died in 2025 and the joint return figures a capital loss carryover to 2026 that includes the deceased spouse's loss.
findings.irs_text: p550 p. 103: "A capital loss sustained by a decedent during the decedent's last tax year (or carried over to that year from an earlier year) can be deducted only on the final income tax return filed for the decedent."
findings.why: A joint return with the surviving spouse can be the decedent's final return, so the decedent's share of the loss cannot carry to 2026. The gate requires "Not a joint return", so the tool never asks and lets that share carry over.

findings.situation: On any return the gate would let through, a filer reading "a filer who died in 2025" may not know whether this covers a spouse who died, or only a sole filer.
findings.irs_text: p550 p. 103: "can be deducted only on the final income tax return filed for the decedent"
findings.why: The question does not say whether it covers a deceased spouse whose final return is filed jointly. Joint returns are in scope, so the question must cover the spouse explicitly.

findings.situation: A student has some tax-free assistance or refunds (worksheet line 3 above zero), but in every academic period they are less than that period's expenses, so the question is asked and the true answer is no.
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 9: "3. Total adjustments (add lines 2a, 2b, and 2c) ... 4. Adjusted qualified education expenses. Subtract line 3 from line 1. If zero or less, enter -0-"
findings.why: The gate opens whenever there is any adjustment, not only when adjustments exceed expenses. This costs one extra question and drops no amount. When line 3 is zero, adjustments cannot exceed a non-negative line 1, so the gated line is correctly false.

findings.situation: The person was married before but was single at the end of 2025 (divorced or annulled before then, or widowed before 2025), so a 2025 joint return including them is impossible, yet the filer answers yes.

findings.why: Only a person married in 2025 can be on a 2025 joint return. A marriage that ended earlier opens the gated question even though its answer can only be no.

findings.why: If the child returned before 2025, the kidnapped-child rule plays no part in 2025, so the gated question is asked needlessly. The gated question itself asks only about being missing in 2025, so it is answered No and nothing is dropped.

findings.situation: On a separate return, the child is a qualifying child of both the filer's spouse and a third person, such as a grandparent who lived with them, so the spouse is not the only other person and the computed condition is false, yet the spouse may still claim the child.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 15: "If the parents don't file a joint return together but both parents claim the child as a qualifying child, the IRS will treat the child as the qualifying child of the parent with whom the child lived for the longer period of time during the year."
findings.why: The parent-versus-parent tiebreaker turns on whether the spouse claims the child, whether or not someone else could also claim the child. Requiring the spouse to be the only other person drops the spouse's claim in exactly the case where it can still defeat the filer's claim.

findings.situation: A married filer who lived apart from the spouse for the last 6 months files as head of household rather than married filing separately, and the spouse, the child's other parent, also claims the child.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 15: "If the parents don't file a joint return together but both parents claim the child as a qualifying child..."; i1040gi p. 17: "(other than your spouse if filing jointly)"
findings.why: The cited text excludes the spouse only on a joint return, so the spouse's claim matters on any non-joint return. The gate tests for married filing separately status and is false for a married filer on a head of household return, so the spouse's competing claim is treated as zero.

findings.situation: The tool decides who else the child 'could be the qualifying child of' from earlier answers, which requires applying the relationship, age, residency, support and joint return tests to every other person.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 17: "If the child meets the conditions to be a qualifying child of any other person (other than your spouse if filing jointly) for 2025, see Qualifying child of more than one person, later."
findings.why: A filer may not know whether another relative in the household also meets all five tests. Earlier answers could then miss a third person, or wrongly include one, which decides whether the 'only other person' condition holds.

locators: p. 17, Step 1, "If the child meets the conditions to be a qualifying child of any other person (other than your spouse if filing jointly) for 2025, see Qualifying child of more than one person, later."

findings.situation: A married dependent under 65 and not blind has $500 of wages, and their spouse files a separate return and itemizes deductions, so the dependent must file, but the filer truthfully answers no because neither dollar limit in the question is exceeded.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 10, Chart B, Married dependents: "Your gross income was at least $5 and your spouse files a separate return and itemizes deductions."; i8962 p. 8, Line 2b: "Only include your dependents who are required to file an income tax return because their income meets the income tax return filing threshold."
findings.why: The question and its help state only the single-dependent limits and never mention the married-dependent $5 gross income rule. This dependent's modified AGI belongs on line 2b, but the gate drops it to zero.

findings.situation: A dependent has $5,000 of wages and $1,000 of interest, so gross income of $6,000 is more than $5,000 plus $450 and they must file, but the question's own list of limits ($1,350 unearned, $15,750 pay) reads as complete, so a filer may answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 10, Chart B: "Your gross income was more than the larger of— $1,350, or Your earned income (up to $15,300) plus $450."
findings.why: The question defines the requirement with a colon followed by two tests, and the combined-income test appears only in the help text. A filer who reads just the question can reasonably take the two tests as the whole rule and answer no.

findings.situation: A parent files Form 8814 for a child whose Form 8814 line 4 is more than $1,350, so the child files no return of their own; the filer may answer no because the child did not have to file, or the filer cannot answer the gated question, which asks for figures from the child's own return.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 8, Form 8814: "If you are filing Form 8814 ... and the amount on Form 8814, line 4, is more than $1,350, you must include on line 1 of Worksheet 1-2 the sum of the tax-exempt interest from Form 8814, line 1b; the lesser of Form 8814, line 4 or line 5; and any nontaxable social security benefits your child received."
findings.why: The parent's election means the child does not have to file, so 'have to file a tax return' can be read either way, even though Worksheet 1-2 still requires an amount for this child.

findings.situation: A dependent who is 65 or older or blind has $2,000 of interest; this is under their $3,350 threshold, but a filer applying the question's stated $1,350 limit answers yes.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 10, Chart B: "Yes. You must file a return if any of the following apply. • Your unearned income was over $3,350"
findings.why: The question applies the lower thresholds to everyone, so it says yes for some dependents who are not required to file. The helper split then zeroes the line for them.

findings.situation: The filer lists a stepchild, foster child or grandchild as 'child', so the tool asks whether the filer is the parent even though the answer can only be No.
findings.irs_text: p501 p. 15, Tiebreaker rules: "the term “parent” means a biological or adoptive parent of an individual. It does not include a stepparent or foster parent unless that person has adopted the individual."
findings.why: A biological or adoptive parent always lists the person as their child (i1040gi p. 20: "An adopted child is always treated as your own child"), so the gate never misses a true parent. It only asks a few extra people who will answer No.

findings.situation: A filer under 19 lived all of 2025 with an older stepbrother or stepsister who files a return and could claim them, and answers No because neither the question nor the help lists step-siblings.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 41, Step 3: "A qualifying child for the EIC is your... Son, daughter, stepchild, foster child, brother, sister, stepbrother, stepsister, half brother, half sister, or a descendant of any of them"
findings.why: The filer is that person's stepsibling, so they could be that person's qualifying child. The gate lists brother and sister, and the help adds half siblings but not step-siblings, so the filer can truthfully answer No and Step 3 question 6 / Step 4 question 5 is never asked.

findings.situation: A filer lived for more than half of 2025 with a step-grandparent, a foster grandparent, a step-aunt or step-uncle, or a great-great-grandparent.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 41, Step 3: "stepchild, foster child, ... stepbrother, stepsister, ... or a descendant of any of them (for example, your grandchild, niece, or nephew)"
findings.why: A descendant of the other person's stepchild, foster child, or stepsibling qualifies by relationship, and so does a more remote descendant. These relatives are not in the gate's list or the help, so a filer can truthfully answer No.

findings.situation: A filer lived with a listed relative, but the shared home was outside the United States for more than half of 2025, or the relative was younger than the filer.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 41, Step 3: "Who lived with you in the United States for more than half of 2025" and "younger than you"
findings.why: The gate holds even though the filer cannot be that relative's qualifying child. This only costs an extra question.

findings.situation: The filer had full-year coverage and column A is the same every month, but the printed column B varies from month to month and is wrong for a reason other than a blank/zero month or an unreported change. Examples: no APTC was paid and the Marketplace filled column B with incorrect varying amounts, or the filer otherwise has reason to believe the Marketplace reported the wrong SLCSP premium. The correct SLCSP premium turns out to be the same for all 12 months.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 14: "If either of these two situations applies to you, or if you have reason to believe the Marketplace reported the wrong applicable SLCSP premium, you must determine the correct applicable SLCSP premium for every month. If the correct applicable SLCSP premium is not the same for every month of 2025, check 'No'"; "1. No APTC was paid for your coverage. ... column B, of Form 1095-A may be wrong, left blank, or reported as -0-."
findings.why: When the form is not printed the same every month, the computed condition counts only 'blank or zero in a covered month, or an unreported change'. It drops the 'no APTC paid' and 'reason to believe the Marketplace reported the wrong' grounds, so the gate is false and the line is forced to false. Under the text, a correction that yields the same premium every month lets the filer check 'Yes' on line 10 and use line 11.

findings.situation: A filer (or spouse) who is a partner, not an employee, gets dependent care benefits under a partnership's dependent care assistance program, reported on Schedule K-1 box 13 code O, and does not think of the partnership as 'your own business'.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1: "Benefits you received as a partner should be shown in box 13 of your Schedule K-1 (Form 1065) with code O."; i2441 p. 5, Line 12: "If you were self-employed or a partner, include amounts you received under a dependent care assistance program from your sole proprietorship or partnership."
findings.why: The gate names only an 'employer' or 'your own business', and its help points only to W-2 box 10. A partner, especially a minority partner in a large firm, could reasonably answer no, which would silently drop the partnership benefits the gated question exists to catch. The gated question names 'a partnership' separately from 'your own business', which shows the two are not the same thing.

findings.situation: A custodial parent whose child under 13 is claimed by the other parent pays for that child's care and reads the helper as asking whether the care was for their own child under 13 who is listed as a dependent on any return, including the other parent's.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1, Special rule for children of divorced or separated parents or parents who live apart: "Even if you can't claim your child as a dependent, they are treated as your qualifying person if ... You were the child's custodial parent."
findings.why: The helper "Was any of the care for a person other than your child under 13 listed as a dependent?" does not say listed on whose return, so this filer could truthfully answer no. With no claimable-dependent answer either, the gate is false and the nondependent qualifying child the special rule covers is dropped.

findings.situation: All care was for a disabled person (or a disabled child 13 or older) whom the filer does claim as a dependent, or the filer can be claimed as a dependent but paid only for their own dependent child under 13.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1, Qualifying Person(s): "Any disabled person ... whom you can claim as a dependent or could claim as a dependent except: ..."
findings.why: The gate is true, but no qualifying person is a nondependent, so the gated line stays false. This costs only an extra question.

findings.situation: Care was for the filer's disabled spouse.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1, Qualifying Person(s): "Your disabled spouse who wasn't physically or mentally able to care for themselves and lived with you for more than half the year."
findings.why: A spouse is "a person other than your child under 13 listed as a dependent," so the gate holds, yet the spouse is not in either situation the gated question lists.

findings.situation: A filer begins living in a newly built or rebuilt home in 2025, but its solar panels, battery or geothermal heat pump were finished in 2024; the help tells them that only installations finished in 2025 count, so they answer No.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 1, Costs: "in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins. For purposes of the residential clean energy credit only, costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins."
findings.why: For a new or rebuilt home, the costs count in the year the filer starts using the home, not the year installation finished. The gate's help states only the installation-completion rule, so the solar, solar water, wind, geothermal and battery lines are dropped for these filers.

findings.situation: A condominium association or housing cooperative installs solar panels, insulation, windows or a boiler on the building in 2025, and a unit owner or tenant-stockholder truthfully answers No because they did not have anything installed.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: "you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation."
findings.why: The question asks whether 'you' had something installed 'at home', and neither the question nor the help mentions work done by an association or cooperative. Yet the IRS treats the member as having paid a share, which feeds the gated lines.

findings.situation: A filer whose only 2025 item was a home energy audit reads the question, which asks only about things 'installed', and answers No.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 2, Part II: "3. The amount paid or incurred for home energy audits during 2025."
findings.why: An audit is not installed and is not equipment. Only the help text says an audit counts, so a filer who does not read the help would answer No and the audit line would be zero.

findings.situation: A filer has solar panels, a wind turbine or a geothermal heat pump installed at a vacation or second home in 2025 and reads 'at home' as meaning only their main home.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 2, Qualified solar electric property costs: "The home doesn't have to be your main home."
findings.why: 'At home' can reasonably be read as the filer's main residence. The IRS text allows Part I property at any home the filer used as a residence.

findings.situation: A filer had energy equipment installed that does not meet Energy Star or other efficiency requirements, or that is at a rental property they do not live in, and answers Yes.
findings.irs_text: i5695 (2025) p. 3, Section B: "To qualify for the credit, qualified energy property must meet certain energy efficiency requirements."
findings.why: The gate asks about any energy-saving installation, so it is broader than qualifying property. This costs only extra questions.

findings.situation: A biomass stove was installed in late 2024 during reconstruction of the filer's home, and the filer's original use of the reconstructed home began in 2025, so the cost is treated as paid in 2025, but the filer truthfully answers that nothing was installed in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "costs are treated as being paid when the original installation of the item is completed, or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins"
findings.why: For a reconstructed home, the year the cost counts is set by when the filer starts using the home, not by when the item was installed. The outer helper asks only about installation in 2025, so this cost is gated out.

findings.situation: A filer who put in a wood or pellet stove or boiler for heating may not think of it as something installed 'to save or make energy' and so answers no to the outer question.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Section B: "Qualified energy property is any of the following. ... Certain biomass stoves and biomass boilers."
findings.why: Biomass heating equipment qualifies whether or not the filer thinks of it as an energy-saving or energy-producing improvement. The phrase 'to save or make energy' does not clearly include heating appliances, so a filer could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: A condominium owner or cooperative tenant-stockholder whose association installed a qualifying biomass boiler in the building may not count it as something installed 'at a home' of theirs.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: "you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation"
findings.why: The filer's share of the association's cost counts on lines 29e/29f. The questions do not say that association-installed property in a shared building counts, so a filer could reasonably answer no.

findings.situation: A biomass stove with a thermal efficiency rating below 75% was installed, so the gate holds, but lines 29e and 29f get no amount.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 7, Line 29e: "biomass stove or biomass boiler that has a thermal efficiency rating of at least 75% (measured by the higher heating value of the fuel)"
findings.why: Only stoves and boilers rated at least 75% efficient qualify, but the gate asks only whether a biomass stove or boiler was installed.

findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: "If you are a member of a condominium management association for a condominium you own or a tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation, you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation."

findings.situation: Exterior doors were installed in 2025 at a second home or vacation home that is not the filer's main home, or the doors do not meet Energy Star requirements.

findings.situation: A filer replaced a broken furnace or boiler in 2025 with a model that meets the CEE highest tier, but bought it because the old unit failed, not to save energy.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3, Section B: "Residential energy property expenditures are costs of new qualified energy property that is installed on or in connection with a home that you used during 2025"; p. 6, Line 24a: "Enter the QMID and amount you paid for the most expensive natural gas, propane, or oil furnace or hot water boilers that achieve the highest efficiency tier"
findings.why: The outer helper asks whether anything was installed "to save or make energy." A filer replacing failed equipment could reasonably answer no, so lines 24a and 24b would be zeroed even though the IRS text gives an amount based only on the property's efficiency tier, not the buyer's purpose.

findings.situation: A condominium association or housing cooperative installed a qualifying boiler or furnace for the building in 2025, and the filer, as owner or tenant-stockholder, is treated as having paid a share of the cost.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: "you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation"
findings.why: A unit owner whose association replaced the building boiler could reasonably answer that nothing was installed at their home, or that they did not install a furnace. Neither the outer question nor the inner question mentions association or cooperative installations, so the filer's proportionate share for line 24a or 24b could be dropped.

findings.situation: A furnace was installed in 2025 that does not meet the CEE highest efficiency tier, or that went into a home the filer did not use.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6, Line 24a: "that achieve the highest efficiency tier established by the CEE that is in effect as of the beginning of the calendar year in which the property is placed in service"
findings.why: The gate holds for any furnace or boiler installation, but the IRS text gives no amount for non-qualifying units. The help text on line 24a screens these out.

findings.situation: A solar water heater was installed in late 2024 in a newly built home the filer first moved into in 2025, so its cost belongs on the 2025 line 2, but the filer truthfully answers that nothing was installed in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "For purposes of the residential clean energy credit only, costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins."
findings.why: The gate is keyed to installation in 2025. For new construction, the IRS times the cost by when original use begins, which can be a year after installation, so the computed condition is false while line 2 has an amount.

findings.situation: A filer reconstructed a home, the solar water heater was installed before 2025 as part of the reconstruction, and the filer's original use of the reconstructed home began in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins"
findings.why: The cost is treated as paid in 2025 even though the installation was not completed in 2025. A truthful no to the 'installed in 2025' question drops line 2.

findings.situation: A condominium association or housing cooperative installed solar water heating property in 2025, and the owner or tenant-stockholder must decide whether something was 'installed at a home' by them.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Association or cooperative costs: "you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation"
findings.why: Neither the gate wording nor the follow-up question mentions association or cooperative costs. A condo owner could reasonably say they installed nothing, which would drop a proportionate share that belongs on line 2.

findings.situation: The filer installed a solar water heater that only heats a pool or hot tub, or that lacks SRCC or state-endorsed certification.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2, Caution: "Costs allocable to a swimming pool, hot tub, or any other energy storage medium that has a function other than the function of such storage don't qualify"
findings.why: The gate holds, but line 2 has no qualifying amount. The question's help text screens these costs out.

findings.situation: A filer, or the spouse on a joint return, replaced a broken gas water heater in 2025 with a unit that meets the CEE highest tier, but did not see it as installed 'to save or make energy', so they answer no to the outer gate.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 3: 'Residential energy property expenditures are costs of new qualified energy property that is installed on or in connection with a home that you used during 2025 ... Qualified energy property is any of the following. ... natural gas, propane, or oil water heaters.'
findings.why: The IRS text sets no purpose test; the property only has to meet the efficiency tier. The phrase 'to save or make energy' lets a filer who replaced an appliance out of necessity truthfully answer no, which silently zeroes lines 23a(i), 23a(ii) and 23b.

findings.situation: A condominium association or housing cooperative installed a qualifying gas water heater that serves the building, and the filer pays a proportionate share but installed nothing in the unit personally.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 2: 'you are treated as having paid your proportionate share of any costs of such association or corporation.'
findings.why: The filer could reasonably read 'Anything was installed ... at a home' and 'A ... water heater was installed' as asking only about their own unit or their own purchases, and answer no. That would drop their proportionate share of the water heater cost.

findings.situation: A filer installed a gas, propane or oil water heater in 2025 that does not meet the CEE highest efficiency tier.
findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 6: 'Line 23a. Enter the QMID and amounts you paid for the two most expensive natural gas, propane, or oil water heaters that achieve the highest efficiency tier established by the CEE'
findings.why: The gate holds for any such water heater, but only units meeting the CEE highest tier give lines 23a and 23b an amount. The help text addresses this.

findings.irs_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "For purposes of both credits, costs are treated as being paid when the original installation of the item is completed, or, in the case of costs connected with the reconstruction of your home, when your original use of the reconstructed home begins."
findings.why: Reconstruction-related window costs count in 2025, but the outer helper asks whether anything was installed in 2025. A truthful filer whose installation finished in 2024 answers no, so lines 20a and 20b become zero.

findings.situation: A condominium association or housing cooperative replaced qualifying windows in the building, and the owner or tenant-stockholder paid nothing directly.

findings.why: The passive question "Anything was installed ... at a home" does not say whether work done by an association counts. A unit owner could reasonably answer no, which drops the proportionate share that belongs on line 20a or 20b.

findings.situation: The filer replaced broken or old windows for repair or appearance and happened to buy Energy Star Most Efficient units.

findings.why: The gate asks about items installed "to save or make energy", but the credit depends on certification, not the filer's purpose. A filer who did not install the windows to save energy could reasonably answer no.

findings.situation: The gate tests only for a current loss or deduction item or a box 16 code D distribution, but the cited Who Must File section has four triggers and the gate drops two of them.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1, Who Must File: "Form 7203 is filed by S corporation shareholders who: • Are claiming a deduction for their share of an aggregate loss ... • Received a non-dividend distribution ... • Disposed of stock in an S corporation (whether or not gain is recognized), or • Received a loan repayment from an S corporation." Gate: "a loss or deduction item, or a distribution (box 16, code D)"
findings.why: The cited text states the filing condition, and the gate's condition is narrower. It omits stock dispositions and loan repayments, so it is not the stated condition.

findings.situation: A shareholder had no current-year loss or distribution but received a repayment of a loan they had made to the S corporation.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1, "Received a loan repayment from an S corporation"; p. 4, Line 34, "The character of the gain on repayment is dependent on whether the debt is evidenced by a formal note or is an open account"
findings.why: Form 7203 is required and Part II applies, since the repayment produces gain measured against debt basis. The computed gate is false, so the loans question is never asked and is treated as false.

findings.situation: A shareholder sold or otherwise disposed of S corporation stock during the year with no loss item and no distribution.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1, "Disposed of stock in an S corporation (whether or not gain is recognized)"; p. 3, "If a portion of your stock is redeemed, sold, or otherwise disposed of during the year, attach two separate forms. Use the first to figure your stock basis at the date of sale"
findings.why: Form 7203 is required, and lines 1 and 2 (beginning basis and additions) determine basis at the sale. The gate is false, so those lines are set to zero.

findings.situation: A shareholder whose current K-1 shows no loss item and no distribution is claiming a loss that was suspended in a prior year for lack of basis.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1, "Are claiming a deduction for their share of an aggregate loss from an S corporation (including an aggregate loss not allowed last year because of basis limitations)"; p. 4, Column (b), "Enter any loss or deduction items disallowed due to basis limitations in prior years that were carried forward"
findings.why: The gate is computed from the current K-1's loss/deduction and code D items, so it does not see a carried-forward loss. Lines 1, 2, the election and the loans question are then never asked.

findings.situation: The K-1 shows a deduction item, but income items exceed it, so there is no aggregate loss and no distribution.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1, "Are claiming a deduction for their share of an aggregate loss from an S corporation"
findings.why: The gate fires on any loss or deduction item, not only on an aggregate loss. It may therefore ask questions when Form 7203 is not required.

findings.situation: A filer has pre-1996 contract reimbursements and reads the gated question after entering line 24, which the instructions say should generally leave those reimbursements out.
findings.irs_text: i8853 p. 9, Line 24: "Generally, don't include on line 24 reimbursements for qualified LTC services you received under a contract issued before August 1, 1996." f8853 p. 2, line 24 Caution: "If you received any reimbursements from LTC contracts issued before August 1, 1996, see instructions."
findings.why: "Was any of that paid back" could refer to the line 24 figure as entered (pre-1996 amounts already left out, so the filer answers no) or to all reimbursements received. Under the first reading, the form's caution, which is triggered by receiving any pre-1996 reimbursements, is never raised. "Paid back" could also be read as the filer repaying money rather than receiving a reimbursement.

findings.situation: A filer's pre-1996 contract was exchanged or modified after July 31, 1996, to increase payments, so its reimbursements correctly belong on line 24, but the filer answers yes and the interview ends.
findings.irs_text: i8853 p. 9, Line 24: "However, you must include reimbursements if the contract was exchanged or modified after July 31, 1996, to increase per diem payments or reimbursements."
findings.why: The yes answer refuses a case the instructions treat as ordinary line 24 reimbursements. This is over-inclusive, not a dropped amount.

findings.situation: A filer is still waiting on an insurance reimbursement for 2025 care, or on a joint return the reimbursement went to the spouse, and reads 'was paid back to you' as covering only amounts already paid to the filer.
findings.irs_text: i8853 p. 9, Line 24: "Enter the reimbursements you received or expect to receive through insurance or otherwise for qualified LTC services provided for the insured for LTC periods in 2025."
findings.why: The past-tense 'was paid back to you' can reasonably be read to leave out reimbursements the filer only expects to receive, and on a joint return it does not clearly include the spouse. Line 24 would then be understated, so line 26 would be understated.

findings.situation: Line 20 is more than zero, but line 21 ($420 times the LTC days) is greater than line 22 and there are no reimbursements, so the line 22 answer does not change line 26.

findings.why: The gate asks for line 22 costs even when line 21 controls line 23. That costs the filer a question but drops no amount.

findings.situation: Line 20 is more than zero and the payment rate changed during 2025, but the filer uses Method 1 (Contract Period), under which a rate change does not create a separate LTC period.
findings.irs_text: i8853 p. 8, Method 1—Contract Period: "your LTC period is the same period as that used by the insurance company under the contract to compute the benefits it pays you"
findings.why: Under Method 1 a rate change does not need separate Sections C, yet a Yes still ends the interview. This is over-inclusive, not a missed amount.

findings.situation: A filer received fixed payments at a weekly, quarterly or annual rate and reads 'a set amount per day or month' literally, so answers No.
findings.irs_text: f8853 (2025) p. 2, line 17: "Gross LTC payments received on a per diem or other periodic basis"; i8853 p. 8: "payments of a fixed amount made on a periodic basis without regard to actual expenses incurred"
findings.why: The IRS covers any fixed periodic basis, not only daily or monthly. The parenthetical about box 3 points toward Yes, but the main wording 'per day or month' invites a truthful No for weekly or annual fixed payments, which would drop lines 17 and 19.

findings.situation: A filer received accelerated death benefits from a life insurance policy at a fixed monthly rate while the insured was chronically ill, and reads 'the payments' as meaning only long-term care insurance payments.
findings.irs_text: f8853 (2025) p. 2, line 19: "Accelerated death benefits received on a per diem or other periodic basis"; i8853 p. 8, Line 19: "These amounts are generally shown in box 2 of Form 1099-LTC"
findings.why: Neither the gate question nor its help mentions life insurance or accelerated death benefits, and the help speaks of payments that 'repaid care costs'. A filer could reasonably answer No about the LTC contract alone, which silently zeroes line 19.

findings.situation: Box 3 of the Form 1099-LTC is blank or wrong even though the payments were in fact a fixed periodic amount.
findings.irs_text: i8853 p. 8: "Box 3 of Form 1099-LTC should indicate whether payments were per diem payments"
findings.why: The IRS says box 3 'should' indicate per diem, not that it always does. The gate defines Yes partly by the checkbox, so a filer could read it either way when the box and the actual payment terms disagree.

findings.situation: A filer with self-only coverage all year divorces in mid-2025; the then-spouse had family HDHP coverage in the early months of the marriage but switched to self-only (or dropped HDHP coverage) before the divorce became final.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4, How To Complete Part I: "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan. Disregard any plans with self-only coverage"; p. 7, Line 6: "Spouses who ... had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025"
findings.why: The family-coverage rule applies in any month of the marriage, and the line itself is defined as "family HDHP coverage in a month of the marriage." The question asks whether the marriage ended "while the other person had" such a plan, so this filer can truthfully answer No, and the family-coverage months are silently dropped.

findings.situation: A filer whose marriage ended in 2025 by a decree of legal separation, or whose divorce was granted in 2025 but took effect later, must decide whether the marriage 'ended during 2025, by divorce or death'.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4, How To Complete Part I: "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage..."
findings.why: The question names only divorce or death, so a filer whose marriage ended by separate maintenance could read it as not applying. That filer could answer No even though there were months of marriage with a spouse who had family coverage.

findings.situation: The former spouse had family HDHP coverage but was not an eligible individual (for example, enrolled in Medicare or covered by a non-HDHP plan) during the marriage.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4: "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage"
findings.why: The rule applies only if both spouses were eligible individuals, but the question does not ask about the spouse's eligibility. A Yes here ends the interview when no amount is actually affected.

findings.situation: A filer made a qualified HSA funding distribution early in 2024 and stopped being an eligible individual during its testing period. They became eligible again by December 1, 2024, used the last-month rule for 2024, and then stopped being eligible again in 2025. Because the 2024 QHFD testing period was already failed, the computed condition is false, so the last-month-rule question is never asked and line 18 is zero.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 9, Part III: 'Use Part III to figure any additional income ... for failure to be an eligible individual during the testing period for: • Last-month rule ... or • A qualified HSA funding distribution'; Line 18: 'Enter on line 18 the excess of the amount contributed over the redetermined amount.' Line 19: 'Enter the total of any qualified HSA funding distribution.'
findings.why: The instructions treat the two testing periods as separate and give each its own line, with nothing saying that failing the QHFD testing period cancels the last-month-rule inclusion. The 'Year parameter hsa.no' branch therefore drops a line 18 amount that the IRS text requires.

findings.situation: A filer's 2024 QHFD testing period and 2024 last-month-rule testing period are both failed in 2025, for example by losing HDHP coverage in mid-2025. The tool treats the QHFD failure as already failed and never asks about the last-month rule.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 2, Testing period: 'If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period ... you will have to include in income the total contributions made that would not have been made except for the last-month rule.' i8889 p. 8, Testing period: '... you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual.'
findings.why: Both inclusions arise in the same year from the same failure, and the IRS text requires each one. A gate that turns off the last-month-rule question whenever the QHFD testing period has failed misses the line 18 amount.

findings.situation: A married person whose own HDHP coverage started, ended or changed type during 2025 (bucket 'changed'), for example self-only from July to December, while the spouse had a family HDHP in those months.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, Line 3, rule 1: "Use the family coverage amount if you or your spouse had an HDHP with family coverage. Disregard any plan with self-only coverage."
findings.why: The 'changed' branch sets the condition to false, so the spouse's family coverage is never asked and is treated as false. Rule 1 applies to every Line 3 computation, including the monthly Limitation Chart and the last-month rule (rules 2, 4 and 5), so the family amount is silently dropped for those months.

findings.situation: A married person with a self-only HDHP on the first day of all twelve months who was not an eligible individual in every month (for example enrolled in Medicare from October), while the spouse had a family HDHP.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, How To Complete Part I: "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan. Disregard any plans with self-only coverage."
findings.why: The condition requires eligibility in every month, so it is false here. In the months when both spouses were eligible, the IRS text treats the filer as having family coverage, which sets the monthly limit under rule 5's worksheet.

findings.situation: A person with a self-only HDHP all year who was married for part of 2025 but not at year-end (divorced or widowed), whose spouse had a family HDHP during the months of the marriage.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, Line 3, rule 1: "Use the family coverage amount if you or your spouse had an HDHP with family coverage."
findings.why: The condition tests marital status only at the end of 2025, while the gated question asks about "any month of 2025". Rule 1 is not limited to year-end marital status, so the spouse's family coverage in the married months is never asked.

findings.situation: A married person with self-only coverage and full-year eligibility whose spouse had a family HDHP but was not an eligible individual in any month (for example the spouse was on Medicare all year).
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4, How To Complete Part I: "if you and your spouse are both eligible individuals and either of you has an HDHP with family coverage, you both are treated as having only the family coverage plan."
findings.why: The question is asked although the deemed-family treatment in this passage requires both spouses to be eligible. This leans to yes and is harmless by design.

findings.situation: A filer with no HSA contributions for 2025 who was an eligible individual in every month of 2025 is still asked about a 2024 IRA-to-HSA transfer, although no testing-period failure occurs in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 8, Testing period: "If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period, other than because of death or becoming disabled, you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual."
findings.why: With no contributions the tool does not know the months of 2025, so it asks anyway; this costs one extra question and drops no amount.

findings.situation: A filer who was not an eligible individual in a month of 2025 that falls after the testing period for the 2024 transfer had already ended (for example a March 2024 transfer and a loss of eligibility in October 2025) is still asked.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 8, Testing period: "The testing period begins with the month in which the traditional IRA or Roth IRA distribution is contributed to the HSA and lasts through the last day of the 12th month following that month."
findings.why: The condition tests any month of 2025 rather than only the months inside the testing period, so it holds where the text gives no amount.

findings.situation: A filer who stopped being an eligible individual in 2025 only because of death or disability is still asked about the 2024 transfer.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 8, Testing period: "If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period, other than because of death or becoming disabled, you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income"
findings.why: The condition does not carve out the death or disability exception, so it holds where the text requires no inclusion.

findings.situation: A filer whose HDHP coverage started, ended or changed type during 2025 (for example self-only January to June, family July to December) was also covered all year by a general-purpose health FSA or HRA, their own or their spouse's.
findings.irs_text: p969 (2025) p. 5, Other employee health plans: "An employee covered by an HDHP and a health FSA or an HRA that pays or reimburses qualified medical expenses can't generally make contributions to an HSA." i8889 (2025) p. 2: "you must be covered under a high deductible health plan (HDHP) and have no other health coverage except certain disregarded coverage."
findings.why: The FSA/HRA bar applies whatever the HDHP coverage pattern, but in the 'changed' branch the condition is forced false, so the FSA question is never asked and the line is treated as false. Unless the month-by-month path (not shown here) separately asks about the FSA/HRA, the refusal is silently dropped.

findings.situation: A filer with the same HDHP type all year truthfully answers no to the three-conditions question for a reason that affects only some months (for example Medicare enrolment from October, or other coverage that ended in March) and also had a general-purpose health FSA or HRA in the other months.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 2: "You must be, or be considered, an eligible individual on the first day of a month to take an HSA deduction for that month"; p969 (2025) p. 5: "An employee covered by an HDHP and a health FSA or an HRA that pays or reimburses qualified medical expenses can't generally make contributions to an HSA."
findings.why: The FSA/HRA still decides eligibility for the remaining months, but the condition is false, so the line is set to false without asking. The gate is only safe if the monthly path captures FSA/HRA coverage on its own, which the cited text and gate do not show.

findings.situation: A filer with a general-purpose health FSA reads the three-conditions question "with no other health coverage that is not disregarded" and may or may not count the FSA as other health coverage.
findings.irs_text: p969 (2025) p. 5: "An employee covered by an HDHP and a health FSA or an HRA that pays or reimburses qualified medical expenses can't generally make contributions to an HSA."
findings.why: The gate wording does not say whether an FSA/HRA counts as other health coverage. One reading answers yes and reaches the FSA question; the other answers no and the FSA line is zeroed without being asked, leaving the outcome to the unshown monthly path.

findings.situation: A filer who met the three conditions in every month with one coverage type had no HSA contributions from any source for 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 4: "Use Part I to figure: Your HSA deduction, Any excess contributions you made (or those made on your behalf)"
findings.why: With no contributions, FSA/HRA coverage changes nothing, yet the question is still asked; this is harmless by design.

findings.why: The helper's three choices do not say that simultaneous coverage counts as family. A truthful self-only answer skips the December 1 question, whose help is the only place this rule is explained.

findings.situation: The account beneficiary died in 2025 with no designated beneficiary or with the estate named. The HSA's value goes on the decedent's own final return, which may be a joint return with the surviving spouse. Asked about the decedent, the gate question gets a truthful no: the decedent was the owner and did not get the HSA because someone else died.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 3: "If the account beneficiary's estate is the beneficiary, the value of the HSA as of the date of death is included on the account beneficiary's final income tax return. Complete Form 8889 as described above, except you should complete Part I, if applicable."
findings.why: On the decedent's final return the HSA's date-of-death value is an amount, and the inherited-case line must not fall back to the spouse-treated-as-own default. The gate question only asks whether the filer received an HSA from someone else who died, so it never reaches the owner's own final return when the estate is the beneficiary.

findings.situation: A non-spouse beneficiary whose benefactor died before 2025 and who received nothing from the account in 2025 answers yes, because the help says to answer yes whatever year the owner died.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 3: "the account ceases to be an HSA as of the date of death"
findings.why: That account stopped being an HSA in an earlier year, so the inherited-case line gives it no 2025 amount. The yes only costs an extra question.

findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8: "you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual"; p. 9: "Include the amount in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual."
findings.why: A failure in 2024 belongs on the 2024 return, so the 2025 line has no amount. The gate holding here only costs extra questions and does not drop an amount. The question's window ("From the month of that transfer") could also be limited to 2025 months.

findings.situation: A filer whose non-rolled-over distributions paid medical bills, but some bills were incurred before the HSA was set up, reimbursed by insurance, or were premiums that don't qualify, could answer the computed helper yes.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8, Line 15: "Only include on line 15 distributions from your HSA that were used to pay you for qualified medical expenses not reimbursed by insurance or other coverage and that you incurred after the HSA was established." p. 2: "Expenses incurred before you establish your HSA are not qualified medical expenses."
findings.why: The helper question says only "used to pay qualified medical expenses" and does not state the after-establishment, unreimbursed and premium limits. A yes skips the detailed question, so line 15 is taken as all distributions and is overstated.

findings.situation: A filer with a deemed distribution (prohibited transaction) or an excess contribution withdrawn after the return due date, whose actual withdrawals all went to medical bills, could answer yes that all non-rolled-over distributions paid qualified medical expenses.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 3: "Any deemed distribution will not be treated as used to pay qualified medical expenses." p. 8, Line 15: "Do not include the distribution of an excess contribution taken out after the due date, including extensions, of your return even if used for qualified medical expenses."
findings.why: Filers may not think of a deemed distribution or a late excess withdrawal as a distribution that 'paid' expenses, or may believe the late excess withdrawal counts because it was spent on medical care. A yes leaves these amounts in line 15 when the text excludes them.

findings.situation: When there were no HSA distributions, the computed condition is false (hsa.no), so the tool asks the medical-expense amount even though lines 14a–14c are zero.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8, Line 14a: "Enter the total distributions your HSAs made in 2025."
findings.why: With no distributions, line 15 has no effect, so asking the question costs only an extra question.

findings.situation: Married spouses with separate HSAs and family HDHP coverage who file a joint return must also split the family limit on line 6, but the computed gate is false unless filing status is married filing separately.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 7, Line 6: "Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025, use the following rules to figure the amount on line 6"; gate: "Filing status married filing separately" = true and "Married at the end of 2025 and treated as having family coverage at any time during 2025" = true
findings.why: The cited condition is spouses with separate HSAs and family coverage, with no filing-status test. The gate adds a married-filing-separately requirement the text does not state. This is harmless only if the tool handles joint returns' separate-HSA allocation somewhere else.

findings.situation: A spouse who had an HSA during 2025 but closed or rolled it out before the filer answers could read 'Does your husband or wife have' in the present tense and truthfully answer no.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 7, Line 6: "Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025"
findings.why: The question asks about now, not 2025. The help says to count an HSA with nothing put into it for 2025, but it does not say to count an account that no longer exists, so a filer could answer no while the line 6 split still applies.

findings.situation: On a married-filing-separately return, the question opens with "For this person (you, or your spouse on a joint return)", which refers to a joint return that cannot exist in this case.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p. 7, Line 6: "divide the amount on line 5 equally between you and your spouse, unless you both agree on a different allocation"
findings.why: A separate filer could be unsure whose HSA is being asked about. The joint-return framing conflicts with the gate's limit to separate returns and with the line's label, "A separate return's spouse had an HSA".

findings.situation: A filer contributed a qualified HSA funding distribution in early 2025 (for example, February 2025) and stopped being an eligible individual later in 2025 (for example, October 2025). Because the testing period began in 2025, not 2024, the computed condition is false.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8: "The testing period begins with the month in which the traditional IRA or Roth IRA distribution is contributed to the HSA ... you will have to include the qualified HSA funding distribution in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual."
findings.why: A 2025 contribution can fail its testing period within 2025, which puts an amount on Part III line 19 for 2025, so the disability exception matters. The gate only recognizes testing periods that began in 2024, so it treats the disability answer as false and the exception is lost.

findings.situation: A filer's testing period for a 2024 qualified HSA funding distribution (or for the 2024 last-month rule) was failed in 2025, and the filer reads the helper question as asking whether the failure happened in 2024.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 9: "Include the amount in income in the year in which you fail to be an eligible individual." Gate helper: "the testing period of a qualified HSA funding distribution contributed in 2024 was failed, or the last-month rule was used for 2024"
findings.why: "Was failed" does not say when, so a filer could answer as of the 2024 return and say no even though the failure occurred in 2025. That wrong no drops the 2025 inclusion.

findings.situation: A filer still holds an HSA but stopped being an eligible individual (lost HDHP coverage) because of disability, and reads "stop being able to have an HSA" as closing or losing the account.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 2: "If you fail to remain an eligible individual during this period, other than because of death or becoming disabled"; p. 2: "You can receive distributions from an HSA even if you are not currently eligible to have contributions made to the HSA."
findings.why: The test is eligibility to contribute, not having an account. A filer who still has the account could answer no to "stop being able to have an HSA" and lose the disability exception.

findings.situation: A filer contributed a qualified HSA funding distribution in March 2024, so the testing period ended March 31, 2025, and lost eligibility in August 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 8: "lasts through the last day of the 12th month following that month"
findings.why: The gate holds because the filer was ineligible in some month of 2025, but that month falls after the testing period ended, so there is no failure and no Part III amount.

findings.situation: A filer used the last-month rule for 2024 or made a 2024 qualified HSA funding distribution, and lost eligibility in 2025 because of death.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 2: "other than because of death or becoming disabled"
findings.why: Death also excuses the failure, so no Part III amount arises even though the gate holds.

findings.situation: Advance payments appear on the Forms 1095-A, but household income on line 5 is 100% of the poverty line or more, so the estimate exception has no effect.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 9: "If the amount on line 5 is less than 100%, you can take the PTC if you meet the requirements under Estimated household income at least 100% of the federal poverty line"
findings.why: The gate checks only whether advance payments were made, not whether income is below the poverty line. Filers above the line may be asked a question that does not matter. findings.situation: Line 5 is below 100 (for example 85), and a family member enrolled in the Marketplace plan is a lawfully present alien who is not eligible for Medicaid because of immigration status. The gate condition (line 5 at least 100) is false, so the alien question is never asked and the line is treated as false.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 9: "If the amount on line 5 is less than 100%, you can take the PTC if you meet the requirements under ... Alien lawfully present in the United States, later." and "Certain aliens with household income below 100% of the federal poverty line are not eligible for Medicaid because of their immigration status."
findings.why: The gated line only matters when line 5 is below 100, which is exactly when the gate condition is false. The gate is inverted and silently drops every case the line exists for. The help text's own reason ('Asked because the income on this return is below the federal poverty line') contradicts the gate.

findings.situation: The cited text makes the alien exception depend on line 5 being less than 100%, but the gate requires line 5 to be at least 100.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 9: "If the amount on line 5 is less than 100%, you can take the PTC if you meet the requirements under ... Alien lawfully present in the United States"; gate: "Household income at least 100% of the federal poverty line (line 5 at least 100)"
findings.why: The source condition is line 5 < 100, the opposite threshold direction of the gate's line 5 ≥ 100. The gate should be the negation of income_100.

findings.situation: Line 5 is 100 or more. The gate holds, but the line's own formula sets it to false (household.no), so the alien question has no effect.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 6: "Generally, you are an applicable taxpayer if your household income for 2025 ... is at least 100% of the federal poverty line"
findings.why: When income is at least 100% of the poverty line, the alien-below-poverty exception is irrelevant. Every case where the gate holds gives the gated line no amount.
