findings.situation: A tax-family member turned down an employer offer, but the Marketplace, given accurate information about the offer, found them eligible for APTC; the computed condition still holds and the gated question is asked.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 5: "employer-sponsored coverage is not considered affordable if, when you or a family member enrolled in a qualified health plan, you gave accurate information about the availability of employer coverage to the Marketplace, and the Marketplace determined that you were eligible for APTC"
findings.why: Here the offer is treated as unaffordable, so the gated line should be false, but the condition is true and a filer may answer Yes. That is extra questions or an unneeded stop, not a dropped amount.

findings.situation: Someone was offered employer coverage they did not take, but only in months with no Marketplace coverage, or only during a waiting period, or only as post-employment COBRA or retiree coverage.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 6: "you are not treated as eligible for that coverage during the waiting period" and "you are not considered eligible for that post-employment coverage unless you actually enroll in the coverage"
findings.why: The second helper does not limit the offer to a month of Marketplace coverage or exclude these cases, so the condition can be true when the gated line has no effect.

findings.situation: A filer who owns a small business buys a group health plan through that business and could have enrolled in it while on Marketplace insurance.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 5: 'MEC includes: ... Most types of employer-sponsored coverage; and • Other health coverage the Department of Health and Human Services designates as MEC.'
findings.why: The gate's help says 'Insurance you bought on your own outside the Marketplace does not count,' so a business owner could read a plan their own company bought as insurance they bought themselves and answer no. The gated question f8962.mec_other names exactly this case ('a plan from a business they own'), and the gate's examples ('a job's plan') do not clearly reach it.

findings.situation: Someone on the return was offered COBRA or retiree coverage and did not enroll, or could only get an employer plan after a waiting period. That person may answer yes because they 'could have had' that coverage.
findings.irs_text: i8962 p. 6: 'you are not considered eligible for that post-employment coverage unless you actually enroll in the coverage.' and 'you are not treated as eligible for that coverage during the waiting period.'
findings.why: The gate holds in these cases, but none of the gated lines carries an amount for them. The help on the job-offer question excludes them, so the only cost is a few extra questions.

findings.situation: A filer (or spouse) owns no shares, gets no Form 1099-DIV and has no taxable interest, but a partnership, S corporation, estate or trust paid foreign income tax and passed it through to the filer on a Schedule K-3 or Schedule K-1.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 1: "Qualified payee statements include Form 1099-DIV, Form 1099-INT, Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), Schedule K-3 (Form 1065), Schedule K-3 (Form 1120-S), or similar substitute statements."
findings.why: The entity paid the foreign tax, so the filer can truthfully answer no to "Have you ... ever paid income tax to a foreign country". The filer also owns no shares and has no interest, so the computed condition is false and a creditable foreign tax is dropped.

findings.situation: Even when the gate opens, the gated question tells the filer to add only box 7 of Form 1099-DIV, box 6 of Form 1099-INT and tax they paid themselves, so foreign tax reported on a Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) or Schedule K-3 is left out of ftc.taxes.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 1: "All the income and any foreign taxes paid on it were reported to you on a qualified payee statement ... Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), Schedule K-3 (Form 1065), Schedule K-3 (Form 1120-S)"
findings.why: The list in the question omits a source of foreign tax that the IRS text names, so a filer following the question literally enters too little.

findings.situation: Foreign tax was withheld at source on foreign royalties, rents or gains, and the filer never wrote a payment to the foreign government.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 2: "You can take a credit for income, war profits, and excess profits taxes paid or accrued during your tax year to any foreign country or U.S. territory"; p. 3: "the day you paid the foreign taxes (or on the day the tax was withheld)"
findings.why: A filer could read "paid income tax to a foreign country" as excluding tax withheld by a payer, and answer no.

findings.situation: The filer has U.S.-only taxable interest or shares of U.S. companies, or paid foreign income tax in some earlier year but not in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 2: "taxes paid or accrued during your tax year to any foreign country or U.S. territory"
findings.why: No creditable foreign tax exists for 2025, so the gate opens with nothing to enter; this is acceptable leaning to yes.

findings.situation: A filer who never paid or accrued any foreign or U.S. territory income tax, but whose 2024 return included another form such as Form 8995 or Form 8889, is asked the carryover question even though no line 10 amount can exist.
findings.irs_text: i1116 (2025) p. 19: "You can carry back 1 year and then forward 10 years any foreign tax you paid or accrued to any foreign country or U.S. territory ... on income in a separate category that is more than the limitation."
findings.why: A carryover can only come from foreign or U.S. territory tax actually paid or accrued, which the first branch already covers. The second branch asks extra questions of filers who can have no carryover, which is acceptable because gates are meant to lean toward yes.

findings.situation: A filer who owned 10% or more of a foreign corporation, or had territory-source income, but never paid or accrued foreign income tax, answers yes to the gate although line 10 can only be zero.
findings.irs_text: i1116 (2025) p. 19, Line 10: "Enter the unused foreign taxes in the separate category from another tax year that are eligible to be carried forward to or back to 2025."
findings.why: Owning a foreign corporation or having territory income does not by itself produce unused foreign taxes, so this branch of the gate is broader than the line requires.

locators: p. 19, Line 10, "Enter the unused foreign taxes in the separate category from another tax year that are eligible to be carried forward to or back to 2025"

findings.situation: The 2024 Schedule B carried a foreign tax forward, but an event before the 2025 filing wiped it out (an IRS audit, a section 905(c) redetermination, or an actual carryback larger than the estimate). A filer can then truthfully answer no to 'Are any of your unused foreign taxes carried to 2025?', so the tool never asks the adjustment question. Yet Schedule B line 1 must still show the 2024 line 8 amount and line 2 must show the adjustment that cancels it.
findings.irs_text: i1116sb p. 1: 'With respect to each separate category of income, if you're filing Form 1116 that has a foreign tax carryover in the prior tax year, the current tax year, or both, you must file Schedule B' and 'Line 2. Adjustments to line 1. Report on lines 2a, 2b, 2c, 2d, etc., any adjustments resulting from events that occurred between the filing of your prior year tax return and the filing of your current year tax return.'; i1116sb p. 2: 'Lines 2c, 2d, 2e, etc. ... Domestic audit adjustments'
findings.why: The gate asks whether a carryover reaches 2025. The Schedule B line 2 adjustment applies whenever the prior year had a carryover, even if the adjustment reduces it to zero. A filer whose 2024 carryover was eliminated answers no, so the change goes unreported.

locators: p. 19, Line 10, "Enter the unused foreign taxes in the separate category from another tax year that are eligible to be carried forward to or back to 2025"

findings.situation: A filer's only foreign taxes fail the holding-period or related-payment rules, so creditable foreign taxes after reductions are $0 and the computed condition is false, yet those taxes can still be deducted on Schedule A.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 2: "even if you take the credit for eligible foreign taxes for the year, you can take a deduction for the following. ... Taxes on income or gain that aren't creditable because you don't meet the holding period requirement"; i1040sca p. 7, Line 6: "Include on this line income taxes you paid to a foreign country"
findings.why: Schedule A line 6 covers foreign income taxes paid, not just creditable ones. Gating sa.foreign_tax_deduct on creditable taxes after reductions being above zero never asks this filer the question, and the deductible amount is dropped.

findings.situation: A partner gets foreign taxes passed through on a Schedule K-3 (Form 1065), or an estate or trust beneficiary gets them on a Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), but owns no shares, received no 1099-DIV, had no taxable interest and paid no foreign tax directly.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 1: "Qualified payee statements include Form 1099-DIV, Form 1099-INT, Schedule K-1 (Form 1041), Schedule K-3 (Form 1065), Schedule K-3 (Form 1120-S)"; p. 2: "You paid or accrued certain foreign taxes to a foreign country or U.S. territory"
findings.why: The helper counts foreign taxes only for share owners, 1099-DIV or interest recipients, or people who 'paid income tax to another country'. A partner or beneficiary whose tax was paid by the entity can truthfully answer no, so the creditable taxes come out zero and the election and Form 1116 questions are never asked.

findings.situation: A filer paid income tax to a U.S. territory such as Puerto Rico or Guam and had no other qualifying trigger.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 2: "You paid or accrued certain foreign taxes to a foreign country or U.S. territory"; "For purposes of the credit, U.S. territories include Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and American Samoa."
findings.why: The helper's trigger is 'ever paid income tax to another country'. A filer who paid tax to a U.S. territory can truthfully say no, so taxes creditable under the IRS text never reach the gated lines.

findings.situation: A filer who once paid foreign income tax in an earlier year, or who owns shares with no foreign tax, is asked the trigger question.
findings.irs_text: i1116 p. 2: "income, war profits, and excess profits taxes paid or accrued during your tax year"
findings.why: 'Ever paid' reaches past years, but the computed amount must still be positive, so this only costs extra questions.

findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 3: "Generally, you can claim the American opportunity credit for a student on a 2025 tax return only if all of the following seven requirements are met."
findings.why: The gate tests only the filers' identification numbers, so it holds where other requirements leave the gated lines with no effect. This direction is acceptable by design.

findings.situation: A filer separated under an interlocutory (not final) divorce decree at the end of 2025 may answer 'no' to 'Were you married at the end of 2025?', even though the IRS treats them as married and they could still be considered unmarried under the live-apart rules.

findings.situation: A filer in a common law marriage recognized by their state may say they have never been married, or answer no to 'Were you married at the end of 2025?', because there was no ceremony or license.

findings.why: The 'has been married at some time' helper and the 'Were you married' question do not mention common law marriage. A filer can read 'married' as formal marriage only, which would skip the considered-unmarried question even though the filer is married for tax purposes.

findings.situation: A married filer who lived apart from their spouse for the last 6 months of 2025 and qualifies as head of household files with status HOH, not MFS. The computed condition is false, so household.mfs_living_if_mfs is forced to together_late and the lived-apart test fails.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 15, Married persons who live apart: "Even if you weren't divorced or legally separated at the end of 2025, you are considered unmarried if all of the following apply. • You lived apart from your spouse for the last 6 months of 2025... • You file a separate return from your spouse."
findings.why: The line is cited for this test, which exists for married people filing separate returns as head of household, whose status is HOH rather than MFS. Gating on status = 'mfs' (and defaulting to together_late 'so that neither lived-apart test is met') denies the lived-apart test to exactly the filers it serves. If filing status is itself derived from this test, the gate is also circular.

findings.situation: The K-1 shows a net section 1231 loss only in box 10, or a loss only in box 11 (other income (loss)), with boxes 1, 2, 3, 8, 9a and 14A zero or positive.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 3: "a partner may only claim their share of a partnership loss (including a capital loss) to the extent it doesn’t exceed their adjusted basis"; p. 8: "These losses and deductions include a loss on the disposition of assets"
findings.why: The basis and at-risk limits reach any partnership loss, including section 1231 and other losses reported outside the six listed boxes. In this case the computed condition is false, so both gated lines are silently set to false.

findings.situation: The K-1 shows a section 179 deduction (box 12), or other deductions such as charitable contributions (box 13), or foreign taxes, but no loss in boxes 1, 2, 3, 8, 9a or 14A.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: "if you have (a) a loss or other deduction from any activity ... and (b) amounts in the activity for which you aren’t at risk, you’ll have to complete Form 6198"; "These losses and deductions include ... the section 179 expense deduction"; p. 3: "a partner’s share of the adjusted basis in partnership charitable contributions ... and taxes ... is subject to this basis limitation"
findings.why: Both limitations apply to deductions as well as losses, and the gate tests only for negative amounts in six boxes. A partner whose deductions exceed basis or amounts at risk is never asked the gated questions.

findings.situation: Box 1 shows positive income, but deductions in other boxes push the partner's net share to a loss larger than basis or amounts at risk.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 3: "There are potential limitations on partnership losses that you can deduct on your return ... the basis limitations, the at-risk limitations"
findings.why: The limitations depend on the combined losses and deductions, not only on the sign of the listed boxes, so a net loss built from deductions in other boxes is missed.

findings.situation: A filer with deductions but no 'loss' reads the basis question 'Were your 2025 losses from it more than your basis' and does not count deductions, or compares against basis after reducing it by the losses.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 3: "to the extent it doesn’t exceed their adjusted basis in the partnership at the end of the partnership’s tax year"; "Basis can’t be less than zero."
findings.why: The question names only losses and defines basis as already reduced by losses. A filer could compare the losses with a basis already reduced by those same losses, or could leave out limited deductions.

findings.situation: A loss in box 14 code A (self-employment earnings) by itself does not create a basis-limited or at-risk-limited partnership loss or deduction.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 3: "potential limitations on partnership losses that you can deduct on your return"
findings.why: Box 14A is self-employment earnings, not a deductible loss item, so including it only causes extra questions.

findings.why: The text bars only limited partners. A non-manager LLC member is not, by this text, a limited partner and could still actively participate, but the computed gate requires item G 'General partner or LLC member-manager' and so drops the decisions line.

findings.why: The gate asks about management decisions even though active participation is impossible here, which costs only an extra question.

findings.situation: A partner who did no work in the business this year (for example, one who retired) but materially participated in at least 5 of the 10 preceding years still materially participates under test 5, yet the helper "Worked in the business, 500 hours or less" reads as false when no work was done, so the gate skips the question.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 (2025) p. 9: "5. You materially participated in the activity for any 5 tax years (whether or not consecutive) during the 10 tax years that immediately precede the tax year."
findings.why: Test 5 depends only on participation in prior years and requires no hours in the current year. The gate requires that the filer worked in the business this year, so a filer who did no work can be passed over and the business's income or loss treated as passive.

findings.situation: On a joint return, a filer may read "worked in the business" and "did you materially participate" as covering only their own work, not their spouse's.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 (2025) p. 9: "Generally, any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through a partnership ... is counted toward material participation."
findings.why: The gate helper and the gated question both refer only to "you", while the IRS text counts the spouse's work toward material participation. A filer whose 5 qualifying prior years rest on the spouse's work could answer no.

locators: p. 9, Individuals (other than limited partners), "You materially participated in the activity for any 5 tax years (whether or not consecutive) during the 10 tax years that immediately precede the tax year"

findings.situation: A filer who is a limited partner but also owned a general partnership interest all year could reasonably answer no to a 'general partner' question, which would make the gate false and skip the substantially-all-participation question (test 2).
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "If you're an individual (either a general partner or a limited partner who owned a general partnership interest at all times during the tax year), you materially participated in an activity only if one or more of the following apply."
findings.why: The gate condition is labeled 'A general partner who worked 500 hours or less', so it is not clear whether the helper covers limited partners who held a general partnership interest all year. Test 2 applies to these filers, and a no would silently treat test 2 as not met.

findings.situation: Test 3 can fail because the filer worked 100 hours or less, even when no one else worked more, but the gate's label says 'less than someone else'.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "You participated in the activity for more than 100 hours during the tax year, and your participation in the activity for the tax year wasn't less than the participation in the activity of any other individual"
findings.why: The gate is correct only if the helper is false whenever test 3 fails for any reason, including 100 hours or less. A helper or label that captures only 'less than someone else' would wrongly skip test 2 for a sole worker with 100 hours or less.

findings.situation: The gate holds for a rental activity of a filer who is not a real estate professional, where material participation has no effect.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "if you have income (loss), deductions, or credits from a rental activity of the partnership (other than a rental real estate activity in which you materially participated as a real estate professional), the amounts from that activity are passive"
findings.why: In this case test 2 never changes the result, so asking the question costs a little time but drops no amount.

locators: p. 9, Individuals (other than limited partners), "constituted substantially all the participation in the activity of all individuals"

findings.situation: A limited partner works 500 hours or less but does substantially all the work in the activity, or more than 100 hours and at least as much as anyone else. The tool then marks test 2 or 3 as met, so the computed condition is false and test 6 is never asked, even though test 6 is one of the few ways a limited partner can materially participate.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "Limited partners. If you're a limited partner, you must meet item 1, 5, or 6 above to qualify as having materially participated." and "6. The activity was a personal service activity and you materially participated in the activity for any 3 tax years ..."
findings.why: The condition requires helper "Worked 500 hours or less and tests 2 and 3 not met" to be true, and nothing shows that helper ignores tests 2 and 3 for limited partners. For a limited partner, meeting test 2 or 3 does not count, so test 6 still decides material participation but the gate closes.

findings.situation: The filer meets test 4 (significant participation activities over 500 hours) or test 7 (facts and circumstances), but tests 1, 2, 3 and 5 are not met, so the gate opens and test 6 is asked even though material participation is already established.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "you materially participated in an activity only if one or more of the following apply."
findings.why: Material participation is met if any one test applies, so the test 6 answer cannot change the outcome. This only costs an extra question.

findings.situation: A limited partner who also owned a general partnership interest all year can meet test 4 or 7, but if item G on their K-1 is checked 'Limited partner or other LLC member', the computed gate is false.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "If you're an individual (either a general partner or a limited partner who owned a general partnership interest at all times during the tax year), you materially participated in an activity only if one or more of the following apply."
findings.why: The IRS text extends tests 4 and 7 to limited partners who held a general partnership interest all year. A gate keyed only to the item G 'General partner or LLC member-manager' box can be false for them, which zeroes t4_if_gp and t7_if_gp.

findings.situation: On a joint or separate return, the spouse did some or all of the work. The gate helper 'Worked in the business' and the questions t4 and t7 ask only about 'your work', so a filer could truthfully answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "Generally, any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through a partnership ... is counted toward material participation."
findings.why: Spouse work counts toward the hour tests, but the wording 'your work' or 'did you work' can be read as the filer alone. This can drop the gate or produce a no to t4 or t7 when the IRS rule gives a yes.

findings.situation: A partner's participation is regular, continuous and substantial on the facts and circumstances, but the t7 question adds 'for more than 100 hours', which the cited text does not state.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "7. Based on all the facts and circumstances, you participated in the activity on a regular, continuous, and substantial basis during the tax year."
findings.why: The question adds a 100-hour threshold that is absent from the cited text. A filer could answer no on the hours even though test 7 as quoted is met.

findings.situation: A general partner who met test 6 (personal service activity) but none of tests 1, 2, 3 and 5 is still asked about tests 4 and 7.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "6. The activity was a personal service activity and you materially participated in the activity for any 3 tax years ... preceding the tax year."
findings.why: Meeting test 6 already establishes material participation, so tests 4 and 7 add nothing for this filer. Asking them only costs extra questions.

findings.situation: A partner did not approve tenants, set rental terms or approve expenditures, but did arrange in a significant and bona fide sense for others to provide services such as repairs, so they truthfully answer no to 'helped make management decisions' and the 10% question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: You may be treated as actively participating if you participated, for example, in making management decisions or arranging for others to provide services (such as repairs) in a significant and bona fide sense. (i1065sk1 2025 p. 11)

findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "If you're an individual (either a general partner or a limited partner who owned a general partnership interest at all times during the tax year), you materially participated in an activity only if one or more of the following apply. ... 3. You participated in the activity for more than 100 hours during the tax year, and your participation ... wasn't less than the participation ... of any other individual"

findings.why: The gated question covers the spouse, but the hours helper that feeds the computed gate is not shown to cover the spouse. If the helper asks only about the filer, a filer whose spouse supplied the 101 to 500 hours could answer no, and the gate would close.

findings.situation: A filer has a prior-year unallowed loss from this partnership, but the 2025 K-1 shows nothing in boxes 1, 2 and 3 (for example, the partnership broke even, or the activity was wound down or disposed of).
findings.irs_text: Column (c). Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582. (i8582 2025 p. 10, Part IV; same for Part V column (c))
findings.why: Column (c) asks for prior-year unallowed losses for each activity regardless of current-year income or loss, so the carryover still goes on line 1c or 2c. The computed gate is false here, so the tool sets the carryover to zero.

findings.situation: The partnership's passive activity produces current-year loss items only in boxes other than 1–3 (such as a section 1231 loss, section 179 deduction or other deductions), or a prior-year unallowed loss arose from such items, while boxes 1–3 are blank.
findings.irs_text: Column (b). Enter the current year net loss for each activity... If an activity has net income on one form or schedule and a net loss on another form or schedule, report the net amounts separately (i8582 2025 p. 10, Part IV); Part V covers 'Passive trade or business activities' (i8582 2025 p. 10)
findings.why: The IRS text treats the activity as a whole, across forms and schedules, not just K-1 boxes 1–3. Gating the prior-year loss question on boxes 1–3 misses activities whose amounts flow through other boxes.

findings.situation: The cited text sets no current-year-activity condition for entering a prior-year unallowed loss, but the gate adds one.
findings.irs_text: Gate: 'Box 1, 2 or 3 shows an amount' vs. i8582 p. 10: 'Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582.'
findings.why: The cited source's condition is that a prior-year unallowed loss exists on the 2024 Form 8582 Part VII column (c). The gate replaces that with a condition on current-year K-1 boxes.

findings.situation: A partner's K-1 has a blank box 1, but it reports deductions or credits from a partnership trade or business activity (for example, a box 13 deduction or a box 15 credit). The partner or spouse worked in that business, yet is never asked the work question.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "Income (loss), deductions, and credits from an activity are nonpassive if you determine that: • You materially participated in a trade or business activity of the partnership"
findings.why: Material participation decides whether deductions and credits from a trade or business activity are passive, not only box 1 income. A filer with a blank box 1 truthfully answers no, so the work line is forced to false even though it still matters.

findings.situation: A trading partnership reports its results in boxes other than box 1 (for example, interest, capital gains, or box 13 deductions) and leaves box 1 blank. The trader question, whose Yes is supposed to end the interview, is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: "If you have net income (loss), deductions, or credits from any of the following activities, treat such amounts as nonpassive ... 3. Trading personal property for the account of owners of interests in the activity."
findings.why: The trading rule applies to all net income, deductions, or credits from the trading activity, not only to box 1 amounts. A filer with a blank box 1 answers no, so the trader line is forced to false and the interview continues when it should stop.

findings.situation: Box 1 shows an amount, but the partner owned no interest during the year and did no work, so the work question has no effect beyond confirming passive treatment.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through a partnership (where you own your partnership interest at the time the work is done)"
findings.why: Asking costs only a question. Gates are meant to lean toward yes, so this does not change the verdict.

findings.situation: The partnership distributes property with a zero adjusted basis (for example, fully depreciated equipment), so box 19 shows code C with $0 or no dollar figure, and the filer may answer that box 19 shows no amount.
findings.irs_text: Code C is used to report the partnership's adjusted basis in property other than money immediately before the property was distributed to you (i1065sk1 2025 p. 25)
findings.why: Box 19 reports the partnership's basis in the property, not the distribution's value, so a real distribution can appear as a code with a zero amount. "Show an amount" can be read as requiring a nonzero dollar figure. A filer reading it that way answers no, and the tool sets b19_other_if_any to false even though box 19 shows a code other than A.

findings.situation: Box 19 shows only a code A cash amount that does not exceed the filer's basis in the partnership interest.

findings.why: The gate holds, but neither gated line ends up with an amount: there is no non-A code and no excess over basis. This only costs two extra questions.

findings.situation: The partnership sold depreciable real property used in its business, so the gain is net section 1231 gain reported in box 10 and its unrecaptured section 1250 portion is reported in box 9c, while box 9a is blank.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 16, Box 9c: "Report unrecaptured section 1250 gain from the sale or exchange of the partnership's business assets on line 5. ... If the partnership reports only unrecaptured section 1250 gain from the sale or exchange of its business assets, it'll enter a dollar amount in box 9c." Box 10: "If the amount is ... a gain, report it in column (g) of Form 4797, line 2."
findings.why: Unrecaptured section 1250 gain from the sale of business assets comes from section 1231 gain, which the partnership reports in box 10, not box 9a. So box 9c can show an amount when box 9a is empty. A filer who truthfully answers no to the box 9a question never reaches the 9b/9c question, and the box 9c amount the Unrecaptured Section 1250 Gain Worksheet needs is dropped.

findings.situation: The partnership's collectibles gain is exactly offset by other long-term capital losses, so box 9a nets to zero or is blank while box 9b shows the collectibles gain.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 16, Box 9b: "Report collectibles gain or loss on line 4 of the 28% Rate Gain Worksheet—Line 18 in the Instructions for Schedule D (Form 1040)."
findings.why: Box 9a is a net figure across all long-term items, so it can be zero while the collectibles component in box 9b is not. The 28% Rate Gain Worksheet still uses the box 9b amount when the filer has other capital gains, so gating on box 9a drops it.

findings.situation: A filer reads the help text "Both are parts of the gain in box 9a" while box 9c reflects section 1231 gain shown in box 10.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 pp. 15-16: "The information reported in boxes 9b and 9c relates to collectibles (28%) gain (loss) and unrecaptured section 1250 gain flowing through the partnership."
findings.why: The IRS text does not say 9b and 9c are parts of box 9a. The help text tells the filer otherwise, which can lead them to assume 9b and 9c don't matter when 9a is blank, and would wrongly support the gate.

locators: p. 15, Box 9a. Net Long-Term Capital Gain (Loss), "Report the net long-term capital gain (loss) on Schedule D (Form 1040), line 12"
p. 16, Box 9b. Collectibles (28%) Gain (Loss), "Report collectibles gain or loss on line 4 of the 28% Rate Gain Worksheet"

findings.situation: A partnership sells depreciable real property used in its business, reports the gain as net section 1231 gain in box 10, and enters the unrecaptured portion in box 9c, leaving box 9a blank because it has no net long-term capital gain.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 16, Box 9c: "Report unrecaptured section 1250 gain from the sale or exchange of the partnership's business assets on line 5" and "If the partnership reports only unrecaptured section 1250 gain from the sale or exchange of its business assets, it'll enter a dollar amount in box 9c."
findings.why: Unrecaptured section 1250 gain from business assets normally comes through section 1231 gain (box 10), not box 9a. So box 9c can carry an amount while box 9a is blank, and the computed condition is false and drops the box 9c amount.

findings.situation: A partnership's collectibles gain in box 9b is exactly offset by other long-term capital losses, so box 9a nets to zero or blank while box 9b shows an amount.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 16, Box 9b: "Report collectibles gain or loss on line 4 of the 28% Rate Gain Worksheet—Line 18 in the Instructions for Schedule D (Form 1040)."
findings.why: Nothing in the cited text makes box 9b depend on box 9a. Box 9a is a net figure that can be zero while box 9b is not, and in that case the gate drops an amount that belongs on line 4 of the worksheet.

findings.situation: The gated lines are labeled "asked only when box 9b or 9c shows an amount", but the computed condition also requires box 9a to show an amount.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 16, Box 9b/9c (no text conditions boxes 9b or 9c on box 9a)
findings.why: The description of the gate and its computation differ, and the extra box 9a requirement has no basis in the cited text. The box 9b/9c helper alone would be the right gate.

findings.situation: A partnership activity has a prior-year unallowed loss carried forward on the 2024 Form 8582, but the 2025 K-1 shows no amount in box 1, 2 or 3. For example, the activity broke even this year, or the K-1 reports only other items.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV/Part V Column (c): "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: Column (c) needs the carried-forward loss for every activity that has one, whether or not columns (a) or (b) show a current-year amount. The computed condition is false whenever boxes 1–3 are blank, so the carryforward is silently dropped from lines 1c/2c.

findings.situation: In a year with blank boxes 1–3, a filer disposes of the partnership interest or keeps it with no current operating items, and still holds unallowed losses from earlier years.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Columns (d) and (e): "Combine income and losses in columns (a) through (c) for each activity, and either enter the overall gain for the activity in column (d) or enter the overall loss for the activity in column (e)."
findings.why: Columns (d)/(e) contemplate an activity whose only entry is column (c). Gating on current-year box 1–3 amounts excludes exactly this case.

findings.situation: A filer is asked whether a loss was "held back on an earlier return" and must classify it as "from the business (box 1)", "rental real estate (box 2)" or "other rentals (box 3)".
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV: "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: The IRS text identifies the amount by the prior Form 8582 Part VII column (c), not by "held back" or by K-1 box. A filer may not recognize a suspended passive loss (or a prior-year CRD) as "held back", or may not know which current-year box an earlier suspended loss belongs to.

locators: p. 10, Part IV, "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582"

findings.situation: A partnership's K-1 shows no amount in box 1, 2 or 3 this year, but the filer's 2024 Form 8582, Part VII, column (c), shows an unallowed loss carried forward from that partnership's business activity. The computed condition is false, so the prior-year loss is zeroed.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part V, Column (c): "Enter the unallowed losses for the prior years for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: The IRS text asks for the prior-year unallowed loss for each activity whether or not the activity has current-year income or loss. Tying the gate to a box 1–3 amount drops carryforwards from activities that are inactive this year. Those carryforwards can still be allowed against other passive income or on disposition.

findings.situation: A filer is asked whether a loss was 'held back' from the business in box 1.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV, Column (c): "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: 'Held back' could be read as losses suspended under the basis or at-risk limits rather than prior-year passive losses unallowed on Form 8582. The question does not point to Form 8582, Part VII, column (c). A filer whose only carryforward is a passive loss could answer no.

locators: p. 10, Part IV, "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582"

findings.situation: A filer carries a prior-year unallowed rental real estate loss from this partnership, but this year's Schedule K-1 shows nothing in boxes 1, 2 and 3 (for example, the activity broke even or had no current-year items), so the outer helper is false and the carryover is set to zero without asking.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV, Column (c): "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: Prior-year unallowed losses carry forward to column (c) whether or not the K-1 shows a current-year amount. Making the gate depend on a nonzero box 1, 2 or 3 drops a carryover the IRS text requires the filer to enter.

findings.situation: The inner helper "Held-back loss from rental real estate (box 2)" does not say whether it means a loss carried over from a prior year's Form 8582 or a loss limited this year, so a filer could answer no about a 2024 carryover.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV, Column (c): "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: "Held back" names neither the year nor Form 8582 Part VII. A filer who reads it as this year's limitation, or who doesn't connect it to the 2024 form, could answer no and lose the carryover.

locators: p. 10, Part IV, "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582"

findings.situation: A filer has a prior-year unallowed loss from a partnership's other-rental activity (box 3), carried on the 2024 Form 8582, but the 2025 K-1 shows no amount in boxes 1, 2 or 3. For example, the activity broke even or was inactive this year.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 10, Part V, Column (c): "Enter the unallowed losses for the prior years for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: The instructions require the prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) whether or not the activity has current-year income or loss. The computed condition is false whenever boxes 1, 2 and 3 are blank, so the carryover is silently set to zero and never reaches line 2c.

findings.situation: A filer who actively participated in a rental real estate activity in both years has a prior-year unallowed loss from it, but the current K-1 shows nothing in boxes 1, 2 or 3.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 10, Part IV, Column (c): "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582. Enter the total of column (c) from your 2025 Part IV on Part I, line 1c"
findings.why: Part IV column (c) also takes the carryover with no requirement that the activity show a current-year amount. Gating on current-year boxes 1 to 3 drops it.

locators: p. 10, Part IV, "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582"

findings.situation: A partner who is a real estate professional receives a K-1 with a rental real estate amount in box 2 and nothing in box 1, and worked more than 500 hours in that rental real estate activity.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "You must determine if you materially participated ... (b) if you were a real estate professional (defined earlier) in each rental real estate activity held through the partnership."
findings.why: Material participation, including the 500-hour test, decides whether the box 2 amounts are nonpassive. The gate is false whenever box 1 is blank, so the hours question is never asked.

findings.situation: A partner's trade or business activity reports items only in other boxes (for example a section 179 deduction, other deductions, or credits), and box 1 is blank or zero.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "Income (loss), deductions, and credits from an activity are nonpassive if you determine that: • You materially participated in a trade or business activity of the partnership"
findings.why: Passive or nonpassive treatment of deductions and credits from a trade or business activity depends on material participation, whether or not box 1 shows an amount. The box 1 gate drops these cases.

findings.situation: A partner in a fiscal-year partnership counts work done during calendar 2025 instead of during the partnership's tax year.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "All determinations of material participation are based on your participation during the partnership's tax year." The gate helper and question say "Worked in the business in 2025" and "more than 500 hours in 2025".
findings.why: The IRS period is the partnership's tax year, while the gate and question use calendar 2025. These periods differ for fiscal-year partnerships, so a filer could truthfully answer no about 2025 even though the partnership-year test is met.

findings.situation: On a joint return, only the filer's spouse worked in the partnership activity.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through a partnership ... is counted toward material participation"
findings.why: The gate helper "Worked in the business in 2025" does not mention the spouse. A filer could read it as asking only about their own work and answer no, so the spouse's hours are never asked. Only the later hours question's help text names the spouse.

findings.situation: A partner did only investor-type work, such as reviewing financial statements, or did work whose main purpose was to avoid the passive loss rules.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "work in connection with the activity isn't counted toward material participation if ... You do the work in your capacity as an investor and you aren't directly involved in the day-to-day operations"
findings.why: Neither "worked in the business" nor "that work add up to more than 500 hours" says whether excluded work counts. A filer could include or leave out those hours.

locators: p. 9, Individuals (other than limited partners), "You participated in the activity for more than 500 hours during the tax year"
p. 9, Work counted toward material participation, "any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through a partnership"

findings.situation: A shareholder's K-1 shows a rental real estate credit (box 13) from the corporation's rental real estate activity, but box 2 is blank, so the gate is computed false and the 10% test is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 5: "If you actively participated in a rental real estate activity, you may be able to deduct up to $25,000 of the loss (or credit equivalent to a $25,000 deduction) from the activity from nonpassive income."
findings.why: The special allowance also covers credits from the activity, so active participation and the 10% test can matter even when box 2 shows nothing. The gate depends only on box 2.

findings.situation: A shareholder has a prior-year unallowed loss from the corporation's rental real estate activity, but box 2 is zero or blank this year, so the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 5: "If you have an overall loss (the excess of deductions and losses, including any prior-year unallowed loss, over income) ... report ... using the Instructions for Form 8582"; "you may be able to deduct up to $25,000 of the loss"
findings.why: Prior-year unallowed losses from the activity can still use the special allowance, which requires active participation and the 10% test. This can matter in a year when box 2 shows no current amount.

findings.situation: On a joint return, only the spouse approved tenants or arranged repairs, and the filer reads the gate question 'Actively participated in the corporation's rental real estate activity' as asking about themselves alone.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 5: "You may be treated as actively participating if you participated, for example, in making management decisions or arranging for others to provide services (such as repairs) in a significant and bona fide sense"
findings.why: The gate question does not mention the spouse, but the gated 10% question and the cited text count the spouse's interest. A joint filer could answer no even though the spouse's participation counts.

findings.situation: A filer only arranged for others to make repairs, but the gate is labeled and referred to as 'Management decisions' ('asked only when you helped make management decisions').
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 5: "in making management decisions or arranging for others to provide services (such as repairs)"
findings.why: If the filer sees the 'management decisions' wording, they could answer no even though arranging services also counts as active participation.

findings.situation: Box 17 shows code V with an asterisk or "STMT" and no dollar figure, because the section 199A information (QBI, W-2 wages, UBIA, section 199A dividends) is on an attached statement; a filer could truthfully say box 17 shows no amount, which skips the code V question and drops the QBI deduction inputs.
findings.irs_text: f1120ssk p. 1: "17 Other information"; i1120ssk p. 17, Code V: "The S corporation will provide the information you need to figure your deduction."
findings.why: Box 17 holds information, not only amounts, and code V is usually reported by statement rather than as a single figure in the box. Asking whether the box "shows an amount" lets a truthful no skip a code that is present.

findings.situation: Box 17 shows only statement-type codes with no dollar figure, such as code D (basis of energy property), AJ (excess business loss statement) or AW (reportable transactions); a filer could truthfully say no amount is shown, so the other-codes question that should stop the interview is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 15, Code D: "If the corporation provides an attached statement for code D, use the information on the statement..."; p. 18, Code AW: "Any information you need to complete a disclosure statement for reportable transactions..."
findings.why: These codes appear in box 17 as information or statement references rather than amounts. A truthful no on "shows an amount" skips the refusal for out-of-scope codes.

findings.situation: A filer sees a code letter in box 17 with "STMT" or "*" where a number would go and must decide whether that counts as box 17 "show[ing] an amount".
findings.irs_text: f1120ssk p. 1: "17 Other information"; footnote "* See attached statement for additional information."
findings.why: "Amount" can reasonably be read as a dollar figure only, or as any entry in the box. The gate should ask whether box 17 shows any code or entry at all.

The passive activity limitations"; i1120ssk p. 4: "You must determine if you materially participated (a) in each trade or business activity held through the corporation"
findings.why: The work question matters to the trade or business items in boxes 11 through 13 even when box 1 is empty. The box-1 gate sets the work answer to false, which treats those items as passive.

findings.situation: The corporation has more than one trade or business activity, and their income and loss net to zero or a blank box 1, while the attached statement shows separate amounts for each activity.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 6: "If the corporation had more than one trade or business activity, it will attach a statement identifying the income or loss from each activity."
findings.why: A filer can truthfully say box 1 shows no amount even though the activities have their own income or loss. Each activity then needs a material participation determination, which depends on the work answer.

findings.situation: Box 1 shows 0, or shows "STMT" with the amounts on an attached statement.

findings.why: One filer could read a printed zero or "STMT" as showing an amount, and another could read it as showing none. A no answer drops the statement amounts and the work question.

findings.why: The gated question asks about calendar 2025, but the IRS test looks at work during the corporation's tax year. A filer could answer for the wrong period.

findings.situation: Box 2 is blank this year, but the shareholder has a prior-year unallowed passive loss from the corporation's rental real estate activity. Active participation still decides whether the $25,000 special allowance can free that loss.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 5: "If you have an overall loss (the excess of deductions and losses, including any prior-year unallowed loss) ... from a passive activity"; "If you actively participated in a rental real estate activity, you may be able to deduct up to $25,000 of the loss"
findings.why: The special allowance applies to the activity's loss, including carried-over prior-year amounts, not only to a current box 2 figure. A filer with an empty box 2 truthfully answers no and the active-participation answer is lost.

findings.situation: The S corporation reports a rental real estate credit (for example, in box 13) but nothing in box 2. The shareholder actively participated and could use the credit equivalent of the $25,000 allowance.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 5: "you may be able to deduct up to $25,000 of the loss (or credit equivalent to a $25,000 deduction) from the activity from nonpassive income"
findings.why: Active participation also matters for credits from rental real estate. A gate on a box 2 amount misses a K-1 that carries only rental real estate credits.

findings.situation: Box 2 shows an amount, but the shareholder cannot use the special allowance, so the active-participation answer has no effect. Examples: a non-individual other than a decedent's estate, a married person filing separately who lived with the spouse, an owner with under a 10% interest, or a box 2 amount that is income.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 5: "Only individuals can actively participate"; "You aren't considered to actively participate ... if ... your interest ... was less than 10%"; "The special allowance isn't available if you were married, file a separate return ... and didn't live apart"
findings.why: The gate asks the active-participation question in cases where the answer cannot matter. That costs only a question.

findings.situation: Box 8c says STMT or points to an attached statement instead of a dollar figure, and boxes 8a and 8b are blank or zero, for example because the long-term gains and losses net to zero. A filer could truthfully answer that no box shows an amount, so the statement question that ends the interview is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 7, Box 8c: "If it reports the other two types of unrecaptured gain, it will provide an attached statement that shows the amount for each type of unrecaptured section 1250 gain."
findings.why: The gate asks whether a box 'show[s] an amount', but the IRS text lets box 8c carry an attached statement rather than a dollar figure. A STMT entry may not count as 'an amount', so the gated box 8c statement line and its refusal are silently dropped.

findings.situation: A filer sees 'STMT', an asterisk or a reference to an attachment in box 8c and must decide whether that box 'show[s] an amount'.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 7, Box 8c: "it will enter a dollar amount in box 8c. If it reports the other two types of unrecaptured gain, it will provide an attached statement"
findings.why: The question does not say whether a statement reference counts as an amount. The gate should ask whether boxes 8a–8c show an amount or a statement reference (for example, 'show an amount, STMT, or a reference to an attached statement').

findings.situation: A shareholder whose S corporation K-1 has no loss in boxes 1, 2, 3, 7 or 8a, but does report a section 179 deduction (box 11) or other deductions (box 12), and whose stock or loan basis was financed with nonrecourse or guaranteed money. The computed gate is false, so the not-at-risk question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "if you have (a) a loss or other deduction from any activity ... and (b) amounts in the activity for which you aren't at risk, you will have to complete Form 6198"; "These losses and deductions include a loss on the disposition of assets and the section 179 expense deduction."
findings.why: The cited text triggers Form 6198 on any loss or other deduction, not only a loss in boxes 1, 2, 3, 7 or 8a. A filer whose only items are deductions, or a section 1231 or other loss (boxes 9 and 10), escapes the gate and is never refused.

findings.situation: The cited text states the Form 6198 condition as a loss or other deduction plus amounts not at risk, but the gate computes only a loss in five specific boxes.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "Generally, if you have (a) a loss or other deduction from any activity carried on as a trade or business or for the production of income by the corporation" vs gate: "A loss in box 1, 2, 3, 7 or 8a"
findings.why: The gate's event (a loss in five boxes) is narrower than the cited condition (any loss or other deduction from the activity).

findings.situation: A shareholder contributed cash or property to the corporation without receiving shares, or holds an interest protected by a stop-loss agreement that does not involve borrowing. This filer may answer no to a question limited to money borrowed to pay for shares or loans.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "Any cash or property contributed to a corporate activity, or your interest in the corporate activity, that is ... (b) protected against loss by a guarantee, stop-loss agreement, or other similar arrangement"
findings.why: The question asks only about borrowed money used for shares or loans. A filer could reasonably read it as excluding capital contributions and non-borrowing stop-loss protection, both of which the IRS text treats as not at risk.

findings.situation: A shareholder who acquired stock before 1987 has a loss from holding real property the corporation placed in service before 1987.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "if you acquired your stock before 1987, the at-risk rules don't apply to losses from an activity of holding real property placed in service before 1987 by the corporation"
findings.why: The gate holds and the question is asked even though the at-risk rules do not apply to this loss.

locators: p. 3, At-Risk Limitations, "you will have to complete Form 6198, At-Risk Limitations, to figure your allowable loss for the activity"

findings.situation: A shareholder's K-1 shows the trade or business activity's items only outside box 1 (for example, a box 11 section 179 deduction or box 12 deductions or credits), or a real estate professional's K-1 shows box 2 rental real estate loss, and box 1 is blank.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "You must determine if you materially participated (a) in each trade or business activity held through the corporation; and (b) if you were a real estate professional (defined earlier), in each rental real estate activity held through the corporation."
findings.why: The helper "Worked in the business" is asked only when box 1 shows an amount and is false otherwise, so the gate stays closed. Tests 2, 4 and 7 can then never be asked, even though material participation still decides whether these items are passive.

findings.situation: A shareholder in a fiscal-year S corporation whose tax year ends in 2025 worked in the business during that corporate year (mostly in 2024) but did not work in it in calendar 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "All determinations of material participation are based on your participation during the corporation's tax year."
findings.why: The gate asks whether the filer worked in the business in 2025, not during the corporation's tax year. This filer can truthfully answer no, which drops tests 2, 4 and 7 for a year in which they may have materially participated.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse did the work in the S corporation's business and the shareholder did little or none of it.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "Generally, any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through an S corporation ... is counted toward material participation."
findings.why: The gate asks whether "you" worked in the business, and the gated question asks whether "you" did the work. A filer could reasonably read either as excluding the spouse's work and answer no, even though the spouse's work counts toward material participation.

findings.situation: A shareholder did a little investor-type work, such as reviewing financial statements, and meets none of the participation tests.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "You do the work in your capacity as an investor and you aren't directly involved in the day-to-day operations of the activity."
findings.why: Such a filer may answer yes to having worked in the business, which opens the gate even though this work does not count toward material participation. This costs only an extra question.

locators: p. 4, Individuals, "Your participation in the activity for the tax year constituted substantially all the participation in the activity of all individuals"; "The activity was a significant participation activity for the tax year, and you participated in all significant participation activities (including activities outside the corporation) during the year for more than 500 hours"

p. 4, Material participation, "Material participation standards for shareholders who are individuals are listed below"; p. 4, Individuals, "You participated in the activity for more than 500 hours during the tax year"

findings.situation: A shareholder who was a real estate professional has an amount only in box 2 (net rental real estate income or loss), so tests 5 or 6 decide whether that rental activity is passive, but box 1 is blank and the computed condition is false.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "You must determine if you materially participated (a) in each trade or business activity held through the corporation; and (b) if you were a real estate professional (defined earlier), in each rental real estate activity held through the corporation."
findings.why: The material participation tests, including the earlier-years tests 5 and 6, also apply to rental real estate activities of a real estate professional. The gate only looks at box 1, so these cases are skipped and the earlier-years answer is treated as false.

findings.situation: A trade or business activity held through the corporation passes through only items reported outside box 1 (for example, a section 179 deduction, other deductions, credits, or other income), and box 1 is zero.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "If the corporation has more than one activity, it will attach a statement ... that identifies each activity ... and specifies the income (loss), deductions, and credits from each activity."; "Passive activities don't include ... Trade or business activities in which you materially participated."
findings.why: Whether deductions and credits from a trade or business activity are passive depends on material participation, which may rest on tests 5 or 6. A box-1-only trigger misses these activities.

findings.situation: Box 1 shows an amount and the filer fails tests 1 and 3 but already materially participates under test 2, 4 or 7, so the earlier-years answer changes nothing.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "you materially participated in an activity only if one or more of the following apply."
findings.why: Meeting any one test is enough, so asking about tests 5 and 6 is unnecessary in this case. This only costs extra questions.

findings.situation: On a 2025 joint return, this S corporation's K-1 belongs to the spouse, whose 2024 passive loss was disallowed on a separate 2024 return (unmarried or married filing separately), so the filer can truthfully say no loss was held back on 'your 2024 return'.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part V, Column (c): "Enter the unallowed losses for the prior years for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: The spouse's carryover from their own 2024 Form 8582 belongs in column (c) of the 2025 joint Form 8582. The question asks only about 'your 2024 return' and doesn't mention a spouse's separate 2024 return, so a truthful no drops the amount.

findings.situation: A loss from this corporation arose in 2022 or 2023 and was still unallowed when the 2024 return was filed, but no new loss arose in 2024, and the filer reads 'held back on your 2024 return' as covering only a 2024 loss.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV, Column (c): "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.why: Column (c) holds all accumulated prior-year unallowed losses, not just 2024's. The gate wording can be read as asking only whether a 2024 loss was disallowed, although the help pointing to Part VII, column (c) lessens the risk.

locators: p. 10, Column (c), "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity"

findings.situation: A shareholder works 100-500 hours in an S corporation trade or business whose Schedule K-1 shows nothing in box 1 but shows other items from that activity, such as a section 179 deduction, other deductions, credits, or box 10 income. The 'worked in the business' helper is false, so the gate is false and test 3 is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "You must determine if you materially participated (a) in each trade or business activity held through the corporation"; "If the corporation has more than one activity, it will attach a statement ... that ... specifies the income (loss), deductions, and credits from each activity."
findings.why: Material participation decides passive treatment for every item from the activity, including deductions and credits. Tying the gate to a box 1 amount drops test 3 whenever the activity's items appear only in other boxes.

findings.situation: A real estate professional works 100-500 hours in a rental real estate activity held through the corporation, reported in box 2 with box 1 blank. The gate is false, so test 3 is never asked for that activity.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "(b) if you were a real estate professional (defined earlier), in each rental real estate activity held through the corporation"
findings.why: The cited text requires a material participation determination for rental real estate activities of real estate professionals. The gate looks only at the box 1 trade or business amount.

findings.situation: A married shareholder filing separately has a spouse who did the work in the activity. The gated question counts the spouse only 'on a joint return', so the shareholder could truthfully answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "Generally, any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through an S corporation ... is counted toward material participation."
findings.why: The IRS text counts a spouse's work regardless of filing status. The question limits the spouse to joint returns and so misses married-filing-separately filers.

findings.situation: A fiscal-year S corporation's tax year does not match calendar 2025, but the gated question measures hours 'in 2025'.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "All determinations of material participation are based on your participation during the corporation's tax year." The gated question asks: "work more than 100 hours in it in 2025".
findings.why: The IRS time frame is the corporation's tax year, not calendar 2025. The 500-hour helper, if it uses the same calendar-year wording, would have the same mismatch.

findings.situation: Spouses who each worked under 100 hours but together worked more than 100 hours could read 'you (or ... your spouse) work more than 100 hours' as asking about each person separately.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "any work that you or your spouse does ... is counted toward material participation"
findings.why: The help text says to combine hours with the spouse's, but the question itself can reasonably be read as a test of each person separately. That reading leads to a wrong no.

findings.situation: A filer whose only work was investor-type work, such as reviewing financial statements, answers that they worked in the business, which opens the gate.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "You do the work in your capacity as an investor and you aren't directly involved in the day-to-day operations of the activity."
findings.why: Investor work does not count toward material participation, so the gate can hold where test 3 cannot apply. Gates lean to yes by design, so this does not change the verdict.

findings.situation: A shareholder who is a real estate professional gets a K-1 showing rental real estate income or loss in box 2 and nothing in box 1, so box1_any is false and the hours question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "You must determine if you materially participated (a) in each trade or business activity held through the corporation; and (b) if you were a real estate professional (defined earlier), in each rental real estate activity held through the corporation."
findings.why: The IRS text requires the material participation tests, including the more-than-500-hours test, for rental real estate activities reported outside box 1. The gate only opens when box 1 shows an amount, so it drops this case.

findings.situation: An S corporation's trade or business activity shows up on the K-1 only through other items, such as a section 179 deduction, other deductions, other income or credits, and box 1 is blank or zero.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "Passive activities don't include the following. 1. Trade or business activities in which you materially participated." and "specifies the income (loss), deductions, and credits from each activity"
findings.why: Whether the activity is passive, and so how those deductions and credits are treated, depends on material participation even when box 1 has no amount. The gate is computed from box 1 alone and is false here.

findings.situation: The S corporation uses a fiscal year, so its tax year does not match calendar 2025, but both the gate and the hours question ask about work 'in 2025'.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "All determinations of material participation are based on your participation during the corporation's tax year."
findings.why: The gate asks whether 'You or your spouse worked in the corporation's business in 2025' and the input asks about hours 'in 2025'. The IRS time frame is the corporation's tax year, which can cover a different period.

findings.situation: A shareholder whose only connection is a rental real estate activity held through the corporation reads 'worked in the corporation's business' and is unsure whether managing the rental counts.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "any work that you or your spouse does in connection with an activity held through an S corporation ... is counted toward material participation"
findings.why: 'Business' could reasonably be read as limited to the trade or business activity. The IRS text covers work on any activity held through the corporation, including rental real estate.

findings.situation: A filer whose only work was as an investor, such as reviewing financial statements without day-to-day involvement, answers yes to having worked in the business.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "You do the work in your capacity as an investor and you aren't directly involved in the day-to-day operations of the activity."
findings.why: Investor work does not count toward material participation, but the gate still opens. This only costs an extra question.

findings.situation: A person born on any day of 1976 after January 1 is only 49 at the end of 2025, yet the computed gate holds and the question is asked.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 97, IRA Deduction Worksheet—Schedule 1, Line 20: "$8,000 if age 50 or older at the end of 2025."
findings.why: Only a person born January 1, 1976 can be treated as age 50 at the end of 2025, because age is reached the day before the birthday. Anyone born after 1975 has the gate open but the line is no. Anyone born before 1976 is clearly 50 or older, so this open-year line is not needed for them.

findings.situation: A filer born in 1971 on any day other than January 1 turns 54 during 2025, so the gate holds but the filer can only answer no and the age-55 amount never applies.
findings.irs_text: i8889 p. 4, Line 3, rule 6: "If, at the end of 2025, you were age 55 or older ... you can increase the amount ... by $1,000"; p. 6 chart: "If you were age 55 or older at the end of 2025, enter $5,300 for the month."
findings.why: Only someone born on January 1, 1971 is close to 55 on December 31, 2025. Everyone else born in 1971 is 54, so for them the question costs a few extra prompts. Filers born in 1970 or earlier are clearly 55 or older; this line, which covers only the uncertain 1971 birth year, assumes that age status is determined elsewhere.

findings.situation: A student has some tax-free assistance or refunds for a term, but less than that term's qualified expenses, so line 3 is above zero and the question is asked even though the answer will be no.

findings.why: The gate is computed as line 3 (total adjustments) > 0, which is true whenever any term's adjustments exceed its expenses, so it covers every yes case. findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93: 'If you were an eligible educator in 2025 ... An eligible educator is a kindergarten through grade 12 teacher, instructor, counselor, principal, or aide who worked in a school for at least 900 hours during a school year.'
findings.why: The IRS test counts 900 hours over a school year, which spans two calendar years. The gate's leading 'In 2025' can be read as limiting the hours to calendar 2025, which would drop that teacher's expenses.

findings.situation: A teacher who started in August or September 2025 and works 900+ hours over the 2025-26 school year had fewer than 900 hours by December 31, 2025, and might answer no.

The IRS text counts the school year itself, and the gate does not say which school year or that a school year overlapping 2025 qualifies.

findings.situation: A sole proprietor in a home-care business receives Medicaid waiver payments that are not in W-2 box 1 and were not reported on any Form 1099-MISC or 1099-NEC (for example, below the reporting threshold or never issued), so the 1099 helper is $0 and the business question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1d: "Enter your taxable Medicaid waiver payments that were not reported on Form(s) W-2 ... If you are a sole proprietor in a business of providing home care services, see the Schedule C instructions for how to report these amounts."
findings.why: In the IRS text, "these amounts" means Medicaid waiver payments not reported on a W-2, not only those on a 1099. The sole-proprietor treatment (Schedule C, and the tool's refusal) applies without a 1099, but the computed condition is false, so the business is silently treated as absent.

findings.situation: On a joint return, one spouse runs a home-care business but has no Medicaid waiver payments on a 1099, while the other spouse's payments are not on a W-2.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1d: "If you are a sole proprietor in a business of providing home care services, see the Schedule C instructions for how to report these amounts."
findings.why: The gate is computed per person from that person's 1099 amount alone. A spouse whose business payments were not reported on a 1099 is never asked, so the business is missed for that spouse.

If you do not have a separate trade or business of providing these services, enter on Form 1040, line 1d, your Medicaid waiver payments reported on Form 1099-MISC or Form 1099-NEC."

findings.situation: A participant born in 1963, 1964 or 1965 turns 62, 61 or 60 during 2025, but the gate is false for them, so the line takes the age-50 parameter and drops the higher $5,250 SIMPLE catch-up limit.
findings.irs_text: p560 (2025) p. 16: "allow participants to make a higher amount of catch-up contributions in a tax year in which they attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63. For 2025 and 2026, the higher limit on catch-up contributions to SIMPLE plans for such participants is $5,250."
findings.why: Attaining age 60–63 in 2025 means being born in 1962 through 1965. The gate tests only 1962 and 1966, and the fallback assumes everyone else is 50–59 or 64 and over, so three birth years in the 60–63 band get no higher limit.

findings.situation: The gate assumes the exact birth date decides the band in the boundary years, but the cited text sets the band by the age attained during the tax year, which the birth year alone decides.
findings.irs_text: p560 (2025) p. 16: "in a tax year in which they attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63" and "age 50 or over at the end of the calendar year"; the gate is "Born in 1962 or 1966 (a year in which the birth date decides whether the SIMPLE catch-up age band is 60 to 63)"
findings.why: Under 'attain age in the tax year', everyone born in 1962 reaches 63 in 2025 and everyone born in 1966 reaches 59, whatever their birth date. The gate's 'open years' do not match the time frame the cited text states.

findings.irs_text: p560 (2025) p. 16: "in a tax year in which they attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63"

findings.situation: A Coverdell ESA beneficiary has an excess contribution from 2024 still in the account at the end of 2025, but the account had no contributions or distributions in 2025, so the inner helper is false and the excess question is never asked.

Line 26: "Enter the excess contributions from line 32 of your 2024 Form 5329." Line 33: "Enter 6% (0.06) of the smaller of line 32 or the value of your Coverdell ESAs on December 31, 2025."
findings.why: A prior-year excess left in the account owes the 6% tax again in 2025 even with no 2025 activity. findings.situation: A parent who contributed too much to a child's ABLE account gets the excess back with its net income, and that income is taxable to the parent, but the parent neither had an ABLE account nor had one held for them and could truthfully answer no.
findings.irs_text: i5329 p. 9, Part VIII: "Any net income distributed from the excess contribution to the ABLE account is includible in the gross income of the contributor in the tax year in which the excess contribution was made."; f5329 p. 1, Part II: "Complete this part if you included an amount in income ... on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8q, from an ABLE account."
findings.why: The person taxed on this ABLE distribution is the contributor, not the account's beneficiary. The gate asks only whether the filer had an account or had one held for them, so it can miss an amount that belongs on Part II line 5.

findings.situation: Part of the gate's citation is the Part IX required-minimum-distribution condition, which has nothing to do with education or ABLE accounts.

findings.situation: A filer itemized for 2024 and got a 2025 reimbursement of 2024 medical bills, but none of the medical bills were deductible because they stayed below the 7.5%-of-AGI floor.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 26, Recovery limited to deduction: "You don't include in your income any amount of your recovery that is more than the amount you deducted in the earlier year."
findings.why: The gate holds and both questions are asked. But the 2024 deduction is zero, so none of the reimbursement is included and the gated lines change nothing. Gates lean to yes, so this costs a few questions but drops no amount.

findings.situation: A filer whose recoveries are fully includible without any worksheet, as in Example 30, still goes through the gate because the computed condition only checks for a 2024 recovery while itemizing.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 25, Example 30: "Your total recoveries are less than the amount by which your itemized deductions exceeded the standard deduction ... so you must include your total recoveries in your income for 2025."
findings.why: The medical lines still matter here, because the deduction caps the amount recovered. So this only shows the gate is broader than the literal "Worksheet 2 is used" label, and it does not narrow coverage.

findings.situation: A filer's lender refunded or credited 2024 mortgage interest in 2025, but no Form 1098 shows the refund in box 4. This can happen when the lender didn't issue a 1098, reported the credit some other way, or the filer has no copy.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24: "If you received a refund or credit in 2025 of mortgage interest paid in an earlier year, the amount should be shown in box 4 of Form 1098."
findings.why: The IRS says the refund 'should be' shown in box 4, not that it always is. A filer could read the gate's parenthetical '(Form 1098 box 4)' as requiring a box 4 amount and answer no, which drops a Worksheet 2, line 2 amount.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse alone holds the mortgage and received the 2025 refund of 2024 interest that the couple deducted on their joint 2024 Schedule A.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 27, Worksheet 2, line 2: "Enter the total of all other Schedule A (Form 1040) refunds or reimbursements"
findings.why: Neither gate question mentions the spouse ('you itemized', 'Was any of it'). A filer could read the question as asking only about their own refunds and answer no for a spouse's Form 1098 refund.
