findings.situation: In 2025 a filer receives a reimbursement of an itemized deduction from a year before 2024, such as a 2023 casualty loss reimbursement. The worksheet for that year needs a line 2 amount, but the gate only asks about money paid back for 2024.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 27: "If you recovered amounts from more than 1 year, such as a state income tax refund from 2024 and a casualty loss reimbursement from 2023, complete a separate worksheet for each year. Use information from your tax return for the year the expense was deducted."
findings.why: Both the gate and the gated lines are tied to 2024. A recovery of an earlier year's Schedule A deduction has no path, so a truthful filer answers no and the line 2 amount for that year is dropped.

findings.situation: A filer who deducted state and local general sales taxes in 2024 and got a refund of those taxes may treat it as a state/local tax refund. That filer could answer no to whether the refund was for "something else you itemized."
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 27, Worksheet 2, footnote 2: "If you deducted state and local general sales taxes and received a refund of those taxes, include the amount on line 2"
findings.why: Sales tax refunds belong on line 2, not lines 1a/1b. The question's "something else" does not say that only state/local income, real estate and personal property taxes are excluded, so a filer could reasonably read a state sales tax refund as already covered.

findings.situation: A filer receives an insurer's reimbursement of 2024 medical expenses or a casualty loss. The filer may not think of it as a "refund" and answers no.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 27, Worksheet 2, line 2: "Enter the total of all other Schedule A (Form 1040) refunds or reimbursements"
findings.why: The gate question asks only whether any of it was a "refund," while line 2 also covers reimbursements from third parties. A filer could reasonably read "refund" narrowly.

findings.situation: A filer paid and deducted real estate tax in 2024 for an earlier assessment period (for example, a 2023 property tax bill paid in 2024), and part of that tax was refunded in 2025.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 26, Worksheet 2a, line 2: "Enter the refunds received for state and local real estate taxes and state and local personal property taxes"; line 4: "real estate taxes, and personal property taxes paid in 2024 (generally, this is the amount reported on your 2024 Schedule A (Form 1040), line 5d)"
findings.why: The worksheet counts refunds of taxes paid and deducted in 2024, whatever period the bill covers. A filer could read "a refund of 2024 real estate or personal property tax" as tax for the 2024 assessment year, answer no, and drop a refund the line requires.

findings.situation: Spouses filed separate 2024 returns, file jointly for 2025, and the only recovery is a 2025 state income tax refund for 2024 that must go through Worksheet 2 (for example, because the 'generally' exception does not apply).
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 27: 'You generally don't need to use this worksheet if you file Form 1040 or 1040-SR and the recovery is for state or local income taxes paid for the immediately preceding tax year'; line 1a 'State/local income tax refund or credit'; 'such as a state income tax refund from 2024 and a casualty loss reimbursement from 2023, complete a separate worksheet for each year'
findings.why: The scope helper excludes state or local income tax refunds outright, so the computed condition is false. But the worksheet only 'generally' excludes them and has its own line 1a for them, so a joint filer with only such a refund never gets the two-separate-2024-returns question.

findings.situation: A filer got an insurance or other reimbursement of an amount deducted in 2024, but does not know whether the deduction actually lowered the 2024 tax (unused credits, AMT, or a credit carryover increase).
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 27: 'A recovery is included in income only to the extent of the deduction amount that reduced your tax in the prior year'; 'any increase to a credit carried over to the current year that resulted from deducting the recovered amount in the earlier year is considered to have reduced your tax in the earlier year'
findings.why: The scope question asks the filer to decide up front whether the deduction 'lowered your tax', which is the very thing the worksheet and refigure rules compute. A filer could reasonably answer no, for example when only a credit carryover changed. The word 'paid back' may also not register as covering a reimbursement from a third party.

findings.situation: A couple files jointly for 2025, but for 2024 they filed separately; the spouse itemized and the filer took the standard deduction. In 2025 the spouse receives a property tax refund or a medical reimbursement for 2024.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 25: "If you recover any itemized deduction that you claimed in an earlier year, you must generally include the full amount of the recovery in your income in the year you receive it"
findings.why: The scope helper covers the spouse, but the second helper asks only "Did you itemize deductions on Schedule A for 2024?" The filer truthfully answers no, so the spouse's taxable recoveries on the 2025 joint return drop to zero.

findings.situation: A filer got an insurance reimbursement or a property tax refund for an amount deducted on the 2024 Schedule A. The filer cannot tell whether the deduction actually lowered the 2024 tax, for example because itemized deductions barely exceeded the standard deduction or taxable income was negative.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24: "You must include a recovery in your income ... up to the amount by which the deduction or credit you took for the recovered amount reduced your tax in the earlier year"; p. 27, Worksheet 2: "A recovery is included in income only to the extent of the deduction amount that reduced your tax in the prior year"
findings.why: The scope question asks the filer to decide in advance whether the deduction "lowered your tax", which is the very result Worksheet 2 exists to compute. A filer who is unsure, or who guesses wrong, may answer no and drop a taxable recovery.

findings.situation: A filer received a credit of 2024 mortgage interest (Form 1098 box 4) or a sales tax refund as a credit, not as a payment.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24: "If you received a refund or credit in 2025 of mortgage interest paid in an earlier year, the amount should be shown in box 4 of Form 1098"
findings.why: "Were you ... paid back an amount" can reasonably be read as excluding credits and offsets, which the IRS text treats as recoveries.

findings.situation: A filer recovered an amount deducted or credited in a year other than 2024, or recovered a nonitemized deduction such as a bad debt, and itemized for 2024.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 27, Worksheet 2: "If you recovered amounts from more than 1 year ... complete a separate worksheet for each year"
findings.why: The scope helper is not limited to 2024 Schedule A items, so the gate opens even when none of the 2024-specific gated lines can have an amount.

findings.why: The two-returns question only matters when a 2025 joint return combines refunds from two separate 2024 returns. findings.situation: A filer reporting a royalty property (for example a copyright or NIL royalty) in a Schedule E column paid advertising for that property, but answers no because the gate asks only about a 'rental property'.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column. You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses..."
findings.why: Lines 5 through 21, including line 5 (advertising), apply to royalty properties as well as rental properties. A gate worded 'For this rental property' lets a royalty filer truthfully answer no, which zeroes a deductible advertising expense.

findings.situation: A filer sees the bare prompt 'For this rental property — Advertising' and cannot tell whether it asks if any advertising expense was paid or incurred in 2025, or asks for something else.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees, agents' commissions, and depreciation."
findings.why: The gate never asks a clear yes/no question such as 'Did you (or your spouse) pay any advertising expenses for this property in 2025?' A filer could read it as an amount field or a category label and answer no, or skip it.

findings.situation: A filer advertised the rented part of a home that is also used personally, or the spouse paid the advertising on a joint return, and is unsure whether that counts.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "If you rent out only part of your home or other property, deduct the part of your expenses that applies to the rented part."
findings.why: The gate does not say that partly personal or spouse-paid advertising counts. A filer could read it as covering only advertising they paid themselves, wholly for the rental, and wrongly answer no.

findings.situation: A filer who did the property's cleaning and upkeep personally, paying no one, could answer yes to the gate even though nothing is deductible.
findings.irs_text: Do not deduct the value of your own labor or amounts paid for capital investments or capital improvements. (i1040se 2025 p. 6)

findings.situation: A filer whose only upkeep costs were repairs or capital improvements might answer yes to the bare 'Cleaning and maintenance' gate.
findings.irs_text: You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, ... Do not deduct ... amounts paid for capital investments or capital improvements. (i1040se 2025 p. 6)
findings.why: Repairs go on another line and capital improvements are not deducted here, so the gate holds while line 7 stays zero.

findings.situation: The gate question is only the bare noun 'Commissions'. A filer who paid an agent a commission to find a renter could read it as asking about commissions they received, or about commissions in some other sense, and answer no, so the paid commissions would never be asked for.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 1: 'Use Schedule E (Form 1040) to report income or loss from rental real estate'. The Line 8 instruction the gate cites does not appear in the page 1 text supplied.
findings.why: The gate never asks whether the filer paid commissions for this property in 2025, though the gated question does ('Commissions paid, for example to an agent who found a renter'). It does not say paid rather than received, does not name the year, and does not cover a spouse on a joint return. A truthful no from a misreading would silently zero line 8.

findings.situation: A filer who paid only a commission to buy the property, rather than to rent it out, could answer yes to the bare 'Commissions' question even though that cost does not belong on line 8.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 1: 'Use Schedule E (Form 1040) to report income or loss from rental real estate'

findings.situation: The gate question is just the word 'Insurance' with no verb, so a filer cannot tell whether it asks if the property had coverage, if they paid premiums in 2025, or if they had a deductible insurance expense.
findings.irs_text: Gate cites i1040se p. 10, Line 9, but the supplied p. 10 text covers only lines 27-28 and Part III ('Line 27 ... Line 28 ... Part III Income or Loss From Estates and Trusts'). It contains no Line 9 instruction.
findings.why: Without a verb or a time frame, a filer could answer no in a case that has a deductible amount. For example, a filer whose 2025 premium was paid by a co-owner or prepaid earlier might answer no. The missing Line 9 text means the gate's scope cannot be checked against the source.

findings.situation: The gated question asks for insurance 'paid in 2025', and the helper says 'Insurance paid in 2025', but the cited Line 9 text is not in the supplied page. So whether a 2025-year share of a premium prepaid in an earlier year should count cannot be confirmed.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 10 (as supplied) has no text for Line 9. The gated input reads 'Insurance on it (the part for 2025), paid in 2025'.
findings.why: A filer who prepaid 2025 coverage in 2024 may read 'paid in 2025' as excluding it. Whether the amount belongs on Line 9 cannot be verified from the supplied text.

findings.why: Line 10 covers royalty properties as well as rental real estate. A gate framed only as 'this rental property' could be answered no for a royalty column that does have line 10 fees.

findings.situation: The filer borrowed against their main home or another asset, for example with a home equity loan reported on Form 1098, and used the proceeds to buy or improve this rental. They could truthfully answer no because there is no mortgage on this rental property itself.
findings.irs_text: In general, you allocate interest on a loan the same way you allocate the loan proceeds. You allocate loan proceeds by tracing disbursements to specific uses. (i1040se 2025 p. 6, Lines 12 and 13)

findings.why: A filer may not know whether ticking it means the property is mortgaged, that interest was paid in 2025, or that interest is allocable to the rental. 'Banks, etc.' also leaves it open whether other lenders count.

findings.situation: A filer paid interest on a loan that isn't secured by the rental (a personal loan, credit card or home-equity loan on another property) whose proceeds were spent on this rental. They could read 'For this rental property — Other interest' as covering only loans on the property and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se 2025 p. 6, Lines 12 and 13: 'In general, you allocate interest on a loan the same way you allocate the loan proceeds. You allocate loan proceeds by tracing disbursements to specific uses.'
findings.why: Under the tracing rules, interest is allocable to the rental based on how the proceeds were used, not on what secures the loan. The gate wording does not signal that such interest counts, so a no is plausible even though the IRS text gives line 13 an amount.

locators: p. 6, Lines 12 and 13

findings.situation: A filer whose only line 14 costs for the property are routine maintenance, such as servicing the furnace, cleaning gutters or repainting a room between tenants, could truthfully answer no to a gate that asks only about 'Repairs', and the deductible maintenance would be dropped.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 14: "You can deduct the amounts paid for repairs and maintenance. ... Repairs and maintenance costs are those costs that keep the property in an ordinarily efficient operating condition. Examples are fixing a broken lock or painting a room."
findings.why: Line 14 covers both repairs and maintenance, but the gate (and the gated question 'Repairs (not improvements)') names only repairs. A filer who reads 'repairs' as fixing something broken would exclude maintenance and answer no.

findings.situation: A filer who paid to repaint a room or do upkeep with nothing broken may not know whether that counts as a 'repair' for the gate.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 14: "Examples are fixing a broken lock or painting a room."
findings.why: The bare gate label 'Repairs' gives no examples and does not say that upkeep and maintenance count, so a filer could reasonably read it either way.

findings.situation: A filer is shown the gate 'For this rental property — Supplies', which is only a line label, and may not know whether it asks if they paid any supplies, which year it covers, or whether supplies used partly for personal purposes count.
findings.irs_text: Gate: 'For this rental property — Supplies' (cites i1040se p. 11, Line 15); gated amount: 'Supplies paid in 2025, before any division for personal use'
findings.why: The gate never asks whether the filer paid for supplies, and it states no year. Its scope is narrower than the gated amount, which counts all supplies paid in 2025 before any personal-use split. A filer whose supplies were partly for personal use, as with a vacation home, could reasonably answer no and lose the amount.

findings.situation: The cited page does not contain the Line 15 (Supplies) instructions, so the gate condition cannot be checked against the IRS text it claims to rest on.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 11 covers only the end of Part III, Part IV (REMICs, columns (c) and (e)), Part V line 42, and the Paperwork Reduction Act Notice; it has no Line 15 text.
findings.why: The citation points to text that does not describe supplies. Whether the gate matches the IRS condition cannot be confirmed from this text, and the citation should be corrected to the page that has the Line 15 instructions.

findings.situation: A royalty owner whose oil or gas payer withheld state or local taxes, and who paid no property tax, truthfully answers no to a question about taxes 'for this rental property', so the withheld taxes are dropped from line 16.
findings.irs_text: Enter on line 4 the gross amount of royalty income, even if state or local taxes were withheld from oil or gas payments you received. Include taxes withheld by the producer on line 16. (i1040se 2025 p. 6, Line 4)

findings.situation: A filer sees the bare gate label 'Taxes' for a rental property and must guess which taxes it means.

findings.why: The one-word gate does not say which taxes count. A filer could read it as property tax only and answer no despite other deductible taxes on the property, such as producer-withheld taxes on a royalty property.

findings.why: Carryovers are tracked for each activity. A filer might answer based on all their rentals instead of this one, though that mostly leads to a wrong yes.

findings.situation: An activity rents more than one class of property, so the simple days-per-stay average across all rentals is over 30, but the income-weighted average the IRS prescribes is 7 days or less (for example, one 365-day rental of a low-income class plus ten 2-day rentals of a class earning 99% of gross rental income: simple average 35 days, weighted average about 5.6 days).
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 3: "If the activity involves renting more than one class of property, multiply the average period of customer use of each class by the ratio of the gross rental income from that class to the activity's total gross rental income. The activity's average period of customer use equals the sum of these class-by-class average periods weighted by gross income."
findings.why: The gate tells the filer to divide total rented days by the number of stays, with no income weighting by class. A filer following that instruction answers no, so the 7-days-or-less exception (Exception 1a) is never asked and the line is forced to false.

findings.situation: A rental period crosses the tax year boundary (for example, a lease that started in a prior year), and the filer cannot tell whether to count all days of the stay or only days in the tax year, or whether to count the stay at all.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 3: "dividing the total number of days in all rental periods by the number of rentals during the tax year"
findings.why: The gate question and its help ("Divide the days it was rented by the number of separate stays") do not say which rentals count or how to count days for a period that spans two years. A filer could reasonably read it either way and land on the other side of 30 days.

findings.irs_text: If you or the plan participant was born before January 2, 1936, you could pay less tax on the distribution. See Form 4972. (i1040gi 2025 p. 30, Lump-Sum Distributions)
findings.why: This is a plan distribution, so the computed condition 'kind ≠ plan' is false and the line is forced to false. When the condition is true, the line's own Choose sends IRA=true to the fixed false, so retirement.born_before_averaging_date_if_plan can never be true.

findings.situation: A retired public safety officer has a governmental-plan pension distribution that paid health or long-term care premiums and elects the exclusion of up to $3,000.

findings.why: The exclusion applies only to plan distributions, where 'kind ≠ plan' is false. The gate therefore zeroes retirement.pso_exclusion_if_plan, and the IRA branch of its Choose also yields false.

findings.why: Cost recovery arises only for pension or annuity distributions, where the computed condition is false. retirement.cost_any_if_plan is therefore always false, so pensions are treated as fully taxable.

findings.why: Disability pensions come from employer plans, so 'kind ≠ plan' is false and retirement.disability_if_plan is forced to false. On the IRA side, its Choose returns false as well.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the distribution came from the spouse's traditional IRA and only the spouse made nondeductible contributions, but the filer answers about their own contributions and says no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 27, Exception 2(1): "You received a distribution from an IRA (other than a Roth IRA) and you made nondeductible contributions to any of your traditional IRAs for 2025 or an earlier year." p. 27: "If you (or your spouse if filing jointly) received more than one distribution, figure the taxable amount of each distribution"

findings.why: "did not deduct on a tax return" can be read as covering only contributions already left off a return that was filed. That reading drops current-year nondeductible contributions, which the IRS text counts.

findings.situation: A filer converted a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA at the same custodian (a Form 1099-R with code 2 or 7, not G). findings.irs_text: "3. You converted part or all of a traditional IRA or traditional SIMPLE IRA to a Roth IRA in 2025." (i1040gi 2025 p. 27, Exception 2); "a rollover to a Roth IRA or a designated Roth account is generally not a tax-free distribution" (i1040gi 2025 p. 30, Rollovers)
findings.why: A conversion moves money into a Roth IRA, which is the case the Roth question exists to catch. findings.situation: A filer under age 59½ gets a distribution from a section 457 plan that did not come from a rollover, but the payer put code 1 (not code 7) in box 7, so the computed condition is false and the section 457 question is never asked.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the Form 1099-R belongs to the spouse, and the filer reads "Were you under age 59½" as asking about their own age.

findings.situation: A filer paid or received alimony only in 2023 or 2024 under a pre-2019 agreement, the first payment year was before 2023, and no 2025 payment or 2025 recapture applies.

findings.situation: A filer sold crafts from a hobby for $800 but spent $1,200 on supplies, and truthfully answers no because the hobby lost money overall.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 31: "You must include on your return income from an activity, even if you don't expect to make a profit from that activity... Enter this income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8j."
findings.why: Line 8j takes gross income, and costs are not netted against it, as the tool's own help says. The gate's "make money" is commonly read as making a net profit, so a filer whose hobby ran at a loss can answer no and drop the receipts.

findings.situation: A filer runs a small farm mostly for recreation, or another activity not engaged in for profit, and does not think of it as a "hobby or pastime".

findings.why: Line 8j covers any activity not engaged in for profit; a hobby is only one example. A filer with a recreational farm or similar activity can truthfully say it is not a hobby or pastime and answer no.

findings.situation: A filer who calls an activity a side business, but who lacks a real profit motive, must decide whether it is "run as a business".
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 31: "income from an activity, even if you don't expect to make a profit from that activity"
findings.why: The IRS test is whether the activity is engaged in for profit, not whether the filer considers or operates it as a business. Filers can reasonably read "not run as a business" either way.

findings.why: A sale of lottery payment rights is not a 2025 win, so the filer can truthfully answer no and line 8b is lost.

findings.situation: A salesperson at a dealer receives prize points from a distributor or manufacturer that can be redeemed for merchandise.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 35, Prize points: "If you're a salesperson and receive prize points redeemable for merchandise ... you must include their FMV in your income. The prize points are taxable in the year they're paid or made available to you"
findings.why: Sales incentive points may not seem like money or a prize won from a contest or award, and the gate's help does not mention them; only the gated prizes question does. A filer could reasonably answer no.

findings.situation: A filer won a contest or drawing in late 2024 but received the prize in 2025, or won in 2025 but receives the prize in 2026.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 35, Prizes and awards: "If you win a prize in a lucky number drawing, television or radio quiz program, beauty contest, or other event, you must include it in your income"
findings.why: The gate is keyed to when the filer won, while income follows when the prize is received or made available. A filer could answer for the wrong year.

findings.situation: A filer whose only prize is an employer award, a prize related to their trade or business, a refused prize, or professional gambling winnings answers yes.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 35: "Cash awards or bonuses given to you by your employer ... must generally be included in your income as wages"; i1040sc p. 6, Line 6: "Prizes and awards related to your trade or business"; p525 p. 33: "If you're in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C"
findings.why: These amounts belong on Form W-2 wages or Schedule C, or are not income at all, so every gated line is zero even though the gate says yes.

findings.situation: A filer who was self-employed before 2025 (for example a freelancer, independent contractor or gig worker filing Schedule C) elected to expense equipment under section 179, and part of it was disallowed by the business income limit. They may not think of themselves as having 'owned a business'.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 5, Line 10: "the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed as a deduction because of the business income limitation"; Line 11: "taxable income from any trade or business you actively conducted"
findings.why: Section 179 applies to any trade or business, including sole self-employment. The scope question asks about owning 'a business', which such a filer could truthfully read as not describing them and answer no. The gate would then drop a real line 10 carryover.

findings.situation: A filer whose pre-2025 section 179 deduction passed through from an LLC taxed as a partnership might not recognize themselves in 'a share of a partnership'.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 5, Line 6, Column (c): "To report your share of a section 179 expense deduction from a partnership or an S corporation, enter 'from Schedule K-1 (Form 1065)'"
findings.why: LLC members often do not think of their interest as a partnership share. They could answer no even though a carried-over deduction from the K-1 belongs on line 10.

findings.situation: A filer who owned a rental or business before 2025 but never elected section 179, or whose deductions were all fully allowed, passes the scope question even though line 10 is zero.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 5, Line 10: "the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed"
findings.why: Owning such property does not by itself create a carryover. The second helper resolves this case, so it costs only one question.

locators: p. 5, Line 10, "The carryover of disallowed deduction from 2024 is the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed as a deduction because of the business income limitation" and "If you filed Form 4562 for 2024, enter the amount from line 13 of your 2024 Form 4562" (owner: the printed amount)
p. 19, Taxable income, "Interest from working capital of your trade or business"
p. 19, Taxable income, "Net income or loss from a trade or business includes the following items" and "Interest from working capital of your trade or business"

findings.situation: A filer has a section 179 deduction limited by business income and has taxable interest, but all of it is personal or investment interest unrelated to any business's operating funds.
findings.irs_text: p946 p. 19: "Net income or loss from a trade or business includes the following items. ... • Interest from working capital of your trade or business."
findings.why: The computed condition holds because there is taxable interest, but none of it is working-capital interest, so the gated line is zero. The question just collects a zero answer.

findings.situation: A filer whose private activity bond interest comes through a mutual fund as exempt-interest dividends, not from a bond payer's Form 1099-INT, reads the gated question's instruction to add up box 9 of Forms 1099-INT and could truthfully answer zero.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 3, Line 2g: "Exempt-interest dividends paid by a mutual fund or other regulated investment company are treated as interest income"; "Each payer of this type of interest should send you a Form 1099-INT showing the amount of this interest in box 9"
findings.why: The cited text counts fund exempt-interest dividends attributable to specified private activity bonds as line 2g interest, and those are not reported in Form 1099-INT box 9. A filer could read the question as limited to box 9 and leave out a line 2g amount. It is also unclear whether the computed helper 'tax-exempt interest and tax-exempt OID' includes these fund dividends; if it does not, the gate's 'at their largest' test would understate the possible 2g amount.

findings.why: The gate holds but line 2g is zero. This only costs one question.

findings.situation: A filer paid a babysitter or gardener small amounts in 2025: under $2,800 to any one person, under $1,000 in every calendar quarter of 2024 and 2025, and no income tax withheld.
findings.irs_text: Household employment taxes. Attach Schedule H (f1040s2 2025, page 1, line 9)
findings.why: The gate holds because the filer paid someone to work in their home, but no Schedule H tax arises, so line 9 is zero. The second question screens this case out, and leaning to yes is intended.

findings.situation: A filer or spouse who is a non-employee director, consultant or contractor exercised nonstatutory options granted by a company that is not their employer, and the income is not on line 1h.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8k: "Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1h."
findings.why: Line 8k covers income from exercising any stock options. The gate asks only about options "from an employer", so a director or contractor could truthfully answer no, and the line would be zero.

findings.situation: Within the gated branch, a filer sold ESPP or ISO shares in 2025 that were bought in 2024 or earlier (a disqualifying disposition), and the employer did not add the income to a W-2.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8k: "Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported"; i6251 p. 4, Line 2k: "a disqualifying disposition of stock acquired in a prior year by exercising an incentive stock option"
findings.why: The gate holds because of the sale, but the inner helper asks whether options were exercised in 2025. That answer is no, so the line is set to false even though the gated question's own help names this exact case.

findings.situation: A filer did a cashless or same-day-sale exercise and never held the shares.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 4, Line 2i: "no income is recognized when an incentive stock option (ISO) ... is exercised. However, this rule doesn't apply for the AMT"
findings.why: "Use stock options ... to buy shares" may not read to such a filer as covering a broker-handled cashless exercise. The "or sell shares bought that way" clause probably still catches it, but a filer could hesitate.

findings.situation: A filer only sold shares in 2025 from nonstatutory options exercised in an earlier year, with the compensation already included on a prior W-2.
findings.irs_text: i6251 p. 4, Line 2i: "If you acquired stock by exercising an ISO and you disposed of that stock in the same year ... no adjustment is required."
findings.why: The gate holds because of the sale, but neither line 8k nor the ISO AMT adjustment gets an amount.

findings.situation: A foreign child or a U.S. child with special needs was placed with the filer in 2023 or earlier, all costs were paid in 2023 or earlier, and the adoption became final in 2025; the filer may answer no because the child joined the family before 2024.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 1: 'You paid qualified adoption expenses in connection with the adoption of an eligible foreign child in: a. 2025 or prior years and the adoption became final in 2025' and '2. You adopted an eligible U.S. child with special needs and the adoption became final in 2025.'
findings.why: The gate asks whether the filer 'adopt[ed] a child' since the start of 2024 but never says the adoption counts when it becomes final, so a filer who dates the adoption from placement could answer no. Both s3.adoption and s3.adoption_earlier would then be zero, and a 2025 credit is dropped.

findings.situation: An employer paid costs for a foreign adoption in 2023, and the adoption became final in 2025, with the child already living with the filer before 2024.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3, Foreign Adoption: 'IF your employer pays for qualifying expenses ... in any year before the year the adoption becomes final THEN take the exclusion in the year the adoption becomes final.'
findings.why: The employer's payment is before 2024, so the gate holds only if the filer reads 'adopt a child' as the adoption becoming final in 2025. The help text does not say this, so scope.adoption_benefits may never be asked.

findings.situation: The filer paid costs in 2024 for a domestic adoption that became final in 2024 and had no other adoption activity.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3, Domestic Adoption: 'the year the adoption becomes final — the year the adoption becomes final.'
findings.why: The credit for these costs belongs on the 2024 return, so no gated line gets a 2025 amount, yet the gate holds.

locators: p. 1, Purpose of Form, "2024 and the adoption wasn’t final at the end of 2024"; p. 3, Domestic Adoption, "any year before the year the adoption becomes final"

p. 1, Purpose of Form, "You may be able to take this credit in 2025 if any of the following statements are true"; p. 3, Domestic Adoption, "any year before the year the adoption becomes final"

findings.situation: The filer paid qualified expenses in 2024 for a U.S. child, the adoption was not final at the end of 2024, it did not become final in 2025 (or was abandoned), and nothing was paid in 2025. The outer question is answered yes and the inner question is truthfully answered no, so the computed condition is false.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 1: "You paid qualified adoption expenses ... in: a. 2024 and the adoption wasn't final at the end of 2024"; p. 3 Domestic Adoption: "any year before the year the adoption becomes final* | the year after the year of the payment" and "you can take the adoption credit or exclusion even if the adoption never became final."
findings.why: Under the domestic table these 2024 payments are credited in 2025 whether or not the adoption is final. The inner question asks only about a 2025 finalization or 2025 payments, so this filer is gated out and the 2025 credit is dropped.

findings.situation: The cited text sets out when the credit may be taken in 2025, and the gate's inner question uses a narrower time frame than that text.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 1: "You may be able to take this credit in 2025 if any of the following statements are true. 1. ... a. 2024 and the adoption wasn't final at the end of 2024 ... 4. You have a carryforward of an adoption credit from 2024." Gate: "adopt a child whose adoption became final in 2025, or pay expenses in 2025 in connection with adopting a child"
findings.why: The gate leaves out statement 1a (2024 payments with the adoption still unfinished at year-end 2024) and statement 4 (a carryforward from 2024), both of which the cited condition includes.

findings.situation: In 2025 the filer's employer paid adoption expenses under a qualified program, for example for a foreign child whose adoption became final before 2025, and the filer personally paid nothing in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 1: "3. You received employer-provided adoption benefits in connection with the adoption of an eligible foreign child in: ... b. 2025 and the adoption became final before 2025"; p. 3: "IF your employer pays for qualifying expenses ... any year after the year the adoption becomes final | the year of the payment."
findings.why: The outer question says "pay (or have an employer pay)" but the inner question says only "pay expenses in 2025". A filer whose employer did the paying could reasonably answer no and lose the 2025 exclusion.

p. 3, Domestic Adoption, "the year after the year of the payment" and "the year the adoption becomes final"; p. 3, Foreign child, "you can’t take the adoption credit or exclusion unless the adoption becomes final"

findings.situation: A filer paid expenses in 2024 for a foreign child's adoption that was not final at the end of 2024; the condition holds, but the gated line ends up false because the answer is No.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3: "If the eligible child is a foreign child, you can't take the adoption credit or exclusion unless the adoption becomes final."
findings.why: The gate opens for any 2024 payment on a non-final adoption, not only for a U.S. child. The gated question then sorts out the foreign case, so this only costs one extra question.

findings.situation: A filer paid adoption-related costs in 2024 that are not qualified adoption expenses, such as costs for adopting a spouse's child or costs reimbursed by an employer; the condition holds even though no credit follows.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 1: "You paid qualified adoption expenses in connection with the adoption of an eligible U.S. child ... in: a. 2024 and the adoption wasn't final at the end of 2024"
findings.why: The helper asks about any expenses paid in connection with an adoption, not only qualified adoption expenses. This leans toward yes, which the gate design intends.

p. 3, Domestic Adoption, "If the eligible child is a U.S. citizen or resident, you can take the adoption credit or exclusion even if the adoption never became final" and "A child is a foreign child if they weren’t a citizen or resident of the United States (including U.S. territories) at the time the adoption effort began"

findings.situation: A filer paid expenses in 2024 or 2025 to adopt a U.S. stepchild without special needs, and the adoption was not final by the end of 2025 (or never became final), so the gate is false and the stepchild line defaults to false, which leaves the expenses treated as qualified.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3: "If the eligible child is a U.S. citizen or resident, you can take the adoption credit or exclusion even if the adoption never became final"; p. 2: "Qualified adoption expenses don’t include expenses: ... For the adoption of your spouse’s child"
findings.why: The spouse's-child exclusion applies whether or not the adoption is final. A U.S.-child credit or exclusion can arise without finality, so the stepchild refusal matters in exactly the case where this gate's finality condition is false.

findings.situation: A filer paid domestic adoption expenses in 2024 for an adoption that was not final in 2025, so the credit is taken in 2025, but the inner helper only asks whether the adoption became final in 2025 or expenses were paid in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3, Domestic Adoption: "any year before the year the adoption becomes final" → "the year after the year of the payment."
findings.why: Expenses paid in 2024 before finality produce a 2025 credit. A filer whose adoption neither became final in 2025 nor had 2025 payments truthfully answers no, so the computed condition is false while the stepchild exclusion still governs that credit.

findings.situation: A filer adopted a stepchild and the employer paid adoption benefits in 2025 for an adoption that is not final, so the exclusion is taken in the year of payment without regard to finality.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3, Domestic Adoption: "IF your employer pays for qualifying expenses under an adoption assistance program in... any year" → "the year of the payment."
findings.why: The domestic exclusion does not depend on finality. Expenses for a spouse's child are not qualified adoption expenses, but the gate drops the stepchild question whenever the adoption was not final.

findings.situation: A filer with more than one adoption, some final by the end of 2025 and some not, must answer "Was such an adoption final by the end of 2025?"
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3, Line 1: "If you can’t give complete information about an eligible child you tried to adopt in 2024 because the adoption was either unsuccessful or wasn’t final by the end of 2025"
findings.why: "Such an adoption" can be read as any one adoption or all of them. The gated question then asks only about children "whose adoption was final", so it never reaches a stepchild whose adoption was not final.

locators: p. 2, Qualified Adoption Expenses, "Qualified adoption expenses don’t include expenses" and "For the adoption of your spouse’s child"; p. 3, Child with special needs, "If you adopt a U.S. child with special needs, you may be able to exclude up to $17,280 and claim a credit"

p. 3, Domestic Adoption, "the year after the year of the payment" and "the year the adoption becomes final"; p. 3, Foreign child, "you can’t take the adoption credit or exclusion unless the adoption becomes final"

findings.situation: A person under 65 retired on permanent and total disability but has no taxable disability income for 2025, or had reached mandatory retirement age by January 1, 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040sr p. 1: "all three of the following statements are true. a. You retired on permanent and total disability. ... b. You receive taxable disability income for 2025. c. On January 1, 2025, you had not reached mandatory retirement age"
findings.why: The condition tests only statement (a), so it is true for some people who are not qualified individuals; the only cost is that the credit question is asked needlessly.

findings.situation: Someone on the return is 65 or older (or retired on disability) but cannot take the credit because of income, alien status, or filing separately while living with a spouse.
findings.irs_text: i1040sr p. 3: "If your AGI or your nontaxable pensions, annuities, or disability income are equal to or more than the income limits, you can't take the credit"; p. 1: "if you lived with your spouse at any time during 2025, you can't take the credit"; p. 1: "Generally, you can't take the credit if you were a nonresident alien at any time during the tax year"
findings.why: The condition holds on age or disability retirement alone, so the credit question is asked even though the credit is unavailable; the gate leans to yes by design.

findings.situation: A taxpayer who died in 2025 before reaching 65 would have turned 65 by the end of 2025, and the age helper may count them as 65 if it works from birth date alone.
findings.irs_text: i1040sr p. 1: "if the taxpayer died on February 12, 2025, the taxpayer isn't considered age 65 at the time of death or at the end of 2025"
findings.why: If the helper ignores the date of death, the condition is true for a person the IRS does not treat as 65; this only adds a question.

findings.situation: A filer's home charger was physically installed in late 2024 but only became operational (energized, inspected) in 2025, and the filer got no clean vehicle in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8911 p. 4, Line 5: "Generally, property is placed in service when it is ready and available for a specific use... For example, an EV charger installed at an individual taxpayer's principal residence will be placed in service when it is operational." i8911 p. 1, Purpose of Form: "alternative fuel vehicle refueling property you placed in service during your tax year"
findings.why: The IRS test is the date the equipment is placed in service (operational), not the date it is installed, so this filer can truthfully answer no to "In 2025, did you... install home equipment". The refueling-credit question (s3.ev_equipment) is then never asked and the 2025 credit is silently dropped.

findings.situation: A partner, S corporation shareholder or similar owner made the Form 1062 election for gain passed through from an entity that sold the farmland, and truthfully answers no because they did not personally sell any farmland.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 117, Line 13z: "If you made the election to defer net income tax attributable to the gain on the sale or exchange of qualified farmland property, use Form 1062 to figure the amount of your applicable net tax liability. On line 13z, enter 75% of your applicable net tax liability from Form 1062, line 14."
findings.why: The IRS text turns only on the filer having made the election, not on the filer being the seller, while the gate asks "did you (or... your spouse) sell farmland?". The page itself does not mention entity sales, so this rests on reading "you made the election" as wider than "you sold"; a no here silently zeroes the 1062NL amount.

findings.situation: A filer sold or exchanged land they never farmed themselves (for example land leased to a farmer, or pasture, orchard or farm buildings with land) and is unsure whether that counts as selling "farmland".
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 117, Line 13z: "gain on the sale or exchange of qualified farmland property"
findings.why: The gate says "farmland" with no explanation, while the IRS text uses the term "qualified farmland property"; a landlord or seller of mixed farm real estate could reasonably answer no.

findings.situation: A filer sold or traded farmland in 2025 but made no Form 1062 election.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 117, Line 13z: "If you made the election to defer net income tax attributable to the gain on the sale or exchange of qualified farmland property"
findings.why: The gate holds but line 13z gets no 1062NL amount; the gated follow-up question resolves this, so it costs one extra question.

findings.situation: A filer (or spouse) elected to pay a net 965 tax liability in installments because of a small interest in a domestic partnership or S corporation that was itself the U.S. shareholder of the foreign company, so the filer's own share of the foreign company, even counted through the entity, was under 10%.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 117, Line 13d: "If you elected to pay your net 965 tax liability in installments, report the deferred amount on line 13d. Enter the amount of net 965 tax liability remaining to be paid in future years."
findings.why: Line 13d depends only on the election and a remaining balance, not on 10% ownership. This filer can truthfully answer no to all three limbs if they never personally paid foreign income tax, so the deferred amount is silently dropped.

findings.situation: A filer took over someone else's remaining section 965 installments (for example as an heir or other transferee under a transfer agreement) and never owned 10% of a foreign company, paid foreign income tax or had territory income.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 117, Line 13d: "Enter the amount of net 965 tax liability remaining to be paid in future years."
findings.why: The line has an amount whenever installment liability remains, but the gate asks about ownership and foreign tax history that this filer does not have. The 965 question is then never asked.

findings.situation: A filer holding foreign shares through a partnership, S corporation or trust cannot tell whether "count shares held through" means the entity's whole holding or only their proportionate slice when testing the 10% threshold.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 117, Line 13d: "If you elected to pay your net 965 tax liability in installments, report the deferred amount on line 13d."
findings.why: Read as a proportionate slice, a minority owner of the entity answers no even though they carry a 965 installment balance. Read as the entity's whole holding, they answer yes.

findings.situation: A filer whose only foreign income tax was withheld at source or paid by a partnership, S corporation or trust (reported on Schedule K-3) may not regard themselves as having "paid income tax to another country"; the help addresses only fund tax in Form 1099-DIV box 7.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 115, Line 1: "all of that income and the foreign tax paid on it were reported to you on Form 1099-INT, Form 1099-DIV, or Schedule K-3 (or substitute statement)"; p. 117, Line 13z: "Use line 13z to report the credit under section 960(c) with respect to an excess limitation account."
findings.why: The IRS text treats tax reported through an entity as foreign tax paid by the filer. A filer who reads "paid" as paid directly could answer no and lose the 960(c) question, unless the 10% ownership limb happens to catch them.

findings.situation: A filer who once paid a small amount of foreign income tax years ago (for example on wages abroad, or on fund dividends claimed on Form 1116), or once had Puerto Rico or Guam income, answers yes although none of the three lines applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 117, Line 13z: "Use line 13z to report the credit under section 960(c) with respect to an excess limitation account ... Also use line 13z to report the amount of U.S. tax allocable to the U.S. Virgin Islands."
findings.why: "Ever" and "any U.S. territory" reach many filers with no 960(c) credit, no 965 installments and no Virgin Islands allocation. This only costs three extra questions.

findings.situation: A filer with an MCC takes the standard deduction, so no home mortgage interest is entered on Schedule A line 8a, yet the credit is still allowed.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 2, Line 3: "If you itemize your deductions on Schedule A, you must reduce the amount of home mortgage interest you would otherwise deduct on Schedule A by the amount on Form 8396, line 3"
findings.why: The credit depends on interest paid on the certified indebtedness, not on itemizing. Unless the tool fills line 8a for non-itemizers too, the computed condition is false and the credit is silently dropped.

findings.situation: The MCC loan interest was not reported on a Form 1098 (for example, a lender that issues only a similar statement), so it goes on Schedule A line 8b and line 8a is zero.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 2, Line 1: "In most cases, this will be the amount in box 1 on Form 1098, Mortgage Interest Statement, or on a similar statement you received from your mortgage holder."
findings.why: Form 8396 line 1 is any interest paid on the certified indebtedness, with or without a Form 1098. A test on line 8a alone misses interest entered on line 8b.

findings.situation: A filer paid no mortgage interest in 2025 (loan paid off, or home sold) but has unused mortgage interest credit carried forward from 2022 to 2024.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 1, lines 4-6: "Enter any 2022 credit carryforward from line 16 of your 2024 Form 8396"; p. 2, Purpose of Form: "Use Form 8396 to figure the mortgage interest credit for 2025 and any credit carryforward to 2026."
findings.why: Carryforwards feed lines 7 and 9 even when line 1 is zero, so the note "the credit is a share of the interest paid" is not true of the whole credit. If the MCC answer is what opens Form 8396 in the tool, forcing it to false drops the carryforward.

findings.situation: The cited text bases the credit on interest paid on the certified indebtedness, while the gate tests the amount deducted on Schedule A line 8a.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 2, Line 1: "Enter the interest you paid during the year on the loan amount (certified indebtedness amount) shown on your MCC"; gate: "sa line 8a > $0"
findings.why: Interest paid on the MCC loan and interest entered on line 8a are different quantities. Line 8a exists only for itemizers, covers only Form 1098 interest, and is itself reduced by Form 8396 line 3.

findings.situation: Most filers with interest on Schedule A line 8a have no MCC, and are still asked the MCC question.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 2, Who Can Claim the Credit: "You can claim the credit only if you were issued a qualified Mortgage Credit Certificate (MCC) by a state or local governmental unit or agency"
findings.why: The condition holds for every itemizer with mortgage interest although only MCC holders get an amount. This is the acceptable lean to yes.

locators: p. 2, Line 1, "Enter the interest you paid during the year on the loan amount (certified indebtedness amount) shown on your MCC"

findings.situation: Kerosene was used in the home for heating, lighting or cooking, but it was dyed (untaxed) kerosene or was bought from a blocked pump, so no credit is available.
findings.irs_text: i4136 (2025) p. 2: "If you are claiming a credit for the tax on undyed kerosene you purchased (other than from a blocked pump) and used in your home during the tax period for heating, lighting, or cooking."
findings.why: The gate asks only about home use of kerosene, so it is yes for kerosene that cannot earn the credit; this costs one extra question and drops no amount.

findings.why: The gate asks only about an AMT liability, which is broader than the cited two-part condition; the gated question then applies the second part. This costs extra questions but drops no amount.

findings.situation: A filer has an unused District of Columbia first-time homebuyer credit (or a mortgage interest or general business credit) carried from 2023 or earlier, and was not required to file, and did not file, a 2024 return because their income was below the filing threshold.
findings.irs_text: f8859 p. 1, Line 4: "You can carry forward any unused credit shown on line 4 until you have used all of it"; i3800 p. 3: "unused general business credits may be carried back 1 year and carried forward 20 years"; f8396 p. 2: "carry forward to the next 3 tax years or until used"
findings.why: Not filing for 2024 does not end the carryforward, so it still reaches the 2025 Form 8859, 3800 or 8396. The help text "If you did not file for 2024, answer No" makes this filer answer no, and the amount is silently set to zero.

findings.situation: The filer's 2024 return includes Form 8582-CR (or another form whose number has a suffix) and no other attachment.

findings.why: A filer could read "8582-CR" as not being a plain four-digit number and answer no, which drops the passive-activity credit carryforward the gated question asks about.

findings.situation: A filer whose 2024 return was Form 1040-SR or 1040-NR alone, or 1040 with an attachment such as Form 8962 or 8867, answers yes but has no carryforward or AMT.
findings.irs_text: i8801 p. 1, Who Should File: "An AMT liability and adjustments or preferences other than exclusion items, • A credit carryforward to 2025 (on 2024 Form 8801, line 26)"
findings.why: The condition holds even when every gated line is zero. This costs only extra questions and is acceptable by design.

findings.situation: A filer has three or more qualifying children (line 16b is $5,100 or more), or line 16a is zero, so the bona fide resident of Puerto Rico status changes no amount on Schedule 8812, yet the condition holds and the question is asked.
findings.irs_text: f1040s8812 (2025) p. 2, after line 20: "Next. On line 16b, is the amount $5,100 or more? No. If you are a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico, go to line 21. ... Yes. If line 20 is equal to or more than line 17, skip Part II-B ... Otherwise, go to line 21."
findings.why: The Puerto Rico routing only matters when line 16b is under $5,100 and line 16a is above zero. When line 16b is $5,100 or more, the filer reaches line 21 the same way whether or not they lived in Puerto Rico. The gate leans to yes by design, so this costs only an extra question.

findings.situation: A filer (or spouse) gave nothing to charity in 2025 but has an unused charitable contribution carryover from an earlier year, for example from gifts made in 2021 through 2024 that exceeded the income limits.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 11, Line 13: "You may have contributions that you couldn't deduct in an earlier year because they exceeded the limits on the amount you could deduct. In most cases, you have 5 years to use contributions that were limited in an earlier year."
findings.why: The gate asks only about gifts given or volunteer money spent in 2025, so this filer can truthfully answer no. The tool then sets sa.charity_limited_if_gifts to false and never asks about the carryover, so the out-of-scope refusal is silently skipped and the line 13 amount is dropped. The gate must also ask about unused charitable carryovers from prior years.

findings.situation: A filer whose only home mortgage interest goes on line 8b, for example a seller-financed loan with no Form 1098, used part of the loan proceeds to pay off other debts. Line 8a is $0, so the tool never asks the other-use question.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "Check the box on line 8 if you had one or more home mortgages in 2025 with an outstanding balance and you didn't use all of your home mortgage proceeds from those loans to buy, build, or substantially improve your home." Line 8b: "Your deductible mortgage interest may be less than what you paid if one or more of the limits on home mortgage interest apply to you."
findings.why: The checkbox and the proceeds-use limit apply to every home mortgage, not only to interest reported on Form 1098. Gating on line 8a > $0 misses filers whose interest is on line 8b, and filers with only line 8c points.

findings.situation: All of a home equity loan's proceeds were used for other purposes, so the deductible amount on line 8a is $0. The box must still be checked.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8a: "Only enter on line 8a the deductible mortgage interest and points that were reported to you on Form 1098." Line 8: "Interest paid on home mortgage proceeds used for other purposes isn't deductible on lines 8a or 8b."
findings.why: Line 8a holds the deductible amount after the limits are applied, so the gate depends on a figure that this very question can reduce to zero. When it does, the gate is false and the line 8 checkbox is dropped.

findings.situation: A filer spent home equity loan proceeds on minor repairs or upkeep rather than a substantial improvement.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "to buy, build, or substantially improve the home securing the loan"
findings.why: The question says "buying, building or improving it", without "substantially". A filer who spent the money on ordinary repairs could truthfully answer No, but under the IRS text those proceeds were used for other purposes.

findings.situation: The other-use proceeds came from a loan taken out on or before October 13, 1987.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "The only exception to this limit is for loans taken out on or before October 13, 1987; the loan proceeds for these loans are treated as having been used to buy, build, or substantially improve the home."
findings.why: Neither the question nor its help mentions this exception. Such a filer would answer Yes, and the interview would end even though the box is not required for these loans.

findings.situation: The cited threshold is 7.5% of adjusted gross income, but the gate asks about 7.5% of "your income", which a filer may read as total or gross income (wages, all receipts) before adjustments.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 1: "You can deduct only the part of your medical and dental expenses that exceeds 7.5% of the amount of your adjusted gross income on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11b."
findings.why: AGI can be lower than the income a filer has in mind, for example after IRA, HSA or self-employment adjustments. Costs can exceed 7.5% of AGI but not 7.5% of gross income, so the filer truthfully answers no and line 1 and the deduction are dropped.

findings.situation: Medicare Part B or Part D premiums are withheld from social security benefits that are wholly or partly untaxed, and the filer's other costs, without those premiums, are under 7.5% of income.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 1: "The supplemental part of Medicare insurance (Medicare Part B)." "The premiums you pay for Medicare Part D insurance."
findings.why: These premiums are deductible, but they were not paid with "money already taxed" in any sense a filer would recognize, so the second helper is truthfully no. If the first helper is also no, the premiums that would push the total over 7.5% of AGI are dropped.

findings.situation: A filer answering the first helper may not count insurance premiums as "medical and dental costs" and so compares only bills to the 7.5% threshold.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 2: "Don't forget to include insurance premiums you paid for medical and dental care."
findings.why: The first helper does not say premiums count. When the second helper also fails, as with untaxed-money premiums, a filer who leaves premiums out can answer no although bills plus premiums exceed 7.5% of AGI.

findings.situation: The filer paid some health insurance with after-tax money, but total medical costs, premiums included, are below 7.5% of AGI.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 1: "You can deduct only the part of your medical and dental expenses that exceeds 7.5% of the amount of your adjusted gross income"
findings.why: The second helper makes the condition true even though no deduction results. This only costs a question.

findings.situation: Costs over 7.5% of income were paid with tax-free HSA or Archer MSA distributions or through a pretax plan, and excluding those amounts leaves costs under the threshold.
findings.irs_text: p969 p. 9: "You can't deduct qualified medical expenses as an itemized deduction on Schedule A (Form 1040) that are equal to the tax-free distribution from your HSA."
findings.why: The first helper does not tell the filer to leave out tax-free-funded costs, so it can be true when the line 1 amount produces no deduction.

findings.situation: A married-filing-separately filer pays mortgage interest to a lender who sends no Form 1098, reports it only on line 8b, and has more than $375,000 of debt (or debt above the home's value); the computed condition is false because nothing is on line 8a.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8b: "If you paid home mortgage interest to a recipient who didn't provide you a Form 1098, report your deductible mortgage interest on line 8b. Your deductible mortgage interest may be less than what you paid if one or more of the limits on home mortgage interest apply to you."
findings.why: The $375,000/$500,000 and fair-market-value limits also apply to interest reported on line 8b, but the gate looks only at line 8a. This MFS filer's over-limit answer is silently set to no.

findings.situation: A married-filing-separately filer whose shared mortgage interest was reported on another borrower's Form 1098 reports their share only on line 8b, so the line 8a helper is false even though the debt exceeds the MFS limit.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, More than one borrower: "If the shared interest was reported on the other person's Form 1098, report your share of the interest on line 8b"
findings.why: Interest paid on a shared mortgage can appear only on line 8b and is still subject to the debt limits. The gate keyed to line 8a misses it.

findings.situation: A married-filing-separately filer whose debt was all taken out on or before December 15, 2017 and totals between $375,000 and $500,000 (and is below the home's value) answers yes to the question's headline wording.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "you can only deduct home mortgage interest on up to $1,000,000 ($500,000 if you are married filing separately) of that debt"
findings.why: No limit applies to this filer. The question's main text names only $375,000, and the $500,000 exception appears only in the help text, so a yes here is a harmless over-ask.

findings.situation: A filer whose debt is between $750,000 and $1,000,000, all taken out on or before December 15, 2017, could answer yes from the question's own wording, although the help text sets the limit at $1,000,000.

findings.why: The question leans to yes, as gates are meant to. This costs only an unneeded refusal, not a dropped amount.

findings.situation: A filer pays a yearly car registration fee figured partly on the car's value and partly on its weight.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5c: "Part of the fee was based on the car's value and part was based on its weight. You can deduct only the part of the fee that was based on the car's value."
findings.why: The gate help says a fee "based on weight, does not count," so a filer whose fee is partly weight-based could reasonably answer no. The value-based part of that fee belongs on line 5c, and only the gated question's help explains the split.

findings.situation: A filer makes a cash charitable contribution in exchange for a state tax credit and applies that credit to a yearly value-based personal property tax, without paying the tax in cash.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3: "to the extent you apply the state or local tax credit to this or a prior year's state or local tax liability, you may include this amount on line 5a, 5b, or 5c, whichever is appropriate"
findings.why: The gate asks whether the filer "pay[s]" the tax. A filer who settled the tax liability with a credit could reasonably say they paid nothing. Under the safe harbor, that amount still goes on line 5c.

findings.situation: A filer pays in 2025 a value-based yearly tax that is not assessed until 2026.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 7: "Only taxes paid in 2025 and assessed prior to 2026 can be deducted for 2025."
findings.why: The gate is yes for this tax, but line 5c gets no amount for it. The gated question already limits the amount to taxes assessed before 2026.

findings.situation: A filer pays only a U.S. territory personal property tax that is allocable to excluded income.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3: "don't include any U.S. territory taxes you paid that are allocable to excluded income"
findings.why: The gate counts territory taxes without this exception, so it is yes even though line 5c gets nothing.

findings.why: The gate question presents a closed list after a colon. Tax on business-use real estate is not deductible on line 5b but is not on that list, so a truthful filer can answer no while a nondeductible amount remains.

findings.why: Escrowed amounts not remitted in 2025 are not deductible, but the question's list does not mention them, so the filer can truthfully answer no.

findings.situation: The filer's only 2025 state estimated tax is a 2024 state overpayment they chose to apply to 2025, and they sent no money to the state in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "State and local estimated tax payments made during 2025, including any part of a prior year refund that you chose to have credited to your 2025 state or local income taxes."
findings.why: The gate asks whether the filer "pay[s]" tax by estimated payments, and its help never mentions a credited refund. A filer who only left a refund with the state could truthfully think they paid nothing and answer no, which drops an amount the gated question itself says to include.

findings.situation: State income tax was withheld from nonemployee compensation or other income reported on Form 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC, not deducted on Schedule C, E or F, and the filer has no other non-salary state tax.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "Forms W-2G, 1099-G, 1099-R, 1099-MISC, and 1099-NEC may also show state and local income taxes withheld"

findings.situation: A filer or spouse receives interest from a bank account, or dividends from stock, as a nominee, and owns no bonds or notes, cashed no savings bonds, and received no loan or sale interest.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "You received interest or ordinary dividends as a nominee." ... "enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total interest you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal"; p. 2 gives the same rule for line 5 dividends.
findings.why: The bond helper is truthfully No, so the computed gate is false and the 'other adjustment' bullet is never asked. The nominee subtraction on lines 2 and 6 is silently dropped.

findings.situation: The gate cites the Schedule B 'Use Schedule B if any of the following applies' list but replaces it with a different condition built on bonds, savings bonds and loan or sale interest.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "Use Schedule B (Form 1040) if any of the following applies ... You received interest or ordinary dividends as a nominee."
findings.why: The gate's condition is 'Bonds or notes owned directly, savings bonds cashed, or interest on a loan or a sale, when taxable interest, ordinary dividends or capital gain distributions are above zero'. This omits the cited nominee item, which has nothing to do with bonds or loans, so the gate does not match the cited condition.

findings.situation: A filer whose only interest is tax-exempt municipal bond interest, from bonds bought at a premium or at an acquisition premium, has no taxable interest, ordinary dividends or capital gain distributions.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "if you acquired a tax-exempt bond at a premium, only report the net amount of tax-exempt interest on line 2a ... Also, if you acquired a tax-exempt OID bond at an acquisition premium, only report the net amount of tax-exempt OID"
findings.why: The 'above zero' helper is false, so the bond-premium question (which itself mentions 1099-INT box 13) is never asked, and the premium adjustment the IRS requires is skipped.

findings.situation: A filer holds Treasury, corporate or other bonds in a brokerage account, bought between interest dates or at a premium, and receives a 1099-INT from the broker.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "When you buy bonds between interest payment dates and pay accrued interest to the seller ... identify the amount to be subtracted as 'Accrued Interest.'" and "If you elect to reduce your interest income on a taxable bond by the amount of taxable amortizable bond premium ... 'ABP Adjustment.'"
findings.why: 'Bonds or notes owned directly' could reasonably be read as excluding bonds held through a broker. A filer reading it that way answers No, and the accrued-interest or premium adjustment is lost.

findings.situation: A filer receives a Form 1099-OID for a long-term certificate of deposit and reports less OID than the form shows.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "If you are reporting OID in an amount less than the amount shown in box 1 or box 8 of Form 1099-OID ... identify the amount to be subtracted as 'OID Adjustment.'"
findings.why: A filer may not consider a CD to be a 'bond or note' and could answer No. The OID adjustment question would then never be asked.

findings.situation: A filer owns bonds directly, or cashed savings bonds, and receives ordinary interest with no accrued interest, premium, OID difference, market discount, seller financing or exclusion.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "Line 1. Report on line 1 all of your taxable interest."
findings.why: The gate holds, but no special treatment applies, so the gated line has no amount. This only costs one extra question.

findings.situation: A filer receives seller-financing interest from a buyer who did not use the property as a personal residence.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "You received interest from a seller-financed mortgage and the buyer used the property as a personal residence."
findings.why: The gate covers any interest on a property sold, which is broader than the cited personal-residence condition. This is harmless leaning to yes.

findings.situation: The filer owns more than 50% of a U.S. corporation, partnership or LLC, or is the grantor-owner of or a >50% beneficiary of a U.S. trust, and that entity holds a bank account abroad; the filer has no foreign account or asset in their own name and no 10% interest in a foreign company.
findings.irs_text: fincen114 p. 5, Financial Interest: 'the owner of record or holder of legal title is ... b. A corporation in which the United States person owns directly or indirectly ... more than 50 percent ... c. A partnership ... d. A trust of which the United States person (i) is the trust grantor and (ii) has an ownership interest ... e. A trust in which the United States person has a greater than 50 percent present beneficial interest'; i1040sb p. 3: 'For definitions of "financial interest" ... see the instructions for FinCEN Form 114.'
findings.why: The account belongs to the domestic entity, so a filer can truthfully answer no to 'did you ... have an account in another country.' The trust helper covers only foreign trusts, and the company helper covers only companies set up outside the U.S. Yet line 7a, the FBAR count and possibly Form 8938 all reach this account.

findings.situation: The filer owns a U.S. single-member LLC (a disregarded entity) or is treated as owner of a domestic grantor trust, and that LLC or trust holds a foreign account, foreign stock or another specified foreign financial asset.
findings.irs_text: i8938 p. 8: 'If you are the owner of a disregarded entity, you have an interest in any specified foreign financial assets owned by the disregarded entity'; 'If you are considered the owner under the grantor trust rules ... of any part of a trust, you have an interest in any specified foreign financial asset held by that part of the trust.'
findings.why: All five helpers ask what 'you' had, owned or were connected to. A filer whose foreign asset is titled to a domestic LLC or domestic trust can truthfully answer no to every helper, which drops Form 8938 and line 7a.

findings.situation: Parents elect on Form 8814 to report their child's interest and dividends, and the child holds a foreign account or other specified foreign financial asset; neither parent has a foreign connection of their own.
findings.irs_text: i8938 p. 8, Interests in Assets Generating Certain Unearned Income of Children: 'If you file Form 8814 ... you have an interest in any specified foreign financial asset held by the child.'
findings.why: The helpers ask only about the filer and spouse, so the child's foreign asset never makes the computed condition true. The Form 8938 question is then never asked, even though the parent has a reportable interest.

findings.situation: The filer directly holds stock or securities of a foreign issuer outside any account (for example, share certificates kept at home), a foreign partnership interest, or a swap or derivative with a foreign counterparty.
findings.irs_text: i8938 p. 7: 'Examples of other specified foreign financial assets include ... Stock issued by a foreign corporation ... A capital or profits interest in a foreign partnership ... An option or other derivative instrument ... entered into with a foreign counterparty.'
findings.why: 'Own anything else of value outside the United States' can be read as asking where the property physically sits, not who issued it. A filer holding foreign-issued stock or a contract in the U.S. could answer no, and the company helper requires a 10% stake or an officer role.

findings.situation: The filer holds an interest in a foreign estate, such as being an heir to an estate administered abroad.
findings.irs_text: i8938 p. 8, Interests in Foreign Estates and Foreign Trusts: 'An interest in a foreign trust or a foreign estate is not a specified foreign financial asset unless you know or have reason to know ... of the interest.'
findings.why: The trust helper names trusts and family foundations, not estates. Whether an expected inheritance counts as 'anything else of value' you 'own' outside the U.S. is open to either reading.

findings.situation: The filer's only connection is an account at a bank in Puerto Rico or Guam, or an officer role in a foreign company that has no accounts the filer can sign for.
findings.irs_text: fincen114 p. 5: 'the United States includes ... all United States territories and possessions'; i1040sb p. 3: 'A financial account is located in a foreign country if the account is physically located outside of the United States.'
findings.why: The condition holds, but line 7a and the FBAR give a territory account no amount; only Form 8938 can reach it. The officer role leads to Form 5471, which is not a gated line.

findings.situation: A filer or spouse holds less than 10% of a foreign corporation's value but 10% or more of its voting power (for example, through voting preferred shares), and reads the helper's 'owner ... of 10% or more' as an equity or value share only.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: 'You may also have to file Form 5471 if, in 2025, you owned 10% or more of the total (a) value of a foreign corporation's stock, or (b) combined voting power of all classes of a foreign corporation's stock with voting rights.'
findings.why: The gate's '10% or more of one' does not say value or votes. A filer could reasonably read it as an ownership share by value and answer no, while the IRS text also counts the voting-power test.

findings.situation: A filer's 10% of a foreign corporation is held through a partnership, corporation, trust or estate they have an interest in, or through options or warrants, rather than directly or by family members.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: 'you owned 10% or more of the total (a) value of a foreign corporation's stock'
findings.why: The gate counts only ownership 'alone or with your family.' The gated question and its help count shares held by entities and option shares, so a filer whose stake is indirect could truthfully answer the gate no and never reach the gated question.

findings.situation: A filer whose only connection is a bank account, investment or trust in Puerto Rico, Guam or another U.S. territory, with no role in or 10% of a foreign corporation.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: 'You may have to file Form 5471 if, in 2025, you were an officer or director of a foreign corporation.'
findings.why: The second helper makes the condition true for territory accounts and investments that have no bearing on Form 5471. This only adds questions.

findings.situation: A filer who is a manager of, or 10% owner of, a foreign entity that is not a corporation, such as a foreign partnership.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: 'officer or director of a foreign corporation'
findings.why: The gate asks about any 'company set up outside the United States,' which is broader than the foreign-corporation scope of Form 5471.
