findings.situation: The trust is administered by U.S. trustees under a state court, but a foreign protector or other non-trustee foreign person can veto substantial decisions, so it is a foreign trust; the filer was its grantor or received a distribution from it, yet truthfully says it is not 'outside the United States' and has no 'trustee abroad'.
findings.irs_text: cfr-26-301-7701-7 p. 4: "Control ... with no other person having the power to veto any of the substantial decisions. To determine whether United States persons have control, it is necessary to consider all persons who have authority to make a substantial decision of the trust, not only the trust fiduciaries."; p. 2: "The term foreign trust means any trust other than a domestic trust."
findings.why: The helper tests foreignness only by location and trustee residence. A trust that fails the control test because of a foreign non-trustee power holder is foreign, but the condition is false.

findings.situation: In 2025 the filer sold or lent property to a foreign trust at arm's length, or borrowed cash or securities from one, or used its property free, and does not see that as having 'gave to it' or as someone who 'may receive from it'.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 3, Line 8: "For this purpose, a loan of cash or marketable securities is generally considered to be a distribution"; "If you were the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust that existed during 2025, you may have to file Form 3520."
findings.why: A transferor includes someone who sells or lends to the trust, and a loan from the trust counts as a distribution. The helper's 'gave to it' and 'may receive from it' suggest gifts and future benefits, so a truthful filer can answer no.

findings.situation: The filer received a final distribution in 2025 from a foreign trust that then ended, or made a transfer in an earlier year to a foreign trust that still existed in 2025 but with which the filer no longer has dealings.
findings.irs_text: f1040sb Part III line 8: "During 2025, did you receive a distribution from, or were you the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust?"
findings.why: The helper is in the present tense ('do you ... have anything to do with', 'may receive'). A filer whose connection ended can truthfully answer no, although line 8 asks about any 2025 distribution and about past grantor or transferor status.

findings.situation: A filer received a 2025 distribution from a foreign trust through an intermediary, such as a nominee, a company or a relative.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 3, Line 8: "If you received a distribution from a foreign trust, you must provide additional information."
findings.why: 'Have anything to do with ... as the person who ... may receive from it' does not say whether indirect receipt counts. The gated question's help says it does, but the gate question gives the filer no such guidance.

findings.situation: The filer has only a U.S. territory account, investment or company, with no foreign trust connection.
findings.irs_text: f1040sb line 8: "did you receive a distribution from, or were you the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust?"
findings.why: The territory helper makes the condition true even though line 8 would be no. This costs only an extra question.

findings.situation: A filer whose only investment income is ordinary bank interest or fund dividends is asked both gated questions, even though none of the bond, savings-bond, seller-financing or nominee situations applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "Use Schedule B (Form 1040) if any of the following applies. ... You received interest from a seller-financed mortgage ... You have accrued interest from a bond ... You received interest or ordinary dividends as a nominee."
findings.why: Having any interest or dividends is only a precondition for these situations, so the gate asks more often than needed. This is harmless because gates lean to yes.

findings.situation: A filer whose only investment income is capital gain distributions (Form 1099-DIV box 2a) is asked the bond and nominee questions.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "Line 5. Report on line 5 all of your ordinary dividends. This amount should be shown in box 1a of your Forms 1099-DIV"; the nominee rules cover only interest (line 1) and ordinary dividends (line 5).
findings.why: With no interest or ordinary dividends, neither gated line can have an effect on Schedule B. Including capital gain distributions only widens the gate.

locators: p. 1, General Instructions, "Use Schedule B (Form 1040) if any of the following applies", "You received interest from a seller-financed mortgage", "You have accrued interest from a bond", "You are reporting original issue discount (OID) of less than the amount shown on Form 1099-OID", "You are reporting interest income of less than the amount shown on a Form 1099 due to amortizable bond premium", "You are claiming the exclusion of interest from series EE or I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989", "You received interest or ordinary dividends as a nominee"

findings.situation: A sole proprietor with no employees in 2025 contributes on their own behalf, as a self-employed person, to a dependent care assistance program and figures the deductible part on Form 2441 for line 14.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 7, Line 14: "If you made contributions on your behalf as a self-employed person to a dependent care assistance program, complete Form 2441, Parts I and III, to figure your deductible contributions to that program."
findings.why: The instructions put a self-employed person's own dependent care contributions on line 14 without requiring any employee. The gate's help says "You are not an employee of your own business," so this filer truthfully answers no, and line 14 is zeroed. The gated question's help ("Not for yourself") also excludes this amount.

findings.situation: A business with no workers during 2025 still pays in 2025 a final paycheck, accident and health or group-term life costs, or deductible plan contributions for people who were employees in an earlier year.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 10, Line 26: "Enter the total salaries and wages for the tax year"; p. 8, Line 19: "contributions you made for the benefit of your employees to a pension, profit-sharing, or annuity plan"
findings.why: "Did this business have employees in 2025" can be read as asking whether anyone worked for the business in 2025, which gives a no. It can also be read as "people it paid wages to" in 2025, which gives a yes. A filer with only former employees could reasonably answer no and drop 2025 amounts on lines 14, 19 and 26.

locators: Schedule C (2025), lines 14, 19 and 26

p. 10, Line 26, "Enter the total salaries and wages for the tax year" and "If you provided taxable fringe benefits to your employees, such as personal use of a car, do not deduct as wages the amount applicable to depreciation and other expenses claimed elsewhere"
p. 8, Line 19

findings.situation: A business bought or produced merchandise in 2025, but all of it was destroyed, stolen, or spoiled before sale, so it sold none and held none at the start or end of the year.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 15, Part III: "if you engaged in a trade or business in which the production, purchase, or sale of merchandise was an income-producing factor, you must take inventories into account"; f1040sc p. 2, line 36 "Purchases less cost of items withdrawn for personal use"
findings.why: The IRS condition is triggered by production or purchase alone, and lines 36 to 39 would carry those costs. The gate asks only about goods sold or held at the start or end of the year, so this filer can truthfully answer no, and the costs are dropped.

findings.situation: A business holds only raw materials or unfinished work in process at year end, or it sold nothing.
findings.irs_text: Gate: "hold goods for sale at the start or end of the year"; i1040sc p. 15: "you must take inventories into account at the beginning and end of your tax year"
findings.why: A filer could read "goods for sale" as finished goods only. The help text says materials that become part of what you sell count, but that help is easy to miss, and unfinished goods are not clearly "for sale."

findings.situation: A small business taxpayer that sells goods but treats inventory as nonincidental materials and supplies, deducting them as they are used and keeping no inventory, answers yes.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 15: "If you are a small business taxpayer, you can choose not to keep an inventory"
findings.why: This filer may have nothing to enter on lines 35 and 41, and possibly no amounts on Part III at all, but the gate still asks the questions. That is acceptable by design.

findings.situation: An accrual-method business incurred 2025 lodging, airfare or business-meal expenses but did not pay them until 2026, so the owner truthfully answers no to 'did this business pay for' in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 9, Line 24a: 'You can't deduct expenses paid or incurred in connection with employment away from home...'; '...only if you did not pay or incur meal expenses on a day you were traveling'
findings.why: The IRS text treats expenses as deductible when 'paid or incurred', but the gate asks only whether the business paid in 2025. An accrual filer with incurred but unpaid 2025 travel or meal costs is dropped. The helper wording 'had expenses' would cover this, but the asked question does not.

findings.situation: An owner traveled overnight on business in their own car (deducted on line 9), stayed free with relatives, bought no meals, and claims the optional $5-a-day incidental expense amount on line 24a.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 9, Line 24a: 'you can use an optional method for deducting incidental expenses only if you did not pay or incur meal expenses on a day you were traveling away from your tax home. The amount of the deduction is $5 a day.'
findings.why: The $5-a-day amount is allowed in place of records of actual spending. A filer who paid nothing for lodging, transport or meals on line 24a could truthfully answer no to 'pay for overnight travel' and lose the deduction.

findings.situation: A filer drove their own vehicle on an overnight business trip and paid for gas but no lodging or airfare.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 9, Line 24a: 'Enter your expenses for lodging and transportation connected with overnight travel for business while away from your tax home.'
findings.why: A filer could read 'pay for overnight travel' to mean only tickets and hotels, not car costs or incidentals. The filer might then answer no even though the trip had overnight travel that can carry incidental or standard-meal-allowance amounts.

findings.situation: An owner bought only their own non-travel lunches or food for their family, which no gated line allows.
findings.irs_text: p587 p. 13, Meals: 'You can never deduct the cost of food consumed by you or your family.'
findings.why: The gate's 'any meals, food or drink' produces a yes here, though every gated line is zero. This is acceptable by design.

findings.situation: A filer whose only service was in 2022–2024, with no 2025 duty, PCS move, travel or repayment, answers yes and then sees three questions that all come back zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93, Line 14: "You can deduct moving expenses if you are a member of the Armed Forces on active duty and due to a military order you move because of a permanent change of station"; Line 12: "National Guard and reserve members who traveled more than 100 miles from home"
findings.why: The moving and travel lines need status or duty in 2025 itself. The look-back to 2022 exists only for reservist repayments, which can come up to two years after active duty ends, so the gate is wider than those two lines need.

findings.situation: A filer who serves in the armed forces (for example, regular active duty with no reservist call-up, PCS move or reserve travel) answers yes, but every gated line is zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 95, Line 20 item 9: "Don't include any repayments of qualified reservist distributions. You can't deduct them."
findings.why: Military service alone gives none of the gated lines an amount. Each line needs a specific 2025 event, so the gate costs only a few extra questions.

locators: p. 93, Line 12, "Certain business expenses of National Guard and reserve members who traveled more than 100 miles from home"
p. 93, Line 14, "You can deduct moving expenses if you are a member of the Armed Forces on active duty and due to a military order you move because of a permanent change of station"
p. 95, Line 20, "Don’t include any repayments of qualified reservist distributions"

findings.situation: A fee-basis state or local government official is paid in fees reported on a Form 1099 or not reported on any form, so the return lists no Form W-2.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93, Line 12: 'Include the following deductions on line 12. ... • Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials. For more details, see Form 2106.'
findings.why: The cited text allows the fee-basis official deduction without requiring a Form W-2, but the computed condition is false whenever no W-2 is listed. The artist/official question is never asked, so the refusal for this deduction is silently skipped.

findings.situation: A filer with a W-2 who did some performing-arts work but does not meet the 'qualified performing artist' rules answers yes to the artist/official question.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93, Line 12: 'Performing-arts-related expenses as a qualified performing artist.'
findings.why: The broad question 'work as a performing artist' covers filers who don't qualify, which costs only an extra question.

locators: p. 93, Line 12, "Performing-arts-related expenses as a qualified performing artist", "Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials"

p. 93, Line 12, "Performing-arts-related expenses as a qualified performing artist", "Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials"; p. 93, Line 12, "For more details, see Form 2106"

findings.situation: A filer who first bought a passive business interest during 2025 (for example a limited partnership, an S corporation share, or publicly traded partnership units) and has a 2025 loss from it must answer the gate no, so the passive-activity refusal is never reached.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 1, Who Must File: "Form 8582 is filed by individuals, estates, and trusts who have passive activity deductions (including prior year unallowed losses)." Purpose of Form: "Trade or business activities in which you did not materially participate for the tax year."
findings.why: Passive activity deductions arise in the year the interest is first held, so owning it before 2025 is not required. The help text routes only 2025 rentals to a later question. A non-rental passive interest acquired in 2025 is silently treated as no.

findings.situation: For the passive-activity refusal, the cited text's own filing condition is having passive activity deductions, but the gate requires owning a business, farm, rental, or partnership or S corporation share before 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 1: "Form 8582 is filed by individuals, estates, and trusts who have passive activity deductions (including prior year unallowed losses)." Gate (citing f1040 lines 8, 10, 13b, 16, 19–20, 27–31): "In any year before 2025, did you ... own a business, a farm, a rental property, or a share of a partnership or an S corporation?"
findings.why: The Who Must File condition has no prior-year time frame. The gate adds a "before 2025" ownership requirement that is not in the cited text.

findings.situation: A freelancer or independent contractor who filed Schedule C in a prior year and elected section 179 might not think of themselves as having "owned a business" and could answer the gate no.
findings.irs_text: i4562 (2025) p. 5, Line 10: "the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed as a deduction because of the business income limitation"
findings.why: "Own a business" can be read as excluding self-employment or sole-proprietor gig work. A section 179 carryover from that work would then be dropped.

locators: p. 5, Line 10, "The carryover of disallowed deduction from 2024 is the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed as a deduction because of the business income limitation" and "If you filed Form 4562 for 2024, enter the amount from line 13 of your 2024 Form 4562" (owner: the printed amount)
, Purpose of Form, "Form 8582 is used by noncorporate taxpayers to figure the amount of any passive activity loss (PAL)"
p. 34, Line 16, "Tax from Form 8978, line 14 (relating to partner’s audit liability under section 6226)"

findings.situation: A filer who held or sold an option or warrant on stock of a foreign investment company in 2025 but no shares (for example, warrants of a Cayman-incorporated SPAC) can truthfully answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 114, Line 17p: "Enter any interest amount from Form 8621, line 16f, relating to distributions from, and dispositions of, stock of a section 1291 fund"; p. 34, Line 16: "Any tax from Form 8621, line 16e, relating to a section 1291 fund"
findings.why: Under section 1298 and its regulations, an option to acquire PFIC stock is treated as stock for section 1291 purposes, so selling the option can produce Form 8621 line 16e tax and line 16f interest. The question asks only about owning 'shares,' and its help does not mention options or warrants.

findings.situation: A filer holding a foreign-domiciled ETF (for example, an Irish UCITS ETF) can read 'other than through a U.S. mutual fund or ETF' as excluding every ETF and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 34, Line 16: "Any tax from Form 8621, line 16e, relating to a section 1291 fund"
findings.why: 'U.S.' can be read as modifying only 'mutual fund,' which would carve out all ETFs, and foreign ETFs are a common kind of PFIC. The help text does not settle this; it should say 'a mutual fund or ETF set up in the United States.'

findings.situation: A filer holding American depositary receipts of a foreign company bought on a U.S. exchange may think they own U.S.-listed securities rather than 'shares of a company set up outside the United States' and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8n: "Section 951 generally requires that a U.S. shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation include in income its pro rata share"; p. 34, Line 16: "Any tax from Form 8621, line 16e, relating to a section 1291 fund"
findings.why: ADRs represent foreign shares for PFIC and CFC purposes, but nothing in the question or help says that depositary receipts or U.S.-listed foreign stocks count.

findings.situation: A filer holding a small number of shares in a large foreign operating company (for example, Toyota or Nestlé) answers yes, although such a company is usually neither a CFC (for an individual small holder) nor a PFIC.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8n: "a U.S. shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation"
findings.why: The gate opens the two follow-up questions for portfolio holdings that give no amount on any gated line. This is acceptable under the lean-to-yes design.

locators: p. 34, Line 16, "Any tax from Form 8621, line 16e, relating to a section 1291 fund"; p. 114, Line 17p, "Enter any interest amount from Form 8621, line 16f"

p. 91, Line 8n, "Section 951 generally requires that a U.S. shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation include in income its pro rata share"; p. 91, Line 8o, "Section 951A generally requires that a U.S. shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation include in income its global intangible low-taxed income"

findings.situation: A filer, or a beneficiary, receives a pension or annuity from a nonqualified deferred compensation plan or a nongovernmental section 457 plan that is reported on a Form 1099 rather than a W-2, and the return has no W-2.
findings.irs_text: f1040s1 Schedule 1 (2025), line 8t: "Pension or annuity from a nonqualifed deferred compensation plan or a nongovernmental section 457 plan"
findings.why: Line 8t is not limited to amounts reported on a W-2. Only the W-2 caution on i1040gi p. 24 ties it to box 1, so the has-W-2 gate drops this amount when the return has no W-2.

findings.situation: A W-2 includes a nonqualified-plan pension in box 1, but the filer reads box 11 as 'deferred pay' rather than a pension paid to them, or box 11 is blank.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24: "If you received a pension or annuity from a nonqualified deferred compensation plan ... and it was reported in box 1 of Form W-2 ... This amount is reported on Schedule 1, line 8t."
findings.why: The IRS text keys the amount to box 1, but the question asks only about box 11 and 'money paid ... from an employer's deferred pay plan'. A filer with an amount for line 8t could truthfully answer no.

findings.situation: A tipped employee received $20 or more in tips in a month, did not report them all to the employer, and has no allocated tips in W-2 box 8.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 112, Line 5: "If you received tips of $20 or more in any month and you didn't report the full amount to your employer, you must pay the social security and Medicare ... tax on the unreported tips."
findings.why: Unreported tips create Schedule 2, line 5 tax even when box 8 and box 12 are empty. The filer truthfully answers no to the box 8 / box 12 question, and the tax is dropped. The same happens if the employer issued no W-2 at all.

findings.situation: A filer received income from a nonqualified deferred compensation plan that fails section 409A, and it is reported in box 15 of Form 1099-MISC rather than on a W-2.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 114, Line 17h: "This income should be shown in box 12 of Form W-2 with code Z, or in box 15 of Form 1099-MISC."
findings.why: The IRS text expressly allows a 1099-MISC source. The has-W-2 gate and the W-2 box question both miss this case.

findings.situation: A filer received an excess parachute payment reported in box 3 of Form 1099-NEC, with no W-2 code K.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 114, Line 17k: "If you received a Form 1099-NEC, the tax is 20% of the EPP shown in box 3. Enter this amount on line 17k."
findings.why: The 20% tax on line 17k applies to 1099-NEC recipients, whom neither the has-W-2 condition nor the box 12 code K question captures.

findings.situation: A fee-basis state or local government official is paid fees not reported on a Form W-2, and the return has no W-2.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93, Line 12: "Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials."
findings.why: The cited text does not require a W-2 for this deduction, so the has-W-2 gate can silently zero it.

findings.situation: A self-employed filer with no W-2 makes elective deferrals to a solo 401(k) above the limit.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1h: "If the total amount you (or your spouse if filing jointly) deferred for 2025 under all plans was more than $23,500 ... include the excess on line 1h."
findings.why: The limit counts deferrals 'under all plans', including plans that are not reported on a W-2. The has-W-2 gate drops the excess when no W-2 exists.

findings.situation: A filer with only SIMPLE plans deferred $20,000, which is over the $16,500 SIMPLE limit but under $23,500.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1h: "This limit is generally (a) $16,500 if you have only SIMPLE plans"

findings.situation: A household employee who works around the home, such as a private driver, yard worker or gardener, is paid without a W-2 and could truthfully answer no to being paid 'for work in someone else's home'.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: "Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2 ... For information on employment taxes for household employees, see Tax Topic 756."
findings.why: Line 1b covers anyone paid as a household employee. The gate's wording 'work in someone else's home' and its examples (nanny, carer, housekeeper) can reasonably be read to leave out household workers whose work is outside the house or away from it.

findings.situation: A babysitter or house cleaner paid small cash amounts by a family, with no W-2 because the pay was under $2,800, may not think of that pay as 'wages, tips or strike benefits' and answer no to the first helper question, which ends the chain.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: "An employer isn't required to provide a Form W-2 to you if they paid you wages of less than $2,800 in 2025."
findings.why: The household question is asked only after a yes to the generic 'wages not on a W-2' question. Informal household pay is exactly the kind a filer may not call wages, so line 1b can be lost before the specific household question is ever asked.

findings.situation: A self-employed house cleaner or carer, an independent contractor rather than an employee, answers yes to being paid for work in someone else's home with no W-2.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: "wages received as a household employee"
findings.why: Line 1b is limited to wages of a household employee, but the gate question does not separate employees from contractors. This only adds questions.

findings.situation: A caregiver is paid by a home care agency, fiscal intermediary or managed-care plan that uses Medicaid waiver funds, gets a W-2 from that agency with box 12 code II, and reads 'did a state Medicaid program pay you' as asking whether the state itself paid them, so answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92, Line 8s: "Certain Medicaid waiver payments you received for caring for someone living in your home with you may be nontaxable. Your nontaxable Medicaid waiver payments should be reported to you on Form(s) W-2 in box 12, Code II."
findings.why: The IRS text turns on the payment being a Medicaid waiver payment, not on who issues the check. Waiver pay usually flows through an agency or intermediary, so a truthful no would drop the box 1 and code II amounts on lines 1a, 1d and 8s.

findings.situation: The person cared for lived in the filer's home and was paid for in 2025 but died or moved out before the return is prepared, and the filer reads the present-tense 'who lives in your home' as asking about now, so answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92, Line 8s: "Certain Medicaid waiver payments you received for caring for someone living in your home with you may be nontaxable."
findings.why: The IRS condition is that the person lived in the home while the care was paid for during 2025. The gate's present tense 'lives' can be read as asking about the current household, unlike the gated questions' 'lived'.

findings.situation: A 2024 business loss was partly disallowed as an excess business loss on Form 461, but the filer's total 2024 income, including large wages, still exceeded the loss. The help text then tells them this is not a carried loss.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 4: "Excess business losses that are disallowed are treated as an NOL carryover to the following tax year."; "An excess business loss is the amount by which the total deductions attributable to all of your trades or businesses exceed your total gross income and gains attributable to those trades or businesses plus the threshold amount"
findings.why: The help defines the carried loss as 'A loss bigger than that year's income'. An excess business loss is measured only against business income plus a threshold, so a filer with a positive overall 2024 income could truthfully answer no. That drops a line 8a deduction and skips the excess-business-loss question.

findings.situation: A filer whose NOL arose in 2024 has not yet deducted it on any return, or whose NOL came from rental property or employee expenses rather than a business or disaster.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 1: "To have an NOL, your loss must generally be caused by deductions from your: • Trade or business, • Work as an employee ... • Casualty and theft losses resulting from a federally declared disaster, • Moving expenses ..., or • Rental property."; p. 2: "Start by carrying the NOL to the first tax year after the NOL year."
findings.why: The help says the loss was 'carried forward on an earlier return' and names only business and disaster or theft sources. A first-year carryforward from a 2024 NOL, or a rental-sourced NOL, can reasonably be read as outside the question.

locators: p. 91, Line 8a, "Enter any deduction for an NOL from an earlier year"

findings.situation: A filer (or spouse) who was a resident alien all of 2025, such as a green card holder or someone meeting the substantial presence test, answers yes to the noncitizen question even though the nonresident answer will be no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 8: "Resident aliens. These rules also apply if you were a resident alien... Generally, you are a resident alien if you meet either the green card test or the substantial presence test for 2025."
findings.why: A full-year resident alien is not a citizen, so the gate opens, but the Form 1040 rules apply to them as to citizens and the gated line stays false. This costs only one extra question.

findings.situation: A filer took the standard deduction for 2024 but itemized for 2023, and in 2025 received a reimbursement of a 2023 itemized casualty loss; following the help text, they answer No.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24, Deductions not itemized: "If you didn't itemize deductions for the year for which you received the recovery of an expense that was deductible only if you itemized, don't include any of the recovery amount in your income."; p. 27, Worksheet 2: "a casualty loss reimbursement from 2023, complete a separate worksheet for each year. Use information from your tax return for the year the expense was deducted."
findings.why: The help tells the filer to answer No based on whether they itemized for 2024. The IRS rule depends on whether they itemized for the year of the deduction, so a taxable pre-2024 recovery drops out and rec.not_2024 is wrongly zero.

findings.situation: In 2025 a filer received a state income tax refund for tax year 2023 (or earlier) and has no other recoveries, so they truthfully answer No because state or local income tax refunds are excluded.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24, Itemized Deduction Recoveries: "You can't use the State and Local Income Tax Refund Worksheet ... and must use this discussion if ... 1. You received a refund in 2025 that is for a tax year other than 2024."; p. 27, Worksheet 2: "If you recovered amounts from more than 1 year ... complete a separate worksheet for each year."
findings.why: A refund for a year before 2024 is exactly the case rec.not_2024 exists to catch. The gate carves out all state or local income tax refunds, so this case never reaches the gated question.

findings.situation: A filer's earlier-year deduction did not lower that year's tax but increased a carryover (for example an NOL or credit carryover) to a later year, so they truthfully answer No to 'lowered your tax'.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24, Tax benefit rule: "For this purpose, any increase to an amount carried over to the current year that resulted from the deduction or credit is considered to have reduced your tax in the earlier year."
findings.why: The gate asks whether the deduction or credit lowered tax on the earlier return. It does not mention that a larger carryover counts as a tax benefit, so a filer with a taxable recovery can honestly answer No.

findings.situation: A filer who claimed a credit on an item later got a downward price adjustment rather than money handed back, and may not consider that being 'paid back'.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 28, Amounts Recovered for Credits: "You had a recovery if there was a downward price adjustment or similar adjustment on the item for which you claimed a credit."
findings.why: 'Paid back' can be read as a cash refund, or even as the filer repaying someone. A filer could reasonably read it to exclude price adjustments that the IRS treats as credit recoveries for rec.nonitemized.

findings.situation: A filer is unsure whether an earlier deduction 'lowered your tax' (for example, because of unused credits, AMT, or the 0% capital gains rate) and answers No rather than refiguring.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 25, Capital gains: "you'll have to refigure your tax for the earlier year to determine if the recovery must be included in your income"; p. 28, Unused tax credits: "you must refigure the earlier year's tax to determine if you must include the recovery"
findings.why: The gate makes the filer judge the tax benefit up front, which the IRS says requires refiguring. That pushes uncertain filers toward a No and works against the gate's intended lean to yes.

locators: p. 24, Example 27, "The maximum refund that you may have to include in income is $500 because it’s less than the excess of the tax deducted"

findings.situation: A member of a religious order who has not taken a vow of poverty does work the order directs at an outside organization that is not church-controlled (for example, a secular hospital or public school). That organization pays them, so they could truthfully answer no: they were not paid by a church or religious body, and they are not a 'minister, priest, rabbi or imam.'
findings.irs_text: i1040sse p. 1: "you must pay SE tax on salaries and other income for services you performed as a minister, member of a religious order who hasn't taken a vow of poverty, or Christian Science practitioner"
findings.why: The gate question and its help name clergy, chaplains and Christian Science practitioners but never members of a religious order. Such a member paid by a non-religious payer could answer no, which drops the scope.clergy line the cited text makes matter.

findings.situation: An ordinary employee of a church (or of a church-controlled school or hospital) whose employer withholds social security and Medicare tax answers yes, although neither gated line applies to them.
findings.irs_text: i1040sse p. 1: "Church employee income is wages you received as an employee ... of a church or qualified church-controlled organization that has a certificate in effect electing an exemption from employer social security and Medicare taxes"
findings.why: The gate asks about any pay from a religious body, not only pay from employers with the exemption certificate. This only costs extra questions.

locators: , Employees of Churches and Church Organizations, "Church employee income is wages you received as an employee (other than as a minister, member of a religious order, or Christian Science practitioner) of a church or qualified church-controlled organization that has a certificate in effect electing an exemption from employer social security and Medicare taxes"

, Ministers, Members of Religious Orders, and Christian Science Practitioners, "you must pay SE tax on salaries and other income for services you performed as a minister, member of a religious order who hasn’t taken a vow of poverty, or Christian Science practitioner"

findings.situation: A filer who leases a vehicle or equipment and subleases it to someone else for pay has rented out personal property, but does not own it, so they could truthfully answer no to a question about 'anything you own'.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 5, Personal property: "Do not use Schedule E to report income and expenses from the rental of personal property, such as equipment or vehicles. Instead, use Schedule C if you are in the business of renting personal property ... If your rental of personal property is not a business, see the instructions for Schedule 1 (Form 1040), lines 8l and 24b"
findings.why: The IRS text covers any rental of personal property, owned or not. The gate's wording 'anything you own' lets a sublessor answer no, so the personal-property answer defaults to false and the case is silently missed.

findings.situation: A filer whose only activity was receiving royalties, or renting only real estate, or offering property for rent without renting it, answers yes to the gate but has no personal-property rental.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 5, Personal property: "rental of personal property, such as equipment or vehicles"
findings.why: Royalties and real-estate rentals do not trigger the personal-property rule, so the extra gated question is asked when it isn't needed. This is acceptable by design.

locators: p. 5, Personal property, "Do not use Schedule E to report income and expenses from the rental of personal property, such as equipment or vehicles"

findings.situation: A filer locked out by an employer received lockout benefits but no strike benefits, wages or tips off a W-2, so they truthfully answer no to the first question and are never asked about the benefits.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 24, Line 1h: "The following types of income must be included in the total on line 1h. • Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts)."
findings.why: The first gate question asks only about "wages, tips or strike benefits that are not on a W-2" and leaves out lockout benefits. The IRS text puts lockout benefits on line 1h, so a truthful no drops the amount.

findings.situation: A filer received strike or lockout benefits from a source other than a union, such as a strike fund or a community or employee group, so they truthfully answer no to the second question.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 24, Line 1h: "Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts)."
findings.why: The IRS text includes these benefits on line 1h whatever their source. The second gate question and the amount question add "from a union," so benefits from other payers are missed.

findings.situation: A filer whose union reported strike benefits on a Form 1099 rather than a W-2 may not know whether to count them as "wages, tips or strike benefits that are not on a W-2."
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 24, Line 1h: "Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts)."
findings.why: The first question groups strike benefits with pay. A filer who does not think of union benefits as pay may answer no, even though such benefits are rarely on a W-2.

locators: p. 24, Line 1h, "Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts)"
p. 24, Line 1h, "The following types of income must be included in the total on line 1h", "Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts)"

findings.situation: A filer whose only unreported tips were cash or card tips not reported in full to the employer answers yes, so the tool asks for noncash tips even though that line has no amount for them.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 24, Line 1c: "This should include any tip income you didn't report to your employer ... Also, include the value of any noncash tips you received, such as tickets, passes, or other items of value."
findings.why: The gate combines unreported cash tips and noncash tips. Filers with only unreported cash tips see an extra noncash question that they answer with zero. This costs one question and drops no amount.

findings.situation: A filer aged 19 to 23 who was not a full-time student, or a filer aged 18 to 23 whose earned income was more than half of their support, is not filing jointly and was under 24, so the condition holds, yet Form 8615 does not apply.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: "b. Was age 18 at the end of 2025 and didn’t have earned income that was more than half of the child's support, or c. Was a full-time student at least age 19 and under age 24 at the end of 2025 and didn’t have earned income that was more than half of the child's support."
findings.why: Being under 24 is broader than condition 3, so some filers get the unearned-income question needlessly. That leans to yes and drops no amount.

findings.situation: A filer under 24 who is not filing jointly and whose parents were both dead at the end of 2025 meets the condition, but Form 8615 does not apply to them.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: "These rules don’t apply if neither of the child’s parents were living at the end of the year."
findings.why: The gate does not test condition 4, so it asks some filers the gated question needlessly. That is harmless over-inclusion.

findings.situation: A filer born January 1, 2002 might answer that they were under 24 at the end of 2025, although the IRS treats them as 24.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: "January 1, 2002 24*** ... *** Don’t use Form 8615 for this child."
findings.why: A literal reading could produce a yes where the form does not apply. That only costs an extra question; no IRS-covered filer is dropped.

findings.situation: A child whose biological parents both died before the end of 2025, but whose stepparent was alive, could read 'was a parent of yours alive' as asking only about biological or adoptive parents and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: 'At least one of the child's parents was alive at the end of 2025.' ... 'For these rules, the term "child" includes a legally adopted child and a stepchild.'
findings.why: The instructions treat stepchildren as children, so a living stepparent can satisfy condition 4. The question does not say that stepparents and adoptive parents count, so a filer could answer no and drop Form 8615.

findings.situation: A filer with more than $2,700 of tax-exempt interest or nontaxable benefits, but not more than $2,700 of taxable unearned income, answers yes to the unearned-income question.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: 'It includes taxable interest, dividends, capital gains ... the taxable part of social security and pension payments'
findings.why: The question asks about any income that was not pay for work, without limiting it to taxable amounts. This over-includes, which is acceptable for a gate that leans to yes.

findings.situation: A child born January 1, 2002 counts as age 24 at the end of 2025 but may answer yes to an under-24 question; a non-student born January 1, 2007 counts as 19 but may answer yes as '18'.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: 'January 1, 2002 ... 24*** ... Don't use Form 8615 for this child.'
findings.why: Calendar age and the IRS's age convention differ by a day, so these filers are asked questions they do not need. This over-includes, which is acceptable for a gate that leans to yes.

findings.situation: A child who meets all the other conditions but is not required to file a return, for example because a parent elects Form 8814, still passes the gate.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1: '2. The child is required to file a tax return.' ... 'If the parent makes this election, the child won't have to file a return or Form 8615.'
findings.why: Neither the gate nor the gated question tests the filing requirement; only the help text mentions it. This over-includes, which is acceptable for a gate that leans to yes.

findings.situation: The filer alone drives the vehicle partly for business and partly for investment (for example 40% business, 30% investment), with no other user and no entertainment use.
findings.irs_text: i4562 (2025) p. 14: 'Generally, a qualified business use is any use in your trade or business. However, it does not include any of the following. • Investment use.' p463 p. 25: 'It doesn't include use for the production of income (investment use)'
findings.why: Investment use by the filer alone removes miles from qualified business use and can bring it to 50% or less, yet the filer truthfully answers no to the gate. qbu_low is then forced false and the vehicle goes on line 26 instead of line 27.

findings.situation: The filer is regularly engaged in the business of leasing passenger automobiles, and this vehicle is held for lease but was not leased or used by anyone else during the year.
findings.irs_text: i4562 (2025) p. 15: 'The business use requirement and the limits for passenger automobiles generally do not apply to passenger automobiles leased or held by anyone regularly engaged in the business of leasing passenger automobiles.'
findings.why: The exception covers vehicles merely 'held' by a leasing business, so nobody but the filer need use the vehicle. The filer truthfully answers no, and the leasing line is forced false.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse uses the vehicle, for example as compensation for services in the filer's business or under a lease from the filer.

findings.situation: A vehicle placed in service in 2024 or earlier, and used 50% or less for qualified business in an earlier year, keeps depreciating in 2025; because it was not placed in service in 2025, the computed gate is false and scveh.prior_low_use_if_earlier is forced to false.
findings.irs_text: p463 p. 25: "If you used your car more than 50% in qualified business use in the year you placed it in service, but 50% or less in a later year (including the year of disposition), you have to change to the straight line method of depreciation." i4562 p. 14: "If you used listed property more than 50% in a qualified business use in the year you placed the property in service, and used it 50% or less in a later year, you may have to include as income part of the depreciation."
findings.why: This line only matters for a vehicle placed in service before 2025. That is exactly when the gate (placed in service in 2025) is false. Inside the gate, the line's own Choose also returns false, so the question can never be asked.

findings.situation: A vehicle placed in service before 2025, with the standard mileage rate used in its first year and actual expenses used in 2025, has its prior-standard-mileage line forced to false because the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: p463 p. 25: "If you used the standard mileage rate in the first year of business use and change to the actual expenses method in a later year, you can't depreciate your car under the MACRS rules. You must use straight line depreciation over the estimated remaining useful life of the car."
findings.why: Prior standard-mileage use can only occur for a vehicle placed in service in an earlier year. The gate excludes that vehicle, so the rule requiring straight line depreciation and a reduced basis is silently dropped.

findings.situation: A vehicle placed in service before 2025 that had a special depreciation allowance claimed in an earlier year has scveh.prior_bonus_if_earlier forced to false, because the gate is false.
findings.irs_text: p463 p. 26: "Decrease your basis by any section 179 deduction, special depreciation allowance, gas guzzler tax, and vehicle credits claimed." i4562 p. 14: "you may have to include as income part of the depreciation, including the special depreciation allowance, deducted in prior years."
findings.why: An earlier-year bonus affects the basis and recapture of a vehicle placed in service before 2025. That is the only case where the line applies, and the gate excludes it.

findings.situation: A car bought for personal use years ago and converted to business use in 2025 may or may not register as "Year of recovery in 2025" = 1, depending on whether the helper uses the purchase date or the conversion date.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 14, Column (b): "If property held for personal use is converted to business/investment use, treat the property as placed in service on the date of conversion."
findings.why: If the year-of-recovery helper counts from the original purchase date, a 2025 conversion would wrongly fail the placed-in-2025 gate. The gate would then drop the acquisition-date question for that vehicle.

findings.situation: A filer with a leased vehicle who answers No to the gate (actual expenses were used in an earlier lease year) is still asked the gated question, even though its own wording forces a No for leased vehicles, so the line can only be false.
findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 6, Line 9: "You can take the standard mileage rate for 2025 only if you: • Owned the vehicle and used the standard mileage rate for the first year you placed the vehicle in service, or • Leased the vehicle and are using the standard mileage rate for the entire lease period."
findings.why: For a leased vehicle the owned-and-first-year branch never applies, so asking it costs a question but drops no amount. When the gate is answered Yes, the rate was used in the first year anyway, so making the line false does not lose the owned-and-first-year path.

findings.situation: A filer answers yes but has no sale that qualifies for the Schedule D totals: a collectible, a sale with no Form 1099-B/1099-DA showing basis reported, an adjustment or code, the Ordinary box or QOF box checked, or a QOF deferral or termination. The routing question is then asked even though every such sale must still go on Form 8949.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 10, Lines 1a and 8a: "the aggregate totals from any transactions (except sales of collectibles) for which: • You received a Form 1099-B or Form 1099-DA ... that shows basis was reported to the IRS and doesn't show any adjustments ... • The Ordinary box ... isn't checked; • The QOF box ... isn't checked; ... • You don't need to make any adjustments"
findings.why: The gate is a free choice and does not test whether a qualifying sale exists, so a yes can lead to questions with no aggregate amount. This costs only extra questions. Reporting every sale on Form 8949 is always allowed ("You can report"), so a no never drops an amount.

findings.situation: A filer sells an oil, gas or mineral royalty interest held as an investment and truthfully answers no, not seeing it as real estate or business property.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 1: "Use Form 4797 to report the following. 1. The sale or exchange of: ... c. Oil, gas, geothermal, or other mineral property"
findings.why: Neither the gate question nor its help mentions mineral property, which Form 4797 covers even when it is not used in a business. Only the gated question names it, and a no on the gate means that question is never asked.

findings.situation: A filer sells small business (section 1244) or SBIC (section 1242) stock at a loss and truthfully answers no, because stock is neither real estate nor business property.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 1: "4. Ordinary loss on the sale, exchange, or worthlessness of small business investment company (section 1242) stock. 5. Ordinary loss on the sale, exchange, or worthlessness of small business (section 1244) stock."
findings.why: These stock losses go on Form 4797, but the gate asks only about real estate or business property, so the filer answers no and the Form 4797 line is zeroed.

findings.situation: Business property or investment property held more than a year is condemned or otherwise involuntarily converted (not by casualty or theft), and the filer answers no because nothing was 'sold or traded'.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 1: "2. The involuntary conversion (other than from casualty or theft) of property used in a trade or business and capital assets held more than 1 year for business or profit."
findings.why: An involuntary conversion is not a sale or trade in ordinary usage, and the gate covers no other kind of disposition. A truthful no drops a Form 4797 amount.

findings.situation: A securities trader who made a mark-to-market election disposes of trading securities and answers no, since securities are not real estate or business property as the help describes it (equipment, a vehicle, a building).
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 1: "6. Ordinary gain or loss on securities or commodities held in connection with your trading business, if you previously made a mark-to-market election."
findings.why: These go on Form 4797, but the gate's wording and examples point the filer away from counting securities.

findings.situation: A farmer disposes of section 126 property, or a filer disposes of other noncapital assets that are not obviously 'business property' as the help describes it.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 1: "d. Section 126 property" and "3. The disposition of noncapital assets other than inventory or property held primarily for sale to customers"
findings.why: The help limits business property to things 'used in a business or rented out, such as equipment, a vehicle or a building', so a filer could reasonably decide these categories do not count.

findings.why: The help tells the filer to answer yes for a home, but a home sold for cash at closing has no Form 4797, Form 6252 or Form 8824 amount.

findings.situation: A filer (or spouse) received no social security payments in 2025 but repaid earlier benefits in 2025, so their Form SSA-1099 or RRB-1099 shows only repayments in box 4 and a negative box 5. The filer could reasonably answer no to 'get social security benefits ... in 2025', even though a form 'reports them'.
findings.irs_text: "Box 4 will show the amount of any benefits you repaid in 2025." (i1040gi p. 31); "if your total repayments in 2025 exceed your total benefits received in 2025 by more than $3,000, you may be able to take an itemized deduction or a credit for part of the excess repayments" (i1040gi p. 31); "Enter the total amount from box 5 of all your Forms SSA-1099 and RRB-1099" (i1040gi p. 32, worksheet line 1)
findings.why: The text gives box 5 a value whenever a filer receives one of these forms, including a repayment-only form with no benefits paid in 2025. The question asks whether the filer 'got' benefits, so a filer who only repaid may answer no. The tool would then drop the net (negative) amount that bears on the excess-repayment deduction or credit.

locators: p. 32, Social Security Benefits Worksheet, line 1; p. 31, Lines 6a and 6b

findings.situation: A filer whose earlier-year lump-sum payment was a railroad retirement benefit treated as social security, reported on Form RRB-1099 rather than Form SSA-1099, may answer no because the question tells them to look for the description on Form SSA-1099.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31, Lines 6a and 6b: "If you received railroad retirement benefits treated as social security, you should receive a Form RRB-1099."; p. 32 worksheet line 1: "Enter the total amount from box 5 of all your Forms SSA-1099 and RRB-1099."
findings.why: The first sentence of the question covers any benefit, but the second points only to the SSA-1099 box 3 description. An RRB-1099 recipient with an earlier-year payment could read the question as not applying to them, which would drop the lump-sum election.

findings.situation: The benefits include a payment for an earlier year, but none of the 2025 benefits are taxable (for example, the worksheet stops at line 7 or line 9).

findings.why: The lump-sum election only reduces a taxable amount, so it does not matter when nothing is taxable, yet the gate still asks the question.

findings.situation: A filer whose tips from one employer came partly from work on the list and partly from work off it may answer no, because not all of 'the work you got these tips for' is on the list, even though the listed portion is qualified.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 103: "If you received tips as an employee in more than one occupation for the same employer, only those tips that were received in an occupation on the list ... are considered qualified tips."
findings.why: The question reads as 'is all of this work on the list,' so a mixed-occupation filer can answer no. That skips the gated other_work question, which exists to catch this case, and silently zeroes the qualified tips from the listed occupation. The question should ask whether any of the work is on the list.

findings.situation: A filer who donated a vehicle, intellectual property, or inventory and expects to deduct $5,000 or less may answer NO because they believe the gift needs no appraisal.
findings.irs_text: i8283 p.2: "Also, use Section A to report donations of ... certain intellectual property described in section 170(e)(1)(B)(iii); a qualified vehicle described in section 170(f)(12)(A)(ii) ...; and inventory and other similar property described in section 1221(a)(1)."
findings.why: The question is framed as "Does this group need an appraisal or other special treatment," and the listed categories are written as examples of that, so it can be read as asking only about appraisal need. Under the IRS text these categories use Section A with no appraisal, but they still get special treatment such as a gross-proceeds limit, a basis limit, or a Form 1098-C, so the reading decides the answer.

findings.situation: A filer gives one clothing or household item that is not in good used condition, is worth more than $500, and for which they claim $500 or less (or the reverse), and could answer either way.

findings.why: The question says "over $500" without saying whether that is the item's value or the deduction claimed. The IRS test uses the deduction claimed.

findings.situation: A filer's EIC was disallowed in an earlier year, but the filer later filed Form 8862, the EIC was allowed for that year, and it has not been reduced or disallowed again, so the filer must answer YES although no Form 8862 is needed for 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: "But don’t file Form 8862 if either of the following applies. • You filed Form 8862 for another year, the EIC was allowed for that year, and your EIC hasn’t been reduced or disallowed again for any reason other than a math or clerical error."
findings.why: The question asks only whether the credit "for any year after 1996" was "reduced or disallowed" and has no carve-out for a later successful recertification. The tool's computation would be correct for this filer because the IRS text requires no Form 8862.

findings.situation: A filer is taking the EIC without a qualifying child, and the only reason an earlier EIC was reduced or disallowed was that a child on Schedule EIC was found not to be a qualifying child.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: "You are taking the EIC without a qualifying child and the only reason your EIC was reduced or disallowed in the other year was because it was determined that a child listed on Schedule EIC wasn’t your qualifying child."
findings.why: The question's phrase "reduced or disallowed for any reason other than a math or clerical error" requires YES, but the IRS text says not to file Form 8862 here. The tool would refuse a credit it can compute correctly.

findings.situation: A filer's CTC, ACTC or ODC was denied or reduced in an earlier year, but the filer filed Form 8862 for 2024 and the credit was allowed for that year, or another exception applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 39: "Don’t file Form 8862 if you filed Form 8862 for 2024, and the child tax credit, additional child tax credit, or credit for other dependents was allowed for that year." i1040s8812 p. 2: "you must attach Form 8862 to your tax return to claim the CTC, ACTC, or ODC unless an exception applies."
findings.why: The question has no exception for an earlier recertification, so this filer must answer YES. The IRS text does not require Form 8862 for this filer, so the tool's computation would be correct.

findings.situation: A filer has a past reduction, disallowance or ban affecting only one credit family, such as the EIC, and claims only the other family, such as the CTC, yet the single answer refuses both lines.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 43: "You must file Form 8862 if your EIC for a year after 1996 was reduced or disallowed" and "10 years after the most recent tax year for which there was a final determination that your EIC claim was due to fraud." i1040s8812 p. 2: "If your CTC, ACTC, or ODC for a year after 2015 was denied or reduced ... you must attach Form 8862 ... to claim the CTC, ACTC, or ODC" and "you will not be allowed to claim any of these credits for 10 years."
findings.why: The question joins both families with "or" and refers to "one of these credits," so a history with either family produces YES and refuses both lines. The quoted IRS text ties each Form 8862 requirement and ban to its own credit family, so the unaffected line would compute correctly.

findings.situation: A filer's earlier CTC or ODC was limited only by the income phase-out or by tax liability, and the IRS never denied or adjusted the claim.
findings.irs_text: i1040s8812 p. 2: "The maximum credit amount of your CTC and ODC may be reduced if either (1) or (2) applies." Compare: "If your CTC, ACTC, or ODC for a year after 2015 was denied or reduced for any reason other than a math or clerical error, you must attach Form 8862."
findings.why: The question's "reduced ... for any reason" does not say the reduction must be an IRS action on a claim, and the instructions also use "reduced" for the ordinary limits. A filer could reasonably answer YES because of a phase-out or tax limit, or NO because the IRS did not change the claim.

findings.situation: A filer covered by a workplace plan has their deduction reduced by the income phaseout on line 7, or limited by a contribution below the annual limit on line 11, so part of their contribution is automatically nondeductible, and they want only the deduction line 12 allows.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 98, IRA Deduction Worksheet line 12: "On line 12a, enter the smallest of line 7a, 10, or 11a... This is the most you can deduct... Or, if you want, you can deduct a smaller amount and treat the rest as a nondeductible contribution (see Form 8606)"
findings.why: The question asks 'Do you want to deduct a smaller amount and treat the rest as a nondeductible contribution?', and the filer never sees the line 12 figure. A filer whose deduction is already capped could read 'smaller amount' as smaller than the annual limit or their full contribution, and 'the rest' as the part that is already nondeductible, so they answer YES although the tool computes line 20 correctly.

findings.situation: A filer who wants to deduct nothing and designate the entire otherwise deductible contribution as nondeductible.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 98, line 12: "if you want, you can deduct a smaller amount and treat the rest as a nondeductible contribution"; p590a p. 16 (cited in gate): "you can even designate otherwise deductible contributions as nondeductible contributions"
findings.why: 'Deduct a smaller amount' suggests a positive but reduced deduction. A filer electing a zero deduction might not see that choice as 'deducting a smaller amount' and answer NO, and the tool would then deduct the full line 12 amount.

question: The most you (and your spouse) can deduct for your traditional IRA contributions is figured on line 12 of the IRA Deduction Worksheet. Do you want to deduct a smaller amount and treat the rest as a nondeductible contribution?

locators: p. 98, IRA Deduction Worksheet—Continued, line 12, "Add the amounts on lines 12a and 12b and enter the total on Schedule 1, line 20"
p. 98, IRA Deduction Worksheet—Continued, line 12, "Or, if you want, you can deduct a smaller amount and treat the rest as a nondeductible contribution (see Form 8606)"

findings.situation: Box 19 shows only code A, but the cash and marketable securities distributed exceed the partner's adjusted basis in the partnership immediately before the distribution, so the excess is a taxable gain.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25, Box 19 Code A: "To the extent the cash and the FMV of the securities (reduced by the reduction amount) received exceed the adjusted basis of your partnership interest immediately before the distribution, the excess is treated as gain from the sale or exchange of your partnership interest ... should be reported on Form 8949 and the Schedule D"
findings.why: The question asks only about codes other than A, so this filer truthfully answers NO. The line then passes the screen and the gain is ignored, even though the cited Code A text says it must be reported.

question: Does box 19 show any code other than A (cash and marketable securities)?

findings.situation: A partner's 2025 box 1 loss alone is within basis, but that loss plus the partner's share of separately stated deductions (box 12 section 179, box 13 charitable contributions or other deductions, box 21 foreign taxes) exceeds basis.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 3: "a partner's share of the adjusted basis in partnership charitable contributions (defined in section 170(c)) and taxes, described in section 901, paid or accrued to foreign countries and to U.S. territories is subject to this basis limitation"; p. 32: "Foreign taxes paid or accrued reduce a partner's basis and are limited to basis."
findings.why: The question asks only whether your 'losses' were more than basis. A filer can truthfully compare just the loss boxes and answer NO, even though the basis limitation applies to losses and deductions together.

findings.situation: A partner has losses or deductions carried forward from earlier years because of the basis limitation, and those amounts plus the 2025 loss exceed 2025 basis (or now become partly allowable).
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 3: "Any losses and deductions not allowed can be carried forward."
findings.why: The question asks only about '2025 losses'. A filer whose current-year loss fits within basis answers NO, and the tool then ignores the suspended carryforward that the basis rule governs.

findings.situation: A partner's nondeductible expenses (box 18 code C), or a decrease in their share of partnership liabilities, bring basis below the 2025 loss, but the filer leaves them out under the question's definition of basis.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25: "Code C. Nondeductible expenses... Decrease the adjusted basis of your interest in the partnership by this amount."; p. 3: "Line 3e... If the sum is negative, enter the amount on line 9a."
findings.why: The definition lists only 'what you put in, plus your share of its income and debts, less losses and money taken out'. A filer using it overstates basis and can answer NO when the losses actually exceed adjusted basis.

findings.situation: A partner has tax-exempt income (box 18 codes A/B) that brings basis above the loss, but the filer leaves it out under the question's definition and answers YES.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25: "Code B. Other tax-exempt income. Increase the adjusted basis of your interest in the partnership by the amount shown"; question: "plus your share of its income"
findings.why: 'Income' on a K-1 is easily read as the taxable income boxes only. Leaving out tax-exempt income understates basis, so the tool refuses a loss that is actually fully within basis and that it would compute correctly.

findings.situation: A filer follows the definition 'less losses' and subtracts the 2025 loss itself before comparing that same loss with basis.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 3: "a partner may only claim their share of a partnership loss ... to the extent it doesn't exceed their adjusted basis in the partnership at the end of the partnership's tax year"; question: "Basis is what you put in, plus your share of its income and debts, less losses and money taken out."
findings.why: The question can be read as comparing the 2025 loss with basis already reduced by that loss. Read that way, a filer with basis 10,000 and a loss of 6,000 answers YES, although the loss is within basis and the tool computes it correctly.

question: Were your 2025 losses from it more than your basis in it at the end of its year? Basis is what you put in, plus your share of its income and debts, less losses and money taken out.

findings.situation: Box 19 code A includes marketable securities treated as money, and the cash plus the securities' reduced FMV exceeds basis, but the cash alone does not.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25, Box 19 Code A: "code A is used to report the distributions the partnership made to you of money, that is, cash and certain marketable securities ... To the extent the cash and the FMV of the securities (reduced by the reduction amount) received exceed the adjusted basis of your partnership interest immediately before the distribution, the excess is treated as gain"
findings.why: The question asks only about "money you took out", and the help never says that marketable securities count as money. A filer who compares only the cash to basis answers NO, and the tool then drops a taxable gain.

findings.situation: The filer's share of partnership liabilities fell during the year, and that deemed distribution of money (alone or with cash) exceeds basis, but the filer took out little or no actual cash.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25, Box 19 Code A: "Code A, however, doesn't include deemed distributions of money under section 752(b); see Code D, later."; p. 3 Line 3e: "If the sum is negative, enter the amount on line 9a"
findings.why: A drop in liability share is a distribution of money that can produce gain above basis. Nobody would describe it as money they "took out", so a filer truthfully answers NO and the gain is treated as zero.

findings.situation: Box 19 shows a code C distribution of other property whose basis, alone or added to cash, exceeds the filer's basis, but no gain arises because no money exceeded basis.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25, Box 19 Code C: "Code C is used to report the partnership's adjusted basis in property other than money immediately before the property was distributed to you"; gain rule under Code A applies only to "the cash and the FMV of the securities"
findings.why: The question points the filer to "(box 19)" as the amount taken out. A filer who totals every box 19 amount, including property, answers YES and is refused even though only money produces gain and the tool's zero is correct.

findings.situation: The filer took cash draws during 2025 that exceed basis at the start of the year but not basis after adding the 2025 share of income from this K-1.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 3: "There may be some transactions or certain distributions that require you to determine the adjusted basis of your partnership interest at the point in time of the transaction or distribution rather than in the order and amounts specified in these instructions."; worksheet adds income (line 4) before decreases
findings.why: "Just before you took it out" can be read as excluding the current year's income share, or as following the worksheet, which adds 2025 income before subtracting distributions. The help does not say which, so filers may answer YES or NO for the same facts.

question: Was the money you took out of it in 2025 (box 19) more than your basis in it just before you took it out?

findings.situation: The partnership itself borrowed on nonrecourse loans, and the filer's share of those loans (in item K1) funds the losses, but the filer contributed only their own cash and borrowed nothing personally.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: "Generally, you aren't at risk for amounts such as the following. • Nonrecourse loans used to finance the activity, to acquire property used in the activity, or to acquire your interest in the activity..."; p. 2: "Nonrecourse loans are those liabilities of the partnership for which no partner or related person bears the economic risk of loss."
findings.why: The question asks about "what you have in it," and the help says a partner who put in their own cash is at risk. A filer will likely look only at their own contribution and answer NO, even though their share of the partnership's nonrecourse debt is an amount not at risk that requires Form 6198.

findings.situation: The filer's investment is protected by an arrangement that is neither a guarantee nor a stop-loss agreement, such as a put or buy-back right or an indemnity.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: "protected against loss by a guarantee, a stop-loss agreement, or other similar arrangement (excluding casualty insurance and insurance against tort liability)"
findings.why: The question names only "a guarantee or stop-loss agreement" and leaves out "other similar arrangement." A filer protected some other way can truthfully answer NO.

findings.situation: Money used in the activity was borrowed from a person who has a non-creditor interest in the activity but is not a partner, or from someone related to that person.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: "Amounts borrowed for use in the activity from a person who has an interest in the activity, other than as a creditor, or who is related, under section 465(b)(3), to a person (other than you) having such an interest."
findings.why: The question covers only loans "from another partner or someone related to one." It misses lenders who hold a non-creditor interest in the activity without being a partner. It also misses such loans made to the partnership rather than to the filer.

findings.situation: The filer borrowed the money on a loan without personal liability, but the loan is secured by the filer's own property outside the activity.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: "Nonrecourse loans ... that aren't secured by your own property (other than the property used in the activity)."
findings.why: The question ("borrowed on a loan you are not personally liable for") makes this filer answer YES. Under the IRS text, a loan secured by the filer's own outside property is not listed as not-at-risk, so the tool would compute this case correctly.

findings.situation: The filer acquired the interest before 1987, and the loss comes from holding real property the partnership placed in service before 1987; the partnership's statement identifies it as not subject to the at-risk rules.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: "if you acquired your partnership interest before 1987, the at-risk rules don't apply to losses from an activity of holding real property placed in service before 1987 by the partnership."
findings.why: Nothing in the question excludes this case, so a filer with nonrecourse or guaranteed financing would answer YES. Form 6198 is not needed for these losses.

findings.situation: The filer personally guaranteed a partnership loan.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: "Cash, property, or borrowed amounts ... that are protected against loss by a guarantee, a stop-loss agreement, or other similar arrangement"
findings.why: The phrase "covered by a guarantee" can be read as "I signed a guarantee," which makes the filer at risk (the help says liability for partnership loans is at risk). It can also be read as "someone else guarantees me against loss," which is not at risk. Filers could answer either way.

findings.situation: The financing is a nonrecourse mortgage on real estate, and the filer must decide whether it is a "qualified real estate loan."
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 8: "See the instructions for item K1, later, for the exception for qualified nonrecourse financing secured by real property."
findings.why: The question uses the undefined term "qualified real estate loan" and gives none of the conditions for qualified nonrecourse financing. A filer may treat any real estate mortgage as excepted and answer NO.

question: Was any of what you have in it borrowed on a loan you are not personally liable for (other than a qualified real estate loan), covered by a guarantee or stop-loss agreement, or borrowed from another partner or someone related to one?

findings.situation: In the year the loss arose, the filer held the interest as a limited partner but owned at least 10% and was consulted on decisions; this year the filer holds it as a general partner.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: "Limited partners can't actively participate unless future regulations provide an exception."; i8582 p. 10: "Don't enter a prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part IV unless you actively participated in the activity in both the year the loss arose and the current tax year."
findings.why: The question tests only decision-making and the 10% ownership share, so this filer truthfully answers NO. But a limited partner cannot actively participate, so that year's loss belongs in Part V and should have been refused.

findings.situation: In the year the loss arose, the filer owned 10% or more at year end but less than 10% for part of that year, for example before buying more of the interest.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: "You aren't considered to actively participate in a rental real estate activity if, at any time during the tax year, your interest ... in the activity was less than 10% (by value) of all interests in the activity."
findings.why: "Owned less than a tenth of it" reads naturally as the filer's ownership share overall or at year end, so the filer may answer NO. The IRS test fails if the share was below 10% at any time during the year, and the question does not say this.

findings.situation: In the year the loss arose, the filer took part only by arranging for others to provide services, such as repairs, in a significant and bona fide way, and made no management decisions.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: "You may be treated as actively participating if you participated, for example, in making management decisions or arranging for others to provide services (such as repairs) in a significant and bona fide sense."
findings.question: Did any of the held-back rental real estate loss come from a year when you did not help make decisions for it
findings.why: The question treats making decisions as the only form of participation, so this filer answers YES and is refused. Under the IRS text the filer may have actively participated, and the tool would compute the loss correctly.

findings.situation: In the year the loss arose, the filer was only nominally involved in decisions, for example rubber-stamping choices the partnership or a manager made.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: "...in making management decisions or arranging for others to provide services (such as repairs) in a significant and bona fide sense."
findings.why: "Help make decisions" has no "significant and bona fide" threshold. A filer with token involvement could reasonably answer either way, and a NO would let a loss without active participation into Part IV.

findings.why: Code C is used only to figure the optional method, and that method is elective. A filer who does not use it has nothing the tool fails to compute, yet the wording forces a YES and a refusal.
