findings.situation: The partnership left box 16 unchecked and attached the notification statement, but the partner asked for and received a Schedule K-3 with international items, so the filer truthfully answers NO and the tool ignores the K-3 items.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 24, Box 16: "If the partnership didn't check the box, the partnership attached a statement ... notifying the partner that the partner won't receive Schedule K-3 from the partnership unless the partner requests the schedule."
findings.why: The question asks only whether box 16 is checked. A filer who holds a K-3 obtained on request, with box 16 unchecked, answers NO even though the K-3 carries items the tool does not compute.

findings.situation: Box 16 is unchecked, but the K-1 reports foreign taxes in box 21, or PTEP-related dividends in box 6a/6b, whose treatment depends on Schedule K-3, so the filer answers NO and the tool treats the international amounts as zero or ignores them.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 32, Box 21: "Don't use this amount to complete your Form 1116 ... See Schedule K-3 to complete your Form 1116 or 1118."; p. 15, Box 6a: "Use Schedule K-3, Part V, to determine your share of distributions ... attributable to PTEP."
findings.why: The IRS text sends these items to Schedule K-3 whether or not box 16 is checked. A screen keyed only to the box 16 checkmark lets such a K-1 through with the K-3-dependent items left uncomputed.

findings.situation: The filer received a Schedule K-3 separately from the K-1 (for example, mailed later or after a request), or box 16 is checked but no K-3 was physically attached, and cannot tell whether to answer by the checkbox or by the attachment.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 24, Box 16: "If the partnership checked the box, see the attached Schedule K-3"; "... or issued a statement prior to furnishing the Schedule K-1"
findings.why: The wording "box 16 checked, showing that a Schedule K-3 is attached" joins two facts that can diverge. One filer may answer by the checkmark and another by whether a K-3 is actually in hand.

question: Is box 16 checked, showing that a Schedule K-3 is attached?

findings.situation: Box 20 shows only code Z, but the partnership was a patron of a specified agricultural or horticultural cooperative, so the filer answers NO even though Form 8995-A and Schedule D (Form 8995-A) are required.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 (2025) p. 30: "If the partnership was a patron of an agricultural or horticultural cooperative (specified cooperative), you must use Form 8995-A to figure your QBI deduction. You must also complete Schedule D (Form 8995-A)"
findings.why: The question lets every code Z item pass, including the cooperative items: W-2 wages allocable to qualified payments and the section 199A(g) deduction. The refusal itself cites code Z as outside the tool, so this patron case is answered NO but not computed unless another screen catches it.

findings.situation: Box 20 shows code AA (section 704(c) information), which only restates amounts already reported in other boxes, so the filer must answer YES and is refused although nothing extra needs computing.

findings.why: "Does box 20 show any code other than A, B, N, Z or AG?" makes any informational-only code trigger YES, even when the amounts already flow through the boxes the tool handles. The same applies to code X (payment obligations), which is reported for basis tracking only.

findings.situation: The partnership had more than one activity and attached a statement splitting box 1, 2, 3, 10 or 15 amounts by activity, but did not check box 22 or 23. A filer who reads the boxes literally answers NO, and the tool reports one undivided amount.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 14: "If the partnership had more than one trade or business activity, it will attach a statement identifying the income or loss from each activity"; p. 14 (box 2): "If the partnership had more than one rental real estate activity, it'll attach a statement identifying the income or loss from each activity"; p. 9: "If the partnership had more than one activity, it'll attach a statement to your Schedule K-1 that identifies each activity"
findings.why: The IRS treats the per-activity statement, and the fact of multiple activities, as what requires separate passive, at-risk and material-participation treatment. The question asks only whether the boxes are checked, so a K-1 where the partnership attached the statement but left the box blank passes the screen.

findings.situation: Box 22 or 23 is checked but no per-activity statement came with the filer's copy, or the filer cannot tell which attached pages are the activity statement.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 32: "When the partnership has more than one activity for passive activity purposes, it'll check this box and attach a statement"; p. 8: "Box 22 of Schedule K-1, Part III, will be checked when a statement is attached"
findings.why: The parenthetical "(with a statement attached)" can be read as a second condition that must also be met. Under that reading, a filer with a checked box but no statement answers NO, even though the partnership still has multiple activities that the tool does not compute.

findings.situation: The filer checks whether the box shows a number or an amount, rather than a checkmark, and answers based on what the box "shows."
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 32: "Box 22. More Than One Activity for At-Risk Purposes ... it'll check this box"; "Box 23. More Than One Activity for Passive Activity Purposes ... it'll check this box"
findings.why: "Showing more than one activity" suggests the box itself states a count of activities. In fact the box is only a checkbox, and the activities are listed on the statement. A filer could therefore look for a count, find none, and answer NO even though the box is checked.

question: Is box 22 or box 23 checked, showing more than one activity (with a statement attached)?

findings.situation: The partnership distributed cash or marketable securities that exceeded the filer's adjusted basis, but the filer kept their whole interest and sold, traded or gave up nothing.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25, Box 19 Code A: "To the extent the cash and the FMV of the securities ... received exceed the adjusted basis of your partnership interest immediately before the distribution, the excess is treated as gain from the sale or exchange of your partnership interest ... reported on Form 8949 and the Schedule D"
findings.why: The IRS treats this as gain from the sale or exchange of the partnership interest, which is the refused case. The filer disposed of nothing, so they truthfully answer NO, and the tool reports no gain.

findings.situation: The partnership's liabilities allocated to the filer went down, creating a deemed distribution of money that exceeded the filer's basis, while the filer took no action on their interest.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25, Box 19 Code A: "Code A, however, doesn't include deemed distributions of money under section 752(b)"; p. 3, Line 3e: "If the sum is negative, enter the amount on line 9a"
findings.why: A deemed distribution in excess of basis produces gain treated as from the sale or exchange of the interest. A filer who sold, traded and gave up nothing answers NO.

findings.situation: The filer's percentage of profits or capital fell because new partners were admitted or allocations were changed, with no transfer by the filer.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 2: "Generally, a partner who sells or exchanges a partnership interest"; question: "did you sell, trade or give up any of your share of this partnership?"
findings.why: "Give up any of your share" can be read as a smaller percentage share, which would lead a diluted partner to answer YES. In fact there was no disposition of the interest, and the tool could compute the K-1.

findings.situation: Part of the filer's interest was redeemed or liquidated by the partnership in exchange for a distribution, rather than sold to a third party.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 25: "if you receive cash or property in exchange for any part of a partnership interest, the amount of the distribution attributable to your share of the partnership's unrealized receivables or inventory items results in ordinary income"; p. 3: "when a partner's entire partnership interest is liquidated"
findings.why: A filer may see a partnership redemption as receiving a distribution, not as selling, trading or giving up their share, so they could answer NO even though a section 751/731 disposition occurred.

question: In 2025, did you sell, trade or give up any of your share of this partnership?

findings.situation: A partner gets a K-1 from a partnership organized under the law of a U.S. territory such as Puerto Rico or Guam. For federal tax purposes that partnership is foreign, but a filer may consider the territory part of 'the United States' and answer NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 9, Foreign Partnerships: "Follow the instructions below in addition to the instructions earlier under Domestic Partnerships." and "you may have to file Form 8865 if ... You controlled a foreign partnership"
findings.why: The parenthetical 'not created or organized in the United States' does not say whether territories count as the United States. A filer whose partnership is organized in a territory could truthfully answer NO, and the tool would then compute the K-1 without the foreign-partnership instructions and Form 8865 that the IRS text requires.

findings.situation: A general partner worked 60 hours in this partnership's activity and 600 hours in another business, so the total exceeds 500 hours, but this activity is not a significant participation activity.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "A significant participation activity is any trade or business activity in which you participated for more than 100 hours during the year"
findings.why: The question applies the 100-hour floor only to the other businesses, not to this one. A filer under 100 hours here answers YES although test 4 cannot apply, and the tool would have computed the activity correctly as not materially participated.

findings.situation: A filer has 150 hours in this partnership plus 2,000 hours in a sole proprietorship where they materially participate under test 1, and nothing else.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "...and in which you didn't materially participate under any of the material participation tests (other than this test)"; test 4: "you participated in all significant participation activities ... for more than 500 hours"
findings.why: Only activities in which the filer did not otherwise materially participate count toward the 500 hours. The question counts every business where the filer worked more than 100 hours, so the filer answers YES although test 4 fails.

findings.situation: A filer has 150 hours in this partnership and a full-time W-2 job at an employer in which they own no interest.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "A significant participation activity is any trade or business activity in which you participated"; "any work that you ... do in connection with an activity held through a partnership (where you own your partnership interest at the time the work is done) is counted toward material participation"
findings.why: Participation means work in trade or business activities the filer holds an interest in. "Other businesses where you worked" naturally includes employment, so this filer answers YES although test 4 is not met.

findings.situation: A filer spent hours reviewing financial statements as an investor, or worked in rental activities, and must decide whether to count those hours as "work" in "businesses."
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "work in connection with the activity isn't counted toward material participation if ... You do the work in your capacity as an investor and you aren't directly involved in the day-to-day operations"; significant participation activities are limited to "trade or business activit[ies]"
findings.why: The question does not exclude investor-type work or rental activities, so a filer could reasonably count them toward the 500 hours or leave them out.

findings.situation: The partnership has a fiscal tax year, and the filer's hours in calendar 2025 differ from their hours during the partnership's tax year.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "All determinations of material participation are based on your participation during the partnership's tax year."
findings.why: The question asks about hours "In 2025." A filer could count calendar-year hours and answer NO even though their hours during the partnership's tax year exceed 500, or the reverse.

question: In 2025, did your work in it and in other businesses where you worked more than 100 hours add up to more than 500 hours?

findings.situation: A general partner in a fiscal-year partnership participated regularly, continuously and substantially for more than 100 hours during the partnership's tax year (for example July 2024 to June 2025), but not during calendar 2025, so the filer truthfully answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "All determinations of material participation are based on your participation during the partnership’s tax year." and test 7: "you participated in the activity on a regular, continuous, and substantial basis during the tax year."
findings.why: The question asks only about calendar 2025. The IRS test uses the partnership's tax year. A partner who meets test 7 for the partnership year can answer NO, and the tool then treats the activity as passive.

findings.situation: A general partner spent more than 100 hours across 2025 reviewing financial statements and monitoring operations as an investor, not in day-to-day operations, and answers YES because that was regular work 'in it'.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "work in connection with the activity isn’t counted toward material participation if ... You do the work in your capacity as an investor and you aren’t directly involved in the day-to-day operations of the activity"
findings.why: The question asks about any 'work in it' and does not exclude investor-capacity work or work done mainly to avoid the passive loss limits. Such a filer does not meet test 7, so the tool's passive treatment would be correct, yet the question makes the filer answer YES and the tool refuses.

findings.situation: The pronoun 'it' does not say whether it means the partnership as a whole or the specific trade or business activity, which matters when the partnership has more than one activity.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 9: "You must determine if you materially participated (a) in each trade or business activity held through the partnership"
findings.why: A filer who worked heavily in one partnership activity but not in another could reasonably answer either way, because material participation is decided for each activity separately.

findings.situation: The partnership's main business sells goods or services, but it also runs a separate trading activity, reported on the attached activity statement, that adds to box 1; the filer answers NO because 'the partnership's business' is not trading.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 11: "If you have net income (loss), deductions, or credits from any of the following activities, treat such amounts as nonpassive ... 3. Trading personal property for the account of owners of interests in the activity."; p. 14: "If the partnership had more than one trade or business activity, it will attach a statement identifying the income or loss from each activity."
findings.why: The rule applies to any trading activity of the partnership, not only to its main business. The question asks about 'the partnership's business', and the help says 'a business that sells goods or services is not', which leads such a filer to answer NO. The tool then treats the trading share under the ordinary participation rules instead of as nonpassive.

findings.situation: A partnership that buys and sells real estate or other non-personal-property investments for its partners puts its ordinary income in box 1, and the filer answers YES because these are 'other investments'.
findings.irs_text: Question: "trading stocks, commodities or other investments for its owners"; i1065sk1 p. 11: "Trading personal property for the account of owners of interests in the activity."
findings.why: The special rule covers only trading personal property. 'Other investments' also takes in real property, whose box 1 income the tool computes under the normal rules, so the tool refuses a case it could handle.

findings.situation: An investment fund or club that mostly holds stocks for its partners, without being in the trade or business of trading, has a small box 1 amount, and the filer answers YES because it 'buys and sells stocks for its partners'.
findings.irs_text: Help: "A fund that buys and sells stocks for its partners is one"; i1065sk1 p. 15: "Portfolio income includes income (not derived in the ordinary course of a trade or business) from interest, ordinary dividends ... and gain or loss on the sale of property that ... is held for investment."
findings.why: The nonpassive trading rule is about an activity of trading. An investor fund's occasional buying and selling is not that activity, yet the help's wording sweeps it in, so the tool refuses box 1 amounts it computes normally.

findings.situation: A partnership trades securities with its own pooled capital, and the filer is unsure whether that is trading 'for its owners'.
findings.irs_text: Question: "trading stocks, commodities or other investments for its owners"; i1065sk1 p. 11: "for the account of owners of interests in the activity"
findings.why: One filer may read 'for its owners' as trading in the partners' individual accounts and answer NO because the partnership trades for itself. Another may read it as trading for the partners collectively and answer YES.

findings.situation: The code Z statement reports the partner's share of a section 199A(g) deduction passed through from a specified cooperative, without labeling anything as a payment, so the filer answers NO and the tool ignores it.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 30: "Section 199A(g) deduction from specified cooperatives. The amount reported reflects your distributive share of the partnership's net section 199A(g) deduction. See the Instructions for Form 8995-A."
findings.why: The question asks only about 'payments from' a cooperative. A pass-through deduction is not a payment, so a truthful filer can answer NO even though the IRS text sends this item to Form 8995-A.

findings.situation: The partnership was a patron of a specified cooperative, and the statement reports W-2 wages or QBI items allocable to qualified payments, or simply states patron status, without showing a payment the partner received.
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 30: "If the partnership was a patron of an agricultural or horticultural cooperative (specified cooperative), you must use Form 8995-A to figure your QBI deduction. You must also complete Schedule D (Form 8995-A)... to determine your patron reduction."
findings.why: The IRS trigger is the partnership's patron status, which requires Form 8995-A and the patron reduction. A filer who sees no payment amount on the statement can truthfully answer NO.

findings.situation: The statement refers to a 'specified cooperative' or an 'agricultural or horticultural cooperative' (for example, a nursery, timber, or livestock marketing co-op), and the filer must decide whether that is a 'farm or garden cooperative.'
findings.irs_text: i1065sk1 p. 30: "Patrons of specified agricultural or horticultural cooperatives"; i1065sk1 p. 30 (Form 8995 condition c): "You aren't a patron in a specified agricultural or horticultural cooperative."
findings.why: 'Farm or garden' is a loose paraphrase of 'agricultural or horticultural.' The statement's term 'specified cooperative' does not obviously match it, so filers could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: A loss was disallowed by the basis limit in a prior year when the filer filed no return, for example because they had only losses and were not required to file. The loss still carries forward, but the filer truthfully says nothing was 'held back on an earlier return.'
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 4: "Column (b). Enter any loss or deduction items disallowed due to basis limitations in prior years that were carried forward."; i7203 p. 1: "Any losses and deductions not allowed this year because of the basis limit can be carried forward indefinitely"
findings.why: The IRS text ties the carryforward to the prior year's disallowance, not to any return. The question's 'on an earlier return' lets a non-filer answer NO, and the tool then treats column (b) as zero.

findings.situation: A filer received the stock from a spouse or former spouse, and the suspended basis-limited losses carried over with it. Those losses were never held back on the filer's own return, so the filer answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 4: "Column (b). Enter any loss or deduction items disallowed due to basis limitations in prior years that were carried forward." (see Regulations sections 1.1366-2(a)(4) and (5), cited in Part III)
findings.why: Column (b) covers any carried-forward basis-limited loss attached to the stock, not only losses from the filer's own earlier returns. 'Held back on an earlier return because your basis' points only at the filer's own history.

findings.situation: A filer whose basis-limited loss arose before Form 7203 existed (it was tracked on the old basis worksheet), or who never filed Form 7203, follows the help text, finds no Form 7203 Part III column (e) amount, and answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1: "Form 7203 and its separate instructions are developed to replace the 3-part Worksheet for Figuring a Shareholder's Stock and Debt Basis"; i7203 p. 1: "(including an aggregate loss not allowed last year because of basis limitations)"
findings.why: The help says 'Your earlier Form 7203 shows it,' so a filer can read the question as asking only about an amount on a prior Form 7203. Carryforwards from the old worksheet era, or from years when Form 7203 was not filed, are still required in column (b).

findings.situation: A loss was suspended by the basis limit in an earlier year and then fully deducted in a later prior year, so no carryforward remains. The filer still truthfully answers YES because the loss 'was held back.'
findings.irs_text: Question: "Was a loss or deduction from this corporation held back on an earlier return because your basis in it was too low?"; i7203 p. 4: "Column (b). Enter any loss or deduction items disallowed due to basis limitations in prior years that were carried forward."
findings.why: Column (b) needs only amounts still carried forward into this year. The past-tense wording catches losses that were already used up, where the tool's zero for column (b) would be correct.

findings.situation: A filer whose prior-year loss was limited by the at-risk rules (Form 6198), not by stock and debt basis, may read 'your basis in it was too low' as covering the amount they had at risk and answer YES.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "Generally, you aren't at risk for amounts such as the following. • The basis of your stock in the corporation or the basis of your loans to the corporation if..."
findings.why: The at-risk rules are explained in terms of stock and loan basis, so 'basis too low' can be read to include an at-risk limitation that does not belong in Form 7203 column (b).

question: Was a loss or deduction from this corporation held back on an earlier return because your basis in it was too low?

findings.situation: Box 10 carries a code with an asterisk and 'STMT' in the dollar space instead of a figure (for example code A portfolio income or code I mineral property disposition), and the filer reads this as box 10 not showing an amount.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 6: "For those informational items that can't be reported as a single dollar amount, the corporation will enter an asterisk in the left column and enter 'STMT' in the dollar amount entry space"; p. 8 Code I: "The corporation will attach a statement that provides ... your share of the amount realized from the disposition"
findings.why: The question asks whether box 10 'show[s] an amount', so a filer whose box 10 shows only a code and 'STMT' can truthfully answer NO. The tool then treats the box 10 income or loss as zero even though the IRS text requires it to be reported and limited.

findings.situation: The corporation owns a CFC and has not made the entity election, so the filer's subpart F or GILTI inclusion appears in Schedule K-3 Part V rather than in box 10, and the filer answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 8: "If Regulations section 1.958-1(d) applies for the tax year ... no information will be provided in box 10 using code F or G. Instead, the corporation will provide information needed to figure your section 951(a) inclusions in Part V of Schedule K-3"
findings.why: The IRS box 10 text sends these other-income inclusions to K-3. Because the screen only asks about box 10, the inclusion and the stock basis increase it causes on Form 7203 line 3i go uncomputed.

findings.situation: Box 10 shows a code with an entry of 0 or a blank amount.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 6: "In boxes 10, 12, 13, and 15 through 17, the corporation will identify each item by entering a code in the column to the left of the dollar amount entry space."
findings.why: It is not clear whether a code entered with a zero or blank dollar entry counts as 'an amount'. Filers could answer either way, which affects both the code-only case and the STMT case.

findings.situation: This year's K-1 shows nothing in boxes 11 and 12, but the filer has section 179 or other box 12 deductions from this corporation that were disallowed in a prior year by the basis or at-risk limits and carried forward.

findings.situation: The filer has loaned money to the S corporation and has debt basis, but the corporation repaid nothing this year, so box 16 shows no code E. The filer truthfully answers NO, and the tool figures the basis limitation with debt basis treated as zero.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 3, Part II: "You must complete this section if you have personally loaned money to the corporation." i7203 p. 1: "the deduction for your share of aggregate losses and deductions ... is limited to the basis of your stock and loans from you to the corporation." i1120ssk p. 3: "Any amounts described in (3) and (4) ... not used ... to reduce your stock basis, are used to reduce your loan basis."
findings.why: The question asks only whether box 16 shows a repayment code. A shareholder with an outstanding loan and no repayment answers NO, yet Form 7203 Part II still sets debt basis, which allows losses beyond stock basis and covers later restoration. The tool ignores this, which wrongly suspends losses or skips the debt-basis reduction.

findings.situation: Box 9 shows 0, or nets to zero across activities, while the attached activity statement shows a section 1231 gain in one activity and a passive section 1231 loss in another.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 8: "If the corporation had net section 1231 gain (loss) from more than one activity, it will attach a statement that will identify the section 1231 gain (loss) from each activity." It also says: "If the amount is a loss from a passive activity ... follow the Instructions for Form 8582 to figure how much of the loss is allowed on Form 4797."
findings.why: A filer could read a printed 0 as "an amount" (YES) or as no amount (NO). If the per-activity statement holds offsetting gain and passive loss, a NO answer skips Form 4797 and Form 8582 reporting that the text requires.

findings.situation: The corporation uses a fiscal year that ends in 2025 (for example, March 2024 to February 2025), and the filer sold, gave away or redeemed shares in 2024 during that corporate year, so the filer truthfully answers NO to 'In 2025'.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 3: "If a portion of your stock is redeemed, sold, or otherwise disposed of during the year, attach two separate forms"; i1120ssk p. 6: "if the corporation's tax year ends in February 2026, report the amounts on your 2026 tax return."
findings.why: The two-Form-7203 rule applies to dispositions during the corporation's tax year whose K-1 is reported on the 2025 return, and that year can include 2024 dates. Because the question limits itself to calendar 2025, the tool would compute a single year-end Form 7203 that ignores the mid-year basis split.

findings.situation: The filer's shares became worthless or were abandoned in 2025, but the filer made no sale, gift or buy-back.
findings.irs_text: i7203 p. 1: "Disposed of stock in an S corporation (whether or not gain is recognized)"; i7203 p. 3: "redeemed, sold, or otherwise disposed of during the year"
findings.why: The question and its help list only sales, gifts and buy-backs. A filer could reasonably decide that shares which simply became worthless or were abandoned were not 'disposed of', even though they are treated as a disposition that needs basis at that date and Form 8949.

findings.situation: The filer worked 100 hours or fewer, or did not do nearly all the work, but on all the facts took part in the business regularly, continuously and substantially during the year (test 7), and answers NO because the question never describes that test.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4, Individuals: "7. Based on all the facts and circumstances, you participated in the activity on a regular, continuous, and substantial basis during the tax year."
findings.why: The question spells out tests 2 and 4 but covers test 7 only as "another test of material participation". The help text points to the K-1 instructions instead of stating the test, so a filer who doesn't know it exists answers NO and the tool treats the activity as passive.

findings.situation: A filer with significant participation activities outside this S corporation may not know whether to count those hours toward the 500.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4, test 4: "you participated in all significant participation activities (including activities outside the corporation) during the year for more than 500 hours"
findings.why: "All such businesses" can be read as only the businesses held through this corporation, or as only businesses like this one. Under the narrower reading, a filer who meets test 4 with outside activities answers NO.

findings.situation: A filer who worked over 100 hours in this business reaches 500 hours in total only by counting businesses where they worked 100 hours or less, or businesses where they already materially participated, and answers YES although test 4 is not met.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: "A significant participation activity is any trade or business activity in which you participated for more than 100 hours during the year and in which you didn't materially participate under any of the material participation tests (other than this test)."
findings.why: "Over 500 hours in all such businesses together" does not limit the count to other businesses with more than 100 hours that were not otherwise materially participated in. A filer can therefore answer YES and be refused although the activity is passive and the tool would handle it.

findings.situation: A filer unsure whether employees' or other non-owners' work counts in "the work done in it" may answer test 2 using only the owners' work.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4, test 2: "substantially all the participation in the activity of all individuals (including individuals who aren't owners of interests in the activity)"
findings.why: The question doesn't say that work by non-owners such as employees counts. A filer who did nearly all the owners' work but not nearly all of everyone's work could wrongly answer YES.

question: Did you do nearly all the work done in it, or work over 100 hours in it and over 500 hours in all such businesses together, or meet another test of material participation?

findings.situation: Boxes 18 and 19 are both unchecked, but the K-1 shows several kinds of items, such as box 1 business income together with box 4 interest or box 2 rental income, and the filer treats these as 'more than one activity' because of the parenthetical.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 4: 'it will attach a statement to your Schedule K-1 that identifies each activity (trade or business activity, rental real estate activity, rental activity other than rental real estate, portfolio income, etc.)'; p. 19: 'When the corporation has more than one activity for passive activity purposes, it will check this box and attach a statement.'
findings.why: The question asks about the checkboxes but restates the test in lay terms as 'the corporation has more than one activity'. A filer whose K-1 reports several kinds of income could take the parenthetical as the real test and answer YES, so the tool would refuse a single-activity K-1 it handles correctly. Another filer would answer NO because neither box is checked.

findings.situation: The filer bought shares or made a loan to the corporation using property, not money, and that property was subject to nonrecourse debt or protected against loss.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "if the cash or other property used to purchase the stock or make the loans was from a source (a) covered by nonrecourse indebtedness ..."
findings.why: The question asks only about paying 'with money borrowed', so a filer who used encumbered or protected property can truthfully answer NO.

findings.situation: The filer contributed cash or property to the corporation's capital without receiving new shares or making a loan, and the contribution was nonrecourse-financed, guaranteed, or borrowed from an interested or related person.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "Any cash or property contributed to a corporate activity, or your interest in the corporate activity, that is (a) covered by nonrecourse indebtedness ..."
findings.why: The question covers only paying 'for your shares, or for loans to the corporation', so a filer whose at-risk problem comes from a capital contribution answers NO.

findings.situation: The filer paid with their own cash, but their stock or interest is protected against loss by a stop-loss agreement, buy-back agreement, or similar arrangement.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "your interest in the corporate activity, that is ... (b) protected against loss by a guarantee, stop-loss agreement, or other similar arrangement"
findings.why: The question reaches loss protection only through 'money borrowed on terms that protect you', so protection of the investment itself, without any borrowing, leads to a truthful NO.

findings.situation: The filer borrowed from someone who has an interest in the activity but is not an owner of the corporation (for example, the corporation itself or a person sharing in its profits), or from someone related to such a person.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "covered by indebtedness from a person who has an interest in the activity or from a person related to a person (except you) having such an interest, other than a creditor"
findings.why: The question names only 'another owner of the corporation or someone related to one', which is narrower than anyone with an interest in the activity.

findings.situation: The filer has losses from a prior year that were disallowed under the at-risk rules and carried forward to this year, but this year's financing is fully recourse.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "Any loss from a section 465 activity not allowed for this tax year will be treated as a deduction allocable to the activity in the next tax year."
findings.why: The question asks only how the shares or loans were paid for, so a filer with an at-risk carryover the tool ignores can answer NO.

findings.situation: The filer financed the stock with qualified nonrecourse financing, or acquired the stock before 1987 and the loss comes from holding real property the corporation placed in service before 1987.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "(except for certain qualified nonrecourse financing, as defined in section 465(b)(6))"; "if you acquired your stock before 1987, the at-risk rules don't apply to losses from an activity of holding real property placed in service before 1987"
findings.why: The question ('a loan you are not personally liable for') makes such a filer answer YES even though the amounts are treated as at risk or the at-risk rules don't apply, so no Form 6198 is needed.

findings.situation: A third party co-signed or guaranteed the filer's own bank loan, and the filer remains personally liable to the bank and to the guarantor.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "protected against loss by a guarantee, stop-loss agreement, or other similar arrangement"
findings.why: The question treats 'one someone guarantees for you' as a YES, but the help says a bank loan 'that you must repay yourself is not meant'. A guarantee of the lender, as opposed to protection of the filer, may not make the filer not at risk.

question: Did you pay for your shares, or for loans to the corporation, with money borrowed on terms that protect you from loss (a loan you are not personally liable for, or one someone guarantees for you), or borrowed from another owner of the corporation or someone related to one?

findings.situation: The filer has a current-year loss or deduction from the corporation's activity and is not fully at risk, for example because stock or loan basis was funded with nonrecourse or guaranteed borrowing, but no loss was limited on any earlier return.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 3: "Generally, if you have (a) a loss or other deduction from any activity carried on as a trade or business or for the production of income by the corporation, and (b) amounts in the activity for which you aren't at risk, you will have to complete Form 6198, At-Risk Limitations, to figure your allowable loss for the activity." i1120ssk p. 6: "If any of the above limitations apply, adjust the amounts on Schedule K-1 before you report them on your return."
findings.why: The question asks only about a loss held back on an earlier return. A filer whose at-risk limitation first applies this year truthfully answers NO. The tool then reports the full loss with no Form 6198 adjustment.

findings.situation: The corporation checks box 18 (more than one activity for at-risk purposes) and the filer has a loss from one activity in which the filer is not at risk, with no prior-year carryover.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 19: "When the corporation has more than one activity for at-risk purposes, it will check this box and attach a statement. Use the information in the attached statement to correctly determine your at-risk limitations."
findings.why: The at-risk limit applies separately to each activity in the current year. The question's wording, which looks only at prior-year carryovers, does not reach this case.

findings.situation: A loss was suspended under the at-risk rules in an earlier year and was fully allowed in a later year, so no at-risk carryover remains for this year.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Was a loss from this corporation held back on an earlier return by the at-risk rules (Form 6198)?" i1120ssk p. 3: "Any loss from a section 465 activity not allowed for this tax year will be treated as a deduction allocable to the activity in the next tax year."
findings.why: The past-tense wording makes this filer answer YES even though nothing carries into the current year. The tool's zero treatment of carryovers would be correct for this filer.

findings.situation: A filer whose loss from this corporation was disallowed in an earlier year by the basis limitation (Form 7203) or the passive rules may not know which rule held it back.
findings.irs_text: i1120ssk p. 6: "If you have losses, deductions, or credits from a prior year that weren't deductible or usable because of certain limitations, such as the basis limitations or the at-risk limitations, take them into account in determining your income, loss, or credits for this year."
findings.why: "Held back" is a lay phrase that covers any suspended loss. One filer could answer YES for a basis or passive suspension, while another answers NO for an actual at-risk suspension, so the answer does not reliably track Form 6198.

question: Was a loss from this corporation held back on an earlier return by the at-risk rules (Form 6198)?

findings.situation: A filer receives damages for emotional distress caused by a physical injury, such as anxiety after a car accident, and answers NO because the payment was labeled emotional distress rather than physical injury.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 32: "Emotional distress itself isn't a physical injury or physical sickness, but damages you receive for emotional distress due to a physical injury or sickness are treated as received for the physical injury or sickness. Don't include them in your income."
findings.why: The question asks only whether damages were paid on account of a physical injury and never mentions emotional distress. A filer who reads that emotional distress isn't a physical injury can truthfully answer NO, and the tool then taxes an excludable amount.

findings.situation: A filer receives a discrimination or reputation settlement that includes an amount for medical care for the resulting emotional distress, so no physical injury is involved and the answer is NO.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 32: "you must include the damages in your income, except for any damages you receive for medical care due to that emotional distress."
findings.why: The medical-care part is excluded even though no physical injury or sickness exists. The question cannot reach this case, so the tool enters the full amount on line 8z.

findings.situation: A filer receives damages for a non-physical personal injury under a written binding agreement, court decree, or mediation award in effect on or before September 13, 1995, and answers NO because the injury was not physical.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 32: "If you receive damages under a written binding agreement, court decree, or mediation award that was in effect (or issued on or before) September 13, 1995, don't include in income any of those damages received on account of personal injuries or sickness."
findings.why: Under the pre-1995 rule, damages for any personal injury are excluded, not only physical ones. The question asks only about physical injury, so the tool includes these excluded damages.

findings.situation: A filer receives a settlement whose underlying claim makes it capital gain or a return of capital, such as compensation for damage to property, and answers NO because no physical injury was involved.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 32: "The character of the income as ordinary income or capital gain depends on the nature of the underlying claim."
findings.why: The tool reports the whole amount as ordinary income on line 8z, and no screen catches settlements that replace capital or restore a loss.

findings.situation: A filer whose award is entirely punitive damages in a physical-injury case must answer YES, although the full amount is taxable and the tool's computation (full amount on line 8z) would be correct.
findings.irs_text: Question: "including punitive damages in a case about one"; p525 p. 32: "Punitive damages in most cases. It doesn't matter if they relate to a physical injury or physical sickness."
findings.why: No split is needed when the award contains no compensatory physical-injury damages, yet the wording sends this filer to a refusal.

findings.situation: A filer missed an RMD whose deadline fell in an earlier year, and that tax belongs to that year's return, but the filer still truthfully answers YES to 'a required minimum distribution ... that you did not receive in full by its deadline'.

findings.situation: A filer has a prior-year qualified business net loss carryforward (a negative Form 8995 line 16 from 2024) that came from section 199A itself, not from a loss suspended by another Code provision.

findings.why: The question asks only about a 'prior-year REIT or PTP loss carryforward' and about losses 'suspended ... by another provision', so this filer answers NO. The tool then ignores the line 3 carryforward that should reduce QBI.

findings.situation: A filer has QBI or a QBI loss from a Schedule C business entered in the tool, but the computed line uses only Form 1099-DIV box 5 dividends.
findings.irs_text: f8995 (2025) lines 1–2: '(c) Qualified business income or (loss) ... Total qualified business income or (loss)'; i8995 p.3: 'Determining if items on Schedule C (Form 1040) are included in QBI.'
findings.why: The question expressly excludes 'the Schedule C businesses entered in this tool', so this filer answers NO. Yet qbi.eligible takes only section 199A dividends, and the refusal says 'Only section 199A dividend income ... is supported', so Schedule C QBI (lines 1–5) is treated as zero.

findings.situation: A filer's Form 1099-DIV box 5 includes REIT dividends on shares held 45 days or fewer, or dividends whose payment is obligated to someone else.
findings.irs_text: i8995 p.3: 'Qualified REIT dividends include any dividends you received from a REIT held for more than 45 days and for which the payment isn't obligated to someone else'
findings.why: The question treats section 199A dividends as fully supported, so this filer answers NO. The tool then enters the full box 5 amount, including dividends that are not qualified.

findings.situation: A filer has losses allowed this year that were suspended earlier but did not come from a qualified trade or business, such as a pre-2018 loss or a non-trade-or-business rental loss, and the tool correctly treats them as zero for QBI.
findings.irs_text: i8995 p.3: 'Losses or deductions from a qualified trade or business that are suspended by other provisions ... In general, losses and deductions incurred prior to 2018 are not qualified losses or deductions and are not included in QBI'
findings.why: The question asks about 'losses or deductions suspended in an earlier year by another provision and allowed this year' without limiting it to qualified, post-2017 trade or business losses. These filers answer YES and are refused even though zero is the correct QBI amount.

findings.situation: A filer who took the 2024 standard deduction receives a 2025 recovery of a 2024 nonitemized deduction, such as payment on a bad debt deducted in 2024. The filer truthfully answers No because nothing relates to a year before 2024, and the tool then enters zero on line 8z because Worksheet 2 is not used.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24: "You may also have recoveries of nonitemized deductions (such as payments on previously deducted bad debts)"; p525 p. 28: "If you recover an amount that you deducted in an earlier year when you were figuring your AGI, you must generally include the full amount of the recovery in your income in the year received."
findings.why: The question only screens for the year of the deduction, not its type. A 2024 nonitemized recovery passes the gate and this screen, but the tool computes line 8z only through the itemized Worksheet 2 branch and otherwise enters zero.

findings.situation: A filer has a taxable 2024 itemized recovery and also gets reimbursed in 2025 for a bill paid in 2023, a year in which they took the standard deduction. The 2023 reimbursement is not income, but the filer must answer Yes because the bill was "paid" before 2024.
findings.irs_text: Question: "for something you paid or deducted in a year before 2024"; p525 p. 24: "If you didn't itemize deductions for the year for which you received the recovery of an expense that was deductible only if you itemized, don't include any of the recovery amount in your income."
findings.why: The word "paid" pulls in pre-2024 expenses that gave no tax benefit and need no Worksheet 2. The tool already computes the correct result for these, since the amount is zero, yet the filer is refused.

findings.situation: A filer whose pre-2024 deduction was recovered as a credit, offset, or rebate rather than cash might not think of it as "money paid back to you" and answer No.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24: "The most common recoveries are refunds, reimbursements, and rebates of itemized deductions"; "If you received a refund or credit in 2025 of mortgage interest paid in an earlier year"
findings.why: "Paid back to you" can reasonably be read to mean cash only, while the IRS treats credits, offsets and price adjustments as recoveries too.

findings.situation: A filer who claimed a credit on an item in 2024 and in 2025 got a downward price adjustment applied to a balance, account credit, or store credit, with no cash refunded, could truthfully answer No to 'money paid back to you.'

findings.situation: A filer whose 2025 business expense was reimbursed in 2025 would answer Yes to 'a business expense refunded,' although a same-year recovery only reduces the deduction and adds nothing to line 8z, so the tool's computation of zero is correct.

findings.situation: The filer's money in the rental is protected against loss by a guarantee, stop-loss agreement, or similar arrangement, or came from a loan the filer is personally liable for but owes to someone with an interest in the activity or a related person. The filer truthfully answers NO because no non-personally-liable loan is involved.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 8: "(b) amounts in the activity for which you are not at risk, your loss may be limited. For more information, see At-Risk Rules, earlier. ... use Form 6198 to figure the amount of any deductible loss." Also p. 2: "At-risk rules apply to losses from rental real estate or royalties."
findings.why: The IRS test is whether any amount in the activity is not at risk. The question tests only one cause of that, nonrecourse borrowing. Protected amounts and certain recourse loans from interested or related lenders are also not at risk and still need Form 6198, but the wording lets the filer answer NO.

findings.situation: The filer used only their own funds, but earlier losses or cash withdrawn from the activity have reduced their at-risk amount below this year's loss. The filer truthfully answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 8 (Line 21): "... amount in the appropriate column of Schedule E, line 21. In the space to the left of line 21, enter 'Form 6198.' Attach Form 6198 to your return."
findings.why: The at-risk limit caps the deductible loss at the filer's current at-risk amount. That amount can fall below the loss without any nonrecourse loan, so the question never reaches this case.

findings.situation: A nonrecourse loan came from a commercial lender that is related to the filer, is the seller, or receives a fee from the filer's investment. The filer answers NO because the lender is 'a bank or other lender in the business of lending.'
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 2: "At-risk rules apply to losses from rental real estate or royalties. ... See At-Risk Rules, later, in the General Instructions."
findings.why: Under the at-risk rules, nonrecourse financing counts as at risk only if it comes from a qualified lender, and a lender with those ties does not qualify. The question exempts every lender in the business of lending.

findings.situation: The filer holds a nonrecourse loan secured by the rental property from, or guaranteed by, a federal, state, or local government. This is qualified nonrecourse financing and is treated as at risk, yet the wording makes the filer answer YES.
findings.irs_text: Question: "borrowed on a loan you are not personally liable for, other than a loan from a bank or other lender in the business of lending"; i1040se (2025) p. 2: "At-risk rules apply to losses from rental real estate or royalties."
findings.why: Government loans and government-guaranteed loans are qualified nonrecourse financing, but the question's only exception is for commercial lenders. The tool therefore refuses a case it computes correctly.

findings.situation: It is unclear what 'it' and 'money you put into it' cover. The filer cannot tell whether a nonrecourse mortgage taken out later (for example, a refinancing), or debt on the property rather than cash the filer contributed, counts.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 8: "amounts in the activity for which you are not at risk"
findings.why: The IRS test covers all amounts in the activity. The question's phrase 'money you put into it' can be read as only the filer's own contributed cash, which would exclude nonrecourse debt on the property itself.

findings.situation: A filer rents a property to make money but shows a net loss this year (for example, because of depreciation and mortgage interest) and may read 'rented not to make a profit' as 'did not make a profit' and answer YES.
findings.irs_text: f1040se (2025) p.1, line 21: "Subtract line 20 from line 3 (rents) and/or 4 (royalties). If result is a (loss), see instructions to find out if you must file Form 6198"; p527 (2025) p.17: "don't use that schedule to report a not-for-profit activity"
findings.why: The IRS test is whether the activity is engaged in to make a profit, not whether it produced one. Schedule E line 21 expressly handles a loss, yet the wording lets a loss-year filer answer YES and be refused a line the tool computes.

findings.situation: A filer rents a unit at fair rental price for most of the year and lets a friend stay a few days at a low rent, then answers YES because the question's own example matches those days.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p.5, Line 2: "A day of personal use is any day, or part of a day, that the unit was used by: ... Anyone who pays less than a fair rental price for the unit"; "Regardless of whether you used the unit as a home, expenses related to days of personal use do not qualify as rental expenses. You must allocate your expenses..."
findings.why: Under the Schedule E instructions, below-fair-rent days to a friend count as personal-use days within a for-profit rental reported on Schedule E, not as a not-for-profit activity. The example 'to a friend at a low rent' does not say whether it means the whole rental or some days, so a filer could answer YES when the property is still a Schedule E profit rental.

findings.irs_text: "If you rent out only part of your home or other property, deduct the part of your expenses that applies to the rented part." (i1040se 2025 p. 6, Renting out part of your home)
findings.why: The IRS allocation rule covers part of any property, not only a home. The question asks only about a property 'you also live in', so the case falls to the computed line, which subtracts unallocated total expenses.

findings.situation: The filer rents a room or one unit of a second home or vacation property they stay in only part-time, or of a home they lived in during 2025 but have since moved out of.
findings.irs_text: "A day of personal use is any day, or part of a day, that the unit was used by: • You for personal purposes" and "expenses related to days of personal use do not qualify as rental expenses" (i1040se 2025 p. 5, Line 2)

findings.situation: In the year the held-back loss arose, the filer helped make management decisions but owned less than 10% (by value) of the activity, so they did not actively participate; they truthfully answer NO and the tool puts the loss in Part IV.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 4: "You aren't considered to actively participate in a rental real estate activity if at any time during the tax year your interest (including your spouse's interest) in the activity was less than 10% (by value) of all interests in the activity." i8582 p. 10: "Don't enter a prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part IV unless you actively participated in the activity in both the year the loss arose and the current tax year."
findings.why: The question tests only whether the filer helped make decisions. Active participation also requires at least a 10% interest, so a filer who took part in decisions with a smaller interest answers NO even though the loss belongs in Part V.

findings.situation: In the year the loss arose, the filer held the rental as a limited partner and took part in decisions, so they answer NO, but they were not treated as actively participating.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 4: "Limited partners are not treated as actively participating in a partnership's rental real estate activity."
findings.why: Taking part in decisions does not make a limited partner an active participant. Under the question's wording this filer says NO, and the tool puts a Part V loss into Part IV column (c).

findings.situation: In the year the loss arose, the filer made no management decisions but arranged, in a significant and bona fide sense, for others to provide services such as repairs; this counts as active participation, yet the filer would answer YES.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Did any of that held-back loss come from a year when you (or your spouse) did not help make decisions for it?" i8582 p. 4: "You may be treated as actively participating if, for example, you participated in making management decisions or arranged for others to provide services (such as repairs) in a significant and bona fide sense."
findings.why: Arranging for services is a separate way to actively participate that the question leaves out. A filer who qualified that way would answer YES, and the tool would refuse a case it computes correctly in Part IV.

findings.situation: A filer who gave only nominal or occasional input, such as agreeing to a manager's choice of tenant, cannot tell whether that counts as helping make decisions.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 4: "...participated in making management decisions or arranged for others to provide services (such as repairs) in a significant and bona fide sense."
findings.why: The question drops the "significant and bona fide" standard. A filer could read any minor input as "helping make decisions" and answer NO when active participation was not met, or read it strictly and answer YES.

question:
Does this distribution involve any of these?

- a disability pension received before minimum retirement age, or a pension partly excludable because you were disabled as a result of a terrorist attack
- a corrective distribution of excess deferrals or contributions
- a qualified charitable distribution or HSA funding distribution
- nondeductible contributions to any traditional IRA
- a conversion or recharacterization (Form 8606)
- a 2024 or 2025 IRA contribution returned to you, or excess contributions for an earlier year returned to you in 2025
- a rollover to a Roth IRA or designated Roth account
- a lump-sum distribution you may report on Form 4972
- a distribution of employer securities with net unrealized appreciation (an amount in box 6)
- a nonperiodic payment received on or after the annuity starting date of an annuity in which you have after-tax cost that is a single-sum payment in connection with the start of the annuity payments, fully discharges the contract, or reduced your later annuity payments
- a distribution the IRS wrongfully levied, any part of which was returned to you and contributed back to a retirement plan or IRA
- a nonqualified annuity
- the retired public safety officer premium exclusion
- a death benefit exclusion
- a military disability pension
- an annuity you receive as the beneficiary of an employee who died before retiring (before their annuity starting date), guaranteed payments you receive as the beneficiary of a retiree under a life annuity contract, or an annuity that is shared among more than one beneficiary (a survivor annuity you receive under a retiree's joint and survivor annuity is not one of these)
- a rollover of property other than cash in which you sold the property and rolled over the proceeds, or rolled over only part of the property you received, or kept the property and rolled over cash or other property instead
- a rollover of a distribution under a qualified domestic relations order
- a qualified disaster recovery distribution (whatever the code in box 7), or a repayment of one, or a recontribution of a distribution to purchase or construct a main home that was canceled because of a qualified disaster (Form 8915-F)
- a plan loan offset
- a Form RRB-1099-R
- U.S. Civil Service retirement benefits under the alternative annuity option (Pub. 721)
- a pension or annuity in which you have after-tax cost whose annuity starting date (for a survivor of a retiree, the retiree's annuity starting date) was before November 19, 1996, or for which the Simplified Method does not apply (the General Rule)

findings.situation: A filer receives a nonqualified distribution from a Roth IRA, or a code T distribution, and has made no conversion, recharacterization or rollover this year, so none of the listed items applies and they answer NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2: "2. You received a distribution from a Roth IRA. But if either (a) or (b) below applies, enter -0- on line 4b ... a. Distribution code T is shown in box 7 ... and you made a contribution (including a conversion) to a Roth IRA for 2020 or an earlier year. b. Distribution code Q ..."
findings.why: Any Roth IRA distribution other than code Q, or code T with a pre-2021 contribution, needs Form 8606 to find the taxable part, and the question never mentions it. The tool would treat everything not rolled over as taxable, or treat the distribution as a qualified Roth distribution and tax none of it.

findings.situation: A filer receives a distribution from one traditional IRA in a year when they converted a different traditional IRA to a Roth IRA, and answers NO because this distribution was not itself a conversion.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2: "If any of the following apply, enter the total distribution on line 4a and see Form 8606 ... 3. You converted part or all of a traditional IRA or traditional SIMPLE IRA to a Roth IRA in 2025."
findings.why: Exception 2 is triggered by a conversion anywhere in the filer's year, and it then governs every IRA distribution. The question asks whether "this distribution" involves a conversion, so a filer can truthfully answer NO for a separate distribution that still needs Form 8606.

findings.situation: A filer takes a non-annuity distribution, before the annuity starting date, from a 401(k) or other qualified plan that holds after-tax contributions (box 5 or 9b), or rolls over such a distribution, and answers NO because only post-start-date nonperiodic payments are listed.
findings.irs_text: p575 p. 17: "If you receive a nonperiodic distribution before the annuity starting date from a qualified retirement plan, you can generally allocate only part of it to the cost of the contract ... Cost of contract x Amount received / Account balance = Tax-free amount"; i1040gi p. 30, Rollovers: "From this amount, subtract any contributions (usually shown in box 5) that were taxable to you when made."
findings.why: The tool figures cost recovery only by the Simplified Method for an annuity, so it would tax the whole distribution or the whole part not rolled over. The question names only nonperiodic payments made on or after the annuity starting date.

findings.situation: A filer with nondeductible contributions to a traditional IRA receives a pension or 401(k) distribution, or a code Q Roth IRA distribution, and is unsure whether that distribution 'involves' the nondeductible contributions.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2: "1. You received a distribution from an IRA (other than a Roth IRA) and you made nondeductible contributions to any of your traditional IRAs"
findings.why: The IRS condition applies only to distributions from non-Roth IRAs. The bullet "nondeductible contributions to any traditional IRA" can be read as a filer-level fact, which would wrongly refuse pension and qualified Roth distributions that the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer has a royalty loss on line 21 that includes amounts for which they are not at risk, and the screen never asks about this.
findings.irs_text: If you have amounts for which you are not at risk, use Form 6198 to determine the amount of your deductible loss. (i1040se 2025 p. 7, Line 21)
findings.why: The question only asks where the royalty came from, so this filer truthfully answers NO. The tool then enters the full line 4 minus line 20 loss without the Form 6198 limit.

findings.situation: A filer has an operating interest in a non-oil/gas mineral property, such as a coal or hard-rock mine, and receives payments from it.
findings.irs_text: Report on line 4 royalties from oil, gas, or mineral properties (not including operating interests) (i1040se 2025 p. 6, Line 4)
findings.why: The question only names an 'oil or gas working interest,' so this filer answers NO. The IRS text excludes all mineral operating interests from Schedule E.

findings.situation: A self-employed creator in a trade the question does not name, such as a software developer, photographer, designer or student-athlete with NIL business income, receives royalty-type income from their business.

If your NIL income is derived from business activities such as sponsorship deals or service income, report your income and expenses on Schedule C, not Schedule E. (i1040se 2025 p. 6, Line 4)
findings.why: The IRS 'etc.' and the NIL rule reach beyond the closed list 'writer, artist, musician or inventor.' A filer outside that list can truthfully answer NO, and the tool then puts business income on Schedule E.

findings.situation: A hobbyist or one-time author or inventor who is not in business as a writer or inventor receives royalties from their own book or patent.

findings.why: 'Your own work' invites a YES from anyone whose own creation produced the royalty. The IRS sends only those in business to Schedule C, so a non-business author belongs on Schedule E, which the tool computes.

findings.why: The question uses 'self-employed' without the IRS's 'in business' qualifier, and the help text does not explain it. Part-time or sporadic creators could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: A payer must pay the mortgage, real estate taxes and insurance on a home owned only by the recipient spouse; all of it can be alimony, so the tool's computed amount is right, but the wording makes the filer answer YES.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 13, Payments to a third party, Example 2: "you must pay the real estate taxes and mortgage payments on a home owned by your spouse. If they otherwise qualify, you can deduct the payments as alimony on your return, and your spouse must report them as alimony received."
findings.why: The question asks about "payments for a home either of you owns." That includes a home owned only by the recipient, which needs no split. Only homes the payer owns, alone or jointly with the spouse, partly fall outside alimony (p. 13 example under Payments not alimony; Table 4).

findings.situation: Alimony decreased or ended during the first 3 calendar years, but the recapture rule does not apply.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 16, When to apply the recapture rule: "You are subject to the recapture rule in the third year if the alimony you pay in the third year decreases by more than $15,000 from the second year or ... decreases significantly from the alimony you pay in the first year. When you figure a decrease in alimony, don't include ... Payments made under a temporary support order ... Payments that decrease because of the death of either spouse or the remarriage of the spouse receiving the payments"
findings.why: The parenthetical defines recapture as any "payments that decreased or ended during the first 3 calendar years." So a filer with a small decrease, a decrease caused by death or remarriage, or a change only to temporary-order payments answers YES. In those cases no recapture is owed and the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A payment includes a part that is not alimony for a reason other than the three sub-bullets, such as a noncash property settlement, the spouse's share of community income, or the use of the payer's property.
findings.irs_text: p504 p. 13, Payments not alimony: "Alimony doesn't include: Child support, Noncash property settlements, Payments that are your spouse's part of community income ..., Payments to keep up the payer's property, or Use of the payer's property."
findings.why: The heading "payments of which part is not alimony:" can be read as a general category, which gives YES. It can also be read as limited to the three listed sub-items, which gives NO. Under the second reading, the tool would take the whole mixed amount from the helper as alimony.

question:
Does any of these apply to alimony you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) received or paid?

- payments under more than one divorce or separation agreement, or paid to more than one person
- a recapture of alimony (payments that decreased or ended during the first 3 calendar years, Pub. 504 Worksheet 1)
- payments of which part is not alimony:
  - child support (including payments that fell short of the total of child support and alimony required, and an amount the instrument reduces on a contingency relating to a child, such as reaching a certain age, or at a time associated with one)
  - payments for a home either of you owns (mortgage, real estate taxes, insurance, repairs; Pub. 504 Table 4)
  - payments of which any part must continue, in cash or property, for any period after the recipient spouse's death (even if the instrument does not say so, for example under state law), or payments for which a payment due after the death is a substitute

findings.situation: A filer has a canceled personal loan or credit card debt whose Form 1099-C shows forgiven interest in box 3. That interest would not have been deductible if paid, so the whole box 2 amount is taxable and the tool computes it correctly.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 20: "If the interest would not be deductible (such as interest on a personal loan), include in your income the amount from box 2 of Form 1099-C."
findings.why: The question says "it includes interest (Form 1099-C box 3) or any other amount ... that would have been deductible." A filer can read this as "any box 3 interest, or other deductible amounts," so any box 3 entry triggers YES. Many credit card 1099-Cs carry a box 3 amount, so these filers are refused even though the tool's box 2 figure is right.

findings.situation: A filer who takes the standard deduction, or whose medical costs would not clear the AGI floor, has a forgiven unpaid medical bill or forgiven mortgage interest.
findings.irs_text: p4681 p. 6: "If you use the cash method of accounting, you don't realize income from the cancellation of debt if the payment of the debt would have been a deductible expense."
findings.why: Filers can read "would have been deductible if you had paid it" two ways. Some will take it to mean a deductible type of expense; others will take it to mean it would actually have lowered their tax given their own deduction choice. So similar filers will answer differently.

findings.situation: A creditor accepts the filer's services instead of money in full satisfaction of a nonbusiness debt. The filer reports the forgiven amount as canceled debt with no Form 1099-C.
findings.irs_text: p4681 p. 3: "You both agreed that you would provide your friend with services (instead of money) in full satisfaction of the debt. You don't have canceled debt. Instead, you have income from services."
findings.why: None of the listed conditions covers a debt paid off with services, so the filer truthfully answers NO. The tool then puts the amount on line 8c as canceled debt, when the IRS treats it as income from services.

question:
Does any of these apply to a canceled debt?

- it was canceled in a bankruptcy case or while you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) were insolvent, or is otherwise excluded from income (Form 982, for example qualified principal residence indebtedness)
- it was a student loan, was canceled as a gift or inheritance, was a reduction of the price of property you bought from the seller, or was owed to a corporation in which you hold stock
- it was a business, rental or farm debt
- it was canceled in connection with a foreclosure, repossession or abandonment of property (Form 1099-C box 7, or a Form 1099-A)
- it includes interest (Form 1099-C box 3) or any other amount (for example an unpaid medical bill) that would have been deductible if you had paid it
- you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) were not personally liable for it (box 5)
- you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) were liable for it together with someone who is not on this return

findings.situation: A filer who plays daily fantasy sports regularly and continuously for profit as a business may truthfully answer NO because they don't think of fantasy sports as 'gambling'. The tool would then put winnings on line 8b that belong on Schedule C.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 33: "Winnings from fantasy sports leagues are gambling winnings. ... If you're in the trade or business of gambling, use Schedule C (Form 1040)."
findings.why: The question doesn't say that fantasy sports, lotteries or similar wagering count as gambling. A business-level fantasy sports player can answer NO, and line 8b would then wrongly include business winnings.

findings.situation: A filer who gambles regularly and continuously for profit as a side business alongside a regular job may read '(a professional gambler)' as meaning full-time only and answer NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8b: "Enter gambling winnings not attributable to a trade or business"; p525 p. 33: "Engaging in gambling activities as a trade or business is considered self-employment."
findings.why: The IRS test is whether gambling is a trade or business, not whether it is the filer's main occupation. The label 'professional gambler' could lead a part-time business gambler to answer NO, while the 'trade or business' wording would lead them to answer YES.

findings.situation: A filer has a line 8z item the tool never asks about, such as a taxable Coverdell ESA or QTP distribution or the taxable part of disaster relief payments, and reads the exception for line 8z as covering all line 8z income.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92, Line 8z: "Use line 8z to report any taxable income not reported elsewhere ... Examples ... • Taxable part of disaster relief payments ... • Taxable distributions from a Coverdell education savings account (ESA) or a qualified tuition program (QTP)."
findings.why: The question exempts "the other income asked item by item for line 8z" but never says which 8z items those are. A filer could treat any 8z income as exempt and answer NO, and the tool would then count an unasked 8z item as zero. Another filer could read it to mean only the items the tool actually asks about and answer YES.

findings.situation: A filer who rents out personal property but not for profit (income the tool computes on line 8j) answers YES because the question gives "income from the rental of personal property" as an example of unsupported income.
findings.irs_text: f1040s1 p. 1, line 8l: "Income from the rental of personal property if you engaged in the rental for profit but were not in the business of renting such property"; i1040gi p. 91, Line 8j: "Activity not engaged in for profit income."
findings.why: The question's example "income from the rental of personal property (8l)" drops the for-profit condition. A not-for-profit rental belongs on line 8j, which the tool supports, yet the example tells that filer to answer YES.

findings.situation: A filer whose stock option income is already in wages on Form 1040 line 1a or 1h answers YES because the question lists "stock options (8k)" without qualification.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8k: "Enter any income from the exercise of stock options not otherwise reported on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1h."
findings.why: Line 8k covers only stock option income not reported elsewhere. The bare example "stock options" could lead a filer with no line 8k amount to answer YES and be refused unnecessarily.

findings.situation: A filer whose entire carryforward arose in tax years beginning after 2017 answers NO, but the carryforward is more than 80% of 2025 taxable income figured without the NOL and QBI deductions, so the allowed deduction is smaller than the amount the tool subtracts.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 1, NOL deduction limitation: "cannot exceed the sum of: (1) the NOLs carried to the year from tax years beginning before January 1, 2018; plus, (2) the lesser of: (a) the NOLs carried to the year from tax years beginning after December 31, 2017, or (b) 80% of the excess (if any) of taxable income computed without regard to deductions for NOLs, or Qualified Business Income (QBI), or section 250 deductions"
findings.why: The question asks only about losses from before 2018, but the 80% cap applies to post-2017 losses too, and line 8a subtracts the whole carryforward. A filer with only post-2017 losses truthfully answers NO and gets the full amount deducted, with no 80% limit applied.

findings.situation: A filer asked about 'the net operating loss carried into 2025' could enter the full carryover from the earlier return or the smaller amount deductible in 2025 after the limitation, and the question and help do not say which.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8a: "Enter any deduction for an NOL from an earlier year"; i172 p. 1, Step 5: "Determine the amount of your unused NOL"
findings.why: The IRS separates the deduction allowed this year from the carryover, but the screen and the amount it asks for use carryover wording. A filer cannot tell whether the tool wants the limited deduction or the raw carryforward.

findings.situation: A filer who had state unemployment insurance contributions withheld from wages in 2025 or an earlier year (as in NJ, PA or AK), but received no unemployment compensation in 2025, must answer YES and is refused. The tool would correctly compute line 7 as zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 89: 'If you made contributions to a governmental unemployment compensation program and you aren't itemizing deductions, reduce the amount you report on line 7 by those contributions.'
findings.why: The IRS adjustment only reduces unemployment compensation actually received in 2025, so it has no effect when none was received. The question asks about contributions in any year and is not limited to filers who received benefits in 2025.

findings.situation: A filer who repaid $3,000 or less in 2025 of unemployment compensation included in income in an earlier year must answer YES and is refused. The line 7 computation, which ignores that repayment, is correct.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 89: 'If, in 2025, you repaid more than $3,000 of unemployment compensation that you included in gross income in an earlier year, see Repayments in Pub. 525 for details on how to report the payment.'
findings.why: The question asks about 'repay in 2025 any unemployment compensation you included in income in an earlier year' with no threshold. The line 7 text gives no adjustment for earlier-year repayments, and only repayments over $3,000 lead to separate reporting treatment.
