findings.situation: A filer who owes no AMT but has an amount on line 7, 9, 13, 14, 15, 16, or 19 (for example, household employment taxes or uncollected Social Security and Medicare tax) can truthfully answer NO, and computed line 21 omits that amount.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 (2025) p. 2, line 21: "Add lines 4, 7 through 16, 18, and 19. These are your total other taxes"; p. 1, line 9: "Household employment taxes. Attach Schedule H"
findings.why: The tool adds only lines 4, 8, 11, 12, and 18, while the question asks only about Form 6251 and AMT adjustments. No listed refusal covers the omitted lines, so line 21 is understated on a NO answer.

findings.situation: A filer who has an AMT adjustment item or must file Form 6251 but owes no AMT on line 2 must answer YES, even though the computed zero on line 2 would be correct.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are you required to file Form 6251 or do you have an AMT adjustment requiring its review?"; f1040s2 (2025) p. 1, line 2: "Alternative minimum tax. Attach Form 6251"
findings.why: Having an adjustment or a filing requirement does not by itself mean a positive amount belongs on line 2. The question therefore refuses some filers whose lines 2, 3, and 21 the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer with a possible AMT preference or adjustment item cannot tell from the question whether it is one "requiring its review" or whether Form 6251 is required without first working through that form.
findings.irs_text: Question: "do you have an AMT adjustment requiring its review?"; f1040s2 (2025) p. 1, line 2: "Alternative minimum tax. Attach Form 6251"
findings.why: The question gives no test for when an adjustment requires review or when Form 6251 must be filed, and the line text supplies none. Similar filers could reasonably answer differently, and a NO could leave AMT owed treated as zero.

findings.situation: A filer with an HSA excess contribution from a prior year that was not withdrawn, and so still owes the 6% tax in 2025, cannot tell whether that is 'the 2025 HSA excess' the tool figures or an 'other amount'.

findings.why: 'The 2025 HSA excess' can mean only contributions made for 2025, or the whole excess subject to tax for the 2025 year, which includes carryover. findings.situation: The filer paid qualified expenses in 2024 toward adopting a U.S. child, the adoption was not final at the end of 2024 and did not become final in 2025 (still pending, or the attempt failed), and the filer paid nothing in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8839 (2025) p. 1, Purpose of Form: "You paid qualified adoption expenses in connection with the adoption of an eligible U.S. child ... in: a. 2024 and the adoption wasn't final at the end of 2024"; p. 3, Domestic Adoption: "any year before the year the adoption becomes final* ... the year after the year of the payment" and "an adoption credit may be allowable for an attempted or unsuccessful adoption, as well as for an adoption that isn't final."
findings.why: The credit for 2024 payments is taken on the 2025 return, but the question asks only about an adoption final in 2025 or expenses paid in 2025. This filer truthfully answers NO and lines 30 and Schedule 3 line 6c/7 are computed as zero.

findings.situation: The filer has an unused adoption credit carried forward from 2024 (for example, from an adoption finalized in 2023 or 2024), with no adoption becoming final in 2025 and no adoption expenses paid in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8839 (2025) p. 1, Purpose of Form: "4. You have a carryforward of an adoption credit from 2024. Any amount of the carryforward credit from 2024 remains a nonrefundable credit."
findings.why: The carryforward is claimed on Form 8839 and flows to Schedule 3 line 6c and so line 7, but nothing in the question mentions a carryforward or earlier-year adoptions. The filer answers NO and line 7 is computed as zero.

findings.situation: The filer first paid adoption expenses in 2025 for a U.S. child whose adoption was not final by the end of 2025 (or for a foreign child whose adoption is not yet final), with no 2024 expenses and no carryforward.
findings.irs_text: Question: "or pay expenses in 2025 in connection with adopting a child or trying to adopt one?" with help "Yes also if the costs paid in 2025 were for an adoption that is not finished." i8839 (2025) p. 1: "b. 2025 and the adoption became final in or before 2025"; p. 3, Domestic Adoption: "any year before the year the adoption becomes final* ... the year after the year of the payment"; p. 3, Foreign child: "you can't take the adoption credit or exclusion unless the adoption becomes final."
findings.why: No adoption credit is allowed on the 2025 return for these payments (the domestic credit is taken in 2026, the foreign one in the year the adoption becomes final). Zero on line 30 and line 6c would be correct, yet the wording and help text force YES and a refusal.

findings.situation: An adoption became final in 2025, but the child is not a special-needs child and the filer paid no qualified adoption expenses in any year.
findings.irs_text: Question: "adopt a child whose adoption became final in 2025". i8839 (2025) p. 1: "2. You adopted an eligible U.S. child with special needs and the adoption became final in 2025. (In this case, you may be able to take the credit even if you didn't pay any qualified adoption expenses.)"
findings.why: Without qualified expenses, only a special-needs adoption gives a credit, so zero is correct here. The question still makes this filer answer YES on finality alone.

findings.situation: The filer's adoption costs in 2025 were paid by an employer under an adoption assistance program rather than out of pocket.
findings.irs_text: i8839 (2025) p. 1: "Qualified Adoption Expenses don't include expenses reimbursed by an employer under a written qualified adoption assistance program ... you must complete Form 8839, Part III, before you can figure the credit, if any, in Part II."
findings.why: "Pay expenses" can be read as covering only the filer's own payments or also employer-paid or reimbursed costs. A filer with only employer-paid costs could answer either way.

findings.situation: In a U.S. domestic adoption, the effort began before the child was born, the child was later born in the U.S. and placed, and the adoption was not final at the end of 2024; the filer may answer No because the child was not yet a citizen or resident when the effort began.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 3: "A child is a foreign child if they weren't a citizen or resident of the United States (including U.S. territories) at the time the adoption effort began." and "If the eligible child is a U.S. citizen or resident, you can take the adoption credit or exclusion even if the adoption never became final ... IF you pay qualifying expenses in any year before the year the adoption becomes final THEN take the credit in the year after the year of the payment."
findings.why: The question asks only about the child's status when the effort began, and the help covers only 'no child placed yet'. A filer whose U.S.-born child did not exist at that time could truthfully answer No. The tool would then zero a 2025 credit for 2024 expenses that the IRS treats as a domestic (U.S. child) adoption.

findings.situation: A filer has more than one adoption effort with 2024 expenses not final at the end of 2024, and may not know which adoption 'such an adoption' refers to.
findings.irs_text: i8839 p. 1: "You paid qualified adoption expenses in connection with the adoption of an eligible U.S. child ... in: a. 2024 and the adoption wasn't final at the end of 2024"
findings.why: The phrase 'a child of such an adoption' relies on the gate's wording, which the filer may not see alongside this question. Some filers could answer only about a foreign-child adoption and miss a separate U.S.-child effort that the tool does not compute.

findings.situation: A filer carries forward an unused credit from a qualified tax credit bond or Build America bond from a prior year, but did not hold any tax credit bond on a 2025 credit allowance or interest payment date, for example because the bond was sold or matured.
findings.irs_text: i8912 p. 2, Line 3: "Enter the amount of the credit carryforward (from prior years) that is attributable to a qualified tax credit bond or a BAB."; p. 3: "you may carry the unused portion of the credit to the next tax year"
findings.why: The question asks whether the filer was allowed a credit for 2025 "as the holder of a tax credit bond," so a filer who held no bond in 2025 would truthfully answer NO. The tool would then enter $0, even though the carryforward belongs on Form 8912 and Schedule 3, line 6k.

findings.situation: A filer's bond credit came through a partnership, S corporation, RIC or trust statement such as a Schedule K-1, or came from a bond held directly with no information return at all, and nothing was reported on Form 1097-BTC or by the issuer.
findings.irs_text: i8912 p. 2, Line 2: "total bond credits from bonds held by you or your nominee(s) and not reported to you on Form(s) 1097-BTC ... may also include bond credits reported to you from a pass-through entity ... that weren't reported to you on Form(s) 1097-BTC"
findings.why: The question says "whether or not reported on Form 1097-BTC," but the help says "Reported on Form 1097-BTC or by the bond's issuer." A filer could read the help as limiting the question to credits reported by the issuer and answer NO for an unreported or pass-through credit.

findings.situation: A filer held a tax credit bond directly or through a nominee, or was passed a bond credit by a partnership, S corporation, estate, trust, RIC or REIT (for example on a Schedule K-1), and received no Form 1097-BTC.
findings.irs_text: i8912 p. 2, Line 2: "This amount is the total bond credits from bonds held by you or your nominee(s) and not reported to you on Form(s) 1097-BTC. This amount may also include bond credits reported to you from a pass-through entity ... that weren't reported to you on Form(s) 1097-BTC."
findings.why: The question asks only about receiving a Form 1097-BTC, so this filer truthfully answers NO. The Form 8912 credit that belongs on Schedule 3 line 6k is then computed as zero.

findings.situation: A filer has an unused credit from a qualified tax credit bond or Build America bond carried forward from an earlier year and received no Form 1097-BTC for 2025.
findings.irs_text: i8912 p. 2, Line 3: "Enter the amount of the credit carryforward (from prior years) that is attributable to a qualified tax credit bond or a BAB." i8912 p. 3: "you may carry the unused portion of the credit to the next tax year"
findings.why: The carryforward is claimed on Form 8912 and flows to line 6k, but no 2025 Form 1097-BTC exists, so the filer answers NO and line 7 is zero.

findings.situation: An audited or AAR partnership furnished its Forms 8986 during 2025 to a pass-through partner, which furnished the filer's Form 8986 in early 2026.
findings.irs_text: i8978 p. 2, Definitions: "Reporting year is the partner's tax year(s) that includes the date the audited or AAR partnership furnished the Forms 8986 to its partners." Example 1 on the same page treats a statement furnished by a pass-through partner on January 15, 2025 as a 2024 reporting year because the audited partnership furnished on March 1, 2024.
findings.why: The filer was not personally furnished a Form 8986 "during 2025" and answers NO. The reporting year is nonetheless 2025, so Form 8978 (line 6l) is required with the 2025 return.

findings.situation: A pass-through partner furnished the filer a Form 8986 in early 2025, but the audited partnership had furnished its Forms 8986 in 2024, so the filer's reporting year is 2024.
findings.irs_text: Question: "were you furnished a Form 8986 ... during 2025". i8978 p. 2, Example 1: "On January 15, 2025, the pass-through partner, in turn, furnishes Forms 8986 ... The reporting year for all three individuals is the tax year that includes March 1, 2024 ... the reporting year is the 2024 tax year."
findings.why: The filer truthfully answers YES and is refused, although Form 8978 belongs on the 2024 return. The 2025 line 6l is correctly zero.

findings.situation: A filer receives a Form 8986 and cannot tell whether "furnished during 2025" means the date they personally received it or the date the audited or AAR partnership furnished its statements (Form 8986, Part II, item G).
findings.irs_text: i8978 p. 2: "The date the audited partnership or BBA partnership that filed an AAR furnished Forms 8986 to its partners is found on Form 8986, Part II, item G."
findings.why: The question and its help text do not point to item G. A filer in a tiered structure could reasonably use either date and reach opposite answers.

findings.situation: A filer under 65 who retired on disability but has no taxable disability income in 2025, or who had reached mandatory retirement age by January 1, 2025, or who was a nonresident alien during the year, may want the credit and answer YES, even though the tool's $0 is correct for them.
findings.irs_text: i1040sr p. 1: "You were under age 65 ... and all three of the following statements are true. a. You retired on permanent and total disability ... b. You receive taxable disability income for 2025. c. On January 1, 2025, you had not reached mandatory retirement age"; "Generally, you can't take the credit if you were a nonresident alien at any time during the tax year."
findings.why: The question asks whether the filer wants to claim the credit, not whether they qualify for it. Its help text mentions only the income limits, so ineligible filers who would like the credit answer YES and are refused although $0 is right for them.

findings.situation: A filer whose AGI is under $17,500 and whose nontaxable social security plus nontaxable pensions is under $5,000, but whose nontaxable annuities or nontaxable disability income bring the total to $5,000 or more, may read the help, believe they are under the limit, and answer YES.
findings.irs_text: i1040sr p. 3: "The second limit is the amount of nontaxable social security and other nontaxable pensions, annuities, or disability income you received ... If your AGI or your nontaxable pensions, annuities, or disability income are equal to or more than the income limits, you can't take the credit."
findings.why: The help states the second limit as "nontaxable social security and pensions under $5,000" and leaves out nontaxable annuities and disability income. Filers who are over the real limit can therefore conclude they qualify, answer YES, and be refused although the computed $0 is correct.

findings.situation: A filer under 65 who stopped working because of a disability that is not permanent and total may treat "retired on disability" in the help as describing them and be unsure whether the question applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040sr p. 1: "a. You retired on permanent and total disability. (See Permanent and Total Disability, later)."
findings.why: The help says "retired on disability" without the "permanent and total" standard, and the question gives no eligibility test. A filer cannot tell whether a temporary or partial disability counts, so whether they should answer YES depends on how they read it.

findings.situation: A filer bought a new or previously owned clean vehicle from a registered dealer before October 1, 2025, transferred the credit to the dealer at the time of sale to lower the price, and so does not want to claim the credit on this return.
findings.irs_text: i8936 (2025) p. 1, Caution: "You must file Form 8936 and Schedule A (Form 8936) if you purchased a new or used clean vehicle from a registered dealer and reduced the amount you paid at the time of sale by transferring the credit to the dealer." Also p. 1, Reminders: "If you elect to transfer the credit, you must file Form 8936 and Schedule A (Form 8936) with your return for the tax year in which the vehicle was placed in service."
findings.why: The question asks only whether the filer wants to claim the credit on this return, so a filer who already took the credit through a dealer transfer truthfully answers No. The tool then goes on without the Form 8936 and Schedule A that the IRS requires for transferred credits, and it never checks whether that advance credit has to be reconciled on the return.

findings.situation: A filer bought a qualifying new or used clean vehicle in 2025, acquired it on or before September 30, 2025, and did not transfer the credit to the dealer. They intend to claim the credit on the return, so they truthfully answer NO, and line 7 is entered as $0.
findings.irs_text: i8936 p. 1, Purpose of Form: "Use Form 8936 and Schedule A (Form 8936) to figure the following credits for clean vehicles you placed in service during your tax year. • New clean vehicle credit. • Previously owned clean vehicle credit."; f1040s3 line 6f "Clean vehicle credit. Attach Form 8936" and line 6m "Credit for previously owned clean vehicles. Attach Form 8936"
findings.why: The question asks only about transfers to a dealer. A filer who claims the clean vehicle credit directly on Form 8936 for line 6f or 6m answers NO, and the tool zeroes line 7 instead of refusing. Unless a sibling screen covers this case, the filer loses a credit the IRS text allows.

findings.situation: A filer bought a clean vehicle and transferred the credit to the dealer in 2024, with the vehicle placed in service in 2024. In 2025 the filer only installed a home charger, or got a different vehicle without a transfer. The gate is satisfied, and the untimed question makes them answer YES.
findings.irs_text: i8936 p. 1, Reminders: "If you elect to transfer the credit, you must file Form 8936 and Schedule A (Form 8936) with your return for the tax year in which the vehicle was placed in service."
findings.why: The question "Did you ... purchase a new or used clean vehicle from a registered dealer and transfer the credit to the dealer at the time of sale" names no year. A transfer for a vehicle placed in service in an earlier year triggers a refusal, even though no 2025 Form 8936 is required for it.

findings.situation: A filer leased an EV in 2025, and the lessor passed through the commercial clean vehicle credit as a lower lease price or capitalized-cost reduction that the paperwork labels as a federal tax credit.
findings.irs_text: i8936 p. 1, Caution: "You must file Form 8936 and Schedule A (Form 8936) if you purchased a new or used clean vehicle from a registered dealer and reduced the amount you paid at the time of sale by transferring the credit to the dealer."
findings.why: The gate help says to count vehicles "bought or leased." The question's phrase "for a reduced price or another immediate financial benefit" and help text about the sales papers showing a clean vehicle credit could lead a lessee to answer YES, even though a lessee makes no transfer election and needs no Form 8936.

findings.situation: A filer has a refundable section 960(c) excess-limitation credit, did not sell farmland or make the Form 1062 election, and so truthfully answers No; the tool then enters $0 on line 14.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 117, Line 13z: "Use line 13z to report the credit under section 960(c) with respect to an excess limitation account ... the amount of the excess is deemed an overpayment of tax and can be claimed on line 13z as a refundable credit."
findings.why: The refusal cites this text, but the question asks only about the farmland deferral election. A filer with a 960(c) credit answers No and loses the credit because line 14 is forced to $0.

findings.situation: A filer must report U.S. tax allocable to the U.S. Virgin Islands (Form 8689) on line 13z, answers No because there was no farmland election, and the tool enters $0 on line 14.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 117, Line 13z: "Also use line 13z to report the amount of U.S. tax allocable to the U.S. Virgin Islands. Enter 'Form 8689' and the amount paid."
findings.why: Line 14 adds all of lines 13a through 13z, but the question covers only the 1062NL entry. The Form 8689 payment is dropped by a truthful No.

findings.situation: A filer has an amount on Schedule 3 line 13a, 13b, 13c, or 13d (Form 2439, section 1341 credit, net elective payment amount, or deferred 965 liability) and answers No to the farmland question.
findings.irs_text: f1040s3 2025 line 14: "Total other payments or refundable credits. Add lines 13a through 13z"; i1040gi 2025 p. 117, Line 13b: "If you are claiming a credit for repayment of amounts you included in your income in an earlier year ... enter the amount on line 13b."
findings.why: The computed line 14 of $0 assumes every component of lines 13a through 13z is zero. This screen does not ask about these components, and no listed refusal covers them.

findings.situation: A filer who sold qualified farmland to a qualified farmer in 2025 intends to elect the deferral on the return now being prepared, but reads the past-tense question as asking about an election already made and answers No.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 117, Line 13z: "If you made the election to defer net income tax attributable to the gain on the sale or exchange of qualified farmland property, use Form 1062 ... On line 13z, enter 75% of your applicable net tax liability from Form 1062, line 14."
findings.why: The election is made with the return for the year of sale. "Did you ... make the election" could be read as asking about an election already made, so the 75% 1062NL entry would be omitted. The help text "If you have not heard of it, the answer is No" adds to this risk.

findings.situation: A filer who has a 2022–2024 mortgage interest credit carryforward from an MCC on a home they have sold (or whose MCC loan was paid off) now pays interest on a new home loan with no MCC, so they truthfully answer NO and the tool enters $0 on line 7, dropping the carryforward.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 1, lines 4–6: "Enter any 2022 credit carryforward from line 16 of your 2024 Form 8396" ... p. 2, Part II: "you may have an unused credit to carry forward to the next 3 tax years or until used"
findings.why: The question asks only about an MCC "for the loan on your main home", but Form 8396 lines 4–6 bring in prior-year carryforwards that remain usable even after the certificate's loan is gone. Those carryforwards still flow to Schedule 3 line 6g and line 7.

findings.situation: A filer who holds a state- or local-issued MCC cannot claim the credit because the interest was paid to a related person, or because the loan was refinanced without the MCC being reissued, and has no carryforward, yet must answer YES and is refused.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 2, Who Can Claim the Credit: "If the interest on the mortgage was paid to a related person, you cannot claim the credit"; Refinanced Mortgage: "You can refinance your mortgage without losing this credit if your existing MCC is reissued"
findings.why: The question "Were you ... issued a mortgage credit certificate (MCC) ... for the loan on your main home?" is satisfied by having been issued an MCC at all. In these cases line 6g is $0, and the tool's $0 would be correct.

findings.situation: A filer whose original MCC loan was refinanced, or who has more than one loan on the home, may not know whether "the loan" means the original MCC-backed loan or the current loan.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 2, Line 1: "If the loan amount on your MCC is less than your total mortgage loan, you must allocate the interest to determine the part that relates to the loan covered by the MCC."
findings.why: "the loan on your main home" assumes a single loan. A filer with a refinanced loan that has no reissued certificate, or with a second loan, could reasonably answer either way.

findings.irs_text: i8801 (2025) p. 1, Who Should File: "Complete Form 8801 if you are an individual, estate, or trust that for 2024 had: • An AMT liability and adjustments or preferences other than exclusion items, • A credit carryforward to 2025 (on 2024 Form 8801, line 26), or • An unallowed qualified electric vehicle credit"; f8801 (2025) p. 2, line 19: "2024 credit carryforward. Enter the amount from your 2024 Form 8801, line 26"
findings.why: The question asks only about a 2024 AMT liability, so this filer truthfully answers NO and line 6b (inside line 7) is computed as $0 although a credit may be allowed. This is a gap unless a separate screen, not shown among the listed refusals, asks about the Form 8801 carryforward.

findings.situation: A filer had no 2024 AMT liability but had a qualified electric vehicle credit that was not allowed for 2024 because of the tentative minimum tax limit, which enters Form 8801, line 20 and can produce a 2025 minimum tax credit.

findings.why: The wording covers only an AMT liability on 2024 Form 6251, line 11, so this filer answers NO and the tool enters $0 on line 7 even though Form 8801, line 21 could be more than zero.

findings.situation: A filer's 2024 AMT liability came entirely from exclusion items (for example the standard deduction, certain itemized deductions, certain tax-exempt interest or depletion) and there is no carryforward, so no minimum tax credit exists and $0 on line 6b is correct.
findings.irs_text: i8801 (2025) p. 1: "An AMT liability and adjustments or preferences other than exclusion items" and "The minimum tax credit is allowed only for the AMT caused by deferral items."; i8801 p. 4, Line 21: "If line 21 is zero or less, you don't have a minimum tax credit or a credit carryforward. Don't complete the rest of this form and don't file it."
findings.why: The question ("have an alternative minimum tax liability for 2024 (2024 Form 6251, line 11)") makes this filer answer YES and be refused, although the IRS condition also requires adjustments or preferences other than exclusion items and the tool's $0 would be right.

findings.situation: A filer first has a tax credit bond credit for 2025 (bought a pre-2018 qualified tax credit bond or BAB during 2025, or first received a Form 1097-BTC or a pass-through share of bond credit for 2025) and had no Form 8912 in the 2024 return.
findings.irs_text: i8912 p. 1: "A taxpayer holding a CREB or qualified tax credit bond ... on one or more credit allowance dates can claim the credit by filing Form 8912 for each tax year in which it holds the bond on a credit allowance date." f1040s3 p. 1: "6k Credit to holders of tax credit bonds. Attach Form 8912"
findings.why: The question asks only whether the 2024 return included Form 8912, so this filer truthfully answers NO and line 7 is computed as $0 although a 2025 line 6k credit exists. Among the refusals listed here, none asks about a current-year bond credit.

findings.situation: A filer's 2024 return included Form 8912, but the whole credit was used in 2024 (or it was a CREB or pre-October 4, 2008 QZAB credit, which cannot be carried forward) and the bond was sold, redeemed or matured before any 2025 credit allowance date, so nothing belongs on 2025 line 6k.
findings.irs_text: i8912 p. 3: "If you can't use all of the credit from Part I (for example, line 12 is smaller than line 4), you may carry the unused portion of the credit to the next tax year"; i8912 p. 2: "Credits attributable to a CREB, or a QZAB issued before October 4, 2008, can't be carried forward."
findings.why: The question ("Does your ... 2024 federal return include Form 8912") forces a YES and a refusal on the mere presence of the form, while a carryforward exists only if part of the credit went unused. For this filer the tool's $0 on line 7 would be correct.

findings.situation: A filer who filed Form 8912 for 2024 and used the full credit reads the help text and cannot tell whether the question is about the form being present or about having an unused credit.
findings.irs_text: i8912 p. 3: "you may carry the unused portion of the credit to the next tax year and add it to any credit allowable to the holder of the same bond in the next tax year"
findings.why: The question asks about the form, but the help says "a credit not used in 2024 carries into 2025", which suggests only an unused credit matters. Such a filer could reasonably answer either YES or NO.

findings.situation: The filer owed AMT for 2024 from deferral items such as depreciation, so a 2025 minimum tax credit exists, but the 2024 return had a Form 6251 and no Form 8801 because there was no earlier credit.
findings.irs_text: i8801 (2025) p. 1, Who Should File: "Complete Form 8801 if you are an individual, estate, or trust that for 2024 had: • An AMT liability and adjustments or preferences other than exclusion items"
findings.why: The credit comes from a 2024 Form 6251 AMT liability, not from a 2024 Form 8801. A filer with no 8801 on the 2024 return truthfully answers No, and Schedule 3 line 6b is treated as zero.

findings.situation: The filer did not file a 2024 return, or filed no form for that credit in 2024, but still has an unused credit from an earlier year: a mortgage interest credit from 2022 or 2023, a D.C. homebuyer credit, a general business credit, a minimum tax credit, or an adoption credit.
findings.irs_text: f8396 p. 2, Part II: "you may have an unused credit to carry forward to the next 3 tax years or until used"; f8859 p. 1, Line 4: "You can carry forward any unused credit shown on line 4 until you have used all of it"; i3800 p. 3: "carried forward 20 years"

findings.irs_text: f1040s3 (2025) lines 6a–6m, e.g. "6g Mortgage interest credit. Attach Form 8396", "6d Credit for the elderly or disabled. Attach Schedule R"; i8839 p. 1: "You paid qualified adoption expenses ... in ... 2025 and the adoption became final in or before 2025"
findings.why: Line 7 is computed as $0, but the question asks only about forms on the 2024 return. A filer whose 6a–6z credit arises entirely in 2025 truthfully answers No, unless some other screen not listed here refuses these credits.

findings.situation: The 2024 return included Form 3800, 8396, 8801, 8582-CR, 8839 or 8912, but every 2024 credit was used in full and nothing carried into 2025 (for example 8396 line 9 equaled line 7, or 8801 line 26 was zero).
findings.irs_text: Question: "Does your ... 2024 federal return include any of Forms 3800, 8396, 8801, 8582-CR, 8839, 8859 or 8912?"; f8396 p. 2: "Complete only if line 9 is less than line 7"; i8912 p. 3: "you may carry the unused portion of the credit to the next tax year"
findings.why: The question asks whether a form was present, not whether a carryforward exists. These filers must answer Yes and are refused, even though no prior-year credit reaches 2025 and the tool's zero is correct for the carryforward.

findings.situation: A filer reading the help text ("alternative minimum tax paid earlier", "credits held back by the passive activity rules") may not know whether the question is about forms on the 2024 return or about having such a credit at all.
findings.irs_text: Help: "Each can leave a tax credit to carry into 2025 (... alternative minimum tax paid earlier, credits held back by the passive activity rules ...)"; i8801 p. 1: "for 2024 had: • An AMT liability"
findings.why: The question names specific form numbers, but the help describes the underlying credits. A filer who paid AMT or had suspended passive credits without those exact forms on the 2024 return could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: A U.S. citizen lived in the U.S. Virgin Islands for part of 2025, moved to the mainland before year end, and earned USVI-source income while living there.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 117, Line 13z: "Also use line 13z to report the amount of U.S. tax allocable to the U.S. Virgin Islands. Enter 'Form 8689' and the amount paid."
findings.why: Form 8689 applies to anyone who was not a bona fide USVI resident at the end of the year, but the help says YES only if you 'were not a resident there.' A filer who lived there for part of the year can truthfully say they were a resident and answer NO, so the tool enters $0 on line 13z.

findings.situation: A filer with USVI-source income spent time in or kept a home in the USVI but does not meet the bona fide residence tests.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 117, Line 13z: "report the amount of U.S. tax allocable to the U.S. Virgin Islands"
findings.why: The help uses the plain word 'resident,' not 'bona fide resident.' A filer could call themselves a resident under everyday usage and answer NO, even though they file Form 8689 and need line 13z.

findings.situation: A filer received nontaxable combat pay (W-2 box 12, code Q), chooses not to include it in earned income for the EIC or for Form 2441, and is not sent to the Schedule 8812 Earned Income Worksheet. The tool's zero amounts on all six lines would be correct, yet the question makes this filer answer YES and be refused.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Did you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) receive any nontaxable combat pay in 2025...?" IRS: "Enter all of your nontaxable combat pay if you elect to include it in earned income" (i1040gi p. 42, Step 5, line 4). "Nontaxable combat pay if you elect to include it in earned income" (i2441 p. 4, Lines 4 and 5). "You can elect to include your nontaxable combat pay in earned income when figuring your exclusion or deduction" (i2441 p. 5, Line 18). "Use this worksheet only if you were sent here from Credit Limit Worksheet B, earlier, or the instructions for line 18a" (i1040s8812 p. 8).
findings.why: On the EIC and Form 2441 lines, combat pay counts only if the filer elects to include it, and Earned Income Worksheet line 1b applies only when the filer is sent to that worksheet. The question asks only whether combat pay was received, so it also refuses filers whose amounts the tool correctly treats as zero.

findings.situation: A filer who was a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico in 2025, with earned-income amount (line 20) equal to or more than line 17, answers YES and is refused, though the result does not depend on Part II-B.
findings.irs_text: f1040s8812 p. 2: "Yes. If line 20 is equal to or more than line 17, skip Part II-B and enter the amount from line 17 on line 27"; "Next, enter the smaller of line 17 or line 26 on line 27" (line 26 is "the larger of line 20 or line 25")
findings.why: The question "Were you ... a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico in 2025?" draws YES from every Puerto Rico resident. When line 20 is at least line 17, line 26 is also at least line 17, so line 27 equals line 17 on either branch. The tool's non-Puerto Rico computation already gives that amount, so it would compute these filers correctly.

findings.situation: A bona fide resident of Puerto Rico whose Credit Limit Worksheet B line 5 is equal to or more than line 1 answers YES and is refused, though line 11 is zero on every branch.
findings.irs_text: i1040s8812 p. 5, CLW B line 6: "No. If you are a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico and line 5 above is less than line 1 above, go to line 7. Otherwise, leave lines 7 through 10 blank, enter -0- on line 11"
findings.why: The Puerto Rico path through lines 7–10 applies only when line 5 is less than line 1. Otherwise line 11 is zero for a Puerto Rico resident too, which the tool already computes, but the question refuses the filer anyway.

findings.situation: A bona fide resident of Puerto Rico who stops at line 12 or line 16a (line 16a is zero) answers YES and is refused, though line 27 is simply zero.
findings.irs_text: f1040s8812 p. 2, line 16a: "Subtract line 14 from line 12. If zero, stop here; you cannot take the additional child tax credit"
findings.why: Part II-B is never reached after these stops, so the tool's zero is correct. The residency question still refuses these filers.

findings.why: The question asks only about charitable limits and carryovers. Nothing in it prompts a YES for line 6 other taxes, which the tool drops to zero.

findings.situation: A filer paid home mortgage interest not reported on Form 1098 (for example, to the seller of the home), or points not reported on Form 1098, answers NO, and lines 8b and 8c are computed as zero.

findings.why: These are interest deductions unrelated to charity. A truthful filer answers NO to a charitable-limit question, and the deduction is lost.

findings.situation: A filer has a line 16 deduction other than gambling losses, such as federal estate tax on income in respect of a decedent, amortizable bond premium, or an ordinary loss on a contingent payment or inflation-indexed debt instrument, answers NO, and the tool includes only gambling losses.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 11, Other Itemized Deductions: "Federal estate tax on income in respect of a decedent. • A deduction for amortizable bond premium ... • An ordinary loss attributable to a contingent payment debt instrument or an inflation-indexed debt instrument"
findings.why: The question's wording is about charitable deductions only, so these line 16 items get a NO and are silently treated as zero.

findings.situation: A filer gave appreciated ordinary income property (for example, inventory or property held one year or less), or gave the use of property, so the deduction must be reduced below fair market value under Pub. 526 even though no percentage-of-AGI limit applies; the filer answers NO and line 12 takes the full value before limits.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 10, Limit on the amount you can deduct: "See Pub. 526 to figure the amount of your deduction if any of the following applies ... 3. You gave gifts of property that increased in value or gave gifts of the use of property."; p. 11: "The cost or other basis of the property if you must reduce it by any ordinary income or capital gain that would have resulted if the property had been sold at its fair market value"
findings.why: The question asks only whether deductions are 'reduced by income limits' or carried over. A basis reduction or a disallowed gift of use is not an income limit, so a truthful filer answers NO.

findings.situation: A filer compares gifts to 'your income' as the help text says, using gross or total income rather than adjusted gross income (Form 1040 line 11b), and concludes no limit applies when one does.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 10: "Your cash contributions or contributions of ordinary income property are more than 30% of the amount on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11b. 2. Your gifts of capital gain property are more than 20% of the amount on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11b."
findings.why: The help text says 'of your income' without naming AGI, line 11b. A filer could reasonably measure against a larger income figure and answer NO.

findings.situation: A filer aged 25 to 64 who is permanently and totally disabled and lives with a parent who files a return, but who provides more than half of their own support, is a qualifying child of the parent for the EIC but cannot be claimed as the parent's dependent, so the filer truthfully answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 42, Step 4, question 5: "Could you be a qualifying child of another person for 2025? ... Yes. STOP You can't take the credit."; p. 41: a qualifying child is one who was "Any age and permanently and totally disabled" and "lived with you in the United States for more than half of 2025" (no support test)
findings.why: The question asks only whether someone can claim the filer as a dependent, which is Step 4 question 6, and its refusal cites only question 6. Step 4 question 5 is a separate bar, because the EIC qualifying-child test has no support test and a person can meet it without being a dependent, so a filer who is only a qualifying child of another person answers NO and the tool allows the credit unless it asks about question 5 separately.

findings.situation: A filer who lived in the 50 states all of 2025 but in 2025 received pay for work done abroad in 2024 (for example, a deferred bonus) and excludes it on a 2025 Form 2555 is told by the help text to answer No.
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 3: "However, if you're filing Form 2555, Foreign Earned Income ... add to the amount on your Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11b, the amount of income you excluded."; f1040s8812 line 2b: "Enter the amounts from lines 45 and 50 of your Form 2555"; i1040gi p. 40: "Are you filing Form 2555 ... Yes. STOP"
findings.why: The question asks only whether the filer files Form 2555, but the help says anyone who lived in the 50 states all year answers No. Filing Form 2555 does not require living abroad during the tax year itself, so this filer answers No and the tool sets the Form 2555 add-backs to zero and allows the EIC.

findings.situation: A filer who lived in the District of Columbia (not one of the 50 states) all year cannot use the help's shortcut and may wonder whether DC counts as abroad or as an exclusion situation.
findings.irs_text: i8863 p. 3: "if you're filing Form 2555 ... or Form 4563 ... or are excluding income from Puerto Rico"
findings.why: The help names only the 50 states, so a DC resident with no exclusions has no stated basis for answering No. A filer could misread the omission as meaning DC residence triggers a Yes.

findings.situation: A filer has charitable contributions from an earlier year that they could not deduct because of the limits and are carrying over into 2025. None of the listed items applies to them, so they answer NO, and the tool enters zero on line 13.

findings.situation: A filer whose Form 1098 mortgage interest may be reduced by the debt limit or the use limit cannot tell from the question whether their loan is affected.
findings.irs_text: f1040sa p. 1, line 8: "If you didn't use all of your home mortgage loan(s) to buy, build, or improve your home, see instructions and check this box"; line 8a: "See instructions if limited"
findings.why: The question says "debt over the limit" but gives no dollar limit and does not say whether a refinanced loan or a home equity loan counts. A filer could answer either way without knowing whether the tool's figure would be correct.

findings.situation: A filer sells S corporation stock, or an interest in a trust, held more than 1 year at a gain, and the entity owns depreciated real property (section 1250 property) but no collectibles.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 12, line 19: 'You reported a long-term capital gain from the sale or exchange of an interest in a partnership that owned section 1250 property.' Compare i1040sd p. 11, line 18: 'an interest in a partnership, S corporation, or trust ... attributable to unrealized appreciation of collectibles.'
findings.why: The question says 'an interest in a partnership, S corporation or trust ... that holds collectibles or section 1250 property', so this filer answers YES. Line 19 looks through only partnership interests for section 1250 property, so the sale is an ordinary long-term gain the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer sells a collectible, or an interest in a partnership, S corporation or trust that holds collectibles or section 1250 property, that was held 1 year or less, or sells such a pass-through interest at a loss.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 11, line 18: 'any long-term gain or deductible long-term loss from the sale or exchange of a collectible' and 'any gain (but not loss) from the sale or exchange of an interest in a partnership, S corporation, or trust held for more than 1 year'; i1040sd p. 12, line 19: 'section 1250 property ... held more than 1 year' and 'a long-term capital gain from the sale or exchange of an interest in a partnership'.
findings.why: The question asks only whether the sale 'involve[s]' these assets, with no holding-period or gain condition, so the filer answers YES. Lines 18 and 19 reach only long-term amounts, and only gain for pass-through interests, so nothing on these lines needs the special worksheets.

findings.situation: A filer sells shares of a REIT or a mutual fund that is legally organized as a trust and owns depreciated real estate.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 12, line 19 covers a REIT or RIC only through 'a Form 1099-DIV or Form 2439 ... that reports "unrecaptured section 1250 gain"', not through a sale of the shares. The look-through for a sale of an interest applies only to 'an interest in a partnership that owned section 1250 property'.
findings.why: The wording 'an interest in a ... trust ... that holds ... section 1250 property' could be read to include REIT or fund shares in a trust-form entity. A filer could reasonably answer YES or NO, even though an ordinary sale of these shares is computed correctly by the tool.

question:
Does any of the following apply to this sale?

Does this sale involve:
- collectibles (works of art, rugs, antiques, metals such as gold, silver or platinum bullion, including shares of an exchange-traded fund or trust that holds gold, silver, platinum or other metals, gems, stamps, coins, alcoholic beverages or other tangible property of that kind)
- a non-fungible token (NFT) whose underlying asset is a collectible, such as an NFT that represents ownership of a work of art or a gem
- qualified small business stock with a section 1202 exclusion
- depreciable real property (section 1250 property: generally, real property for which depreciation was allowed or allowable (claimed, or that you could have claimed), such as a home you once rented out or used in part as a home office)
- an interest in a partnership, S corporation or trust (including S corporation stock) that holds collectibles or section 1250 property directly or through another entity, such as stock of an S corporation that owns art or gold worth more than its cost
- a loss on stock held 1 year or less on which you received an extraordinary dividend (one that equals or exceeds 10% of your basis in the stock, 5% for preferred stock) reported as a qualified dividend
- a gain from a constructive ownership transaction on a financial asset (an interest in a partnership, S corporation, trust, mutual fund or REIT), such as a forward contract to acquire it

Or does it dispose of an investment in a qualified opportunity fund (QOF), or is any of its gain deferred by an investment in a QOF?

findings.situation: A filer whose foreign accounts together exceeded $10,000 at some point in 2025 but were closed or emptied before the filer answers (or who first passed $10,000 in 2026) cannot tell which year's FBAR requirement the present-tense question means.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 3, Line 7a—Question 2: "A U.S. person that has a financial interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts must file the form if the aggregate value of foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000 at any time during 2025."
findings.why: The question asks "Are you ... required to file FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR)?" without naming calendar year 2025, unlike the gate question, which says "At any time in 2025". A filer who reads it as their current situation could answer NO although line 7a Question 2 and the line 7b country list apply, or YES for a requirement that arises only for 2026.

findings.situation: A filer employed in 2025 as a mid-level manager (for example a sales or store manager) of a foreign company, who was neither an officer nor a director and owned no stock, reads 'managing director or manager' and answers YES.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2, Part II TIP: "You may have to file Form 5471 if, in 2025, you were an officer or director of a foreign corporation."
findings.why: The question says "an officer, director, managing director or manager of a foreign corporation or other company", while the IRS text names only officers and directors. An ordinary managerial employee is refused although the tool computes lines 2, 3 and 6 correctly for them.

findings.situation: A filer who was a manager or officer of a foreign entity that is not a corporation (for example a foreign LLC or partnership-type company taxed as a partnership) answers YES.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2, Part II TIP: "an officer or director of a foreign corporation" and "10% or more of the total (a) value of a foreign corporation's stock"
findings.why: The question says "a foreign corporation or other company, whatever it is called", which takes in entities that are not corporations. The IRS text ties Form 5471 only to a foreign corporation.

findings.situation: A filer who owns no stock personally but has a small interest in a partnership, corporation, trust or estate that holds 10% of a foreign corporation counts all of that entity's shares and answers YES.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2, Part II TIP: "You may also have to file Form 5471 if, in 2025, you owned 10% or more of the total (a) value of a foreign corporation's stock, or (b) combined voting power of all classes of a foreign corporation's stock with voting rights."
findings.why: The question says "counting shares owned by ... partnerships, corporations, trusts or estates you have an interest in", with no proportionality or minimum interest. The IRS text speaks only of stock "you owned", so a filer with a trivial stake in such an entity is refused.

findings.situation: A filer who was an officer or director of a corporation organized in Puerto Rico, Guam or another US territory cannot tell from the IRS text whether that is a "foreign corporation".
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2, Part II TIP: "an officer or director of a foreign corporation ... For details, see Form 5471 and its instructions"
findings.why: The question treats companies "organized outside the 50 states and the District of Columbia, including in Puerto Rico, Guam or another US territory" as foreign. The supplied text does not define "foreign corporation", so this may be correct or over-inclusive.

Failure to file Form 8938 may result in penalties and extension of the statute of limitations. See IRS.gov/Form8938 for more information."
findings.why: The wording asks for a legal conclusion that the filer can only reach from the Form 8938 instructions, so a filer who actually must file could in good faith answer NO (for instance, by assuming no FBAR means no Form 8938). findings.situation: A filer whose only connection is a foreign pension plan, a foreign mutual fund or a similar pooled investment vehicle answers Yes because each 'holds property for beneficiaries', though none is a trust distribution, grantor or transferor situation under line 8.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.3, Line 8: 'If you received a distribution from a foreign trust ... If you were the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust that existed during 2025, you may have to file Form 3520.' The same instructions treat 'shares in a mutual fund or similar pooled fund' and cash-value insurance as financial accounts under line 7a (i1040sb pp.2–3), not as trusts.
findings.why: The question says 'another arrangement that holds property for beneficiaries counts as a trust' and adds 'if you are not sure whether an arrangement is a trust ... answer Yes'. A filer with only a foreign pension or fund would answer Yes and be refused. The IRS text handles these as line 7a foreign accounts, and the tool computes lines 2, 3 and 6 for that filer.

findings.situation: A filer who received a loan of cash or securities from a foreign trust on terms they consider arm's-length, or who sold property to a foreign trust for full value, cannot tell whether that counts.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.3, Line 8: 'a loan of cash or marketable securities is generally considered to be a distribution'; 'If you were the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust ... you may have to file Form 3520.'
findings.why: The question says a loan 'counts' and that anyone who 'sold' property to the trust is a transferor, with no exceptions. The IRS text says only 'generally' and 'may have to file' and points to the Form 3520 instructions, which are not part of the text provided. A filer cannot tell whether the IRS qualifiers change the answer.

question: During 2025, did you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) receive a distribution from a foreign trust, including money or property that reached you through another person or company (a loan of cash or marketable securities counts, and so does free or below-market use of a home, car or other property the trust owns), or were you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) the grantor of, or a transferor to, a foreign trust that existed at any time during 2025, even one created or funded in an earlier year (a transferor is anyone who gave, sold, lent or otherwise transferred money or property to the trust, directly or through another person, in 2025 or any earlier year)? A foreign foundation, a waqf or another arrangement that holds property for beneficiaries counts as a trust; a trust counts as foreign unless a court in one of the 50 states or the District of Columbia (not one in Puerto Rico, Guam or another US territory) can supervise its administration and US persons (US citizens or residents, or US companies such as a US bank) control all of its substantial decisions, so it is foreign if anyone else can make or veto any of them, even if the trust was set up under US law or has a US address; if you are not sure whether an arrangement is a trust or whether a trust is foreign, answer Yes.

findings.situation: A filer bought a tax-exempt municipal bond at a premium and nets the amortized premium only against the tax-exempt interest on Form 1040 line 2a, which does not change Schedule B lines 2, 3 or 6.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "if you acquired a tax-exempt bond at a premium, only report the net amount of tax-exempt interest on line 2a of your Form 1040 or 1040-SR"; question: "bond premium adjustment"
findings.why: The question says "bond premium adjustment" without limiting it to taxable bonds, so this filer would truthfully answer YES. The ABP Adjustment on Schedule B applies only to "interest income on a taxable bond," so the tool computes these lines correctly for this filer.

findings.situation: A filer's payer already reported a net amount of interest or OID that reflects amortizable bond premium or acquisition premium, so no Schedule B reduction is allowed and the 1099 amount is correct as reported.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "if the payer reported to you a net amount of interest income on the bond reflecting the offset of the gross amount of interest income by the amortizable bond premium, no reduction of the amount of interest income reported to you by the payer is permitted on Schedule B"
findings.why: A filer who holds premium bonds may answer YES to "bond premium adjustment" even though no adjustment is made on Schedule B. The tool's unadjusted sum of the reported amounts is correct here.

findings.situation: A filer has OID that differs from Form 1099-OID, or has OID with no Form 1099-OID at all, and the wording "in an amount other than on Form 1099-OID" does not match the IRS trigger of reporting less than box 1 or box 8.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "If you are reporting OID in an amount less than the amount shown in box 1 or box 8 of Form 1099-OID ... identify the amount to be subtracted as 'OID Adjustment.'"
findings.why: "Other than" can be read as "different from" (which includes reporting more) or as "not on a 1099-OID." A filer cannot tell whether OID that has no 1099-OID, or OID above the form amount, counts.

findings.situation: A filer sold a market discount bond and part of the gain is treated as interest under the market discount rules, but the filer never elected to accrue market discount.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "Also include any accrued market discount that is includible in income and any gain on a contingent payment debt instrument that is includible in income as interest income."
findings.why: "Accrued market discount" may read to a filer as applying only after a current-inclusion election. Some filers in this situation could answer NO and leave includible interest out of line 2.

findings.situation: A filer has some unusual interest or dividend item and must decide whether it is "other special treatment."
findings.irs_text: question: "or other special treatment?"; i1040sb p. 1: "Report on line 1 all of your taxable interest."
findings.why: The catch-all has no defined scope, so filers could reasonably answer either way for items such as interest not reported on any Form 1099 or tax-exempt items that do not affect these lines.

findings.irs_text: i1040sc p. 7, Line 14: "You must reduce your line 14 deduction by the amount of any credit for small employer health insurance premiums determined on Form 8941"; p. 9, Line 23: "Reduce your deduction by the amount shown on Form 8846, line 4"; p. 10, Line 26: "Work Opportunity Credit (Form 5884) ... Empowerment Zone Employment Credit (Form 8844) ... Credit for Employer Differential Wage Payments (Form 8932) ... Employer Credit for Paid Family and Medical Leave (Form 8994)"
findings.why: The wording "other than the employment credits asked about with the special items of this Schedule C" does not name which credits are carved out. A filer who reads Form 8941 or Form 8846 as an 'employment credit' answers NO here, and if the other question lists only the line 26 wage credits, the Form 3800 credit passes both screens.

question: Do you value closing inventory by a method other than cost or lower of cost or market, or was there any change in determining quantities, costs or valuations between opening and closing inventory (line 34)? Answer No if you have no inventory

locators: p. 15, Line 35
p. 15, Lines 33 and 35
p. 15, Part III, Line 33; Schedule C (2025), lines 33 and 34

findings.situation: A filer changing their inventory accounting method beginning with 2025 refigures last year's closing inventory under the new method, so opening and closing 2025 inventory are on the same basis and the filer can truthfully answer No if the new method is cost or lower of cost or market.
findings.irs_text: If you are changing your method of accounting beginning with 2025, refigure last year's closing inventory using your new method of accounting and enter the result on line 35. If there is a difference between last year's closing inventory and the refigured amount, attach an explanation and take it into account when figuring your section 481(a) adjustment. (i1040sc 2025 p. 15, Line 35)
findings.why: The question asks only about a change between opening and closing inventory, which misses a change between 2024 closing and 2025 opening inventory. The tool's input instructs the filer to enter the 2024 closing amount, rather than the refigured amount, and does not handle the explanation or section 481(a) adjustment.

findings.situation: A filer who consistently uses an IRS-approved method other than cost or lower of cost or market, with no change in method, must answer Yes even though line 35 is simply last year's closing inventory, which the tool's input takes correctly.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Do you value closing inventory by a method other than cost or lower of cost or market"; IRS: "Your inventories can be valued at cost, the lower of cost or market, or any other method approved by the IRS." (i1040sc 2025 p. 15, Line 33)
findings.why: The Line 35 text requires refiguring only when the method of accounting is changing, so consistent use of an approved other method does not make the entered amount wrong. For this line, the question refuses a case the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A small business taxpayer who chooses not to keep an inventory but holds unsold goods, or tracks them in books under a financial accounting method, could read "no inventory" as either no goods on hand or no formal inventory kept.
findings.irs_text: If you are a small business taxpayer, you can choose not to keep an inventory, but you must still use a method of accounting for inventory that clearly reflects income. (i1040sc 2025 p. 15, Part III, Exception for small business taxpayers)
findings.why: The wording does not say whether this filer should use the "Answer No" instruction. That choice can decide whether a filer whose treatment is neither cost nor lower of cost or market answers Yes and is refused, or answers No and has line 35 computed, possibly as zero.

findings.situation: A filer whose inventory counts or unit costs simply differ between the start and end of the year, with no change in method, could read "any change in determining quantities, costs or valuations" as covering those ordinary differences.
findings.irs_text: Question: "was there any change in determining quantities, costs or valuations between opening and closing inventory"; compare: "If you are changing your method of accounting beginning with 2025" (i1040sc 2025 p. 15, Line 35)
findings.why: The question means a change in how amounts are determined, but it does not use the words "method" or "accounting method". A filer could read it as covering ordinary changes in the amounts and wrongly answer Yes, even though the tool computes line 35 correctly.

findings.situation: A filer has grouped a single rental with a trade or business activity, or with an activity held through a partnership or S corporation, rather than grouping two of their own rentals together, so they truthfully answer NO even though their activities are grouped for Form 8582.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 1: "Regrouping due to net investment income tax (NIIT). You may be able to regroup your activities ... See Regrouping Due to NIIT under Grouping of Activities"
findings.why: The refusal rests on i8582 Grouping of Activities, which covers grouping of activities in general. The question asks only about "two or more of your rentals", so any other grouping that changes the passive loss allowed on line 22, and therefore lines 25 and 26, is not caught.

findings.situation: A filer who treats several rental properties as one rental real estate enterprise under the QBI safe harbor answers YES, even though that treatment has no effect on the passive activity computation of lines 24 through 26.
findings.irs_text: i8995 (2025) p. 1: "Rev. Proc. 2019-38 provides a safe harbor under which a rental real estate enterprise will be treated as a trade or business for purposes of the QBI deduction."
findings.why: "Treat two or more of your rentals as one activity" describes the QBI enterprise aggregation as well as section 469 grouping. The question never says it means passive activity grouping, so a filer whose case the tool handles correctly is refused.

findings.situation: A filer who owns one multi-family building, or who rents several units of one property and reports them together in a single Schedule E column, could think they treat several rentals as one activity.
findings.irs_text: f1040se (2025) p. 1: "Type of Property: ... 2 Multi-Family Residence"; "1a Physical address of each property"
findings.why: The question does not define "rentals" or "one activity". Neither the question nor its help ("A Yes ends the interview here") points to the formal grouping that Form 8582 is about, so a filer could reasonably read it as asking about units versus properties.

findings.situation: A real estate professional who elected to treat all interests in rental real estate as one activity for material participation could answer either way.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 3: "each interest in rental real estate is a separate activity unless you elect to treat all your interests in rental real estate as one activity"
findings.why: This election is separate from the i8582 grouping rules the refusal cites, yet its wording closely matches the question. It is unclear whether the question means to include it.

findings.situation: A filer whose rental qualifies as a trade or business for the QBI deduction answers YES, but Schedule E line 26 is the same sum of lines 24 and 25 either way, so the tool refuses a line it would have computed correctly.
findings.irs_text: f1040se (2025) p. 1, line 26: "Total rental real estate and royalty income or (loss). Combine lines 24 and 25." i8995 (2025) p. 1: "Rev. Proc. 2019-38 provides a safe harbor under which a rental real estate enterprise will be treated as a trade or business for purposes of the QBI deduction."
findings.why: The question asks: "Do you treat a rental as a business for the qualified business income deduction...?" Trade-or-business status for QBI matters only to the Form 8995 deduction. Nothing in the text of line 26 depends on it, so a YES on this question has no bearing on the line that gets refused.

findings.situation: A filer whose rental meets the section 162 trade-or-business standard but who never chose the safe harbor could read "Do you treat" as asking about an election and answer NO, or read it as asking about the rental's status and answer YES.
findings.irs_text: i8995 (2025) p. 1: "The ownership and rental of real property may constitute a trade or business if it meets the standard described above. Also, Rev. Proc. 2019-38 provides a safe harbor..."
findings.why: The wording "treat" and the safe-harbor example ("250 hours or more a year of rental services, with separate books") suggest a choice the filer makes. The IRS text says a rental can be a trade or business without the safe harbor, so the same filer could truthfully answer either way.

findings.situation: A self-employed general contractor, builder or developer who spends most of a 2,000-hour year on construction or redevelopment, and materially participates in a rental, could answer NO because they don't see construction as a 'real estate business.'
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "A real property trade or business is any real property development, redevelopment, construction, reconstruction, acquisition, conversion, rental, operation, management, leasing, or brokerage trade or business."
findings.why: The IRS definition includes construction, development and conversion trades, but 'real estate businesses' suggests brokerage or rentals to most readers. That filer would answer NO, and the tool would then treat a nonpassive rental loss as passive and omit the line 43 reconciliation.

findings.situation: A landlord who personally manages and operates their own rental properties full time, with no other job, could answer NO because they don't think of owning rentals as working in a 'business.'
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "... rental, operation, management, leasing ... trade or business" counts toward "more than 750 hours of services during the year in real property trades or businesses in which you materially participated."
findings.why: The question doesn't say that hours spent running your own rentals count. A full-time self-managing landlord who qualifies under the IRS test may truthfully believe they don't work 'in real estate businesses.'

findings.situation: A W-2 employee with no ownership stake, such as a leasing agent, property manager or employee broker at a real estate firm, works full time there and answers YES, although none of that time counts and the tool would compute the rentals correctly as passive.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "Services you performed as an employee are not treated as performed in a real property trade or business unless you owned more than 5% of the stock (or more than 5% of the capital or profits interest) in the employer."
findings.why: The question counts any work time in a real estate business. The IRS excludes employee services unless the employee owns more than 5%, so this filer is not a real estate professional but is refused anyway.

findings.situation: A filer who works more than 750 hours, and more than half their time, in real estate businesses but does not materially participate in those businesses or in any rental answers YES, although the tool computes their rentals correctly as passive.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "performed in real property trades or businesses in which you materially participated" and "any rental real estate activity in which you materially participated is not a passive activity."
findings.why: The question never mentions material participation. Both IRS hour tests count only businesses in which the filer materially participated, and the status changes nothing on line 26 unless a rental is materially participated in.

findings.situation: A filer working in real-estate-adjacent fields such as mortgage lending, appraisal or title work cannot tell whether that is a 'real estate business.'
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "development, redevelopment, construction, reconstruction, acquisition, conversion, rental, operation, management, leasing, or brokerage trade or business."
findings.why: The question doesn't define 'real estate businesses.' The IRS list is closed, and lending, appraisal and title work are not on it, so readers will reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: It is unclear whether 'all your work time' covers only work in trades or businesses, and whether investor-type hours such as reviewing statements count.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "More than half of the personal services you performed in trades or businesses during the year were performed in real property trades or businesses..."
findings.why: 'Work time' is vaguer than 'personal services ... in trades or businesses,' so filers near the 50% line could compute the fraction differently.

findings.situation: A filer whose Form W-2 box 1 includes wages earned while an inmate in a penal institution reads 'wages' as a kind the question is not about and answers NO, so the tool leaves the amount on line 1a and puts nothing on line 8.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 23, Line 1a: "If you earned wages while you were an inmate in a penal institution, report these amounts on Schedule 1, line 8u. Do not report these wages on line 1a."
findings.why: The question excludes 'wages' and names only 'wages or tips not on a Form W-2', so W-2 wages that must move to Schedule 1 line 8u (and into Form 1040 line 8) are not caught.

findings.situation: A filer with wages plus a receipt that is not reportable income (a state general-welfare payment, a utility rate reduction, a reimbursed union convention expense) answers YES because it is 'other income' outside the six listed kinds, although line 8 is correctly zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p. 23: "Generally, you must report all income except income that is exempt from tax by law." p525 (2025) p. 36: "The amount of the rate reduction or nonrefundable credit isn't included in your income."
findings.why: The catch-all 'any other outside the wages, interest, dividends...' is not limited to income that must be reported on the return, so exempt receipts trigger a refusal the lines do not need.

findings.situation: A filer with only wages who would claim a credit or special computation (for example the claim-of-right repayment credit, a foreign tax credit, or a mortgage interest credit carryforward) cannot tell whether that is a 'return treatment outside the kinds listed'.
findings.irs_text: p525 (2025) p. 36: "if the amount you repaid is more than $3,000, you may be able to take a credit against your tax for the year in which you repaid it"; f1040 (2025) line 20 "Amount from Schedule 3, line 8" and line 31 "Amount from Schedule 3, line 15"
findings.why: 'Return treatment' is undefined, and the listed kinds and examples are all income items, so a filer could read the question as being about income only and answer NO while lines 20 and 31 are computed as zero.

findings.situation: A filer who received a qualified disaster recovery distribution in 2025 on a Form 1099-R, or who made a 2025 repayment of a distribution received in a year other than 2023 or 2024, cannot tell whether the Form 8915-F item applies to them.
findings.irs_text: p575 p. 35: "Use Form 8915-F to report qualified disaster recovery distributions and repayments." and "you can include $6,000 in your income in 2023, 2024, and 2025. However, you can elect to include the entire distribution in your income in the year it was received."
findings.why: The wording names only distributions 'received in 2023 or 2024' and 'a 2025 repayment of one', while 'Form 1099-R distributions' is listed as a kind the question is not about, so a 2025 distribution or its repayment can be read as either NO or YES.

findings.situation: A filer (typically an S corporation shareholder) had a section 965(i) triggering event in 2025 with no transfer agreement, so the triggered deferred net 965 tax liability belongs on line 16, but nothing in the question's list names it.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 36, Line 16: "Triggering event under section 965(i). If you had a triggering event under section 965(i) during the year and did not enter into a transfer agreement, check box 3 and enter the amount of the triggered deferred net 965 tax liability and enter “965INC” on the line next to that box."
findings.why: The list omits 965(i)/965INC, and a triggering event such as selling the S corporation stock can leave the filer owning no CFC or PFIC stock, so a truthful NO is plausible. The only catch is the vague stem "any additional Form 1040 line 16 tax", which a filer cannot be expected to map to this item.

findings.situation: A filer who claims the foreign earned income exclusion, housing exclusion or housing deduction on Form 2555 must figure line 16 with the Foreign Earned Income Tax Worksheet, which the computed line (Schedule D Tax Worksheet or the non-SDTW method) does not use.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 36, Line 16: "If you claimed the foreign earned income exclusion, housing exclusion, or housing deduction on Form 2555, you must figure your tax using the Foreign Earned Income Tax Worksheet."
findings.why: Form 2555 is not named in the question, and it is a different way of figuring the tax rather than an "additional" line 16 tax, so the filer can answer NO. This is a gap only if no other screen (not shown here) already refuses Form 2555 filers.

findings.situation: A filer born on January 1 (2008, 2007 or 2002) counts their age at the end of 2025 by ordinary reckoning and answers YES to the Form 8615 age test, although the IRS treats them as a year older and Form 8615 may not be required (for example, born January 1, 2002 and a full-time student, or born January 1, 2008 with earned income over half of support).
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 36: "A child born on January 1, 2008, is considered to be age 18 at the end of 2025; a child born on January 1, 2007, is considered to be age 19 at the end of 2025; and a child born on January 1, 2002, is considered to be age 24 at the end of 2025."
findings.why: The question says "you were under 18 at the end of 2025, or 18 with earned income of not more than half your support, or a full-time student 19 to 23" without the January 1 birthday rule. These filers answer YES and are refused even though the ordinary tax computation the tool performs would be correct for them.
