findings.situation: A filer whose only Schedule 1 item is a Schedule C business in which they do not materially participate (a passive activity) answers NO, because Schedule C is one of the items 'this tool asks about separately'.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 40, Step 2, question 4: "Do any of the following apply for 2025? ... You have income or loss from a passive activity. Yes. Use Worksheet 1 in Pub. 596 to see if you can take the credit."
findings.why: The question names passive activities only through Schedule E and K-1 items and carves Schedule C out, so eic.step2_other computes 'No' and skips Pub. 596 Worksheet 1 for a passive Schedule C activity.

findings.situation: A self-employed Schedule C filer (such as the tour guide in the IRS example) who received qualified tips in the business answers NO, because Schedule C is asked separately, and the tool enters $0 on Schedule 1-A line 5.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 104: "Line 5. Include the qualified tips you and/or your spouse received in the course of a trade or business, but only to the extent the trade or business in which you received the qualified tips has net income." and "You enter $7,000 on Schedule 1-A, line 5."
findings.why: Nothing in the wording makes a tipped Schedule C filer answer YES; the question even says Schedule C and Schedule 1-A are handled elsewhere, yet this screen is what guards the line 5 zero.

findings.situation: A filer with qualified overtime compensation included in Form 1099-NEC box 1 or Form 1099-MISC box 3, reported on Schedule C or as other income the tool asks about, answers NO and the tool enters $0 on Schedule 1-A line 14b.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 108: "Enter on Line 14b only the qualified overtime compensation amount that is included in Form 1099-NEC, box 1, or Form 1099-MISC, box 3."
findings.why: The question never mentions overtime paid on a Form 1099, and the Schedule C carve-out means a truthful NO, so the deduction is silently zeroed instead of refused.

findings.situation: An options or commodities dealer filing Schedule C has section 1256 contract gains or losses (reported through Form 6781 and Schedule D, not Schedule 1) that must be added to earned income, and answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040s8812 p. 8, Earned Income Worksheet line 2b: "Options and commodities dealers must add any gain or subtract any loss (in the normal course of dealing in or trading section 1256 contracts) from section 1256 contracts or related property"
findings.why: This adjustment does not arise from any Schedule 1 item other than Schedule C, so the screen is answered NO and, as far as the listing shows, s8812.eiw_3 is figured without it.

findings.situation: A filer with church employee income under $108.28, or a minister with an approved Form 4361 who has only W-2 wages and files no Schedule SE, must answer YES and is refused.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 42, Step 5, question 1: "Are you filing Schedule SE because you were a member of the clergy or you had church employee income of $108.28 or more? ... No. Complete the following worksheet. 1. Enter the amount from Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1z"
findings.why: The question's bullets "church employee income (wages from a church ... that elected exemption ...)" and "income as a minister" have no Schedule SE or $108.28 condition, although the IRS text sends these filers to the ordinary line 1z worksheet the tool computes.

findings.situation: A filer who rents out personal property (for example equipment) as a business reported on Schedule C cannot tell whether the bullet 'rental of personal property' applies to them.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 40, Step 2, question 4: "You are reporting income from the rental of personal property not used in a trade or business."
findings.why: The question drops the IRS qualifier 'not used in a trade or business', so a Schedule C rental business could read it as YES (bullet) or NO (Schedule C is asked separately).

findings.situation: A filer with a Schedule 1 line 8 item (for example gambling winnings, prizes or hobby income) cannot tell from 'the line 8 items asked one by one' whether their item is one the tool asks about separately.
findings.irs_text: f1040 p. 1, line 8: "Additional income from Schedule 1, line 10"
findings.why: The exclusion list does not name the supported line 8 items, so the filer could reasonably answer either YES or NO for the same income.

findings.situation: The help text tells the filer to answer Yes for anything 'other than the items in the parentheses', but the question contains no single parenthetical list of the separately asked items.
findings.irs_text: f1040 p. 1, line 10: "Adjustments to income from Schedule 1, line 26"
findings.why: The only parentheses in the question sit inside YES bullets (Form 4797, Schedule E or K-1, Schedule F, line 8s, solo 401(k)), so a filer following the help literally could treat those refused items as the excluded ones and answer NO.

question:
Any income or adjustment requiring Schedule 1 other than the ones this tool asks about separately, including any of the following?

Income:
- statutory-employee wages or income as a minister, a member of a religious order who has not taken a vow of poverty, or a Christian Science practitioner
- church employee income (wages from a church or qualified church-controlled organization that elected exemption from social security and Medicare taxes)
- a refund or other recovery of an amount you deducted or took a credit for in an earlier year, other than a state or local income tax refund, for example:
  - a refund of general sales tax, real estate tax or personal property tax
  - a refund of mortgage interest in box 4 of Form 1098
  - a reimbursement of medical expenses
  - a payment on a bad debt you deducted
- sales of business property (Form 4797)
- a net operating loss deduction
- rental real estate, royalties, partnerships, S corporations, estates or trusts (Schedule E or a Schedule K-1)
- rental of personal property
- farm income (Schedule F)
- an exclusion of Medicaid waiver payments (Schedule 1 line 8s)

Adjustments:
- other qualified retirement plans for the self-employed (such as a solo 401(k) or other Keogh plan)
- an adjustment on Schedule 1 line 12, 14 or 23

The ones this tool asks about separately:
- business income or loss from Schedule C
- a taxable state or local income tax refund
- alimony under an agreement made before 2019
- unemployment compensation
- the line 8 items asked one by one
- educator expenses
- the HSA deduction
- the deductible part of self-employment tax
- self-employed SEP and SIMPLE contributions
- the self-employed health insurance deduction
- the penalty on early withdrawal of savings
- the IRA deduction
- student loan interest
- jury duty pay you gave your employer

Schedule 1-A deductions are asked separately.

findings.situation: A filer born before January 2, 1961 has income high enough that the enhanced senior deduction phases out to zero, so Schedule 1-A line 38 is $0. The tool's $0 on line 13b would be correct, but the filer answers YES because of their birth date.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.2, line 12d: "You: Were born before January 2, 1961"; line 13b: "Additional deductions from Schedule 1-A, line 38"
findings.why: The question names the deduction as "the enhanced deduction for a filer born before January 2, 1961," so birth date alone reads as qualifying. Any filer who checks the line 12d box would answer YES and be refused, even when the Schedule 1-A amount is zero. The income phase-out itself is not in the supplied text.

findings.situation: A filer received tips (line 1c or W-2) or overtime pay but does not know whether these count as "qualified tips" or "qualified overtime compensation."
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.1, line 1c: "Tip income not reported on line 1a (see instructions)"; p.2, line 13b: "Additional deductions from Schedule 1-A, line 38"
findings.why: "Qualified" is a defined term that none of the supplied text explains, so a filer with tips or overtime could reasonably answer either way. If they answer NO when the items do qualify, line 13b becomes $0 and a deduction they are owed is missed.

findings.situation: A filer meets the basic conditions for a Schedule 1-A item (tips, overtime, vehicle loan interest, or age), but the computed deduction may be limited or reduced to zero.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.2, line 13b: "Additional deductions from Schedule 1-A, line 38"
findings.why: "Qualify for any Schedule 1-A deduction, whether or not you planned to claim it" can mean meeting the eligibility conditions or having a nonzero amount. Filers whose amount works out to zero could answer either way.

question: Is there a capital loss carried into 2025 from any earlier year?

locators: Schedule D (2025), Parts I–III

findings.situation: A filer with a short-term or long-term capital gain or loss passed through on a partnership, S corporation, estate, or trust Schedule K-1, but no prior-year capital loss, truthfully answers NO, and lines 5 and 12 are entered as zero.
findings.irs_text: 5 Net short-term gain or (loss) from partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts from Schedule(s) K-1 ... 12 Net long-term gain or (loss) from partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts from Schedule(s) K-1 (f1040sd 2025, p. 1)
findings.why: The question asks only about carryovers. Pass-through capital gain or loss is a separate source that the wording never mentions, so the tool treats it as zero without refusing.

findings.situation: A filer with an installment-sale gain (Form 6252), a casualty or theft gain or loss (Form 4684), a section 1256 or straddle result (Form 6781), a like-kind exchange (Form 8824), a Form 4797 Part I gain, or undistributed long-term gain (Form 2439) truthfully answers NO, and lines 4 and 11 are entered as zero.
findings.irs_text: 4 Short-term gain from Form 6252 and short-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824 ... 11 Gain from Form 4797, Part I; long-term gain from Forms 2439 and 6252; and long-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824 (f1040sd 2025, p. 1)
findings.why: None of these sources is a carryover from an earlier year, so a truthful NO zeroes lines 4 and 11. The line labels ('zero only after unsupported source/carryover screening') assume a source screen that this question does not perform.

findings.situation: A filer had a net capital loss on the 2024 Schedule D, or negative 2024 taxable income, but does not know whether any of the loss remains after the $3,000 deduction, so cannot tell whether a loss is 'carried into 2025'.
findings.irs_text: 6 Short-term capital loss carryover. Enter the amount, if any, from line 8 of your Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet in the instructions ... 14 Long-term capital loss carryover. Enter the amount, if any, from line 13 of your Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet (f1040sd 2025, p. 1)
findings.why: The carryover amount is the result of the worksheet, so 'is there a capital loss carried into 2025' can only be answered after the worksheet the tool declines to prepare. A filer whose prior loss may have been fully absorbed could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: A filer who repaid more than $3,000 of income included in an earlier year under a claim of right chooses the section 1341 credit, which belongs on line 13b and flows into line 14. The filer answers NO because no Form 2439 was received, and the tool enters $0.
findings.irs_text: f1040s3 (2025) p.1: "14 Total other payments or refundable credits. Add lines 13a through 13z"; "b Section 1341 credit for repayment of amounts included in income from earlier years"; i1040gi (2025) p.117: "If you are claiming a credit for repayment of amounts you included in your income in an earlier year ... enter the amount on line 13b."
findings.why: Line 14 sums every line 13a through 13z, but the screen asks only about Form 2439 (line 13a). A filer with a line 13b credit truthfully answers NO and loses the credit.

findings.situation: A filer has a net elective payment election amount from Form 3800 (line 13c) or a deferred net 965 tax liability (line 13d). The filer answers NO to the Form 2439 question, and the tool sets line 14 to $0.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p.117: "Line 13c Enter any net elective payment election amount from Form 3800, Part III, line 6, column (j)." "Line 13d If you elected to pay your net 965 tax liability in installments, report the deferred amount on line 13d."
findings.why: These amounts are part of the line 14 total, and nothing in the question asks about them. A truthful NO leaves them out.

findings.situation: A filer has a line 13z amount, such as a section 960(c) excess limitation credit, U.S. tax allocable to the U.S. Virgin Islands (Form 8689), or 75% of the applicable net tax liability from Form 1062. The filer answers NO, and the tool computes line 14 as $0.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi (2025) p.117: "Line 13z Other refundable credits. Use line 13z to report the credit under section 960(c) ... Also use line 13z to report the amount of U.S. tax allocable to the U.S. Virgin Islands. Enter 'Form 8689' ... On line 13z, enter 75% of your applicable net tax liability from Form 1062, line 14."
findings.why: Line 13z feeds line 14. The screen's wording is limited to Form 2439 and does not reach these credits.

findings.situation: A filer receives Form 2439 from an ETF, a closed-end fund or another regulated investment company that the filer does not think of as a 'mutual fund'. That filer could answer NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd (2025) p.6: "your share of the undistributed long-term capital gains of the regulated investment company (including a mutual fund) or real estate investment trust." ... "Include on Schedule 3 (Form 1040), line 13a, the tax paid as shown in box 2 of Form 2439."
findings.why: The question names only 'a mutual fund or a real estate investment trust (REIT)', but any regulated investment company can issue Form 2439. A filer who reads 'mutual fund' narrowly could miss the line 13a credit.

findings.situation: A filer whose only Form 4797 amount is a loss or a gain that is not a Part I gain (for example, ordinary gain from Part II) must answer YES, although nothing from that form reaches Schedule D and the zero on line 11 is correct.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are there gains or losses from (or that belong on) Forms 4797..."; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "Gain from Form 4797, Part I"
findings.why: Line 11 takes only gain from Form 4797, Part I, while the question counts any gain or loss on the form. The filer is refused on these Schedule D lines even though the tool's zero is correct for them.

findings.situation: A filer with a personal casualty or theft whose Form 4684 result is a loss that does not go to Schedule D, or that is not deductible, is told to count it and answers YES, although lines 4 and 11 are correctly zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Count section 1256 contracts and a casualty or theft of property whether you held the property directly or through an entity."; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 4: "short-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The lines take only amounts that Form 4684 sends to Schedule D, but the question counts a casualty or theft without that limit. The routing of personal casualty losses comes from Form 4684, which is not in the supplied text, so this rests on knowledge of that form.

findings.situation: A filer with a casualty or theft that produced no gain or loss, such as one fully reimbursed at basis, cannot tell whether the event itself counts or only a resulting gain or loss.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Count ... a casualty or theft of property"; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "long-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The second sentence can be read as an instruction to count every such event, or only as clarifying what counts as a gain or loss under the first sentence. The first reading gives YES and the second gives NO, and with no amount for Schedule D the correct answer is NO.

findings.situation: A filer with a fully deferred like-kind exchange on Form 8824 has a realized gain but no recognized gain, and could read "gains" either way.
findings.irs_text: Question: "gains or losses from (or that belong on) Forms ... 8824"; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "long-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The question does not say whether a deferred gain counts or only an amount the form carries to Schedule D. If nothing carries over, line 11 is correctly zero, but a filer could still answer YES because the deferred gain appears on the form.

findings.situation: A filer whose Schedule K-1 shows only net section 1231 gain might answer NO because the K-1 does not label it a capital gain, even if that gain belongs on Form 4797, Part I and reaches line 11.
findings.irs_text: Question: "or capital gains or losses on a Schedule K-1"; f1040sd (2025) p. 1, line 11: "Gain from Form 4797, Part I"
findings.why: The clause "or that belong on" Form 4797 technically requires YES, but the K-1 clause suggests that only items labeled capital count. A filer who does not know this routing could answer NO, and the tool would then wrongly treat line 11 as zero. The routing of K-1 section 1231 gain comes from text not supplied here.

findings.situation: A filer whose 2025 benefits include an earlier-year payment, but none of whose benefits turn out to be taxable, may still answer YES because they want the election. The tool would have computed that return correctly with line 6b at zero.
findings.irs_text: "If any of your benefits are taxable for 2025 and they include a lump-sum benefit payment that was for an earlier year, you may be able to reduce the taxable amount with the lump-sum election." (i1040gi 2025 p. 31, Line 6c; same condition in the TIP on p. 32)
findings.why: The question "Do you want to figure the tax on that earlier year's payment with the lump-sum election method?" asks only whether the filer wants the method. It does not limit YES to filers with taxable benefits, which is the only case where the election can change the result. Filers who would get zero taxable benefits anyway are refused needlessly.

findings.situation: A filer disabled in a terrorist attack, whose SSDI converted to retirement benefits at full retirement age before 2025, could read the question as covering their benefits and answer YES, even though the IRS text excludes nothing for that year and the tool's computation would be correct.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31: "Because you became eligible for a full retirement benefit in May, the month after you turned age 66, you can exclude only 4 months (January through April) of your annual benefit from income ($6,000). You must report the remaining $12,000 on line 6a."
findings.why: The question asks whether benefits are 'disability payments for injuries incurred as a direct result of a terrorist attack' but does not say that benefits paid for months after full retirement age no longer count. A filer whose benefits still stem from the attack injury could answer either way.

findings.situation: A filer receiving auxiliary benefits (as a spouse, child or survivor) on the record of someone disabled in a terrorist attack could read 'disability payments for injuries' as including their benefits and answer YES, or read it as covering only their own injuries and answer NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31: "Don't include in your income any disability payments (including Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) payments) you receive for injuries incurred as a direct result of a terrorist attack"
findings.why: The question does not say whose injuries must be involved. The IRS text does not settle whether benefits paid on another person's disability record qualify, so a filer could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: A filer's only year-designated box 12 amount is code G (for example "G 24") from a nongovernmental 457(b) plan, or is entirely nonelective, so the filer must answer YES even though the amount does not count on Form 8880 line 2 for any year and the line would correctly exclude it.
findings.irs_text: Question: "any amount with a year after its code". iw2w3 (2025) p. 20: "Code G—Elective deferrals and employer contributions (including nonelective deferrals) to any governmental or nongovernmental section 457(b) deferred compensation plan." f8880 (2025) p. 2, Line 2: "Elective deferrals ... to a 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457(b), SEP, SIMPLE, or the federal TSP."
findings.why: The question applies to every year-designated code G amount, but line 2 counts only elective deferrals to a governmental 457(b). This filer is refused although the amount is zero for line 2 regardless of the year it relates to, which matches the tool's governmental-elective-only treatment of code G.
